en: Thus the sixth book is complete.
Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Rādhā and Gokulananda.
The First Chapter:
The Dialogue between Śrī Viṣṇu and the Messengers of Yama within the Narrative of Ajāmila.
Śrī Parīkṣit said:
The path of cessation was first taught by the Blessed One, whereby,
through the attainment of the sequential yoga, there is no further transmigration into saṃsāra by means of Brahman.
Śrīdhara:
In the holy forest shines the lion named Nṛsiṃha alone;
at his roar, the elephants of great sin flee away.
"Viṣṇu protects with all his forms the living beings born of emission who abide within their own bounds"— thus it is established in the fifth [chapter].
In the nineteenth chapter of the sixth book, nourishment is described,
characterized by the protection of devotees who have transgressed all bounds.
Just as Ajāmila among men was protected despite his great sins,
and Vāsava among the gods, though he was the slayer of Viśvarūpa and others.
The messengers of Viṣṇu recognized Ajāmila’s status as a devotee,
which arose from his attachment to affection for his son through the use of the Lord’s name as a mere convention.
Even Indra was a devotee of the Blessed One, serving Upendra as his friend;
his sovereignty over the gods and his very life depended on him for the conquest of his enemies.
Therein, first, the story of Ajāmila is told in three chapters;
then, for the purpose of declaring Indra’s faults, the account of Viśvarūpa is told in six chapters.
Then, with eight [verses], there is the narrative of Vṛtra for the purpose of stating Indra's fault;
and with two [verses], the narrative of the Maruts—such is the sequence of the sections.
Therein, first, during the liberation of the sinner by Viṣṇu’s messengers,
the characteristics of Dharma and the other [deities] were described by the messengers of Yama for the purpose of making that person's sins known.

Now the sixth book (*skandha*) is explained. Following a restatement of what was previously mentioned, he asks about the means for avoiding the hells just described by means of six verses beginning with "The path of cessation" (*nivṛttimārga*).
First, in the second book, it was stated: "He goes to Vaiśvānara" (*bhā.pu.* 2.2.24), and so forth.

By you, the Blessed One, in the manner that it truly is, by the upward path, through gradual yoga consisting of the attainment of the Radiant and other stages, Brahman is perceived; through that, liberation occurs as non-rebirth together with Brahman.
When the dissolution has arrived, all those [attain] together with Brahman.
"Those who have perfected themselves enter the supreme state at the end of the other," according to this statement.
Regarding the *kramasaṃdarbha*: "In the *kramasaṃdarbha* of the sixth [chapter], there is a compendium of the *saṃdarbhas*."
He who acts according to my command is my refuge, for I have no other resort.
Now, regarding the structural arrangement of the sixth book:
wherever it was not made explicit by the venerable master, or where it was made explicit but unclear in some respect,
in each such instance this arrangement known as the "Sequence" (krama) is to be recorded.
Wherever there may be satisfaction for a Vaiṣṇava,
from that very place one should write down some portion of the Vaiṣṇava doctrine with courtesy alone.
He restates what was previously mentioned as being applicable to the matter to be inquired about, with the five verses beginning with "nivṛtti.
In that regard, there are first two paths to the other world: one in accordance with the Vedas, and another by transgressing them.
Here, the first is of two kinds, characterized by renunciation (*nivṛtti*) and engagement (*pravṛtti*); whereas the latter...
It is of one kind, characterized by non-dharma. Here, it has been stated that "being the path" means being the cause for the application of sequential practice (*kramayoga*).

Regarding the phrase "by means of the attainment of sequential practice": knowledge and devotion, however, because they grant immediate attainment, are not intended here as the "path. Having this in mind, he says [this] in the first two and a half verses.
In that regard, "cessation" constitutes a pair of verses. ||1||
Viśvanātha: Om, salutations to Kṛṣṇa!
Having again bowed to the venerable Guru, who is powerful and an ocean of compassion...
I take refuge in that glorious Guru, the Lord of the World and the Eye of the Universe.
To the Lord, who is dearer than life to the cowherd women and people,
and to His beloved servant, I offer myself and my own.
In the fifth [chapter], it is declared that the protection of the inhabitants of Pātāla and heaven by one who maintains his own boundaries is designated by the term "station" (sthāna).
The protection of devotees, even those who transgress the boundaries of dharma,
is what is proclaimed by the wise as "nourishment" (poṣaṇa).
Even for the sinner Ajāmila, devotion was attained through the mere appearance of the Name;
even Indra’s betrayal of his guru is declared to be the devotion of one who has been authorized.
And because of His nourishing those two as well as Citraketu and others— how much more so!—
the affection for His devotees is described in the nineteenth chapter.
In this [section], however, the narrative concerning Jāmbavat is contained in three chapters;
that concerning Viśvarūpa in six; and then the account of Vṛtra in eight.
The narrative of the Maruts is proclaimed in two chapters,
wherein Indra’s continued devotion to Diti during the *puṃsavana* rite is described.
In this regard, it is said that while Ajāmila was being liberated by the messengers of Viṣṇu, his bonds were severed by the servants of Yama.

With a heart softened by compassion upon hearing of the torments of the fall into hell for human beings, [the Blessed One], in order to inspire the enthusiasm for providing an answer to the question regarding the means of deliverance from that state,
and to establish the capacity for grasping the taught meaning through a restatement of what was previously said—

He makes his own [intention] manifest by saying "nivṛtti" (cessation) and so forth. "Yathā-yathāvat" means as it truly is. First, in the second book, by the passage beginning with "He goes to Vaiśvānara" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 2.2.24), and likewise in the third book, by the passage beginning with "Those who do not violate their own duties" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.32.5)—by whichever path and in whatever manner [the Lord acts].

Liberation is non-return to worldly existence (asaṃsṛti) together with that Brahmā who has been reached through the method of gradual progression. This is according to the Vedic revelation: "When the dissolution has arrived, at the end of the Supreme [Brahmā], all those perfected souls enter the supreme state along with Brahmā. (1)
O Sage, this very characteristic of phenomenal activity, which is the domain of the three *guṇas*,
is that emission of the *guṇas* from the unshaken primordial nature (*prakṛti*) that occurs again and again.

Śrīdhara: For that person whose [only] object is the attainment of the three qualities—the pleasure of heaven and so forth—and whose primordial nature (*prakṛti*) has not dissolved [into him], the path consisting of the repeated creation of the qualities in the form of the undertaking of a body for the sake of experience has been described in the third [chapter]: "By the southern path of Aryaman..."
"Those go to the world of the ancestors," and so forth [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.32.20]. ||2||
Kramasandarbha: This has not been explained.

Viśvanātha: And that which is characterized by worldly activity was indeed described in the third [chapter] itself, beginning with the words "But those here whose minds are unattached" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.32.16), as the threefold qualities consisting of the happiness of heaven and so forth.

That very [state] belongs to one for whom the object is attained; for that transmigrating being whose primordial nature (prakṛti) is dissolved, there is creation by means of the qualities (guṇas) alone, from which arises birth again and again. ||2||
The various hells characterized by unrighteousness have been described,
as well as the first Manvantara, that of Svāyambhuva, from which [the account] proceeds.
Śrīdhara: This has been described in the immediately preceding chapter and explained at the beginning of the fourth [chapter], "yato yasmin" (from which and in which). ||3||

The sequential arrangement: "Adharma" constitutes one half-verse; "the characteristics of adharma" and "those that indicate it" [are explained] by two and a half verses; and "the Manvantara" [is explained] by two [verses], because [it occurs] in those two paths. ||3||
Viśvanātha: [The word] *yataḥ* means "from which" or "in which. ||3||
the lineage and the deeds of Priyavrata and Uttānapāda;
[and] the islands, regions, oceans, mountains, rivers, gardens, and trees.
The Lord created this configuration of the terrestrial sphere according to its divisions, characteristics, and measurements, as well as the celestial bodies and the subterranean cavities.

Śrīdhara: The meaning is that the Lord has explained how he created the continents and so forth—according to their divisions, characteristics, and measurements—as well as the configuration of the terrestrial sphere and the configuration of the luminaries and the subterranean cavities. ||45||

The sequence of composition: "dvīpa" and so forth constitutes one and a half verses. The mention of "caves" (*vivarāṇām*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the hells (*narakāṇām*). ||45||

Viśvanātha: The syntactical connection is that he has explained how he created the continents and so forth. This means that he has explained how he created this configuration of the terrestrial sphere and the luminaries, such as the sun and others, according to their divisions, characteristics, and measurements. ||45||
Now, O highly fortunate one, you ought to explain to me how a man here might avoid being led to those various fierce torments of hell.
Śrīdhara: You should now explain to me how—that is, by what means—one might not go to those hells which contain various terrible torments. ||6||

The sequence of the composition: He states what is to be asked—"Now, here... The sense is that while those two [means] for accomplishing what is desired by people have been known, the means for avoiding what is undesired must likewise be known. ||6||

Viśvanātha: So that one may not go—that is, may not enter—those hells characterized by various terrible torments; the sense is that just as the two means for accomplishing what is desired and what is undesired by people are known, so too must the means for avoiding the undesired be known. ||6||
Śrī Śuka said:
"If you do not perform atonement for your sin right here,"
If one should perform for another what has been done [for oneself] through mind, speech, or hand,
he will certainly, after death, encounter those hells of sharp torments which I have described to you.

Śrīdhara: Regarding this, he says in two verses beginning with "If not," that without the expiation prescribed by Manu and others, hell is difficult to avoid. If one does not perform the atonement (*prāyaścitta*) for the sin committed through the mind, speech, and body—by means of those very same [faculties]—in this very life, then he...
After passing away—that is, having died—a person certainly goes to the hells, which I have described to you;
those hells contain sharp and terrible torments. (7)

The sequential arrangement: therein, in order to introduce his own view regarding expiation by means of a question, he restates the opinion of another school, beginning with the words "If not" (na cet). ||7||

Viśvanātha: Therein, examining the proficiency of his own disciple Parīkṣit in his own doctrine, [the Lord] describes the remedy for hell according to the view of those who follow ritual action (karmis) in two verses beginning with "na cet.
He describes the expiation for the sin committed in this very life through the mind, speech, and body, whether individually or collectively.
If one does not perform the expiation in this very life, then [the consequences] will be sharp and terrible. ||7||
Therefore, before this, one should strive here for the expiation of evil so that one’s self does not fall into the power of death.
Having observed the relative gravity or lightness of a disorder, one who knows the causes of diseases should treat it just as a physician would.

Śrīdhara: Since this is so, one should therefore strive for the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) of sin. When? Before death. Furthermore, by means of a self that is "unfallen"—that is, a body that has not decayed—or else, as long as one is "unfallen," meaning free from calamity; and with a "restrained self," meaning with a controlled mind; and even then, quickly. Otherwise, [the opportunity will be lost].

However, if a long time has passed, one must undergo double the vow, because of the resulting doubling [of the offense]. In that case, having considered the magnitude or smallness of the sin, one should strive for an expiation corresponding to it; just as a physician who knows the causes of diseases would treat them with a corresponding remedy. ||8||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Since this is so, therefore [one must act] even before death, and there too quickly; otherwise, if a long time has already passed, one would incur a doubling of the penance, as it is said that one deserves double the vow [for a transgression committed after a long delay].
"May I not suffer misfortune"—the meaning is that as long as there is no incapacity for vows and the like due to old age, disease, and so forth.

Regarding this, he says "of the fault," indicating that an authoritative person (*vyavasthāpaka*) who is learned and understands the intent of the *dharmaśāstra* must be sought; [he refers to] the gravity and lightness, that is, the weightiness and the insignificance. (8)
Śrī Rājā said:
Even though one knows that a sin committed through seeing or hearing is harmful to oneself, [one still persists].
Furthermore, how can one who is rendered powerless perform an act of expiation?

Śrīdhara: Here he raises an objection with two verses. "Seen" refers to [punishment] such as royal penalty; "heard" refers to [retribution] such as falling into hell. Even though one knows that sin is harmful to oneself through these two, one commits it again after performing atonement. Therefore, for what reason [is there] a twelve-year penance and so forth?

Regarding expiation (*prāyaścitta*): the sense is that by it, the fault together with its root is not eliminated; or, even if it were eliminated, there would be no possibility for the sin to sprout again. ||9||
The sequential arrangement: likewise, he asks—"Is it seen? ||9||

Viśvanātha: Refuting this [objection] and considering it to be false, he says with two verses beginning with "dṛṣṭa": "Having seen" [the consequences of royal punishment] and so forth, and "having heard" [of the fall into hell] and so forth—one performs for oneself the expiation for that sin which is harmful [as a result of those two], following the performance of the penance; for such is observed in the world. Therefore, [it is so]. "Atho" means "ataḥ" (therefore).
The meaning is: how is expiation (prāyaścitta) destructive of sin? The implication is that once it has destroyed the sin, there can be no further growth of that sin. ||9||
"— in one case he turns away from what is inauspicious, and in another he engages in it again;
therefore, I consider such expiation to be as useless as the bathing of an elephant."
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, at some time or place, one may turn away from evil or sin;

yet at another time, one commits that very same act again. Just as an elephant, even after bathing, defiles itself with dust, so too, because sin is difficult to restrain, a fall into hell is inevitable.
I consider the act of atonement to be futile. ||10||

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: In some cases, such as youth and so forth, one turns away from evil (*abhadrāt*) or sin; yet again, in some cases, such as old age, one commits that very same sin. Therefore, for this reason, it is purposeless (*apārtham*) or futile (*vyartham*).
"Like the purification of an elephant": for even after bathing, an elephant again makes itself dirty with dust. ||10||
Śrī Bādarāyaṇi said:
The removal of karma by means of karma is not desired as being ultimate.
Since the authority for expiation belongs to the ignorant, it is a matter for deliberation.

Śrīdhara explains: Through ritual action—that is, through penances such as the *kṛcchra*—the removal or destruction of the act of sin is not seen to be absolute or root-and-branch. This is because it pertains to that which has ignorance (*avidyā*) as its substrate; therefore, since there is no destruction of ignorance, even when that sin has been destroyed [by ritual means], [it remains].

Through that residual impression (*saṃskāra*), the sprouting of other sins occurs again and again. What, then, is the primary expiation? To this he says: "But the expiation is investigation, which is knowledge" (11).
The sequence of composition: He speaks to state his own view, beginning with the words "by action" (karmaṇā). ||11||

Viśvanātha: Having passed the examination, Parīkṣit, who is to be examined once again, makes known the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): by means of ritual action, such as penances like the *kṛcchra*, the destruction of sinful action is not absolute, but rather a temporary subsidence; this is the meaning. An ignorant person is a living being (*jīva*) bound by ignorance (*avidyā*).

The meaning is this: for whomsoever this [ignorance] is predominant, that is their *bhava* (state of being); therefore, because the root of sin—namely, ignorance—is present, there is the repeated sprouting of sin. What, then, is the primary atonement? Examining this further, [the author speaks] of the wise...
He states his own view: "Knowledge is reflective awareness (vimarśana), because it alone is the remover of ignorance"—this is the sense. ||11||
For diseases indeed overcome even wholesome food when it is not eaten;
likewise, O King, one who observes such a rule gradually becomes fit for security.

Śrīdhara: But that [state] is attained gradually by one who is constantly vigilant, and not by anyone else; thus he says "no," along with an illustration. Just as diseases do not afflict those men who eat only wholesome food, so too the practitioner of restraints and other disciplines becomes capable of attaining security, which is the knowledge of reality. ||12||
The sequence of composition: one who establishes rules and one who practices those rules. ||12||

Viśvanātha: Now, if it is argued that in the presence of sin there is an absence of purity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and since that is the case, how can there be any possibility of knowledge? True. He states, with an illustration, that even by means of the instruments of knowledge, sin is pacified: "Just as diseases do not [afflict] men who eat only wholesome food..."
Just as those [obstacles] cause harm, so too the performer of restraints and other practices gradually becomes capable of securing well-being and destroying evil. ||12||
By means of austerity, celibacy, tranquility, and self-restraint;
by renunciation, truthfulness, purity, and by restraint or observance.
The wise, who know the Dharma and are endowed with faith, cast away even great evil born of body, speech, and mind, just as fire consumes a thicket of bamboo.

Śrīdhara: He clarifies this very point with two verses. "By austerity" means by one-pointedness; for it is stated in the Smṛti that "the supreme austerity is the one-pointedness of the mind and the senses. "By celibacy" means by the eightfold [celibacy].
As it has been said:
Remembering, chanting, playing, gazing, speaking in secret,
forming intentions, making resolutions, and the actual performance of the act itself.

"The wise declare this eightfold sexual union; its opposite, characterized by these same eight qualities, is celibacy (*brahmacarya*). Here, *śama* is the restraint of the mind; *dama* is the restraint of the external senses; *tyāga* is generosity; and *yama* consists of non-violence and so forth.
The rule consists of recitation and so forth. ||1314||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* has not been commented upon.
Viśvanātha clarifies this very point with two verses: by "austerity" (*tapas*), meaning freedom from worldly enjoyment;
by "celibacy" (*brahmacarya*), meaning the abandonment of looking at women; and by "tranquility" (*śama*), meaning the restraint of the mind according to one's capacity.

By *dama*, which is the restraint of the external senses; by *tyāga*, which is generosity; by *yama*, such as non-violence and so forth; and by *niyama*, such as the recitation of mantras (*japa*) and so forth. ||1314||
Some, solely through devotion, being intent upon Vāsudeva,
shake off their evil entirely, just as the sun dispels the mist.

Śrīdhara: Because this [practice] is extremely difficult to perform, he states another primary expiation, beginning with "some. By this, he shows that such devotion is preeminent and rare. "By means of exclusive [devotion]" (kevalayā) means independent of austerity and other such practices. "Those who have Vāsudeva as their supreme goal" (vāsudevaparāyaṇāḥ) is not merely a qualification of the qualified person (adhikāriviśeṣaṇa).
However, because others do not engage in it due to a lack of faith, [the teaching] effectively results in those [others] alone; thus, it is a mere restatement (anuvāda). ||15||

* Caitanyamata-mañjūṣā*: "Some," and so forth. "Some" refers to those rare individuals who are devoted solely to Vāsudeva; that is, by means of [devotion] alone, independent of [ritual] knowledge, and in its entirety, consisting of a total uprooting [of sin]. The sense is that through mere expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) and the like, sin does not depart in its entirety.
In this regard, there is an illustration: "as if mist," [verse 15].
Sanātana (Ha.bha.vi. 11.548):
[He is attained] through austerity, celibacy, tranquility, self-restraint, renunciation, truthfulness, purity, restraint, or observance.
The wise, who know the Dharma and are endowed with faith, cast away even great evil born of body, speech, and mind, just as fire consumes a thicket of bamboo.

Since the expiation (prāyaścitta) thus described is extremely difficult to perform, he states another primary expiation with the words "some" (kecit). By the word "some," he shows that such devotion (bhakti) is predominant and rare. "By means of exclusive [devotion]" means independent of austerity and other such practices. "Those who have Vāsudeva as their supreme goal" (vāsudevaparāyaṇāḥ).

This is not a qualifying attribute of the qualified person (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*); rather, because others do not engage in it due to lack of faith, it results in those very [qualities] by implication, and is thus merely a restatement (*anuvāda*). "In its entirety" means from the root and from the limbs. A corresponding illustration is: as the sun [dispels] mist and the darkness produced by it. Thus...

Here, the intended meaning is the destruction of all sins without exception, together with their roots and constituent parts. Previously, in the passage "as fire [destroys] a thicket of bamboos," the complete eradication of all sins along with their roots was described through the power of fire to consume even the ashes and other residues remaining underground. Nevertheless, one should understand that there is a distinction between this [present case] and the previous one.
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.

*Viśvanātha*: Here too, by means of the analogy of the bamboo thicket and fire, he speaks on behalf of the devotees to the king whose mind is not yet appeased, because the regrowth of sin is again indicated—some [say]:

The sense is that these [other means] are, moreover, of rare occurrence. By "exclusive" (kevalayā) is meant being devoid of ritual action, knowledge, and so forth, and disregarding even those qualities such as ritual action and knowledge that may be present but remain subordinate.
Here, because of the use of the term "completely" (kārtsnyena) and the analogy of the frost and the sun, it is shown that the total eradication of sin occurs through devotion alone and not otherwise.
It has been indicated. ||15||
For, O King, a sinner is not purified by austerities and the like in the same way as one whose life is dedicated to Kṛṣṇa is purified by serving His devotees.

Śrīdhara: And he says that this is even superior to the path of knowledge (*jñāna-mārga*): "In that way he would not be purified"—that is, he would not become pure—by serving those persons through whom his life-breaths have been offered to Kṛṣṇa. ||16||

*Caitanyamatamañjuṣā*: Let it be granted that the worship of Vāsudeva is the destroyer of sins; however, the worship of his [Vāsudeva’s] devotees alone is likewise so. Thus he says, "Not so. The address "O King" is significant, implying: "Know that what I am saying here is indeed the truth."
It is meaningful. The reason for having one's life-breaths (*prāṇa*) offered to Kṛṣṇa is "by service to His attendants" (*tatpuruṣaniṣevayā*); this is the sense.

By serving His attendants, one offers one's life-breaths to Kṛṣṇa; the point here is that hunger and thirst are indeed attributes of the life-breath, and when the life-breath is offered to Him, those two cease to exist. One is not afflicted by these two.
It comes to be. ||16||

Kramasaṃdarbha: This has not been explained. Viśvanātha: Here too, according to the opinion of those who understand the essential purport of the scriptures on devotion (*bhakti-śāstra*), it is improper for the Great Goddess of Devotion to apply herself to such a trivial matter as the pacification of sin.

Prefacing his own view with a refutation of other opinions, he says: "No. By the complete surrender of oneself, thinking, "Whether He who has His life dedicated to Kṛṣṇa casts me, a doer of evil deeds, into hell for the sake of appropriate disciplinary punishment, or does not cast me there, He alone is my refuge; I belong to Him alone," [one attains liberation].
The meaning is that he is one whose devotion is pure even while not performing atonement for hellish rebirths.
To the question, "How can there be the state of having one's life-breaths offered to Kṛṣṇa? he says: "tatpuruṣa... (verse 16).
For this is the path in this world that leads straight ahead, secure and free from fear;
it is where the virtuous and noble ones dwell, devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa.
Śrīdhara: The reason for this is that it is *sadhrīcīna*, meaning correct or favorable. This path is the path of devotion (*bhakti-mārga*).

It is because it is secure (*kṣema*). The reason for its security is that there is no fear from any source, such as obstacles and the like. He states that very point: those on this path are of good character, compassionate, saintly, and free from desire. On which path? On this path.

They are established in the Dharma; therefore, they have no fear caused by the necessity of solitude as found on the path of knowledge (jñānamārga), nor do they have fear of those possessed by envy and other vices as found on the path of ritual action (karmamārga). This is the intended meaning. ||17||

*The Casket of the Mind of Consciousness*: It is said that one should abandon the paths of knowledge (*jñāna-mārga*) and take refuge in the path of devotion (*bhakti-mārga*) alone—beginning with the words "concordant" (*sadhrīcīna*).
That which moves together is "concordant" (*sadhrīcīna*); because it is easy to serve, the path itself is the goal to be reached. The movement together suggests a state of uniformity.

Because it is "fearless from all sides," where there is no fear from any quarter; whereas the path of knowledge and the like is "fearful on all sides. He speaks of its being "concordant": "where the virtuous are," meaning only the virtuous travel there, not robbers. On a path seized by robbers, neither virtuous men nor merchants [can proceed].

They move about. Who are these virtuous ones? To this he says: they are those whose character (*śīla*) is excellent—that is, whose pure conduct consists of the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. He demonstrates that very point: "devoted to Nārāyaṇa"; Nārāyaṇa is Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is supreme even over Nārāyaṇa and others; he [is devoted to him].
Those for whom this very [state] is the path and the support. ||17||

Sanātana (Ha.bha.vi. 11.565): This path is the path of devotion (*bhaktimārga*); it is *sadhrīcīna*, meaning correct or appropriate. Because it is *kṣema*, meaning auspicious. The reason for its being *kṣema* is that in it there is no fear from anything, such as obstacles (*vighna*) and the like. Or rather, *kṣema* means having the nature of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) and being free from fear from any quarter. That...

Thus he says: on whichever path there are virtuous, compassionate, and selfless holy men (*sādhu*), there is no fear caused by a lack of companionship as in the path of knowledge (*jñānamārga*), nor is there fear of those possessed by envy and other vices as in the path of ritual action (*karmamārga*). Through association with them, there is security in every respect.
The state of being. ||17||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Nor should it be said that the yoga of devotion (*bhaktiyoga*) is intended only for those incapable of the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*), vows, and so forth;
thus he says—*sadhrīcīnaḥ*. For (*hi*) is certain. This alone is the best of all, not...

The sense is that where there is fear of obstacles and the like from any source whatsoever, such as in the path of knowledge (*jñānamārga*), there is no fear caused by a lack of assistance— as is the case with "virtuous saints" (*sādhavaḥ*) who possess good character— nor is there fear caused by envy and the like, as occurs in the path of ritual action (*karmamārga*). ||17||
O King of kings, expiations performed by one who is averse to Nārāyaṇa do not purify him,
just as rivers cannot cleanse a jar of liquor.

Śrīdhara: It has been stated that devotion is independent of anything else; however, he says "Prāyaścittāni" (Expiatory rites) to show that rites such as the Kṛcchra do not purify in the absence of devotion. He provides an illustration for their inability to purify even great sins: "Like rivers [overflowing] a jar of liquor. (18)
The Caitanyamata-mañjūṣā also demonstrates this by means of contrast, stating: "Expiatory rites.
Even when performed, expiatory rites such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* do not purify one who is averse to Nārāyaṇa; the sense is that they purify him only in some limited way. In that regard:

The illustration is: "like a river [emptying] a jar of liquor. For even though a jar of liquor has been washed, it does not abandon its foul odor, nor indeed can it ever again be used for practical purposes. Therefore, even one who has performed penance, though he be a devotee of the Lord with a purified inner self, does not become [fully pure].
The sense is that it is not even fit for conventional usage. ||18||

Sanātana: Even those things performed and committed do not purify, nor do they cleanse. As an illustration of the fact that even great deeds do not effect purification, he says: "like a jar of wine" and "like rivers. (Ha.bha.vi.
Kramasandarbha: This has not been commented upon.)

Viśvanātha: Furthermore, through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is observed that devotion alone is the pacifier of sin, and not knowledge, ritual action, and so forth; thus he says: "Atonements" (*prāyaścittāni*). By the use of the plural number, the meaning is that all [means] consisting of ritual action and knowledge [are excluded]. One who is turned away from Nārāyaṇa...
Although both devotion (*bhakti*) and the excellence of the devotee (*bhakta-utkarṣa*) have been heard of [in scripture], they do not purify one who lacks faith therein; however,
devotion purifies even one devoid of knowledge, ritual action, and so forth, because of the previously stated principle that "by devotion alone."—
Those who have once fixed their minds here upon the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa, being enamored of His qualities,
do not [fear] Yama, nor the wielders of nooses, nor his soldiers.
For those who have performed the required expiation see [these things] even in their dreams.

Śrīdhara: He says that even very slight devotion purifies indeed—with the words "once" (sakṛt). That mind which possesses merely attachment to His qualities, but not [theoretical] knowledge; by that much alone, the expiation has been performed by those [who possess such a mind]. ||19||
*The Casket of the Doctrine of Consciousness*: To introduce the narrative, he provides the introductory verse beginning with "once" (*sakṛt*).

Let it be granted for now that [the devotee] possesses the qualities previously mentioned in the preceding verses, such as being solely devoted to Vāsudeva and having offered his life-breaths to Kṛṣṇa.

Those who have fixed their minds even once upon the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa—minds that are attached to his qualities, such as His affection for His devotees and other virtues—do not see Yama. Let them not see Yama;
for what can the noose-bearing one do when he arrives at some point to summon them, having disregarded His majesty?

Or they do not even see its soldiers; let alone in person, not even in a dream, because they have performed the expiation—having completed their atonement—merely by fixing their minds upon it once. ||19||
The Structural Arrangement (*kramasaṃdarbha*): Now, he speaks of that which consists of the semblance of passion (*rāgābhāsa*), which is even superior to the former, using the word "once" (*sakṛt*).

Here, "passion" (*rāga*) is characterized merely as a coloring, an appearance of erotic love (*ratyābhāsa*), because of the use of the word "once. It is not, however, direct joy arising from the knowledge of the actual sweetness of its qualities. For this very reason, in that case...

It has been stated that even "once" [is sufficient] because there is no other intent; for if delight were direct, the fixing of the mind upon that would necessarily occur repeatedly. Those who place their minds on You once, [knowing You] to be the Self, which is eternal bliss—
"But they do not resort again to dwellings that carry away the essence of man" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.87.35).
Because of this praise in the Śruti, it is stated in the Ṭīkā: "He has only attachment toward the qualities, but no knowledge."

Whatever is mere passion is simply passion; and knowledge is experience according to reality. Nevertheless, there is a distinction between these [devotees] and those such as Ajāmila; thus he says: "They do not go to Yama," and so on. Therefore, their superiority over the former is established here by the presence of a semblance of devotion toward the fruit, even though Yama and others remain within the range of their vision.

Because it was impossible for them to go there, he manifested a form of great majesty. In this context, the qualifying phrase "one who is attached to his qualities" serves to destroy even their capacity to enter the range of his vision; such is the power of recollecting him in that manner.
It should be understood that this indicates a specific excellence of power (*prabhāvaviśeṣa*). As stated by Śrī Yama in the *Nārasiṃha Purāṇa*:
"I was appointed as Yama by the Creator, who is worshipped by the hosts of immortals, to determine what is beneficial and harmful for the world."
"I punish those mortals who are averse to Hari and the Guru, and I bow down to those who prostrate at the feet of Hari.
Thus it is said. Likewise, there is a statement of Skanda in the *Amṛtasāroddhāra*:
"Neither Brahmā, nor Śiva, Agni, Indra, nor I, nor any other dwellers of heaven are able to effect the restraint of the high-souled Vaiṣṇavas. (19)

Viśvanātha: He says that even an abundance of devotion is not required here—"even once," how much more so "repeatedly"? "Even with the mind," how much more so with the ears and other senses? And that mind, though attached to objects and enamored of the *guṇas*, [is purified];
how much more so one who is free from attachment to the *guṇas*? "Even in a dream," how much more so when it is manifest?
Those by whom the expiation (*niṣkṛta*) or atonement (*prāyaścitta*) has been performed through meditation (*dhyāna*) alone to that extent; here,

by the words "once" (*sakṛt*) and so forth, it is meant that even if sins were to recur for some pure devotee due to fate, they are as ineffective as the bites of snakes whose fangs have been pulled out.

To be made the object of such a censure is altogether improper, like the purification of an elephant; for this is evident from such scriptural statements as, "Even if one of very wicked conduct worships Me" (Gītā 9.30), and so forth. ||19||
In this regard, they cite this ancient history;
learn from me that dialogue between the messengers of Viṣṇu and Yama.
Śrīdhara: He establishes this point by means of an ancient narrative (itihāsa), beginning with "And here... The word "me" means from me. ||20||

The sequential arrangement: Now, in order to demonstrate the "how much more so" (kaimutya) argument in various instances, he introduces a historical narrative with the words "And here... (atra ca). ||20||
Viśvanātha: Here, the very meaning introduces a narrative. "In this regard"—understand from me that dialogue which occurs therein. (20)
In Kānyakubja, there was a certain twice-born man named Ajāmila, the husband of a maidservant;
he had lost all virtuous conduct and was defiled by his association with that slave woman.
Śrīdhara: In the city of Kānyakubja, there was a husband of a maidservant named Ajāmila. ||21||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*, Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— He who has adopted a censurable livelihood through prostrations, deceit, and theft.
Supporting his family while remaining impure, he caused embodied beings to suffer.
Śrīdhara: *Vṛttim* means livelihood; *bibhrat* means supporting or nourishing; *yātayāmāsa* means he tormented. ||22||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: "By that" means by the dragging of the people who were bound in chains;
and by means of dice—that is, gambling—and by deceits, such as fraud, he caused his livelihood (*vṛtti*) to be exhausted.
He oppressed [them]. ||22||
O King, as he lived in this manner fondling his sons,
eighty-eight years of his life passed away.
Śrīdhara: A great period of time related to his lifespan has passed. To address the inquiry as to how much that was, he says: "Eighty-eight years," meaning years or full cycles. (23)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: A great period of time related to [his] lifespan has passed. To address the expectation of how much that was, he says: "years," meaning *saṃvatsaras*, joined with the number eighty-eight. (23)
He had ten sons; among them,
the youngest was a boy named Nārāyaṇa, who was dearly beloved by his parents.
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha [comment]: "Pravayasaḥ" means of one who is old. ||24||
The sequence of the composition: By stating that [the son] was beloved by both parents, it is said that the mother’s purpose was also fulfilled—
he, with his heart bound to that child who spoke with the sweet voice of a young elephant...
Beholding that divine play, the aged sage rejoiced exceedingly.
Śrīdhara: One by whom the heart is bound; *jaraṭha* means old or aged. ||25||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Jaraṭha means old or aged. ||25||
Eating, drinking, and chewing, constrained by affection for his child,
the fool who feeds and nourishes him does not perceive the approaching end.

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, this act of fondling him and so forth should also be understood as being for the sake of the established conclusion—that through the greatness of uttering the name of Śrī Nārāyaṇa, it was indeed devotion to Him that arose. ||26||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not commented upon. Viśvanātha: Eating, that is, chewing. ||26||
While he was conducting himself in this manner, when the time of death had arrived,
that wise man set his mind upon his young son named Nārāyaṇa.
Śrīdhara: Not commented upon.

Viśvanātha: Furthermore, this—such as his fondling [of the child] and so forth—should also be understood as being for the sake of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), namely that through the greatness of uttering the name of Śrī Nārāyaṇa, devotion to Him alone arose.
By the venerable feet of the Lord [Śrī Svāmī]. ||26||
Seeing those three exceedingly cruel men with nooses in their hands,
with curved snouts and bristling hair, who had come to lead him away—
With his senses agitated, he called out in a loud, tearful voice to his son named Nārāyaṇa, who was playing with toys at a distance.
Śrīdhara: Those whose snouts or mouths are curved; those whose body hairs stand erect;
by that which has been made to float, i.e., brought to a state of floating. [2829]
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Regarding the word "three"—although the sins committed by Ajāmila were infinite, because they are of three kinds—bodily, vocal, and mental—only three messengers of Yama arrived.

Because the name Nārāyaṇa consists of four syllables, it should be understood that the four attendants of Viṣṇu have arrived. "By the *plāvita*" means having been brought to a state of floating. ||2829||
O Great King, hearing the glorification of Hari from the mouth of their dying master, the attendants suddenly fell down.
Śrīdhara said: Having heard the glorification of Hari, they fell down, because that is the name of their Master. (30)
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: They fell [down] upon hearing the glorification of Hari. Of what kind [of person]? Of their master (bhartṛ), who was uttering his name. ||30||
As they were dragging Ajāmila, the husband of the maidservant, from within his heart,
the messengers of Viṣṇu forcibly repelled the servants of Yama.
Śrīdhara: [This is part of] the *Kramasaṃdarbha*; it has not been commented upon.
Viśvanātha: "Do not drag away this Vaiṣṇava Ajāmila! O, do not drag him away! If you wish to live," they said, thus restraining them. (31)
Having been thus forbidden, those messengers leading the way to the city of Vaivasvata said to them:
"Who are you that seek to obstruct the command of the King of Dharma?"
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha: the servants are leading the way. ||32||
The sequence of composition has not been explained.
Whose [are you], from where have you come, and for what reason do you forbid this?
Are you gods or secondary deities, or are you the most excellent of the Siddhas?
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha: Restrain his gaze! ||33||
The sequential arrangement has not been explained. —
All have eyes like lotus petals and wear yellow silken garments.
Wearing crowns and earrings, and adorned with shimmering garlands of lotuses.

Śrīdhara says: "Do not be angry, thinking 'we do not know you,' for you are beings of a superhuman nature," as they say in the two and a half verses beginning with *sarve*. They possess shimmering garlands of lotuses (*puṣkaramālā*).
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— All [the deities] possess youthful forms, and all have beautiful four arms.
The splendor of the bow, quiver, sword, mace, conch, discus, and lotus.
Śrīdhara: "Nūtna" means those whose age is new (youthful). A "niṣaṅga" is a quiver. Those who possess beauty (śrī) or splendor through their bows, quivers, and so forth, are [described as such]. (35)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.
*Viśvanātha*: "And by your very appearance, you are perceived to be truly most refined," thus they say—"all of you. (35)
Making the quarters of the sky bright with light and free from darkness by your own splendor,
for what reason do you restrain us, the servants of Dharmapāla?

Śrīdhara: [They say: "They make the quarters such that the darkness has vanished and there is light—that is, illumination—for others. They state, "This is improper for you," and ask, "For what reason? //36//
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Those [nights] in which darkness has vanished and there is the light of others; yet, how is it that they are unrefined by their actions? Thus they ask—"For what purpose? (36).
Śrī Śuka said:
When this had been spoken by the messengers of Yama, those who carry out the commands of Vāsudeva [replied].
They replied to them with a laugh, in a voice as deep as the roar of a thundercloud:

Śrīdhara: "Aha! These are nothing but thieves who, being devoid of knowledge regarding who deserves punishment and who does not, speak this falsehood out of fear of us, claiming to be the servants of Dharmarāja. Laughing with amazement at them, they spoke in reply [with a voice whose resonance was like that of a cloud]. (37)

Kramasaṃdarbha: This has not been explained. Viśvanātha: [The word] "having laughed" [means]: "O, you do not even know dharma; why do you say out of fear of us that we are the servants of Dharmarāja? But you are merely a specific kind of ghost (preta)."
The sense is: "Having thus fallen into our hands, how will you live today? ||37||
— the Śrī Viṣṇu messengers said:
"If you are indeed the executors of the commands of Dharmarāja,"
Declare to us the true nature of dharma and the defining characteristic of adharma.
Śrīdhara: *Tattva* is the essential nature (*svarūpa*); *lakṣaṇa* is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). ||38||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Now, [one might ask]: "We are indeed the messengers of Dharmarāja; who then does not recognize us?
To this they say: "You... The instruction is the instruction regarding our true nature.
The intrinsic nature, the definition, and the means of valid cognition. ||38||
How indeed is the rod of punishment wielded, and what is its desired scope? Are all offenders subject to punishment, or only some among men?

Śrīdhara: *Katham svid* means "in what manner? *Sthānam* means "the sphere of experience. *Kāriṇaḥ* means "those who perform actions" (the agents). By saying *nṛṇām* ("of men"), it is meant that only humans [are intended], not animals and so forth; and even among them, only a few—this is the meaning. ||39||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "How? is a question regarding the manner (*prakāra*) of the rod (*daṇḍa*). "It stands from this" (*tiṣṭhaty asmāt*), thus it is the "basis" (*sthāna*); this is a question regarding the cause (*kāraṇa*) of the rod. "Of the doers" (*kāriṇām*), that is, "of the agents" (*karmiṇām*); this is a question regarding the object (*viṣaya*).
Regarding the word "all": does this include even animals and so forth, or does it refer only to some among human beings?
This is the question concerning the determination of the scope. (39)
The messengers of Yama said:
"Dharma is indeed that which is ordained by the Vedas; adharma is its opposite."
We have heard that the Veda is Nārāyaṇa himself, the self-existent.
Salutations to Śrī Vedavyāsa, the author of Madhva’s works.

Since the all-pervading Hari alone is the first speaker of the Vedas, therefore those who expound the Vedas say that the Vedas have Viṣṇu as their soul. Thus [it is stated] in the *Śabdanirṇaya*, verse 40.

Śrīdhara: Dharma is that which is enjoined or prescribed by the Veda; the meaning is that it has the Veda as its authority (*pramāṇa*). By this, both the essential nature and the authority are stated: that which has the Veda as its authority is dharma, and that which is dharma has the Veda as its authority. As Jaimini said: "Dharma is a matter characterized by Vedic injunction (*codanā*)."

Thus it has been explained by the Bhaṭṭas: "Two things are defined by a single sūtra through both direct statement (śruti) and implication (artha). They state the nature and definition of *adharma*—even though it was not asked about—in order to describe the basis for punishment: "That which is the opposite of that [dharma], being prohibited by the Veda, is *adharma*."

And the meaning is that negation is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding that [the Veda]. The reason for the authority of the Veda is that the Veda has emerged from Nārāyaṇa; he himself is [the source] directly, which is a figurative expression (*upacāra*). And as for the term "self-existent" (*svayaṃbhū*), it means that it exists by itself through mere exhalation. And thus says the Śruti: "Of this Great..."
"This Rigveda is the very breath of that which has come to be" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.10). ||40||
The composition of the sequence: the meaning is that it was established and ordained in the Veda. "Directly" means by himself alone; for this very reason, he is the Self-existent (Svayambhū). ||40||

Viśvanātha: [Dharma] is that which is enjoined or prescribed by the Veda. Since the nature of dharma is "being ordained by the Veda," it has been stated there that the Vedic injunction itself is the authority (*pramāṇa*) regarding its nature.
Furthermore, because adharma was also inquired about through the question concerning the cause of punishment, the nature and the authority of adharma [are likewise explained].

And they say: that which is the opposite of that [dharma], being prohibited by the Veda, is *adharma*; the meaning is that the very prohibition in the Veda is the authority (*pramāṇa*) for it. "Self-existent" (*svayaṃbhū*) means that he exists by himself through the mere breath of Nārāyaṇa. And thus says the Śruti: "The breath of this great Being..."
"This is what is called the Rigveda" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.10). ||40||
By which [power] these entities, composed of rajas, sattva, and tamas, are manifested in their own abode according to their true nature through qualities, names, actions, and forms.

Śrīdhara: Who is this Nārāyaṇa? To that they reply: By him—in his own abode, which is his essential nature (*svarūpa*)—these beings (*bhāva*), namely living creatures; these qualities (*guṇa*), such as tranquility and so forth; these names (*nāman*), such as "Brāhmaṇa" and so on; these activities (*kriyā*), such as Vedic study and so forth; and these forms (*rūpa*), such as the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*) and so forth, are manifested (*vibhāvyante*), that is, they are differentiated.
"Yathātatham" means "as it truly is. He is Nārāyaṇa. ||41||
The sequence of composition: "By which" means by which supreme cause. ||41||

Viśvanātha: Who is this Nārāyaṇa? To this they reply: He who, remaining even while situated in his own abode, Vaikuṇṭha, [creates] these beings—living entities—by mere volition alone; as well as the qualities such as tranquility and so forth;
the names such as "Brāhmaṇa" and so on; the activities such as study and so forth; and the forms such as the castes and stages of life (varṇāśrama) and so forth.
By them they are manifested; they are created in their various forms, according to their respective natures and as they truly are. ||41||
The sun, fire, space, the wind-god, the moon, the twilight, day and night, the quarters, heaven,
earth, and Dharma himself— these are indeed the witnesses of the embodied being.
Śrīdhara: Nevertheless, how is it known that unrighteousness has been committed by him? To this they say: "The sun," etc.
*Ahanī* means day and night. *Kam* means water. *Kuḥ* means the earth. Of the embodied living being (*daihyasya jīvasya*). As they have said: [citation].
The sun and the moon, the wind and the fire, heaven, earth, water, the heart, and Yama;
day and night, and both twilights—
And Dharma knows the conduct of a man. Thus [ends verse 42].
The sequence of arrangement: the witnesses. In the examination consisting of mantras, such as "From the beginning until the moon," and so forth, they reveal what is auspicious or inauspicious. ||42||

Viśvanātha: "May no one know [of it]"—thus is sin committed by men in secret; here, the connection with the preceding verse is that the sun and other luminaries are perceived as witnesses to the embodied soul (*jīva*). Day and night; *kam* means water; *kuḥ* means the earth. As they have said:
The sun and the moon, the wind and the fire, heaven, earth, water, and Yama;
day and night, and both twilights.
And Dharma knows the conduct of a man. Thus [ends verse 42].
—o)0(o— By these [means], unrighteousness is recognized; it is appropriate that there be a place for punishment.
All perpetrators deserve punishment in accordance with their actions.
Śrīdhara says: "They declare this to be the place; it is recognized by these causal signs. They declare those who are subject to punishment to be 'all' [of them]. ||43||
The sequential composition is appropriate; the meaning is "it comes into being. ||43||
Viśvanātha says: "They say this is the place"—meaning by these [verses]. Daṇḍin says: "Indeed, all living beings, O sinless ones, experience both auspicious and contrary events."
For those who perform actions, there is attachment to qualities; indeed, one who possesses a body is not without action.

Śrīdhara: Even unfavorable and inauspicious results occur for those who perform actions, because they possess attachment to the *guṇas*. If someone were a non-doer (*akartā*), then inauspicious results would not accrue to him;
however, this is not the case, as they say: "Indeed, there is no embodied being who is a non-doer. Therefore, all...
The meaning is that since sin is inevitable for those who perform actions, all such actors deserve punishment. ||44||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: The reason why all are subject to punishment is given by the words "they occur" (*sambhavanti*). "Viparītāni" means inauspicious or evil deeds. For those who act—that is, those who perform actions—there is indeed an attachment to the *guṇas*. And the *guṇas*...

Beings and so forth are indeed the causes of merit and demerit; however, the designation "this person is righteous or unrighteous for as long as he lives" is made on account of the preponderance [of such actions]. Now, it is said that attachment to qualities belongs only to those who act; if someone were a non-doer, he would simply be exempt from punishment. To this they reply: "one who possesses a body. That is, one who bears a body.
A person; moreover, the claim that he is devoid of action contradicts direct perception—this is the meaning. ||44||
Whatever dharma or non-dharma has been pursued here by anyone, in whatever manner, to that same extent one surely experiences its fruit in the next world.

Śrīdhara: To the question, "How indeed is the rod (daṇḍa) wielded?", the answer is given by the word "by which" (yena). The phrase "or like dharma" is an illustration; the meaning is that punishment follows adharma just as happiness follows dharma.
This sequence of the composition has not been explained [elsewhere].

Viśvanātha: They provide the answer to the question "How is the punishment [meted out]?"—to whatever extent (yāvān), meaning of what measure (yat-pramāṇaka), and in whatever manner (yathā) unrighteousness or righteousness has been committed; the fruit thereof, whether suffering or happiness, is of that same measure, according to the perspective of the scriptures—this is the implied sense. ||45||
Just as here among the foremost of gods a threefold nature is perceived due to the diversity of qualities in beings, so it is inferred elsewhere.

Śrīdhara says: Not only the sun and other such phenomena are indicators of dharma and adharma, but also presumptive testimony (arthāpatti); thus they say, "as follows": O best of gods, in this birth, [one's nature] is known through being peaceful, terrible, or deluded; or through being a mixture of pleasure and pain; or through being righteous and so forth.

Just as the threefold knowledge is perceived among living beings, so too is it inferred in another birth; it is postulated because its existence cannot otherwise be accounted for by means of this threefold nature. ||46||
The sequence of composition: it is inferred even by mortals—this is the ellipsis. ||46||

Viśvanātha says: "Let the association with qualities such as *sattva* be perceived directly"—thus they say. Just as there is a threefold division among men in this world due to their meritorious, sinful, and mixed karma, so too is there a threefold division elsewhere—in the next world or in another birth—by way of happiness, mixture, and suffering.
The threefold nature is inferred; the sense is that this occurs solely through the perspective of the scripture. ||46||
Just as the present time indicates the qualities of the other two times [past and future],
so too does this [present] birth serve as an illustration of merit and demerit for the other two births.

Śrīdhara says: They state, with an illustration, that through one's present birth there arises knowledge of the dharma and adharma of previous and subsequent births. The "present" is the current season, such as spring; it is the indicator (*abhijñāpaka*) of those qualities—such as flowers, fruits, and so forth—which belong to the other two, the past and future springs.
Just as this birth indicates the merit and demerit of the other two births—the past and the future—so it is. ||47||

The sequential arrangement (*kramasaṃdarbha*) refers to the present time, such as the preceding twilight or the spring season. Just as it manifests the qualities of its own prior time— such as the night or the cold season— in its former part, and the qualities of its own subsequent time— such as the day or the summer heat— in its latter part, so too [does it function].
The meaning is that even the present birth [is known] from one's own previous births and so forth. ||47||

Viśvanātha says: They state, with an illustration, that through one's present birth alone, there arises knowledge of the dharma and adharma of previous and future births. "The present" refers to the current season, such as spring. It is the indicator (*abhijñāpaka*) of those qualities—such as flowers and fruits—belonging to the other two, namely the past and future springs.
Just as this very birth indicates the merit and demerit of the other two births—the past and the future—so it is. ||47||
In the city of the mind, the divine Lord perceives his former form;
the unborn Blessed One contemplates that which was previously unknown by means of the mind.

Śrīdhara says: This is the manner in which others know dharma and adharma; however, they say that Dharmarāja perceives everything by means of his mind alone. Even while remaining in the city of Saṃyaminī, the divine Yama—whether as the inner controller (antaryāmī) residing within the body or as the specific prior form of the individual soul (jīva) endowed with dharma, adharma, and so forth—[perceives it].
He sees; immediately thereafter, he investigates the unprecedented form; he deliberates upon that which is appropriate to each, because that Blessed One is unborn. 48.

The sequential arrangement: In the view of the Yamas, the Blessed One is "Aja" (the Unborn); because he is their manifestation (*vibhūti*), he is designated as non-different from them through devotion. ||48||
Viśvanātha: This manner of knowing dharma and adharma is common among others;

however, they say that Dharmarāja perceives everything with certainty by means of his mind alone. Even while remaining in his city, Saṃyamanī, the god Yama beholds the former form—that is, the nature of previous births.
He perceives that which is joined with merit, demerit, and so forth; immediately thereafter, he investigates the unprecedented, the present, and future forms.
He deliberates upon whatever corresponds to what [is being examined]; the Blessed One is omniscient, unborn, and equal to Brahmā. ||48||
Just as one endowed with darkness worships only the manifest according to his understanding,
so too, having lost the memory of his previous births, he does not know what came before or what comes after.

Śrīdhara says: "The individual soul (jīva), however, perceives only the present body presented by the Lord, and not the previous or the future one—as it is said: 'Just as...'. The ignorant soul, whose limiting adjunct is ignorance (avidyopādhi), indeed attends only to the manifest, present body and so forth manifested by past karma, and thinks, 'I am [this]'"—so they say.
He does not know what is before or what is after. The reason for this is that his memory of births has been lost.

Here is an illustration: just as one who is possessed by darkness—meaning sleep—in a dream attends only to the manifest body and so forth, and not to the waking body or to anything belonging to a previous dream, such is the case here; this is the meaning. ||49||

Kramasaṃdarbha: This has not been explained. Viśvanātha says: Since the individual soul lacks knowledge of what precedes and follows, its engagement in sin and so forth is not surprising; they say this is just as a beast or similar creature, possessed by darkness, clearly acts only toward its present body.

Just as [the deity] attends to him with desired food and so forth to provide comfort, so too does the man; "whose memory is destroyed by birth" is the reason for the absence of knowledge regarding what preceded and followed. ||49||
With five he accomplishes his own purposes, and with another five he knows the five Vedas;
but with the sixteenth he enjoys three, while the seventeenth himself experiences all.

Śrīdhara: [The author] elaborates upon the transmigratory existence of such a living being (jīva) in five verses. Through the five organs of action, he performs the taking up of objects for his own sake and so forth;
through the five organs of knowledge, he perceives the five [objects], sound and the rest; and together with the mind as the sixteenth, he constitutes the seventeenth.

Although it is included among the sixteen adjuncts (*upādhi*), it is itself indeed one alone. Because it synthesizes the objects of all the sense organs, it attains the threefold objects of the organs of knowledge, the organs of action, and the mind.
Kramasaṃdarbha: not commented upon.
Viśvanātha: —o)0(o—
This great sixteen-fold liṅga, consisting of the three powers,
maintains the cycle of transmigration for the individual soul, bestowing joy, sorrow, fear, and affliction.

Śrīdhara: Thus, this subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*), consisting of the three powers and being the effect of the three qualities (*guṇa*), is great and beginningless; it maintains its connection with the individual soul (*puruṣa*, *jīva*) throughout the cycle of transmigrations.
The sequential arrangement [of the commentary] has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: O Lord,
the ignorant man, though unconquered by the sixfold group of passions, is made to perform actions against his will.
Like a silkworm, one deludes oneself by enveloping oneself with one's own actions.

Śrīdhara: "Whether willing or even unwilling, he is made to perform actions by this very [bondage]. The *kośakāra* is a specific kind of silkworm. "He is deluded; he does not know the means of escape.
Regarding the sequence of the composition, no explanation has been provided.
Viśvanātha:
No one indeed ever remains for even a moment without performing action.
For one is made to act against one's will by the inherent qualities through their force.

Śrīdhara: Regarding the statement "it is caused to act," they cite experience as the proof, saying "not indeed. [The text continues: "By the qualities" means by passion and other effects of the qualities (*guṇa*); "inherent" means produced from the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of prior karma. The sequence of the composition has not been explained.
Viśvanātha:
Having obtained the unmanifest cause, it indeed becomes manifest and unmanifest.
According to the womb and according to the seed, by virtue of its own powerful nature.
Śrīdhara says: They state that by the power of karma, a body corresponding to it arises; thus he says, "having obtained.

Having obtained the unmanifest—the unseen cause—one comes to possess a manifest-unmanifest body, both gross and subtle, corresponding to that [karma]. "According to the womb" means similar to the mother; "according to the seed" means...

"Similar to the father": *svabhāva* means latent impression (*vāsanā*). The meaning is that even though the semen and blood are one, the body becomes similar to the mother and father due to the latent impressions of karma.
Regarding the sequence of the composition: "having obtained," etc.; those which are reached in the womb and the seed by means of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) as the instrumental cause.
The meaning is that the body comes to be in accordance with its own nature. ||54||
Viśvanātha:
This is the error of the Puruṣa due to its association with Prakṛti.
He existed for a short time, but through union with the Lord, he is dissolved.
Śrīdhara: Concluding the discussion on the wheel of saṃsāra, they describe the manner of liberation with the words "This...
[verse 55]. Through association with the Lord—that is, through the worship of the Supreme Lord. ||55||
The sequential arrangement is as follows: "This" refers to fear, which arises from attachment to duality, as in the verse: *bhayaṃ dvitīyābhiniveśataḥ syāt* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.2.37). ||55||
Viśvanātha: "This" refers to the following: the meaning is that bondage and liberation arise solely from the conjunction of primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa). ||55||
For he is endowed with learning, a repository of virtuous conduct, observance, and qualities;
firm in his vows, gentle, self-controlled, truthful in speech, skilled in mantras, and pure.

Śrīdhara: Thus, having concluded the general determination of dharma and so forth, they describe the unrighteousness of the subject at hand, Ajāmila, and state his deservingness of punishment, beginning with "This man indeed," and continuing until the end of the chapter. Therein, by two [verses], that...
The narration of the previous events is for the purpose of demonstrating the excess of injustice. *Śīla* is good character;
*vṛtta* is right conduct; *guṇāḥ* are qualities such as forbearance and the like; he is the abode (*ālaya*) of these. (56)
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: Having thus described the nature of dharma, adharma, and so forth, he elaborates upon adharma—in the passage beginning with "For this [man]" and so on—in order to make known the culpability of the subject at hand, Ajāmila. In that regard as well...
To indicate that such excellence is inappropriate, they describe his righteousness through two qualities: *śīla* is a good disposition;
*vṛtta* is virtuous conduct; and *guṇas* are qualities such as forbearance and the like. ||56||
—o)0(o— Devoted to serving his guru, the sacred fire, guests, and elders; free from egoism;
a friend to all beings; virtuous; moderate in speech; and free from malice.
Śrīdhara: "Free from egoism" means devoid of the sense of "I. ||57||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
Once that twice-born man went to the forest to carry out his father’s command.
Having taken fruits, flowers, sacrificial fuel, and kuśa grass, he then returned.
Śrīdhara: Then, having turned back from the forest, he returned. ||58||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha states that this has not been explained.
He saw a certain lustful Śūdra together with his female servant.
And having drunk the honey-wine *maireya*, her eyes were rolling with intoxication.

Śrīdhara: Having drunk *maireya*—a type of honey-wine or spirituous liquor made from flour—by means of a *bhujiṣyā*, that is, a woman for pleasure or a female slave; she whose eyes were rolling and wandering due to intoxication. (59)
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Maireya is a spirituous liquor made from flour; it is *madhu*, wine. [She] was being enjoyed by a *bhujiṣyā*, a female slave. ||59||
With his waist-knot loosened by intoxication, devoid of shame,
he was playing, singing along, and laughing in her presence.
Śrīdhara: [The phrase] "with her whose waist-knot (nīvī) was especially loosened"; "fallen" means deviated from proper conduct (*svācāra*).
The sequence of the composition has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: [He is] free from fear of the world, together with her. ||60||
Seeing her embraced by that arm smeared with passion, he,
utterly deluded, suddenly fell under the sway of desire.
Śrīdhara: [The phrase] "smeared with the ointment of passion" refers to being anointed with that body-unguent such as turmeric and the like, which kindles desire;
this has not been explained in the *Kramasaṃdarbha*.
Viśvanātha: "Smeared with passion" means anointed with the essence of turmeric, which kindles desire. (61)
Though restraining himself by his own self as much as possible according to what he had heard,
he was unable to compose his mind, which was trembling with passion.

Śrīdhara: *Sattva* means fortitude; *śruta* means learning. Even though he steadied [his mind] by the power of those two, he was unable to compose or restrain his heart, which was trembling with passion. (62)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Self, mind, essence, fortitude, learning, and knowledge. ||62||
Seized by the demon of Cupid under the pretext of that cause, he became senseless;
meditating on her alone in his mind, he indeed desisted from his own duty.
Śrīdhara: He was seized by that very sight, which was the cause of the crocodile in the guise of love; he was rendered unconscious, his memory having departed. ||63||

The Sequential Composition (*kramasaṃdarbha*): In this section, through the words of the messengers of Yama, it is shown that although he was endowed with Vedic learning—as in the passage beginning "For he was possessed of scriptural knowledge" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 6.1.56)—he was not protected from falling into a lower state by his adherence to such duties; rather, he was protected solely by a semblance of devotion (*bhaktyābhāsa*).
This is the intention of Śrī Śukadeva. ||63||

Viśvanātha says: [The Lord] ceased [speaking]. By such steadfastness in his own duty and by his knowledge, he was not able to protect himself from falling; however, even by the mere semblance of His name, [the Lord] protected him from such a downward fall and sent him to Vaikuṇṭha.
By means of the meaning of this section, the individual power of the knowledges of the dharma and the knowledges of the categories has been demonstrated. ||63||
He gratified her with as much ancestral wealth as was necessary,
and with such delightful worldly pleasures as would cause her to be pleased.
Śrīdhara: By the whole [of it]. ||64||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.
*Viśvanātha*: The ellipsis is "by exactly as much meaning as [is necessary] for it to remain"; the ellipsis is "he explains it in such a way that she may become pleased. ||64||
That sinner, his mind pierced by the sidelong glances of a wanton woman, soon cast aside his own young wife, a Brahmin woman born into a noble family.
Śrīdhara: "Lambhitām" means married. ||65||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: "Obtained" means given by her father only after due deliberation.
The sandhi [elision] in *svairṇyāpāṅga* is an archaic (Vedic) usage. ||65||
From here and there, he brought wealth by both fair and foul means;
this dull-witted man supported the household of his wife.
It has not been explained by anyone;
for he, having transgressed the treatise, acted according to his own will and was thus utterly censured.
For a long time, he lived an impure life, seeking evil and defiled by sin.
Śrīdhara: [The word] *malāt* means "from one whose life is of the nature of impurity," because he consumes that person's food and so forth, which are nothing but impurity. //67//
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: He is one whose life (āyuḥ) has the form of sin (*agha*) or is for the sake of sin; he eats only the filth that is the leavings of a prostitute. ||67||
"Therefore, we shall lead him, who has committed an offense and has not yet performed atonement, into the presence of Daṇḍapāṇi, where he may be purified by punishment."
Śrīdhara: "Akṛtanirveśam" means one who has not performed atonement. And they say, "We shall lead him [to the goal] for his very benefit," in the verse beginning with "yatra. (68)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: The sense is: "How can you restrain us, who are engaged solely in assisting those who become purified even without having performed penance? (68)
Thus ends the first chapter of the sixth [book] in the *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted to the Lord; it is well-received by the virtuous.
Thus ends the sixth book in the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā, the Pāramahaṃsyam, within the Brahmasūtrabhāṣya of the glorious Bhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa.
The First Chapter: The Dialogue between Śrī Viṣṇu and the Servants of Yama in the Narrative of Ajāmila.
Now begins the Second Chapter.
In the narrative of Ajāmila,
Śrī Bādarāyaṇi said:
"Thus addressed by the messengers of Yama, those messengers of the Blessed One..."
Then, O King, having reflected upon those words, those experts in policy replied.
Śrīdhara:

In the second [chapter], it is told how a certain twice-born man, having been made to hear by Vaiṣṇavas the wondrous greatness of the names of Viṣṇu, was led from the realm of Yama to the world of Viṣṇu.
They are skilled in guidance and proficient in logic. ||1||

Caitanyamatamañjuṣā: In the second and third chapters, although everything is indeed my own doctrine within the narrative of Ajāmila, nevertheless, I shall demonstrate some aspects of my own doctrine here according to my understanding. ||1||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha:
In the second [chapter], by the greatness of the Name, the messengers of Yama were repelled.
The renunciation of Ajāmila and his ascent to Vaikuṇṭha are now described.
As those skilled in guidance and knowledgeable in the treatises on ethics say: ||1||
—o)0(o— The messengers of Śrī Viṣṇu said:
"Alas, what a tragedy! Even unrighteousness touches the assembly of those who perceive the Dharma!"
Where punishment is wielded in vain by those against those who are not deserving of punishment and are sinless.
Śrīdhara: Unrighteousness touches the assembly of those who perceive dharma. Regarding this, they say:
"In whatever assembly," "by whomsoever who perceive dharma," "of them—that assembly. (2)

The sequential arrangement: Now, as for the fact that the messengers of Yama demonstrated their own master’s status as Dharmarāja and as a world-protector through the passage beginning with "Who are you? (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.1.32), they challenge that by way of a concessive argument (abhyupagamavāda) in five verses beginning with "Alas, what misery! (aho kaṣṭam). ||2||

[In this regard, as in the words of the Blessed Lord, "Whatever one performs," it is taught that on the path of action, the injunction for the best of people consists solely in being devoted to the performance of their own duty (*svadharma*), even while desiring the fruits of action.
Viśvanātha: Ah, you are recognized! You are recognized! You are indeed the servants of Dharmarāja himself.

They said, "Enough with your idle talk; rather, we know that the very nature of Dharmarāja is characterized by its opposite. The sense is: "Alas! Until this very day, this report has not reached our ears. "Kaṣṭam" (alas/woe) expresses such great injustice.

The sense is: "What will be the fate of the worlds? Now, who indeed are being thus censured? To that we reply: "Listen, O listen! they say. Even in the assembly of those who perceive dharma—those who see dharma—it is adharma alone that touches them; the sense is that even regarding what is dharma, they perceive only adharma.

The sense is that in whatever assembly punishment is inflicted upon people who are not wicked—even those who are not wicked and thus ought not to be punished—that very thing is a manifestation of unrighteousness. ||2||
If there were indeed partiality among those who are the fathers of subjects, who are teachers, virtuous,
and impartial, to whom would the subjects go for refuge?
Śrīdhara: The fathers are like fathers—protectors, instructors, and those who discipline through punishment. Inequity consists in the failure to punish. ||3||

Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: "Listen! Is that which is heard regarding the fatherhood, the authority, the goodness, and the impartiality of your masters now indeed become a mere falsehood?"
They said: "Because of their affection for their subjects, they are fathers; because they instruct them in dharma, they are teachers; because they act for their welfare, they are virtuous men;

and because they perceive equality between their own happiness and suffering in all circumstances, they are impartial. To speak of partiality toward them would mean that even fathers oppress their children, and even teachers do not [teach] dharma even to their own servants."

The meaning is this: even the virtuous instruct those who act for their own harm; yet, being themselves ignorant of the suffering of others, whom can they reach? This sight of the world's misery is simply unbearable for us.
Whatever a superior person practices, another strives to do;
whatever standard he sets, the world follows.

Śrīdhara: They say that a great calamity occurred because another person would also practice this unrighteousness thus set in motion—expressed by the words "whatever... whatever. *Śreyān* means the most excellent. ||4||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not commented upon.
Viśvanātha: Thus, they say that in this way this path of dharma will soon be destroyed—"whatever... [it is]" (verse 4).
He upon whose lap the world rests its head and sleeps in peace,
himself knowing neither dharma nor adharma, just like a beast.

How can he, who has surrendered himself and practiced friendliness toward the insentient world, yet be worthy of milking— that is, exploiting— the trustful beings while remaining devoid of compassion?

Śrīdhara: They say [the sin] is even greater than the betrayal of one who trusts—by means of two verses beginning with "yasya" (of whom). *Nirvṛtaḥ* means free from anxiety. ||5|| [He refers to] one by whom the self has been completely surrendered through trust.
*Viśrambhaṇīyaḥ* means worthy of being trusted. [This applies] if he is compassionate. ||6||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Furthermore, they say [in the two verses beginning with] "Of whom... (*yasya...*): What sin greater than the betrayal of trust can we speak of? [He refers to one] by whom the self has been completely surrendered through trust. How?
Regarding the word "trusted," they say: he is one who inspires trust among living beings and is compassionate. (6)
for he has indeed expiated even the sins of ten million births,
since, though helpless, he uttered the name of Hari as a prayer for well-being.
Śrīdhara: Now, as for why this reproach is directed at the punishment of this sinner, they say:
"For he... Since, even though helpless, he uttered the name of Hari;
it is not merely that the name of Hari serves as an expiation, but rather it is a means of well-being (*svastyayana*) and a means to liberation (*mokṣa*).
Moreover, according to the Smṛti: "By whomsoever the two syllables 'Ha-ri' are uttered even once, the girdle has been fastened by him for the journey toward liberation. (7)

Sanātana: This Ajāmila has performed his expiation—that is, his atonement—by which means he uttered, even though helpless, the name of Hari. Not only is the name of Hari a mere expiation, but it is also a blessing and a means to liberation (*mokṣa*). Or rather:
It is also the supreme abode of auspiciousness. (Ha.bha.vi.
