11.331) The sequence of the composition: "Even if helpless," the sense is that let alone for this very son, there is greatness by means of his name being clearly uttered by each preceding person. [Having attained fulfillment] 7.
[Having performed expiation; furthermore, the fifteenth verse should be consulted here.
Viśvanātha: Now, why have we—or rather, our masters—wished to lead Ajāmila to hell, even though he had already performed expiation for thousands of great sins, if only to purify him?
Regarding the objection that "you have committed an offense by thus censuring him," they reply:

"For he has certainly performed his atonement; not only for the sins committed in a single lifetime, but even for those of ten million lifetimes—because, though helpless, he uttered the name of Hari."
"For as much power as the name of Hari possesses in removing sin, a sinful man cannot commit that much evil. Thus it is said:
"When His name is uttered even involuntarily, [one is freed] from all sins."
"A person is instantly liberated, like deer terrified by a lion"— so says the Smṛti. Thus,
the name of Hari is not merely an expiation, but also a means of well-being and a means for liberation.
"By whomsoever the two syllables 'Ha-ri' are uttered even once, by him the preparation for proceeding toward liberation has been made," according to the Smṛti. (7)
By this very act, the expiation for the sin of this sinner would indeed be accomplished,
when he uttered the four syllables: "Nārāyaṇāya."

Śrīdhara: Now, it is indeed appropriate that the name of Hari brings about the perfection of ritual action, according to such scriptural statements as: "I salute that Acyuta, by whose remembrance and utterance of His name, what is deficient in penance, sacrifice, ritual acts, and the like, immediately attains completeness."
But how could the name of Hari remove sin independently?

To this they say: "By this very [name]. *Aghonaḥ* means "of one who possesses sin" (*aghavataḥ*). Its form is like that of the word *maghavan*. There is a division after *yat* and *ā*. *Ā* means "slightly," merely a manifestation; the four-syllabled name which he uttered—by that very [name].
"By the word 'kevalena' (by itself), the superiority [of the name] is also shown. How did he speak?
In the form of a loud cry calling his son: 'O Nārāyaṇa! Come here! This is the intended meaning:

even though the name of Hari is an auxiliary part of ritual action (*karmāṅga*), like the *svādi* and *rat* suffixes, it possesses distinctness through its separate connection (*saṃyogapṛthaktvena*).”

It is indeed logical that this serves as a universal expiation (sarvaprāyaścitta). For it is said: "Even by one who acts involuntarily, when his name is uttered, a person is instantly liberated from all sins, just as deer are terrified by a lion."

From such passages in the Purāṇas, the independence of the Name is understood in thousands of instances. Nor should it be suspected that these are merely *arthavādas* (explanatory or glorificatory statements), because they lack the status of being supplementary to an injunction (*vidhi*). Furthermore, one should not assume that they are subordinate to something else simply because no injunction is heard; for instance, [in the case of the statement]: "The cake on eight potsherds is for Agni."
Thus, as in these and other such passages, since the meaning is not already established, it is logical to assume an injunction. Furthermore, in the mantras—
such as "O mortals, we meditate upon your many names, O immortal Jātavedas,
we the wise," and "Knowing his name, they proclaim it"— there is the superiority of all dharmas, such as austerity and charity, over [the mere] name.

This is understood. Furthermore, it has been established in the *Devatādhikaraṇa* that even mantras and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) possess authority regarding their own literal meaning. Therefore, by the mere manifestation of the name of Śrī Nārāyaṇa, the expiation of all sins shall be accomplished. ||8||

The Sequential Composition (*Kramasaṃdarbha*): Now, one might object: "In that case, since the destruction of the sins of ten million births occurred through that very name at the time of his naming, it would be more appropriate to say that the exhaustion of the sins committed by him repeatedly thereafter was accomplished by this [name] alone. Anticipating this doubt:

He himself states the intended meaning of the previous statement with the words "by this very [means]": even if he had not previously uttered that [formula], the sense there was that by this very [means] the expiation would have been accomplished; thus, the fact that it is a subsidiary part of something else is all the more avoided. ||8||

Viśvanātha: [Objection: "But surely the name was not taken as an expiation with the thought that it was the name of Hari; rather, it was merely a call to one's own son out of fear arising from our philosophical system. [Reply: You do not know the truth! Being turned away from the truth, you do not understand. Thus they say: "By this very fact, it is indeed certain."

"Aghonaḥ" means "of one possessing sin" (*aghavat*); its form is like that of the word "maghavan. The meaning is: even in the absence of a conscious intention to expiate sin through the mere calling of the son's name; that is, how much can this present calling of the son's name accomplish toward the expiation of sin? However, when previously—

Even at the time of the naming ceremony and other rites, he spoke even in the Apabhraṃśa language, saying, "O Nārāyaṇa, Āya, come from your mother’s lap to my lap"; the meaning is that at that very moment, the expiation for his sins was accomplished. Regarding the phrase "four syllables," this refers to the name Nārāyaṇa, even by means of one or two of its syllables.
The meaning is that there shall be the destruction of all sins. ||8||
the thief, the drinker of spirituous liquor, the betrayer of friends, the slayer of a Brahmin, the violator of the Guru’s bed,
the killer of women, kings, ancestors, or cows, and others who are sinners;
For all who have committed sins, this alone is the perfect atonement:
the utterance of Viṣṇu’s name, for it directs the mind toward Him.

Śrīdhara: Now, one might object: "How can this single expiation suffice for thousands of great sins committed through desire, which have been repeated many times and cannot be removed even by twelve hundred million years?
To this they reply with two verses beginning with "stena" (the thief): [9] "It is a well-performed, excellent expiation."

The reason for this is as follows: because of the utterance of the name, Viṣṇu’s thought arises regarding that object—that is, regarding the person who has uttered the name—thinking, "This is mine; I must protect him from all sides. ||10||

Sanātana: But how can this be a single atonement for thousands of great sins committed out of desire, which have been repeated many times and which cannot be remedied even by millions of twelve-year penances? To this, the venerable attendants of Viṣṇu reply with two verses beginning with "stena": "It is well-expiated... [and so forth].

This alone is the most excellent expiation. The reason for this is that from the utterance of the name—that is, from the act of pronouncing the name directed toward a person—the thought arises in Viṣṇu: "This one is mine; he is to be protected by me in every way and is to be especially favored. (Ha.bha.vi. 11.332333)

The sequence of the composition: "From which" means that from which even the experience of that Viṣṇu arises; or, because it is naturally inherent in His essential nature. For the supreme devotees (paramabhāgavatas), even hearing a single portion of that [scripture] is a source of delight. This being so:
The sense is: how much is characterized merely by the destruction of evil? ||10||
Viśvanātha: Now, let it be granted that there is indeed the destruction of sins;

however, how can there be expiation for thousands of great sins committed intentionally, repeated many times, which cannot be removed even by twelve crores of years, merely by the appearance of the Name once? To this [he says]:

They say: "He is a thief. For one who has stolen gold, this alone is the most excellent atonement (*prāyaścitta*) because it completely eradicates sin; it is not [the penance] lasting twelve years and so forth, for although that too destroys sin, it lacks the power to uproot it entirely. Nor does it have this as its sole result, since [the goal is attained] through the invocation of the Name.

The venerable teachers [hold that] Viṣṇu’s thought becomes directed toward that object—namely, the person uttering the name—with the realization, "This is mine; he must be protected by me in every way.
Thus, as if hearing His own name, or rather, merely by remembering Ajāmila who uttered it, He [sent us] to bring him.
The sense is: "How much more so would his mind be directed toward Viṣṇu as an object of service?
Therefore, the messengers of Viṣṇu spoke of Ajāmila’s utterance of that name at that time as an expiation for all sins, merely to show the messengers of Yama directly. But in reality, however—
It should be explained that among the many names uttered on numerous occasions during the son's naming ceremony and subsequent invocations,

it was that very first name which became the pacifier of all sins, whereas the others were merely means for achieving devotion; this is understood from the use of the third-person reference "yad vyājahāra" (that which he uttered), indicating the first [name].
It was stated specifically with reference to the name. "Helpless" (vivaśaḥ) should be explained as "helpless through affection for his son.
Furthermore, it is not for the sake of pacifying all sins—such as frequenting prostitutes, drinking liquor, and so forth—which may arise repeatedly even after one has repeatedly uttered the name.

It must be stated that only the utterance of the name arising at the final moment is required— that after which there is no further production of sin— because of the inclusion of the word "entire" (*aśeṣa*) in the verse: "They know the chanting of the name of Vaikuṇṭha to be the remover of all sins" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.2.14).
"Whatever sin exists in the present, whatever has occurred in the past, and whatever will occur in the future—
all that is quickly consumed by the fire of the chanting of Govinda's name. Thus, from hearing his name even once...

"Even a Pukkasa is liberated from saṃsāra. [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.16.44] "It is wonderful that one who has gone far away might take up Your name even once; by that, he immediately casts off bondage. [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 5.1.34]

This is because of the application of terms such as "bondage to saṃsāra" and so forth; and because no specific restriction regarding the particular *samaya* is mentioned in those various instances, it is understood from the mere mention of the first name that all sins, their latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and even the ignorance (*avidyā*) that is their root, are destroyed. Furthermore...
Because of the impossibility of the growth of sin.
But then, why did Ajāmila not depart immediately after uttering the first name, having become disillusioned?
Even in the absence of the growth of sin, he remained attached to that very same servitude and committed that very same sin.

On the contrary, it was performed for that duration. It is said: by the force of residual impressions (*saṃskāra*), even for those liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), their karma likewise persists for that duration; yet even though that very same sin is produced again and again, it does not generate a fruit, just like the bite of a snake whose fangs have been pulled out.

Alternatively, this should be explained as follows: even in the absence of the seed of sin, the Lord himself might again cause one to engage in sin so as to uproot the notion [of sin] held by other schools of thought; otherwise, if it were explained as a mere eulogistic statement (*arthavāda*) or through some other figurative interpretation, then—given the possibility of the offense against the Name mentioned in the *Padma Purāṇa* that "one falls due to the offense against the Name, which is the friend of all"—even the Name itself would be subject to such an offense.
"Regarding the word 'below' (adhaḥ): that man who entertains doubt toward the name of Hari is the most sinful among men; he clearly falls into hell. Thus [it is said].
Any person who, having heard of the various fruits of chanting the names [of the Buddha], lacks faith and considers them to be mere empty praise—
that person I shall cast here into a mass of suffering.
His body was oppressed by the various terrible afflictions of saṃsāra.

"Those who would say that those passages in the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas which speak of the greatness of the Name are merely *arthavāda* (laudatory statements), for them there is no end to their stay in hell"— according to these and thousands of other such statements from the *Pādma-saṃhitā*, the *Kātyāyana-saṃhitā*, and others, they shall surely suffer a downward fall.
For this very reason, Śrī Viṣṇurāta said:
"In one case he turns away from the inauspicious, and in another he engages in it again;
therefore, I consider expiation to be as useless as the bathing of an elephant" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.1.10).
Furthermore, while one who invokes atonement upon seeing the recurrence of sinful conduct might indeed do so, in the context of devotion,
no such invocation is made even when some devotee is seen to repeatedly engage in sinful conduct. Moreover, just as Ājāmila, despite his wicked conduct, [was saved] by the power of the Name...

Just as Vaikuṇṭha was attained [by the devotees], so too those who follow the Smṛtis and other traditions, who possess good conduct and are learned in the scriptures— even if they have frequently uttered the Name—
may still fall into the terrible cycle of worldly existence due to the power of offenses against the Name, such as the conceptualization of it as mere *arthavāda* (laudatory rhetoric).
Therefore, one should not even suspect that the universal liberation of all beings follows from the majesty of the Name alone.
Thus, O Blessed One, although this very name destroys evil with its very roots even when uttered but once,
it generally displays the sign of its own fruit in the world after a slight delay, according to the maxim: "Even a tree that bears fruit bears it only in due season."

It is understood as the established doctrine that, for the sake of not destroying the views of those who follow external scriptures, [the Teacher] does not reveal [the truth] everywhere, but leads his own interlocutors— rendering them free from their own faults— to the abode of the Blessed One.

Granted that those who commit offenses such as the recitation of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) may indeed suffer a downfall caused by their offense—we do not dispute this point. However, does the destruction of all sins occur through the cause of uttering the Name or not?

If the former is true, then among the ranks of those who perform ritual works (*karmi*), those possessed of knowledge (*jñānin*), practitioners of yoga (*yogin*), devotees (*bhakta*), and even other men distinct from them—

No one at all should go to those hells accessible through adultery, violence toward others, and so forth. In the second [type of hell], however, even devotees must go to the hells for the sake of experiencing their own sins, just as the *karmis* and others do;
regarding this, it is said that just as a great multitude [of people] [acts] according to the degree of refuge taken by those dependent upon them...

Even while making distinctions in the degree of protection, He protects those very same beings; for if they were offenders against Him, His lack of favor alone would be the cause for not protecting those who have taken refuge in Him, rather than any incapacity to protect them being imagined. It is precisely through the gradations in the exhaustion of their own offenses that [He acts] toward them.

And there is a gradation in grace (*prasāda*). When all offenses have been exhausted, there is grace alone. Likewise, for those who resort to the Goddess Bhakti—designated by that very name—as a subordinate factor for the sake of attaining the fruits of ritual actions and so forth, even though Bhakti exists in them as a subordinate element...

According to the maxim that "designations are made on the basis of predominance," they are designated by such terms as *karmi* (performer of rituals) or *jñānī* (possessor of knowledge), but not by the term *vaiṣṇava*. Furthermore, they are offenders against the single name [of the Lord] by their very nature. As it is said:
It has been said:
negligence is the equality [of indifference] toward all auspicious actions, such as the abandonment of religious vows and the offering of oblations.

The meaning is this: even the identity of the Name with dharma and the other virtues is a fault, let alone its being subordinate as a constituent part of dharma and so forth; yet, even that [identity] is maintained by these [virtues] through the mere grasping of a small fraction of the qualities belonging to such a refuge, lest their practice of *karmayoga* and the rest become fruitless.

Thinking "let it be so," the Goddess of Devotion, out of her own courtesy, accepts even her own inferiority; yet, just as she brings about the fruit of their actions and the like without obstacle precisely because she has become an auxiliary to those very actions, so too does she destroy their sins precisely because she has become an auxiliary to the rite of expiation (*prāyaścitta*). It is not otherwise.

Therefore, those very individuals who have not performed atonement must indeed go to those respective hells for the sake of experiencing the fruits of their various sins, but this is not the case for Vaiṣṇavas. Furthermore, even if they were to commit other offenses against the Name, such as slandering others through figurative speech (*arthavāda*) or by claiming to be virtuous, while still performing dharma and so forth—
When they do not perform [the rites], then even though the Name has become an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the Dharma and so forth, it does not produce those respective fruits.
"O best of Brahmins, what are those offenses committed against the Blessed One’s Name?
They destroy the efficacy of men's actions and indeed bring about their degradation. From such statements as these.

Furthermore, even for them, having desisted from those respective offenses and being intent upon the chanting of the Name and other practices that pacify them, there is a gradation in the attainment of the fruits of karma according to the degree to which the offense against the Name has been exhausted. When all offenses against the Name are exhausted through the power of association with the virtuous (sādhu), [liberation ensues].
However, by the perfect grace of the Goddess Bhakti, the attainment of the fruit of the Name is indeed beyond dispute.

But surely, even in the case of Ajāmila—through the words of Yama’s messengers, such as "For he was endowed with Vedic learning" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.1.56)—his former state as a ritualist is understood. True; yet, due to his drinking of liquor...
Even his status as a Brahmin has been utterly destroyed, let alone his eligibility for ritual action. As it is said:
"Thus, having subverted all dharmas, he is the husband of a slave-girl, fallen through his contemptible deed" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.2.45).
At the very moment his karma was exhausted, even his subordinate devotion vanished; yet once again,
through such acts as calling out to his own son, he possessed a devotion that was purely and solely focused on the utterance of the name Nārāyaṇa.

Now, if there indeed exists an injunctive statement such as "one should practice devotion" [prescribing] devotion as a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) to ritual action, knowledge, and so forth, then how can there be the offense of misnaming them? It is said in reply: all duties (*dharma*) are perfectly accomplished by devotion alone; even great sins (*mahāpātaka*) are destroyed by even a mere fragment of devotion, and so on.

The Vedic scripture, being composed of compassion, [teaches] that devotion may arise even for those who do not trust the words of hundreds of other scriptures, who have faith only in ritual action and knowledge, who are averse to devotion, and whose minds are impure and crooked— by this very method, as an auxiliary to the knowledge of dharma and so forth.
Since [the scripture] enjoins devotion (*bhakti*), the scriptural statement is not to be censured. Consequently,

just as the fault of that violence does not depart even when heaven is attained through the power of the injunction for the ritual slaughter of an animal (*vaidha-paśu-hiṃsā*), so too [is it with one] who possesses the offense consisting in making devotion subordinate.
Even when the fruit of action is obtained through the power of ritual injunctions, it should be understood that this occurs only upon the removal of one's transgressions.

Now, as for those who, being indeed offenders, have taken a Vaiṣṇava guru through Vaiṣṇava initiation and rely exclusively or primarily upon the Goddess of Devotion (Bhaktidevī) by means of the chanting of the Name and other such practices—

Even for those who worship the Blessed One and are designated by the term "Vaiṣṇava," there is a gradation in the exhaustion of their offenses and a gradation in the arising of the primary fruit of devotion, according precisely to the gradation of the grace of the Goddess Bhakti. As it is said:
It was said by the Blessed One himself:
"In whatever way this self is polished by means of hearing and reciting my meritorious verses..."
"In this way, one perceives even the subtlest object, just as the eye when treated with collyrium" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.14.26); and likewise,
"Devotion, the experience of the Supreme Lord, and dispassion" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.2.42), and so forth.
For those who hear his own stories, Kṛṣṇa— whose hearing and chanting are meritorious,
who dwells within the heart, and who is the friend of the virtuous— shakes off all misfortunes.
Thus, as indicated by such statements, their ascent through the fourteen stages occurs precisely in due order.
This is to be understood. For this very purpose, the injunctions regarding faith, conduct, and so forth are prescribed here and there. In this context as well, it is said:

"Indeed, the cultivation of goodness is the praise of virtues" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.2.13). Therefore, for those who have reached the Blessed Lord only after all their faults have been exhausted, there is no rebirth.

But for those who are sinless, there is no delay in attaining the Lord; for them, indeed, there are only two stages: the chanting of the Lord’s name and the ascent to Vaikuṇṭha, as was the case with Ajāmila and others. As it has been said:

"For those devoted to Vāsudeva, no inauspiciousness exists anywhere, nor does the fear of birth, death, old age, or disease ever arise. Thus it is said: "A man who is steadfast in his own duty for a hundred births..."
"Beyond that, the devotee of the Lord indeed attains me,
the unmanifest Vaiṣṇava state,
just as I am, O gods, at the end of the cosmic cycles. [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 4.24.29] Thus it is said.

Even for some who are innocent, yet who desire to attain a particular degree of love, there may be a slight delay in attaining the Blessed One; as was the case with Ādibharata, who underwent three births. Furthermore, among those who are guilty, if some—due to a lack of practice in devotion—have not exhausted their prior sins, [they too face such delay].
Even if there were offenses consisting of the sins they committed, they still should not go to the hells after abandoning their bodies;
for even upon seeing their own person with noose in hand, [they would turn back].
It is said that Yama whispers into his ear:
"Avoid those intoxicated by the stories of the Blessed Lord; I am the master over other debtors, but certainly not over the Vaiṣṇavas. (Bhāgavatamāhātmya 6.99)
"Neither they nor we have the power to inflict punishment," according to the words of Yama;
for the brother of Yamunā has indeed told us again and again with great insistence:
"O Vaiṣṇavas, you must avoid those men who worship Viṣṇu."

Thus it is from the words of the divine messenger (*devadūta*) in the *Māghamāhātmya* of the *Padma Purāṇa*. Furthermore, from the Lord’s own words: "O Uddhava, there is not even the slightest destruction of My dharma at the commencement of its limbs," it follows that even a mere sprout of devotion possesses an imperishable nature and cannot be overcome by sins and the like.

And because it is unfailing, their birth must necessarily be for the sake of future leaves, flowers, and so forth; it does not have as its cause sins or merits that are in a state of perishing. As it has been said: "For Vaiṣṇavas, there exists no birth bound by karma. Therefore, in another birth, theirs...

Through the chanting of the Name and other practices arising from the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of prior devotion, and upon the exhaustion of sins and offenses, one attains the Blessed One by the grace of the Goddess Bhakti. As it has been said:
"Indeed, a person shall never, under any circumstances, fail to go [to Him]."

"O dear one, a person who relishes the aesthetic flavor (*rasa-grāha*) and remembers the embrace of Mukunda’s feet would not wish to abandon it again, even while wandering through worldly existence like others, as he serves Mukunda. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.5.19)

In this context, the phrase "like others" means that he does not undergo the cycle of transmigration consisting of the experience of the fruits of merit and demerit like ordinary people born of karma; rather, he experiences the cycle of transmigration consisting of pleasure and pain as bestowed by the Blessed One.
As it has been said in the Śruti: "One who realizes You does not perceive the auspicious or inauspicious arising from You."
"Whether endowed with virtues or vices" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.87.40).
As long as there is no destruction of their offenses against the Name, their sins remain undestroyed even if they have already begun to yield their fruits;
however, through the increase of devotion and the non-repetition of those offenses, once the offenses against the Name are destroyed, [the result occurs] immediately.

Because one attains the Blessed One through the destruction of evil along with its roots, even those who are Vaiṣṇavas attain Him after one, two, or three births for the sake of increasing their devotion. The worldly pleasures seen in them arise from the dharma of devotion. As it has been said:
For one who possesses the dharma that leads to liberation, wealth does not serve the purpose of wealth;
nor is desire intended for the acquisition of wealth by one whose sole aim is dharma.
"The gratification of the senses is not the attainment of desire; one should live with only as much as is necessary for life.
For a living being, the inquiry into reality is the goal, and not that wealth which is acquired here through ritual acts.
Thus, certain sufferings were [described] by the Blessed One, who is skillful in increasing devotion to His own devotees.

These were given by me like a physician administering emetics, bitter medicines, and the like, intended to increase one's hunger; for it is said: "Whomever I favor, I shall gradually take away that person's wealth" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.88.8).

Which, however, are the most powerful fruits of offenses against the Name? For among the ten offenses against the Name, three—namely, the fabrication of a different meaning for an *arthavāda*, the assumption of a different meaning, and equating the Name with other meritorious acts—are direct destroyers of Vaiṣṇava status itself. Among the others, two are exceedingly powerful.
Regarding the engagement in evil due to the power of a great offense: for how can one endure the censure of that which has attained renown?
Indeed, it is by the power of a name that one’s mind turns toward evil.
For him, purification through restraints does not exist.
Thus, because this specific threat has been uttered, those two are pacified only by the continuous chanting of the Name accompanied by the endurance of appropriate suffering, and not otherwise;
whereas other offenses against the Name are pacified precisely through the continuous chanting of the Name and so forth. And as for those which...

Those who are offenders by name— devoid of ritual action, knowledge, and so forth, yet possessing devotion through hearing, chanting, and other such practices— are nevertheless designated by the very term "Vaiṣṇava," because they have not taken refuge at the feet of a guru and are thus uninitiated. For instance, this is established in the sūtra *sāsya devatā* ("he whose deity is this"), as well as in the various sūtras concerning various forms of bhakti.

And because [the goal] is accomplished through this, some say that those who have been made into deities by means of initiation (*dīkṣā*)—that is, those for whom Viṣṇu has become the deity—and those who have been made into objects of worship by means of devotion (*bhajana*)—that is, those for whom Viṣṇu has become the object of worship—are both indeed Vaiṣṇavas due to the absence of any other designation;
therefore, for them as well, there would be no falling into hell and so forth, just as before. This is not so.

"Properly associated" (*susaṃgatam*): because of the statement in the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* (10.20.17), "Since the human body is the first [means]," and so forth, that "the Guru is the helmsman," people do not easily attain the Lord without a Guru;
therefore, it is only by the power of their devotion to Him that, upon attaining a human birth in another life, they take refuge at the feet of a Guru.

They declare that the attainment of the Blessed One occurs through devotion for the virtuous, and not otherwise. Yet, it is indeed observed that even Ajāmila, who had no spiritual teacher, attained the Blessed One with ease;
therefore, the settled conclusion here is this: those whose senses are directed toward sense-objects alone, like cattle or donkeys, [do not attain Him].

They constantly practice [the chanting of the Lord's name], yet they do not know—even in their dreams—who the Blessed One is, what constitutes devotion, or who the Guru is; for those like Ajāmila and others, who have taken the name of Hari even through a mere semblance of its sound, liberation occurs without a Guru, provided they are free from offense. Hari alone is truly to be worshipped.

The vessel [of devotion] is precisely that which leads to Him; the teacher is indeed the one who instructs it. Although they possessed a particular excellence of discernment—such as the fact that only those devotees instructed by the guru attained Hari in the past—it is said:
"He does not look with even the slightest regard toward initiation, nor toward virtuous rites, nor toward preparatory worship."
"This mantra, consisting of the name of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, bears fruit even when it merely touches the tongue" (Padyāvalī 29).
According to this authoritative evidence and the example of Ajāmila and others, he thought: "What is the use of my laborious effort in making him my guru?
My attainment of the Lord will surely come about through the chanting of His names alone. Thus reflecting, he—
One does not attain the Blessed One solely due to the great offense characterized by disrespect toward the guru; rather,
whether in that very life or in another birth, upon the exhaustion of that offense,
one attains Him only by taking refuge at the feet of the venerable guru.
Some maintain that for those who worship other deities, there is a fixed rule regarding sin and transgression similar to that of ritualists (*karmī*).

Others hold that because they share the common quality of taking refuge in a deity through devotion (*bhakti*), they are nonetheless situated on a lower level than [the devotees of the Supreme Deity]. As it has been said:
Even those who, devoted to other deities, worship them endowed with faith,
they too, O son of Kuntī, worship me alone, though not according to the prescribed rule.
For I am indeed the enjoyer and also the lord of all sacrifices;
yet they do not recognize me in truth, and therefore they fall.
"Those devoted to the gods go to the gods; those devoted to the ancestors go to the ancestors;
those who worship the spirits go to the spirits; and those who sacrifice to me go to me" (Gītā 9.25).
However, for those who are entirely devoid of devotion, there is no liberation at all, as it has been said:
Those hateful, cruel, and most base among men, who are inauspicious, I cast perpetually into the very wombs of the asuras within the cycles of worldly existence.
"Having entered the womb of an asura, deluded from birth to birth,
they fail to reach Me, O son of Kuntī, and from there they go to the lowest state" (Gītā 16.19–20).
As for those among them such as Kaṃsa and others:
"Out of desire, hatred, fear, or affection, as well as through devotion, many have fixed their minds upon the Lord; having abandoned their sins, they have attained His state.
By the force of such scriptural statements, liberation occurs through the destruction of offenses against the Name by means of absorption in the Blessed One alone.
Some say that the mere names [of the Lord] remove sin; this is an elliptical expression for meditation (*dhyāna*) and other practices as well.

Therefore, others maintain that the repeated practice of meditation itself is "possession" (*āveśa*). However, in the case of the incarnations of Kṛṣṇa, this is not invariably true, because some among the hosts of Naraka, Bāṇa, and the Kauravas were devoid of such possession.
Others say that some attained it through the power of his death, while others through the power of even merely seeing him; this has already been stated previously. ||910||
Even by means of expiations uttered by those who discourse on Brahman,
a sinner is not purified in that way through vows and other such rites.
Just as the utterance of Hari’s names and words brings about the perception of the qualities of that One of Excellent Renown.

Śrīdhara [comments]: By two verses beginning with "Not so," they establish that very superiority. One is not purified by the expiations such as vows and the like taught by the exponents of Brahman, such as Manu and others;
rather, one is purified by the utterance of the aforementioned names, by which even the connection with actions such as "I bow" (namāmi) is implied.

It has been shown that [the name] is not required for that purpose. Furthermore, the utterance of His name and the words [describing Him] serves as a means of perceiving and making known the qualities of the Lord of Excellent Renown (uttamaśloka); it does not, however, have its utility exhausted merely by the removal of sin, like the Kṛcchra or Cāndrāyaṇa penances—this is the meaning. ||11||
Sanātana establishes this very superiority [of the name]: "No. One is not purified in that way by the vows and other expiations (niṣkṛta) taught by the exponents of Brahman such as Manu and others;
rather, [one is purified] by the utterance of the cited names, by which even the connection with actions such as "I bow" (namāmi) is implied.

It has been shown that [the name] is not required for that purpose. Furthermore, the utterance of those names serves as a means of perceiving and making known the qualities of the Lord of Excellent Renown (uttamaśloka);
the meaning is that it is not exhausted merely by the removal of sin, like the Kṛcchra or Cāndrāyaṇa penances. ||11||

(Ha.bha.vi. 11.334) The composition of the sequence: "by the exponents of Brahman" (*brahmavādibhiḥ*). Here, "Brahman" refers solely to the section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*), as in the passage: "The proponents of the Vedic tradition are deluded" (Bhāgavatapurāṇa 11.5.5).

It is not by means of names and words alone that the recitation of those names and words is exhausted merely by the purification of sins; rather, even a single name of the Lord of Excellent Renown (uttamaśloka), through its constituent parts, becomes both a means of perceiving His qualities and a cause for direct experience. ||11||

Viśvanātha: They say that even though the Name serves as an expiation for all great sins (mahāpātaka), it is supremely distinguished—this they state in two verses beginning with "No" (na). By the teachers of Brahman, such as Manu and others, through the words of the Name; that is, by means of the Names as mere indicators through conventional designation and so forth. Or rather, even by a single name such as Nārāyaṇa and the like.

The meaning is that even by the word alone—that is, by the mere nominal form (*subanta-śabda*)—the plurality [of the suffix] is due to its weight (*gaurava*), and thus even the expectation of the meaning (*arthāpekṣā*) need not be considered. The meaning is that even by the examples being uttered—that is, even by their mental presentation (*manoniveśa*)—it need not be considered. One who possesses sin (*aghavān*), such as a ritual agent (*karmin*) and so forth, is indeed distinct from *papī*.
It should be explained according to the reasoning already stated. Furthermore, they say that the Name is not exhausted merely by the cessation of sin along with its roots;

rather, that Name also causes one to perceive and experience through love the qualities of the One of Excellent Renown (Uttamaśloka), such as His sovereignty, sweetness, and beauty. Thus it is called "tat" (that).
Alternatively, one might ask: "How can that which is averted by great hardships such as austerities and vows be averted merely by the easy utterance of its name? To this, they say:
"That [very thing]. It is that very [sin] of the Supreme Lord Hari, the one of great fame, through the power of His qualities.
The meaning is that this too is one of the supreme lordships of the Supreme Lord, serving as a proof of it. ||11||
For that [peace] is not absolute; even when atonement has been performed,
if the mind runs again toward the path of evil.
For those who desire the accomplishment of that karma, the recitation of Hari’s qualities is indeed the cultivation of the sattva-nature.

Śrīdhara: It is neither absolute nor an ultimate purifier; therefore, it is considered insufficient. If, even when that has been performed, the mind still runs toward the wrong path, the way of evil, then for those who desire the complete removal—that is, the total destruction—of sinful actions, the recitation of the qualities of Hari alone is the true atonement (prāyaścitta). For He is...
Indeed, the cultivation of sentient beings is the purifier of the mind. ||12||
The sequential arrangement: Not only is the name such, but the qualities are also so; thus they say, "not absolute. This is also a restatement of the qualities. ||12||

Viśvanātha: They say that the penances [prescribed] for twelve-year periods and so forth are inferior to that [practice], stating: "That penance is not definitive nor is it an absolute purifier. If, even when that has been performed, the mind still runs toward the evil path—the way of sin—then from that [penance], one must seek "nirhāra," which is absolute destruction [of the fault].

For those who desire [liberation], the recitation of Hari’s qualities—just as there is a recitation of His names—is the subsequent narration of those qualities; that is, the recounting from someone else's mouth of things previously heard. According to Amara, the word *anu* signifies "subsequent" (*paścāt*) and "similarity" (*sādṛśya*). It is a purifier of the *sattva* quality because it destroys even the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that constitute the nature of *sattva*.

If it is argued: "But how can the repeated commission of sin after performing an expiation be censured, given that it too depends upon latent impressions (*saṃskāra*)? We must explain this as being like a snake whose fangs have been pulled out," then you are mistaken; such an explanation is not ours.

This is solely in accordance with the scriptural statements establishing that the Name destroys sins along with their latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and not something fabricated by one's own imagination. For in your *prāyaścitta* scriptures, such statements do not exist;
indeed, since no transgression (*pratyavāya*) arising from an *arthavāda* is even heard of in the path of ritual action (*karmamārga*), how could it be so for you?
It has already been stated that there is the capacity to explain [it]. ||12||
"Therefore, do not remove him, for he has performed every expiation for his sins,
since he, while dying, O Blessed One, grasped your name."

Śrīdhara: Therefore, do not lead him away by a wrong path. By whom the atonement for all sins has been performed—because he has fully recited [the name]; the sense is that even a single part of the name is sufficient. By the word "mriyamāṇa" (dying), moreover...

It has been stated that there is no possibility of other sins [occurring at that time], but it was not intended that the name must be uttered at that specific time. For at that moment, just as the injunction for performing *kṛcchra* and other penances would be impossible, so too would the injunction for uttering the name be impossible. Furthermore, there is no authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*) that the utterance of a name—which occurs by mere chance like the "crow and the palm fruit" (*kākatālīya*)—is a remover of sin in the absence of an injunction. ||13||
The sequential arrangement: Now, regarding the phrase "Then him..."—for this very reason, even at other times when Ajāmila was uttering the name of Nārāyaṇa as used for his son:
"That name which, when remembered by men, [delivers them] both at the time of death and at any other time."
The flood of sins perishes instantly; salutations to that Self of Consciousness!
Thus, according to the *Padmadevadyuti-stotra*: "Even in the state of old age and death, Your names, formed from Your qualities, dispel all impurities" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 5.3.14);
and by the inclusion of the word "even" (*api*) as stated in the fifth verse, it follows that [the effect occurs] simply through the utterance of the first name.

Even for one whose every sin has been exhausted, the mention of his name at the time of death is heard as nothing but praise; and in that regard, it is repeated: "Then him... Here, the word *aśeṣa* (without remainder) extends to the latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and the word *agha* (evil) extends to transgressions (*aparādha*). In this context of death, even for all [others], there is wretchedness and so forth.
It should be understood that this is the gateway to the supreme grace of the Blessed Lord. The meaning is "even while dying.

Based on the strength of what will be stated in the passage beginning with *sāṃketyam* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.2.14), it is not intended that this [recollection] must necessarily occur only at that specific moment of death. ||13||

Viśvanātha: Now, since this is so, therefore do not lead him away. "By the name by which all duties were performed"—the meaning is that it was by his very first name at the time of the naming ceremony for his son. By this, one understands that Ajāmila was free from the transgressions associated with both ancient and modern names. Since he was indeed sinless because of this...

The sense is: how indeed could the name appear on the tongue of a sinful being while he is dying? As it is said in the *Gītā*, beginning with: "But for those whose sin has come to an end... (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 7.28).
"And at the time of death, whoever departs casting off the body while remembering Me alone, he attains My state; there is no doubt about this" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 8.5).
Therefore, it is precisely at the time of death that the presence or absence of an offense against the Name depends upon the manifestation or non-manifestation of the Name.
They explain [the term] as "in the object of inference" (anumeye). ||13||
Whether it be for the sake of convention, in jest, as a mere exclamation, or even in derision,
they know that the utterance of the name of Vaikuṇṭha removes every single sin.
"Madhvaḥ": This refers to Nārāyaṇa; when spoken of as an object of contempt by others, it removes sin. "The name of Viṣṇu removes all sins when preceded by devotion;
if uttered without devotion, it will not yield any fruit at all."

Since remembrance of Him arises through His being the Master, the chanting of the Name is prescribed for the devotee even in times of emergency and the like. Thus it is said in the *Nāradīya*: "Even Ajāmila was not released from death because of his remembrance [of Nārāyaṇa] with devotion. (14)
Śrīdhara: Now, it may be argued that this person has taken the name "son" and not the name of the Lord; regarding this, they say:

*sāṃketya* is that which is designated by convention, as in the case of a son and so forth; *pārihāsya* is that which is done in jest; *stobha* is that which is done for the purpose of filling out a song or conversation; and *helana* is even that which is done with contempt, such as asking, "What does Viṣṇu have to do with this? and so on.
The utterance of the name Vaikuṇṭha. ||14||

*Sanātanaḥ* (Ha.bha.vi. 11.335): Now, one might object: "Did he not take this as his son's name, rather than the name of the Lord? To this they reply: *Sāṃketyam* is that which is designated by convention, as in the case of a son and so forth; *pārihāsyam* is that which is done in jest; *stobham* is that which is done for the purpose of filling out a song or conversation, and so on; *helanam* [is that which is said] "What... *(Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with "kiṃ".)*
Or even the utterance of the name Vaikuṇṭha with contempt, such as "By Viṣṇu! ||14||

The sequence of the composition: "Pārihāsya" (jest). Here, *parihāsa* refers to speech containing affection that involves the disparagement of another, but not speech containing censure; for the latter is called *upahāsa* (mockery). Therefore, the meaning is that whatever name of the Blessed One is uttered serves as a support for *narma* (affectionate jesting). In this context, *helanam* (disregard) [is intended].

It should be understood that this refers to a lack of effort—as in the expression "the mountain was lifted with ease"—and not to an attitude of contempt; for if it were the latter, there would be no fault even in the case of a flute-player.
Furthermore, regarding the ten offenses concerning the Name, a fault is heard of even when teaching it to those who are faithless and so forth.
However, some maintain that even when an offense is committed, there must indeed be a destruction of past sins. ||14||

Viśvanātha: In response to the inquiry as to what kind of name might be the remover of all sins, they state [the following] by way of a *kaimutya* (argument a fortiori): "Sāṃketyam" means a convention regarding a son or the like; the suffix *ṣyañ* is used in its own sense (*svārthe*). In all instances, the nominative case is used in the sense of the instrumental; thus the meaning is "even by means of conventions and so forth. "Parihāsyam" means... [laughter/ridicule].
It should be imbued with affection (*prītigarbha*) and not with censure (*nindāgarbha*). For example: "O you of renowned fame!
O you named Kṛṣṇa! Having seen your glory, I am unable to lift myself up.
*Stobha* is that which is performed for the purpose of filling out a narrative, song, conversation, and so forth. Here, *helanam* means "the mountain was [tossed] with ease" (*helayā girir*).

By the expression "extracted" (*uddhṛta*), it is simply meant that there is an absence of effort; for instance, even in matters such as eating, walking, or sleeping, however many names of Kṛṣṇa this person utters with utter indifference, others would not be able to utter even that many, even with great exertion.
It does not, however, imply censure or contempt, for if that were the case—

From the passage beginning with "Hearing the censure of the Blessed One," it follows that even for one who censures the Blessed One, or for one who treats with contempt Viṣṇu or even a flute-player (veṇa) and so forth, [the Lord] brings about harm; therefore, [the Name] removes all sins without exception, destroying every evil up to and including its latent impressions (vāsanā). ||14||
Whether fallen, stumbled, broken, bitten, scorched, or struck,
a man who involuntarily utters the name "Hari" does not deserve torments.

Śrīdhara: Now, it might be argued that he did not utter the name "Vaikuṇṭha" preceded by a formal resolve (saṃkalpa), but rather while overcome by affection for his son; to this they reply with the words "fallen. Even one who utters "Hari" involuntarily does not deserve torment. By the word "person" (pumān), it is indicated that there is no restriction here regarding caste, stage of life (varṇāśrama), and so forth.
It has been said. They speak of being "powerless" as follows: fallen from a palace or similar structure; stumbled on the path;

broken with fractured limbs; bitten by snakes and the like; tormented by fever and so forth; struck by a staff or similar object (Haṭhayogapradīpikā 11.336). Now, one might object: "But this [state] is not preceded by volition."

He received the name Vaikuṇṭha; however, being overcome by affection for his son, they said of him there, "He has fallen. Even one who involuntarily utters the name "Hari" does not deserve torment. By the word "person" (pumān), it is stated that here there is no restriction regarding caste, stage of life, and so forth. They describe this very lack of volition: he fell from palaces and other such heights.
Stumbled on the path; broken with shattered limbs; bitten by snakes and the like; tormented by fever and the like; struck by sticks and the like. ||15||

The sequence of the composition: They say that such a state exists not only through convention and so forth, but also through the desire to eliminate the suffering at hand. Regarding the phrase "even involuntarily": as before, the plural form "yātanāḥ" (torments) is used in some instances. ||15||
Viśvanātha: He describes the varieties of helplessness belonging to a fifth type of person, distinct from those mentioned previously such as the *sāṃketika* (conventional) and so forth:
one who has fallen from a palace or similar height; one who has stumbled on the path; one who is broken, meaning with broken vessels;
one who is bitten by snakes and the like; one who is tormented by fever and the like; one who is struck by a staff and the like; [such is] the man.
It should be understood through the reasoning already explained that [the self] is distinct from the agent and the others. ||15||
The great sages, having understood them, have declared the heavy and light penances for heavy and light sins, respectively.

Śrīdhara: Now, it may be argued that for a great sin, a great expiation alone is appropriate, and not a small one such as the mere utterance of the Name; for as there is a gradation of penances like the *kṛcchra* and others according to the degree of the sin, [the author] says two verses regarding this: "For heavy sins, there are heavy expiations, and for light ones, light ones."
Having understood this gradation, the rules were stated by Manu and others; therefore, the established order applies there exactly as described.

However, this rule does not apply to the name of Hari, because of the scriptural statement: "By the mere remembrance of Viṣṇu, one is liberated from all sins. Nor [does it apply] in the case of drinking even a drop of liquor.
Just as there is a traditional teaching regarding its being a great sin (mahāpātaka), it is an excessive burden to claim that this name prescribes the specific expiation for it. ||17||
The sequential arrangement [of the commentary] on the words "of the gurus" is as follows: by means of these three verses alone, the intended meaning is set forth.

Those expiations which have been prescribed certainly purify those very sins; however, the latent impression (durvāsanā) is purified only through following the Lord. Therefore, that which is the name of the One of Excellent Verses (Uttamaśloka), moreover—due to ignorance—[is not understood].
Or rather, the meaning is that once it has been proclaimed by means of knowledge, even the sin of an ordinary person would be consumed entirely, just as fire consumes fuel. ||17||
Viśvanātha: Furthermore, even by those [means] of such a kind, they are purified—that is, destroyed—at the destruction of the person;

however, the heart born of unrighteousness, which is the root and subtle form of sins, is not purified and does not perish. Even that [is destroyed] through service to the feet of the Lord, through devotion to the feet of Hari, and through the nine types of devotion.

In the midst of this, even by means of a single act of glorification related to the context, because it destroys sins up to the very limit of their latent impressions (*vāsanā*), that too is purified. ||17||
By means of austerity, charity, vows, and the like, those sins are purified;
yet that heart born of unrighteousness is not [purified] even by service to the feet of the Lord.

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, by those [acts] such as austerity and charity, those very sins are purified—that is, they perish. However, the heart of that evildoer, which has become stained due to unrighteousness (*adharma*), is not cleansed; or rather, the subtle form of those sins, known as the latent impression (*saṃskāra*), is not purified. Even that [is purified] by service to the feet of the Lord.

The meaning is that one is purified by chanting (*kīrtana*) and so forth. This is the underlying idea: even great sins perish by the mere single utterance of the Name, just as dense darknesses are dispelled by a lamp lit but once.
Through its repetition, however, there is the non-arising of further sin, just as by holding a lamp, no more darkness remains.

And from that, through the exhaustion of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), there is purification of the heart. It is for this very purpose that the performance of recitations is prescribed here and there. Furthermore, the destruction of evil occurs for those who remember Him day and night, as stated in such passages.
That very point is also expressed here: "The praise of His qualities indeed brings about the cultivation of *sattva*. This...

And it is said: "Even by service to the feet of Īśa. Therefore, for this person, the destruction of all sins occurs through the name of Hari alone, whereas the destruction of latent impressions (vāsanā) occurs through such means as the vision of Great Beings (mahāpuruṣa). ||17||

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: Furthermore, by those [means], even such a person is purified—that is, [the heart] is destroyed. The root *puñ* means destruction. The heart, which is the root and subtle form born of unrighteousness (*adharma*), is not purified—that is, it does not perish.

It perishes; even that is purified through service to the feet of the Lord, by means of devotion to the feet of Hari—even by a single form of the nine types of devotion relevant to the present context, namely *kīrtana*—because of the destruction of sins up to their very latent impressions (*vāsanā*). ||17||
Whether through ignorance or through knowledge, the chanting of the name of the One of Supreme Fame burns away a person's sin, just as fire consumes fuel.

Śrīdhara: If it is argued that [the mantra] was not uttered because it was known to be an expiation for sin, they say in response: "Out of ignorance. Just as fire cast into a pile of wood by a child burns it even though he is ignorant, so it is here. (18)

Sanātana (Ha.bha.vi. 11.337): Now, if it is argued that even so, this was not uttered because it was known to be an expiation for sin, they say in response: "Out of ignorance. Whether through knowledge or ignorance of this Śrī Viṣṇu—even if thrown out by a child out of ignorance—it burns the heap of wood, just like fire.
It is the same as that. ||18||

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: If it is argued that this was not uttered because, although it was known to be a penance (*prāyaścitta*), [the author] did not mention it, they say in response: "due to ignorance. Just as fire might be cast [into water] by a child even out of ignorance.
It burns a heap of wood; it is just like that. ||18||
Just as a most potent medicine, when taken by chance even by one who is unaware of its own qualities, produces its effect; so too does a mantra produce its result when it is recited.

Śrīdhara: But how can this [remedy] be an expiation for one who has not been instructed by the assembly and lacks faith? To this they say: "Just as... *Agada* means medicine. Although it should have been said "most powerful" (*vīryavattama*), it is stated as "most potent" (*vīryatama*). This refers to that which is used by chance, being devoid of faith and so forth.

Even if one does not know it, the consumption [of a substance] from the mouth of an assembly would produce health as its own quality; likewise, a mantra consisting of mere names would certainly perform its own function. The meaning is that the power of a thing does not depend upon faith and so forth. Thus it is said in the *Viṣṇudharma*:
"Even when remembered by those with wicked minds, Hari removes sins;
for fire indeed burns even when touched unintentionally.
This is the sequence of composition: "according to the prescription. Here, the word *mantra* refers to the utterance of the name, because it is the essence of the mantra.

Because such power depends upon faith and other factors, whereas this [power] does not depend upon them; it should be understood that the primary application of the word "mantra" occurs precisely here—this is the intended meaning. Alternatively, the entire verse may be taken as providing another illustration for the preceding verse. (19)
Viśvanātha: It is not merely that he burns away sins;
rather, through the proximity of divine love and other qualities, he does more. Therefore, they offer another illustration:
"Just as a medicine (agada) is to be called 'most potent' (vīryatama)," though it should have been said "most powerful" (vīryavattama); this is due to the elision of the possessive suffix *matup*.
The word *vīrya* may end in the suffix *ac* according to the rule for words beginning with *arśas*. "By chance" (*yadṛcchayā*) means unexpectedly, even through ignorance;

the meaning is that the mantra, being of the nature of consciousness (*jāgradrūpa*), performs its function in that very same way. Or rather, this mantra, consisting of name (*nāmātmaka*), must indeed perform its own effect, for the power of a thing [is not dependent on knowledge].
The meaning is that it depends upon knowledge and so forth. ||19||
Śrī Śuka said:
O King, having thus thoroughly determined the Bhāgavata dharma, they...
Having released him from the nooses of Yama, they liberated that brahmin from death.
Śrīdhara: They released—that is, they caused that brāhmaṇa to be liberated. ||20||

The sequence of the composition: "having well-determined" (*suvinirṇīya*). Although the messengers of Yama did not then fully understand that at the time, nevertheless, the meaning is that they made a restatement after having thoroughly determined it within themselves.
In this regard, as in the passage beginning with *atra sāṃketyam* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.2.13), even by the mere appearance of the name once—

By the expression "shaking off all sins without remainder," the destruction of even the residual impressions (*vāsanā*) is indicated. As for the statement that [the removal of faults] occurs through the repetition of devotion in passages such as "repeating the virtues" and so forth, that should be understood respectively with reference to being free from offenses against the Name and to worshipping while possessed of such offenses.
"Even for those who have committed offenses against the Name, the names themselves remove their sin;
for when applied without ceasing, they alone accomplish the goal. Thus, from the *Padma Purāṇa*.
Therefore, although the Name is thus independent in all respects, it is nevertheless employed as an ancillary (*aṅga*) to ritual action and the like for the sake of fulfilling them.

Even that which has been performed as a transgression— namely, the equality of all auspicious rites such as fire-offerings and so forth— is reckoned as a fault within the state of the *pādma* [condition]; therefore, even that [service] must be understood as being solely for the purpose of pacifying such a transgression through service to the feet of the Lord.

If this were indeed the case, why did the attendants not lead him to Vaikuṇṭha immediately upon his death? For it is heard that even those who merely imitate the incarnations, qualities, and activities of the Lord [attain liberation].

"Those who, even involuntarily, utter His names when in distress—having instantly cast off the impurities of many births—they attain the unobstructed Truth. I take refuge in that Unborn One. [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.9.15] Thus it is said.

To this it is replied: indeed, the utterance of the name of the Blessed Lord occurs in two ways—as a mere utterance and as one joined with affection. Among these, by the former alone that name surely causes one to attain His world immediately; and by the latter, it even causes one to attain proximity to Him.
"Indeed, devotion to me leads all beings to immortality;
it is by good fortune that you have had such affection for me, which removes all fear.
Thus it is from his words.
"But,
O friends, although I do not favor living beings even when they worship Me,
I do so for the sake of following their own inclinations"— according to the direction of these words.

He causes [them] to reach [their goal] with delay. As for their affection, it is their continued devotion; their very mode of life and the cause of their subsistence is service to me alone—this is the intention shown by the phrase "for that purpose. This being so, even this Ajāmila, who had merely assumed that name...

Through his connection with his son, he felt affection even for that name; and in that name of his own, the intense pride of the Blessed Lord is also seen, because of the phrase "the mind directed toward him. Since even among the attendants (*pārṣadas*) great reverence for that [name] is observed, therefore—

Knowing that the Lord, through the medium of affectionately addressing him by his own name and directly proclaiming His own glories with longing, desires to take him away by bestowing His supreme personal love, they suddenly took Him along with themselves.
Thus, everything is consistent. [Bhaktisandarbha 152] Viśvanātha: Not commented upon.
Thus addressed, O subduer of enemies, the messengers of Yama went to the presence of Yama and reported everything exactly as it was to King Yama.
Śrīdhara: Having been rebuffed and driven away, they went and reported the matter correctly to Yamarāja. ||21||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: "Pratyuditāḥ" means those who have been rejected by Yamarāja, that is, by the King of Death. ||21||
Released from the noose, the twice-born man became free from fear and returned to his natural state;
filled with the joy of the vision, he bowed his head to the servants of Viṣṇu.
Śrīdhara: He for whom there is a festival through the sight [of the Lord]. ||22||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
Intending to speak of that [work], the servants of the Great Being [say]:
O sinless one, as he was looking on, they suddenly vanished there.
Śrīdhara: Having perceived him as desirous of speaking—that is, wishing to speak—[he addressed him]. ||23||

The sequence of composition: "desiring to speak to him. By that, having increased the longing for conversation with him, Viśvanātha understands that renunciation is indeed for that purpose alone, in order to bring about perfect devotion. "They disappeared": even though there was a remainder of his lifespan, it was [obstructed] by sins alone.
Having understood, according to the scriptures, that the end of his lifespan has arrived, the messengers of Yama began the process of dragging him away;

it is this very moment that is conventionally designated as the "time of death. In reality, however, it should be understood that because his sins have been exhausted, there is no actual breaking of his life-force. ||23||
Then Ajāmila, having heard from the messengers of Yama and Kṛṣṇa the pure Bhāgavata dharma and the Vedic path which rests upon the [three] qualities (guṇas),— o)0(o—
Through hearing the majesty of Lord Hari, he quickly became devoted to the Blessed One;
as he recalled his own misdeeds, a great sense of remorse arose within him.

Śrīdhara: "Having heard" (ākarṇya) should be construed with "the threefold dharma"—that which is propounded by the three Vedas and based on the [three] qualities (guṇas)—and "the Bhāgavata dharma," which is the dharma of the messengers of Yama and the messengers of Kṛṣṇa, composed by the Lord (bhagavat), pure, and free from the qualities (nirguṇa). The phrase "he became possessed of devotion" (bhaktimān āsīt) is to be supplied as a continuation from the subsequent verse. ||24||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: Having heard the dharma of the messengers of Yama and the messengers of Kṛṣṇa—[specifically] the pure, transcendent quality (guṇātīta), Bhāgavata dharma proclaimed by the Lord for the messengers of Kṛṣṇa, and [the dharma] of the messengers of Yama...
The "threefold science" (traivedya) is that which is expounded by the three Vedas; it is the locus of the [three] qualities (guṇa) and is impure. ||2425||
Alas, what supreme misery has come upon me, who have failed to conquer my self! For by me, whose mind was corrupted, the Veda was defiled through procreation with a woman of low caste.

Śrīdhara: He elaborates upon his remorse with four verses beginning with "Aho. By me—who, as a son born of a Śūdra woman—by that very self, the *brahman*, the Brāhmaṇa caste, was "violated," meaning destroyed;
this is the sequence of the composition. He demonstrates the direct worship of Him preceded by intense longing, beginning with "Aho."
By such statements as these, ending with "I shall fix my pure mind upon the Blessed One through the chanting of his glories and so forth," Viśvanātha says:
"By me, through myself, being born as a son to a *vṛṣalī*, Brahman—meaning the status of a Brāhmaṇa—has been violated, that is, destroyed. (26)
"Fie on me, censured by the virtuous for this wicked deed that stains my lineage!
For, abandoning a young, chaste woman, I have gone to an unchaste woman who drinks liquor."
Śrīdhara: "Duṣkṛtam" means the perpetrator of a fault; "kulasya kajjalam" means the stain of the lineage. ||27||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: *Duṣkṛtam* means that which is of the nature of sin, or the perpetrator of a fault. ||27||
"My aged parents are helpless and have no other kin; they are pitiable. Alas! By me, ungrateful as a base man, they have now been abandoned."
Śrīdhara: There is no other kinsman, such as a son or the like, for those two who are suffering ascetics;
[this happened] right now, at that very moment. (28)
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Now, in this birth... ||28||
Thus, I shall clearly fall into a most dreadful hell,
where those who destroy righteousness and are full of lust undergo the torments of Yama."
Śrīdhara: This has not been explained.

Kramasaṃdarbha: "I, being such, shall clearly fall. This is said solely from the perspective of seeing one's own fault, whereas from the perspective of seeing the greatness of the Name, it will be stated otherwise: "of one who is dying. (29)
Viśvanātha: [This has not been explained.
—o)0(o— Is this a dream, or rather is this a wondrous thing seen directly here?
Where have those gone today who, with nooses in hand, dragged me away?
Śrīdhara: Now, with eight verses beginning with "What is this?", he describes the sequence of liberation preceded by inquiry. "Directly" means perceived here by one who is awake. (30)
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o)— Now, where have those four Siddhas of beautiful appearance gone?
Having bound him with nooses, they released him as he was being led down to the underworld.
Śrīdhara: And where have those who liberated me gone? (31)
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Being led toward hell beneath the earth. ||31||
Nevertheless, for me, an unfortunate one, there must be some auspicious omen regarding the sight of the supreme among the wise, by which my soul may find peace.

Śrīdhara: Although I am unfortunate and sinful in this birth, yet in another birth I must surely have been meritorious; thus he says: "by the sight of the best of the wise. This is a locative of cause (*nimitta-saptamī*). For the sake of seeing them, there must have been a great merit in the form of auspiciousness from a previous life, by which—
By means of vision. ||32||
The sequence of the composition: By the words "athāpi" (nevertheless), it is understood that although he possessed devotion to the ancients, it was obscured by some offense. ||32||

Viśvanātha: Regarding the vision of the most excellent of the wise, it must be inferred that the cause is some auspiciousness, which is itself nothing other than the compassion of a certain devotee, for without that, the sowing of the seed of devotion therein would be impossible. This is precisely why his own son was given the name Nārāyaṇa.
He did so. ||32||
Otherwise, how could the tongue of one who is dying impure as the husband of a *vṛṣalī* be fit to utter the name of Vaikuṇṭha in this world?
Śrīdhara: "Otherwise" means without prior merit (*pūrvapuṇya*). Of what nature is the name "Vaikuṇṭha"?
It is called *grahaṇa* because by it the mind is grasped, that is, brought under control.
Kramasandarbha: This has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: [It means] to speak or to act. Alternatively, that by which the name Vaikuṇṭha is grasped or attained is "vaikuṇṭhaprāpaka"; this is the meaning. ||33||
Where am I— a deceitful, sinful wretch, a slayer of Brahmins, and devoid of shame—
and where is this auspicious name of the Blessed One, "Nārāyaṇa"?
Śrīdhara: A slayer of a Brahmin is one who destroys his status as a Brahmin. ||34||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha states: "It has not been explained."—
Therefore, I shall strive in such a way that my mind, senses, and breath are restrained.
So that I may not sink my self again into the blinding darkness.
It has not been explained by anyone whatsoever.
A friend to all beings, peaceful, friendly, compassionate, and self-possessed.
May I release my own self, which has been swallowed by my own illusory power consisting of woman,
by whom I, like a wretched play-deer, have been made to sport.
Śrīdhara: [Not commented upon].
Viśvanātha: Just as the base world is like a plaything for a deer, so too have I, though a superior Brahmin, been made a plaything by her. ||3637||
Abandoning the false-minded notion of "I" and "mine" regarding the body and so forth,
I shall place my pure mind upon the Blessed One through his glorification and other such acts.

Śrīdhara: Being one whose intellect is fixed upon the non-illusory reality, and having thus abandoned the notion of "mine" and "I" regarding the body and so forth, I shall fix my mind [upon that reality]. (38)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: One who possesses the cognition that these objects, such as the body and so forth, are indeed false; and being such a person, having abandoned the notion of "I" and "mine. (38)
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus, having developed a profound sense of renunciation through his momentary association with the saintly, he spoke.
Having abandoned all attachments, he went to Gaṅgādvāra.
Śrīdhara: He by whom every bond, such as affection for sons and so forth, has been relinquished. ||39||

The Structural Arrangement (*kramasaṃdarbha*): Having thus described the fruit of the Name up to the point of association with the saintly, he now states the specific fruit of association with the saintly—beginning with "iti.
One who has become such that renunciation (*nirveda*) has arisen well, preceded by the generation of devotion to the Lord. (39)
Viśvanātha: One whose every bond has been released, having abandoned attachment to wife, sons, and so forth. ||39||
Seated there in that abode of the gods, established in yoga and having withdrawn the collection of his senses, he joined his mind to the Self.
Śrīdhara: One by whom the collection of the senses has been withdrawn. ||40||

The Sequence of Composition: Regarding that which was previously investigated with the words "When there is steadiness of mind" (*sati dhairye manaḥ*) and so forth, by means of the performance of its glorification and other such acts, and by means of a purified mind characterized by a particular flash of realization attained thereby, this [next stage] is again investigated:
even for such a mind, there may not yet be a reach extending as far as the Blessed Lord.
According to the principle stated in *Gītā* 14.27, "For I am the foundation of Brahman," that which is higher than the highest is indeed the state with attributes; therefore,
I shall strive solely for the sake of experiencing Brahman, which is characterized by the manifestation of that very reality as devoid of attributes.

Therefore, that fire shall indeed be extinguished by the Great Compassionate One, the Blessed Lord himself. Having reflected on this, he shows what was done by him in two verses beginning with "sa tasmin" (He, in that...). 40.
Viśvanātha: Yoga means the yoga of devotion (bhaktiyoga) toward the Self, Hari. ||40||
Then, having detached the self from the qualities through self-concentration,
he united it with the Brahman that is the abode of the Blessed One and whose nature is pure experience.

Śrīdhara: Having separated and purified the self from the qualities consisting of the body, senses, and so forth, [one should meditate] upon the abode—the essential nature—of the Blessed One through self-concentration, which is one-pointedness of mind. ||41||

*Caitanyamatamañjuṣā*: From the words "tato guṇebhyaḥ" (from the qualities) onwards; even though Brahman, whose nature is consciousness and experience, exists in the abode of the Lord—in the *śrīvigraha* (divine form) of the Blessed Śrī Kṛṣṇa—the word *dhāma* refers to the house, body, splendor, and power, according to Amara.

"His mind was yoked" means that he assumed a form identical to His own, the form of a personal attendant (*pārṣada*), because it will be stated later: "He immediately assumed his true form, standing by the side of the Blessed One" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.2.43). He did not attain absolute liberation (*kaivalya*). Or rather, O Brahmanical one!

O Parīkṣit! You too, indeed, O dear one, become that very Self which is the abode of the Blessed Lord—that Śrī Kṛṣṇa; the meaning is: become intent upon Him. Or rather, "experience" refers to knowledge, characterized by detachment and so forth at that time, which is the means for devotion to the Blessed Lord.

He joined his own self—his mind—to that quartet of attendants who were identical in form to himself; the singular number is used because they are non-different from one another. Of what nature were they? They were the abode of the Blessed One, possessing the forms of the Lord, bearing conches, discs, and other emblems, being Brahman—the vast and all-pervading. Therefore, he...
He became the form of an attendant, and likewise: "Whatever state of being one remembers when leaving the body at the end, to that very state one goes" (Gītā 8.6), and so forth. ||41||
The sequence of composition: By the phrase "when [He] has ceased," it is established that even after the experience of Brahman, the manifestation of the glory of Śrī Vaikuṇṭha occurs. ||41||

Viśvanātha: Having separated [the mind] from the objects of the senses—that is, having detached it—one should [meditate] upon the abode of the Blessed One, which is the true nature of the Blessed One, through self-concentration, that is, through one-pointedness of mind. ||41||
When his mind was withdrawn from that [vision] and he beheld men before him,
the twice-born one, having recognized those whom he had previously perceived, bowed his head in salutation.

Śrīdhara: He whose intellect was stilled and motionless in that abode of the Blessed One—at that time, he saw [them] "in front," that is, before him. And then, having perceived those very same ones previously apprehended, and having recognized them, he paid homage. ||42||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: In that abode of the Blessed One, one whose intellect is stilled—meaning whose mind is motionless—[sees] those previously known right before him, in front. ||42||
Having cast off his body at the sacred ford of the Gaṅgā immediately after seeing [the Lord],
he instantly assumed his true form in the presence of those standing by the side of the Blessed One.
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha have not commented [on this].
Caitanyamatamañjuṣā: For this very reason, he shows: "He immediately assumed the form of those standing by the side of the Blessed One. "Immediately" means without any interval. ||43||
Through this sequential arrangement, he immediately became liberated while yet living (jīvanmukta). ||43||
Together with the servants of the Great Being, the brahmin ascended a golden celestial chariot through the air and went to where the Lord of Śrī resides.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
Thus, he has caused all phenomena to dissolve.
The husband of a slave woman, fallen due to contemptible deeds and cast down into hell because he had violated his vows,
was immediately liberated while uttering the name of the Blessed One.
Śrīdhara concludes with two verses beginning with "evam": [He is one] by whom all dharmas have been washed away;
he is one whose vow—the restraint regarding one's own wife and so forth—has been destroyed. (45)
The sequential composition: regarding those who commit offenses against the Name, he says with two verses beginning with "He who thus... [45]:
"Even one who is inauspicious and an offender against the Name... [45]
Viśvanātha: Not explained.
—o)0(o— Thereafter, there is nothing that cuts through the bonds of karma.

For those seeking liberation, the mind does not again become attached to ritual actions through the chanting of the names of the Lord whose feet are the source of all holy places; otherwise, it remains defiled by passion and ignorance.

Śrīdhara: There is nothing superior to this for cutting—that is, severing—the bondage of karma which has sin as its root. Superior to what? Superior to the chanting of the name of the One Whose Feet are the Holy Places (tīrthapada). The reason for this is:
"from which," that is, from the chanting of that [name]. Otherwise, there would be no need for other forms of expiation.
That mind which remains turbid and defiled by rajas and tamas does not again become attached to actions. 46.

Sanātana: Thus, it has been shown that [the Lord] is the preventer of ill-conceived undertakings (*duṣprārabdha*). Revealing that very point, he writes with the words beginning "Nothing beyond this" (*nātaḥ param*) and ending with "the man shines forth" (*bhāsate naraḥ*, *Haṭhayogapradīpikā* 11.374). [This is] the cutter—that is, the destroyer—of that which is bound by karma and rooted in sin; beyond this, there is nothing further.
