It does not exist. Why? Because of the glorification of the Blessed One, the Tīrthapada. The reason for this is: "because of the glorification from which [it arises]. From that glorification; otherwise, that mind remains indeed turbid and defiled by *rajas* and *tamas* even after other forms of atonement.

Although the phrase "severing the bonds of karma" refers here to the cutting off of all *prārabdha* karma without exception, nevertheless, since the fall of the body would necessarily follow upon the destruction of the entirety of *prārabdha*,
what is intended is the destruction only of the *duṣprārabdha* (evil or adverse) *prārabdha*. For this very reason:

It is written in the *Nāmaśrutibhāṣya*: "The power to remove even commenced karma (*prārabdha-pāpa*) occurs sometimes by the force of the devotee's will; otherwise, there would arise a contradiction with the cases of Ajāmila and others presented here. Alternatively, it may occur through the destruction of difficult-to-overcome commenced karma by means of the eradication of diseases and so forth, up to the liberation from the jaws of death.
Even when the fall of the body occurs, by the power of chanting the Name,

according to the principle of the constant dissolution (*nityapralaya*), there arises at that very moment another suitable body for the sake of worshiping the Blessed One; or else, [he attains it] through that very same previous body.

It should be inferred that he attained [the state] as if it were new, by virtue of possessing specific qualities suitable for the worship of the Lord as Sadyojāta; just as when Śrī Dhruva was ascending to the supreme abode, he attained his own previous body as if it were distinct, due to its being endowed with the bodily qualities appropriate for an attendant (pārṣada). And bearing that form—
In passages such as "made of gold" (*hiraṇmaya*), this has already been clearly explained by the venerable Śrī Svāmipāda.
Likewise, in the *Bṛhannāradīya*:
The scriptural statement beginning with, "A person who mutters 'Govinda' every day with senses restrained,
being liberated from all sins, shines like a god" (Harivaṃśa 11.374),
is well-consistent with this. And as for that which externally bears the fruits of pleasure and pain...

Even when the *prārabdha* karma has been exhausted, at some point, for someone, some slight external pleasure or pain may still be observed in the body and so forth; and this [is explained] by the Blessed Lord or by the devotee for the purpose of concealing the greatness of devotion in the world.
It should be understood that by that very means, one manifests according to one's capacity for the sake of concealing the self. Thus, everything is faultless. (Haribhaktivilāsa 11.371).
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* has not been commented upon [here].

Viśvanātha: Because the mind itself does not become attached to worldly actions through the chanting [of this name], whereas otherwise it would remain turbid and defiled even by other forms of atonement. ||46||
He who,
endowed with faith, hears this supreme secret history that destroys evil, and he who recites it with devotion.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
Indeed, he does not go to hell, nor is he seen by the servants of Yama.
Even if a mortal is inauspicious, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Śrīdhara: And he is not observed. ||48||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— Dying while uttering the name of Hari, as performed by his son...
Even Ajāmila went to the abode; how much more so one who chants with faith?
Śrīdhara: Even one who is dying, being devoid of control and lacking faith... ||49||
Sanātana: "The abode of Hari. (Ha.bha.vi. 11.436) Kramasandarbha: "From which, while dying... (11.436).

Viśvanātha: Having concluded the section, yet for the sake of ensuring complete understanding, he states the established doctrine regarding the greatness of the Name in a single sentence: "Even while dying" (*mriyamāṇa*).
Because one is in the very act of dying, even if one recites it without faith—how much more so if with faith—even while dying...

How much more so for one who is alive—this applies even to a son; how much more so for Ajāmila himself, even though he was a great sinner; and how much more so for one who is sinless—such is the fourfold determination. ||49||
Thus ends the second chapter, perfectly composed for the virtuous, in the sixth book of the *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted.
Thus ends the Sixth Canto in the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā, the Pāramahaṃsyasaṃhitā, which is the Commentary on the Brahma-sūtras within the glorious Mahāpurāṇa Śrīmad Bhāgavatam.
The second chapter in the narrative of Ajāmila.
Now begins the third chapter in the narrative of Ajāmila.
The illustrious King said: Having heard what was described by his own soldiers,
did the Lord Dharmarāja say anything to them as well?
Thus, this world of people has been brought under the control of Murāri by his messengers, who have struck down the ignorant and destroyed their enemies.
Śrīdhara:
But in the third [chapter], even Yama, having consoled his own messengers by describing the excellence of the Vaiṣṇavas, made those messengers servants to the Vaiṣṇavas.

The third chapter begins in order to confirm, through the mouth of Yama, the meaning of the scriptures as determined by the messengers of Viṣṇu. Regarding what was stated there— "and they reported everything to King Yama" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.2.21)— the author asks what occurred thereafter with the word "niśamya" ("having heard").

Thus thwarted by the messengers and servants of Murāri—indeed, by those very ones whose commands he himself has violated—who is this person under his control that even he speaks out against them? ||1||
The sequence of composition: "the doubt of the world"—the implication is that for himself, however, there was no doubt.
Viśvanātha:
But in the third [birth], those messengers said to Yama, "This is our own humiliation."
And he taught them the wonderful sovereignty of devotion.
Although Yama was censured by his own devotees who were devotees of Kṛṣṇa, he did not become angry; on the contrary, he felt remorse for having failed to instruct them properly.

The third chapter begins in order to confirm, even through the mouth of Yama, the meaning of the scriptures as determined by the messengers of Viṣṇu. Regarding what was stated there— "They reported everything to King Yama" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.2.21)— he asks what happened after that, beginning with the word "niśamya" (having heard) from the perspective of Murāri.
Those who were obstructed by the followers of Hari—who carry out his commands—he himself, having disregarded the command, struck down. ||1||
"O Sage, the breaking of the staff of the god Yama has never before been heard of from any source."
O Sage, you cut through this doubt of the world; for it is my firm conviction that no one other than you can do so.
Śrīdhara says: "This is most wonderful," and thus states: *yamasya* etc. O Sage, the breaking of Yama’s staff had never before been heard of from anyone whatsoever; this refers to that very matter.
Or rather, it was not heard of before; and this [event], namely the repelling of Yama’s messengers, also occurred. Therefore...
A doubt exists for all the world, and it is my firm conviction that no one other than you can sever it; therefore, please explain it—this is the implied request. ||2||
The sequence of composition has not been explained. Viśvanātha says: "From anywhere"—O Sage! never heard before from any source whatsoever; this, this—o)0(o—
Śrī Śuka said:
O King, their efforts thwarted by the servants of the Lord,
the messengers of Yama reported the matter to their master, Yama, the lord of Saṃyamanī.
Śrīdhara: Those whose efforts have been thwarted by the messengers of the Blessed One; "the messengers of Yama" refers to the sequence of the composition. Viśvanātha: This has not been explained.
The messengers of Yama said:
"O Lord, how many instructors are there here in the world of the living who cause the manifestation of the fruits of action performed through the threefold [path]?"

Śrīdhara: "How many are there? is a rhetorical question. *Traividya* means threefold; the suffix *ṣyañ* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*). Alternatively, it refers to one who performs action in such a way as to possess the threefold knowledge. Thus, the question is: how many are the causes for the manifestation of the fruit of that action? ||4||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "We, who bring about the humiliation of all the worlds, even we must endure such humiliation; therefore, today, having caused the punishment of those four four-armed ones, [I shall deal with] him..."

"We shall certainly lead Ajāmila to hell; if we are unable to bring him there, then from now on we shall no longer perform the service of this firefly. Thus they spoke with reproach, their words faltering with inner anger—"How many? refers to the threefold nature [of the messengers], which is itself threefold. ||4||
If there were many teachers in the world wielding the rod of punishment,
to whom would death belong, or to whom would immortality belong? Or perhaps neither?

Śrīdhara: Let there be many; what is the objection to that? To this they say: "If... Death is suffering, and immortality is happiness. In the event of their disagreement, to whom would both belong? To no one at all, because both are mutually obstructed by their opposition. But in the case of unanimity, to whom would they not belong? To everyone.

Could they not both exist? One desires to bring about happiness, while the other desires to bring about suffering. And if there were unanimity between them through mutual approval of each other's actions, then since both would be attained by both, for whom would those two not belong?
This is the meaning. ||5||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha*: not commented upon. Viśvanātha: To the objection that there may be many [such fruits] therein, what is the contradiction? they say: "If...
For the fruit of action is indeed twofold: death and hell, or immortality and heaven; of these two alone...
Among those who wish to establish their own position, for whom would both [the two views] be possible?

Rather, the meaning is that when there is contradiction, even hell [would befall them]. But if, by chance, they were to reach a consensus and there were no contradiction, for whom would both not be possible? Indeed, both of those [views] would belong to everyone, and not just one.
"Because there is no decisive reason [to choose one over the other]"—the sense is that there would simply be a contradiction once again. ||5||
But if there were a plurality of teachers, then for many practitioners here,
the status of being a teacher would be merely figurative, just as it is for those presiding over a mandala.

Śrīdhara: [Objection] "But surely, let there be many teachers for the many ritualists according to their respective systems; if that were the case, this fault would not arise. To this they reply: "If there were a plurality of teachers due to the systematic arrangement of many ritualists, then 'teacherhood' (śāstṛtva) might indeed exist—that is, it would be possible. However, in that case, regarding the one who is the teacher of all..."

The primary status of being a teacher would then exist only as a mere metaphorical designation for a portion of it; just as the primary status of being a teacher belongs only to a universal monarch (cakravartin), while for those ruling over a single region it is merely metaphorical, because they lack absolute sovereignty. ||6||

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: Now, one might object: "Let there be many teachers for the sake of the systematic arrangement of the many ritualists; if that were so, this fault would not arise. To this they reply: "But what [is the point]? (kiṃ tu).

Teacherhood belongs primarily to the Teacher alone; in others, it is merely figurative. Just as teacherhood is primary only for a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), whereas for those who rule over a single region or for mere craftsmen, it is only figurative due to the absence of unimpeded power. (6)
Therefore, you alone are the supreme lord over all beings who possess lords;
you are the ruler, the wielder of the rod of punishment for men, and the discriminator between the auspicious and the inauspicious.
Śrīdhara: Since, for this reason, a plurality of teachers is not tenable, you alone are the Teacher;
thus, because you distinguish between the auspicious and the inauspicious, you are so called. (7)
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— The punishment ordained for you does not exist in the world now.
Your command has been deceived by four marvelous accomplishments.
Śrīdhara: "Vipralambhitā" means deceived; that is to say, transgressed. ||8||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: "Vipralambhitā" means deceived; that is to say, a woman who has been neglected (*khaṇḍitā*). ||8||
Being led by us to the houses of torment at your command,
those [beings] forcibly released that sinner by cutting his bonds."
Śrīdhara says: They state that very point as follows: "being led," etc. (9).
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* has not been explained.

Viśvanātha says: To the question "In what manner?", they reply: "being led. [The meaning is: having brought them here by that means, if you are able to inflict punishment for their offense, only then are you a ruler (*śāstā*).
The sense is that even our fire of suffering is extinguished. ||9||
"We wish to know them, if you consider us worthy;
when 'Nārāyaṇa' was uttered, they came swiftly, saying, 'Do not fear!'"

Śrīdhara: "From you"—that is, from yourself—if you consider it appropriate and beneficial for us. Otherwise, if that [advice] is disregarded through ignorance, there will be misfortune even for you; for their power is unfathomable, since when merely the name "Nārāyaṇa" is uttered, they say, "Do not be afraid."
They have arrived quickly. ||10||
The sequential arrangement: Now, let some activity and so forth be described for the sake of their knowledge; regarding this, they say—"Nārāyaṇa" (verse 10).

Viśvanātha: [Objection] "But they have now gone to the abode of their own Lord; who can bring them here now so that I may punish them? To this, they reply: "Because of your supreme omniscience, we wish to know about them—from whom they are messengers and where they dwell."
The sense is: "We ourselves shall bring them by force. The sense is: "If you consider this to be appropriate and beneficial for us;

otherwise, out of an inability to endure defeat, we shall surely die. If [you say], "Tell us something so that we may know them and their activities," then—oh, alas!—how extraordinary is their audacity!
They said, "It is not so. The sense is that they even spoke thus to the sinner, saying, "Do not fear, do not be afraid! Oh, what injustice! ||10||
Śrī Bādarāyaṇi said:
Thus questioned, that god Yama, the restrainer of living beings, replied.
Remembering the lotus feet of Hari, he spoke joyfully to his own messengers.
Śrīdhara: He is so called because he restrains his subjects. ||11||

The sequence of the composition: "He was pleased. Prior to the determination that Śrī Nārāyaṇa was the Supreme Person (Puruṣa), there had arisen the sorrow of perceiving him as belonging to another. ||11||
Viśvanātha: The meaning is that he was pleased merely by hearing the name "Nārāyaṇa," while remembering it with love. —o)0(o— Yama said:
There is another, distinct from me, who is the support of all that moves and stands; wherein the entire universe is woven like a cloth, warp and woof,
and from whose parts its existence, birth, and destruction proceed.
And he under whose control the world is, like a nose-string.
"Madhvaḥ": woven like a cloth.
As rags and cloths exist as they are, woven lengthwise and crosswise with thread, so this entire universe exists woven lengthwise and crosswise in Viṣṇu; thus it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa. (12)

Śrīdhara: There exists another, the supreme Lord, who is higher than both the moving and the stationary world; I, however, am a servant of that Lord, being the master only of the moving, and even among them only of men, and even there only of sinners. He, on the other hand, is the Lord of all. Who is he? He in whom the entire universe is woven like warp and woof.

Like a cloth formed from threads extending upwards and across; he from whose parts—Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Rudra—the maintenance and other functions of this world arise, and under whose control the world exists, like oxen tied to a nose-rope. 12.
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "O you offenders, why do you prattle? Listen to the truth," he says with the words "para" (the Supreme). From me—who you know to be the teacher of the world—and from those indicated by me...

There is a Supreme Lord who is even higher and more excellent than Indra and the other gods. But I am [the master] only of moving beings, and even among them, only of sinners; and even there, I am merely their servant, whereas He is the Lord of all. Who is He?
He in whom the universe is woven like a cloth upon warp and woof threads—vertically and horizontally—from whose parts [it arises].
To Viṣṇu and Rudra; [the suffix] na is applied as in *nasyota* ("yoked by the nose") and *protabalīvarda* ("yoked by the neck"). ||12||
He who binds people to his own speech by means of names, as one binds cattle to a rope on a tethering post.
To whom these people, bound by the fetters of their names and deeds, offer tribute with trembling.

Śrīdhara explains this in detail: He binds people with bonds upon His own tongue, which is like a rope or a tethering-line, using names such as "Brāhmaṇa" and so forth, just as one binds oxen with ropes. These living beings are bound by name and action, which serve as means for firm bondage, and [they offer] tribute to Him.
They carry; the meaning is that they perform actions under its control. ||13||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: He elaborates on this very point with the words "He who... and so forth. Bound by those very constraints—the names such as Brāhmaṇa and others, and the rituals such as sacrifice and others—which are the characteristics of the Veda and serve as fetters, they are bound within speech.
— I am Mahendra, Nirṛti, Pracetas, Soma, Agni, Īśa, Pavana, and Viriñci.
The Ādityas, the Viśvedevas, the Vasus, as well as the Sādhyas, the hosts of Maruts, and the hosts of Rudras together with the Siddhas.
And others— the creators of the universe, the lords of the immortals,
Bhṛgu and the rest— who, though untouched by passion and darkness,
are yet affected by Māyā and do not know His purposeful activity.
Are those others, even though characterized by a predominance of sattva, different from that?
Śrīdhara: And because his pastimes (*līlā*) are difficult to conceive, he says [the following] with two verses beginning with "I am" (14).

Those by whom *rajas* has not been touched, and who do not know what is intended or what is performed [by Him], are those touched by *māyā*—that is, touched by illusion. Therefore, since even they do not know [Him], how much less so others?
It must be stated. ||15||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: He is not only superior to those like me, but even we—including all those up to Viriñci—though omniscient, do not know when or what he might do.
He said: "I am. "Īhitam" means that which is desired to be done. As it has been said: "O King, no man ever knows His purpose;
for even the wise, though engaged in the desire to know Him, are indeed bewildered" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.9.16).
Although they have not touched rajas or tamas, they have been touched by the māyā consisting of sattva;
therefore, they are characterized by the predominance of sattva.
Indeed, that which those who bear the auspicious do not perceive with their senses, nor with their minds, nor with their breaths, nor with their hearts, nor with their auspicious speech;
The Self, dwelling within the heart, is perceived by the self through the senses, just as forms are perceived beyond them.

Śrīdhara: It has been stated that they do not know [Him] because they are deluded by His *māyā*, and because He is beyond the scope of the senses; thus he says, "Him whom... They do not perceive or see Him with the "cows"—that is, the senses—or with the heart, which is the mind.
This is according to such scriptural passages as, "That which is not expressed by speech," and "That which the mind does not think."

The Self of the selves, that is, of the individual souls (*jīvas*); the Seer; just as the eyes do not know their own forms or shapes because they are the instruments of action, therefore [the Self] is the illuminator of those very forms. The point is that the knower is never an object of the means of knowledge. Such is the Supreme Lord, who exists as none other than myself.
The connection is with what precedes it alone. ||16||

The sequential composition: It reveals that he whom [the Vedas] praise is indeed the form of the Blessed Lord himself, described by the Śrutis as being beyond the reach of speech and other senses; thus, his self-luminosity is manifested, and [those who do not perceive it] do not behold him—that is, they do not take him as their object. ||16||

Viśvanātha: He says "him" (yam) to show that because he is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), we do not know him all the more clearly. They do not perceive—that is, they do not know—him with the "cows," which are the organs of knowledge (*jñānendriya*); with the "mind" (*manas*) through conceptualization (*savikalpatayā*); with the "vital breaths," which are the organs of action (*karmendriya*); and with the "heart" (*hṛd*), which is the intellect (*citta*), through non-conceptualization (*nirvikalpatayā*). [This refers to] the selves, the individual souls (*jīva*).
The one Self alone is the inner ruler of many; just as the eye is the form for various shapes, so He is the illuminator who stands beyond all that is to be illuminated. 16.
Of that self-dependent Hari, the supreme Lord, the master of Māyā, the Great Soul;
Generally, messengers here indeed move about as enchanting, possessing forms, qualities, and natures corresponding to those [of the one they serve].

Śrīdhara: Let it be that there is another Supreme Lord of such a nature; but who are those who, having rebuked us, protected the sinner? He speaks of them with two verses beginning with "tasya" (of him).
Those whose form, qualities, powers, and so forth, as well as their very nature, consist of affection for devotees and the like, are [the ones]. (17)

Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: Now, let there be such another Supreme Lord; we do not seek to know him. But who are those who, having rebuked us, protected us from sin? To this [it is said]:
He said: "Of him. The sense is that while [these things] are generally pleasing to you, they are not pleasing to you [in this context].
(o)0(o)—The elements of Viṣṇu are worshipped by the gods.
The great wonders, whose forms are difficult to perceive,
protect those devoted to Him from others, from me, and from all mortals everywhere.

Śrīdhara: Those whose forms or appearances (*liṅga*) consist of Viṣṇu’s beings (*bhūta*), which are servants (*bhṛtya*) and difficult even to behold; they protect those devoted to Him—the devotees of Viṣṇu—from others, that is, from enemies, from me, and from all sides such as fire and so forth. (18)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "Worshipped by the gods. The sense is: "O fools, you who have failed to worship them are indeed offenders. And [the phrase] "from me" refers to those devoted to Him (Śiva) and the devotees of Viṣṇu.
The sense is: "How wretched they are! ||18||
But neither the sages nor even the gods truly know the Dharma as it was directly proclaimed by the Blessed One.
Not even the principal Siddhas and Asuras are humans; how much less so the Vidyādharas, Cāraṇas, and the like?
Śrīdhara: [Objection: But if they were devotees of Viṣṇu, how could they have taken the side of unrighteousness? To this he says: "Dharma... etc. The sages are Bhṛgu and others. (19)

The *Caitanyamatamañjuṣā* states: "But the Dharma is directly [revealed]," and so forth. The meaning is that the *bhāgavata-dharma* is that which was composed by the Blessed One (*bhagavat*), composed for the sake of the Blessed One, and composed for the purpose of attaining the Blessed One.
The word *vai* signifies certainty. The sages (*ṛṣi*), such as Bhṛgu and others, and the gods (*deva*), such as Indra and others, do not know [it]. (19)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Now, if this is so, then how can they be partial toward unrighteousness? [The answer is:
How could fools like you understand the true nature of dharma? [Only] great scholars...
He says "the dharma" to show that even sages do not know it. ||19||
Svayambhū, Nārada, Śambhu, Kumāra, Kapila, Manu, Prahlāda, Janaka, Bhīṣma, Bali, Vaiyāsaki, and we ourselves.
O warriors, we twelve know this Bhāgavata Dharma, which is secret, pure, and difficult to understand; by knowing which, one attains immortality.

Śrīdhara: [Objection: "If some do not know him, what is the proof for his existence? To this he says, "Self-existent" (*svayambhū*). "Kumāra" refers to Sanatkumāra. By saying "we," he points to himself, esteeming his own personage highly. ||2021||
*The Casket of the Mind of Consciousness*: If, then, no one knows [it], what is the proof for its existence?

To this he says with two verses beginning with "Self-born" (*svayambhū*). As the Blessed Lord himself said: "In the beginning, I taught this Dharma, whose essence is I, to Brahmā" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 11.14.33).

The Self-Existent One (Svayambhū) knows it as it truly is because he taught it; Nārada also knows it by having heard it from his own mouth; Śambhu [knows it] because he is non-different from the Blessed One; Kumāra [knows it] because of his direct vision; Kapila [knows it] because he is an incarnation of him; and Manu [knows it] because he was instructed by Brahmā according to the truth. So too Prahlāda.

Janaka, because of his supreme devotion (*paramabhāgavatatva*); Bhīṣma, because through association with devotees he prayed for love for the Blessed One at the time of his departure from life; Bali, because of the touch of the lotus feet [of Vāmana]; Vyāsa’s son (Śuka), because of the instruction in the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavata*; and I myself, for this same reason.

"We"—we know this because of the perception [of them] here; for although Bhīṣma and the others are not ancient, nevertheless there is a designation and enumeration of them as if they were past. "Kumāra" refers to Sanatkumāra alone, and not to the class of Kumāras. For Sanatkumāra is...

"By devotion to the playful beauty of the petals of whose lotus feet..."—thus he instructed Pṛthu. By this, the implication is that even Vyāsa, the author of the Purāṇas and other works, does not know [this].
Through the instruction of Nārada, at the time of composing the Bhāgavata, he knows the greatness of the yoga of devotion to the Lord.

The meaning is as follows: it is difficult to understand and hard to discern for those who follow contrary paths. "Having known" means merely by knowing; the sense is: "What need is there to mention practicing it?"—for by knowing it, one attains the nectar (*amṛta*), which is the wine of the lotus-feet of the Blessed One. ||2021||

The sequence of the composition: the meaning is that we indeed know [this], yet we do not state it explicitly in our own traditional works (*smṛti*) and so forth. The reason for this is that it is secret (*guhya*), meaning it must be concealed in order to preserve worldly conventions (*lokamaryādā*). Furthermore, it is difficult for ordinary people to understand. The reason for its being difficult to understand is that it is pure (*viśuddha*); for those who are impure [cannot grasp it].
The specific reason for its secrecy is that [only] the Arhats are worthy to know it in its pure form. Regarding the word "yam" (it): O soldiers!
Therefore, the meaning is that you do not understand it at all. ||21||
Viśvanātha: [Objection: But if some do not know [it], then what is the proof for its existence?

To this he says: "Self-existent" (*svayambhū*). The meaning is that we shall explain it clearly even in our own composed Smṛti-śāstras, rather than leaving it merely to be known [by intuition]. The reasons for this are: it is secret because it is the supreme reality (*paramatattva*).

It is to be established merely from the standpoint of conventional reality, because the very reason for this is seen in the *Rājavidyārājaguhyādhyāya*: "Hear from Me once more that which is the most secret of all secrets"; furthermore, because the pure [Self], which transcends qualities (*guṇātīta*), is unfit to be described in scriptures concerning the recollection of [the Lord] with qualities (*saguṇa-smṛti-śāstra*), it is difficult to be understood by those engaged in ritual action (*karmibhiḥ*).
Because it is difficult to understand for those whose inner faculties are clouded by defects such as mere explanatory passages (arthavāda). ||2021||
In this world, this alone is recorded as the supreme duty for men:
the yoga of devotion toward the Blessed One through such means as chanting His names.
Śrīdhara says: He states that very same dharma [in the verse] beginning with "etāvān" (so much). ||22||

*Sanātana* (Ha.bha.vi. 11.559): By the phrase "through the utterance of the name and so forth of that Blessed One," it is intended that the primary importance lies in the utterance of the name. ||22||

The Caitanya-matamañjūṣā states that the Bhāgavata-dharma alone is the supreme dharma, saying: "This much alone," and so forth. It is recorded as the supreme dharma for men. What is it? It is the yoga of devotion (bhakti-yoga) toward the Blessed Lord.
Of what nature is it? To this he says: "By means of chanting His names and so forth. (22)

The sequence of composition: "in this world" means here in this universe. The instrumental case in the phrase "by means of mentioning his name and so forth" is used in the sense of the instrument, as in the expression "a handsome man by nature. ||22||
Viśvanātha says: "In that case, protect us, your servants, by teaching us that very dharma.

The sense is that although there is a great multiplicity of divisions, in reality it is only this much. The word *para* (the Supreme) is used as a qualifier for the subject being discussed. [The phrase] "by means of grasping His name and so forth" refers to that.

Yoga characterized by the dedication of action (*karmārpaṇa*), which possesses attributes, has been excluded. This alone is the essential subject matter of the *Śrīmad Bhāgavata*. As it was stated at the very beginning of the scripture: "In this [work], the supreme dharma is that which is free from hypocrisy" (BhP 1.1.2); for that indeed is the highest [dharma] for men.
"Dharma" [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.2.6]. ||22||
O sons, behold the greatness of chanting the name of Hari,
by which even Ajāmila was liberated from the noose of death!
Śrīdhara says: "And no proof needs to be stated here because it is observed," thus he says: "By the utterance of the name.
That by which alone, when uttered even once— ||23||

The Caitanyamatamañjuṣā demonstrates the greatness of uttering the Name through two verses beginning with "The greatness of uttering the Name": he attained liberation, which is the salvation consisting of becoming identical in form with the attendants (pārṣada-sārūpya). ||23||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Nor is any external authority to be sought here, because it is directly perceived;
thus he says: "By name" (nāma) ||23||
This much alone is sufficient for the removal of the sins of men:
the chanting of the qualities, deeds, and names of the Blessed One.
Even the sinful Ajāmila, while dying, attained liberation after crying out to his son, "Nārāyaṇa!"
Śrīdhara: But how can there be the destruction of all sins through a mere semblance of the name?

For it is also prescribed that one must practice with faith, devotion, and repetition. Indeed, as it is said: "Chanting with devotion morning and evening, one is liberated from the multitude of sufferings" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.3.29). This [is to be done] every day.
"Listening with reverence" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 4.23.39);
"Hearing, chanting, and meditating upon Hari of wondrous deeds, as well as His births, activities, and qualities, and performing every action for His sake" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.3.27).
Such passages are recited here and there in this very Purāṇa, and in another Purāṇa it is said:
"And the destruction of sins occurs for those who remember Him day and night. And in this very [text]:
"Therefore, the chanting of Viṣṇu's names is an auspiciousness for the world and a destroyer of sins."

"O Kauravya, know that even for the great, there is complete atonement through right chanting alone" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.3.31). By such statements, one is liberated through chanting alone. Furthermore, if that were the case, why would Manu and others prescribe penances lasting twelve years and so forth? Therefore...

This seems untenable; therefore, he says "not merely by this much. That which is called the "perfect glorification of the names, deeds, and qualities of the Blessed One" is not sufficient—that is, it is not adequate—for the removal of men's sins or for the mere destruction of evil. Here, the word *alam* is used in the sense of prohibition.
As Amarasimha says: "The word *alam* expresses ornament, sufficiency, capability, and prohibition.

[The text] speaks precisely of the absence of utility. Ajāmila, though a great sinner, cried out "Nārāyaṇa," but he did not chant [the name] correctly; and he cried it out for his son, not for Hari. He was burdened by sin and impure.
Even while dying and with a mind in an unstable state, he attained liberation, and not merely the removal of sins.
Therefore, the reality is simply this: even by the mere appearance of the Name, there is the destruction of all evils.
It has already been stated that the injunctions regarding repetition, faith, and so forth, are for the purpose of destroying the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of sin, [according to] Hari.
Indeed, the recitation of virtues is the cultivation of the thought of enlightenment; thus it is said here. ||24||
*Sanātanaḥ* (Ha.bha.vi. 11.427): [This refers] to the qualities, actions, and names of the Blessed One;

or rather, it means that the proper chanting of the many diverse names associated with His qualities and actions serves for men merely to remove evil—that is, to destroy sin. By this much being stated...

There is no need [for further elaboration]. Why? Because even Ajāmila, though a great sinner, merely cried out "Nārāyaṇa," but did not properly chant the specific name distinguished by the sweetness of the qualities and deeds associated with the Avatāra. Furthermore, he called out to his son, and not to Hari.

"Sinful" means impure, or even one who has not performed atonement; "dying" means even with a distressed mind, he attained liberation, and not merely the removal of sin. Since Ajāmila’s body was still present at that time, his state as one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) is established. Therefore, by the mere semblance of the Name, in whatever way it may be...
If even liberation may occur through its mere birth, what need is there to mention the destruction of sins? This is the intended meaning. ||24||
Regarding the phrase "etāvatā" (by this much), the commentary on the passage "for the sake of exhausting sinful tendencies" (*pāpavāsanākṣayārthā*) explains that its meaning is:

"nevertheless, for the sake of exhausting those sinful tendencies which persist by taking recourse to great offenses and the like. However, at the time of death, [this occurs] only for one who is indeed free from offense, in his very presence.

The intention is that there would be the manifestation of the Name. This very point has been explained in the second [chapter], at the verse "This much [is attained] through Sāṃkhya and Yoga" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 2.1.6). But in the end, it is the supreme gain. Thus it has been said:
The living being who, at the time of death, abandons life while uttering "Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa,
Kṛṣṇa," for that person the first word leads to liberation.
"The other two remain standing, bent with shame, veiled.
Thus, [the phrase] "he shall attain liberation" is said with reference to *jīvanmukti* (liberation while living). ||24||

Viśvanātha: But how can there be the destruction of all sins by the mere utterance of the name once? [The answer is: By the recollection of that name and so forth; for you yourself have included the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), implying that it occurs through the yoga of devotion consisting of the ancillaries such as chanting and hearing, which is the supreme dharma.
Since it has been stated that liberation is attained preceded by the destruction of all sins, he says: "By this much.

The mere proper glorification of the qualities, deeds, and names of the Blessed One is not sufficient—that is, it does not serve as the means—for the removal of evil or the mere destruction of sin for men. The word *alam* here [indicates insufficiency].

The meaning is that even by the incorrect recitation of any one of the names beginning with "Nāma," the accomplishment of the removal of obstacles is achieved; for it was done by crying out, and not by reciting correctly. And that was by crying out to the son by the name "Nārāyaṇa," and not to Hari.

Though he was sinful and impure— and not merely pure, nor one who had committed only minor sins— Ajāmila, though a world-renowned perpetrator of great crimes— and not some other sinner— attained liberation (mukti), and not merely the removal of his sins, even while dying and helpless under the pain of death— and not with a healthy mind. Therefore:
"By means of taking His name and so forth" refers to:
"Hearing, chanting, and meditating upon Hari of wondrous deeds, as well as His births, activities, and qualities; and every action performed for His sake. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.3.27)

Therefore, regarding injunctions such as "the chanting of Viṣṇu" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.3.31) and "listening to this daily with reverence" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 4.23.39), which prescribe various limbs of devotion—
including faith, the proper mode of practice, and correctness— these apply to those who are free from offenses.
It is for the sake of increasing love, and for those who have committed offenses against the Name, it is also for the sake of exhausting those offenses.
Having begun with the words, "Faith in my nectar-like story... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.19.20), it continues:
"Thus, O Uddhava, through these duties, men who know the Self..."
"Devotion arises toward Me; what other goal remains for him? (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.19.24).

Here, by the word "devotion" (*bhakti*), love alone is meant, because liberation is excluded by the phrase "what other [goal remains]?"—for even those who have committed offenses against the Name, the Names themselves take away their sin.

"Those very [practices], when performed without rest, are indeed productive of the goal. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and there is the destruction of evil, as one remembers [the Lord] day and night," one should explain that by virtue of the word "and" (ca), there is also the destruction of offenses against the Name, as well as loving devotion (*premabhakti*). Thus, "evil" refers to its latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
The destruction of ignorance, which is the root of that [bondage], and even the mere semblance of a name such as *sāyujya* or *sālokya*, is seen to be the fruit of this very narrative alone. ||24||
Generally, this world knows it not; alas, the minds of these great people have been utterly deluded by the illusory power of the Goddess.
His mind dulled by the three Vedas which blossom with honey,
he was engaged in the great sacrificial ritual.
Śrīdhara: As for what was said—that the traditional recollection of [the duration of impurity] as twelve years and so forth would then be useless—the response is:
"mostly" (*prāyeṇa*). "Great people" (*mahājana*) refers to Manu and others. This is the point:
just as physicians who do not know the life-restoring elixir (*amṛtasañjīvanauṣadhi*) [cannot cure disease].
They remember the *trikaṭuka*, *nimba*, and so forth; likewise,
this great multitude, apart from the twelve beginning with Svayambhū and Śambhu, remembers the twelve-year period and so on without knowing this supreme secret.

Furthermore, this person, whose mind has been utterly deluded by the goddess Māyā— whose intellect is rendered dull and attached to the three Vedas, which are as captivating as a flowering tree with their flowery exhortations (arthavādas) that are like blossoms, just as honey is sweet— therefore, with faith, engages in great ritual action.

One who is engaged in practice does not apply himself to what is insignificant; for it is observed that ordinary people have faith in great things such as mantras, but lack faith in what is insignificant. Therefore, they did not say that there is no one to grasp this [teaching].

Alternatively, just as people do not employ a lion— which is under their own control— to ward off dogs, jackals, and the like, so too, because sin is utterly trivial, they do not remember the name of Hari, the supreme auspiciousness, for its removal.
Alternatively, because the consequence would be universal liberation if one were to know the greatness of the Name—this is the general direction;
however, for fear of excessive prolixity in the text, it is not elaborated further. ||25||

*The Jewel Casket of the Caitanya Doctrine*: [Objection: "But, O Lord, since the chanting of the Lord's names and other such practices exist, why indeed have penances such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* been prescribed by the great men?
[Reply: He says "no," beginning with the words "generally, the Veda...
The "great men" (*mahājana*) are Vyāsa, Yājñavalkya, and others. They are distinct from the twelve [starting] with Svayambhū.

He knows [the truth] only partially, or not at all, or according to his own whim. Why? To this he says: "He is especially deluded by divine Māyā. He states the indicative mark: "His intellect is rendered dull regarding the three Vedas," because he is joined by that very [Māyā], and not [truly] united [with the Supreme]. ||25||
The sequential arrangement: "The great person" refers to the twelve [sages] and others such as Munya; he is characterized by such traits as having his mind deluded by the Goddess. ||25||

Viśvanātha: Now, if this is so, why do learned men generally fail to teach and practice the worship of the Lord through the chanting of His names and other such means—which are the most excellent of all dharmas, the means to liberation, and exceedingly easy—yet instead teach and perform only *karmayoga*? To this he replies with the word "generally" (*prāyeṇa*). [The great person (*mahājana*)...]
Jaimini and others did not know this.

But one might ask: since he is the author of the Śāstra, how could he not have known it? To this he replies: by the Goddess, who possesses supreme sovereignty (*paramaiśvarya*). The implication is that there is indeed no power whatsoever in deluding one who is ignorant; therefore, she would delude one who is already learned all the more.

For this very reason, his mind was rendered dull— deprived of discernment due to excessive attachment— by the three Vedas, which are like a flowering tree from which the flowers of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) have blossomed so as to be sweet like honey. Consequently, he remained devoted to the sacrificial ritual (*vaitānika*), which abounds in the elaboration of materials, procedures, mantras, and so forth.

The meaning is that one who is engaged in great ritual acts such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices— which involve much exertion— for the sake of worldly status and the like, does not take delight in activities involving little effort, such as the chanting of names (*nāmakīrtana*). ||25||
Having reflected thus, the wise indeed establish the yoga of devotion with their whole being toward the infinite Blessed One.
They do not deserve punishment from me; moreover, even if they were to commit a sin, the chanting of the names of the Wide-Striding One destroys it.

Śrīdhara: [He speaks of] the yoga of devotion (*bhāvayoga*), which is the yoga of devotion (*bhaktiyoga*). For these people, sin shall certainly not exist. Even if it should exist, there is the speech—namely, the chanting—of the Wide-strider (*urugāya*). ||26||
The sequential arrangement: Thus, the manner of the greatness of devotion to the Lord as previously described [is shown].
By the words "with one's whole being," the abandonment of obligatory and occasional duties is stated. Likewise, they do not deserve punishment.
In that regard, if by some chance there should be sin due to the performance of forbidden acts, even that [is dealt with] in whatever way possible.
The meaning is that the mere mention of it destroys [evil]. ||26||
Viśvanātha:
Nevertheless, O Lord, it is only one who is graced by even a small fraction of the favor of Your two lotus feet [who can do so].

"O Blessed One, no one else knows the reality of Your majesty, even if they were to search for it for a long time"— from this statement by Brahmā, it follows that even those who know the scriptures may remain ignorant of the true nature of the Blessed One.

He says "thus" (evam) to show that even those who have not studied the scriptures, being favored by the Blessed One and possessing pure intellects, become discerning and indeed worship the Blessed One— not with only a portion of their mind for the sake of performing obligatory and occasional rites, but with their whole self, that is, with their entire mind.

The meaning is "having abandoned. "Daṇḍa" refers to the demerit produced by the non-performance of obligatory duties (*nityakarman*). If, by chance, there should be a transgression (*pātaka*) characterized by the performance of forbidden acts, [one should abandon] "vāda," which means reputation. ||26||
Those holy ones who are praised in pure verses by gods and siddhas, who possess an even vision, and have taken refuge in the Blessed One;
Do not approach them, for they are protected by Hari’s mace;
neither we nor our strength have the power to punish them.

Śrīdhara: Having thus determined the true nature of dharma, he instructs his servants with the words "Those [who... and so on. Those who have taken refuge in the Blessed One are such that their pure songs are sung by the gods and siddhas, and their pure stories are described by them; therefore, do not approach them—do not even go near them.
Even the passage of time has no power over him. ||27||
*Sanātana* (*Ha.bha.vi.* 10.218): Thus,

since the majesty of the Lord’s devotees shines forth in every chapter of the *Śrīmad Bhāgavatam*— which is the essence of all scriptures and the embodiment of the fruit of the entire Veda— I have now written [this] according to the sequence of its chapters.

As before, although there is no direct [statement] regarding their greatness, because certain statements ultimately culminate specifically in their greatness by way of their intended meaning (*tātparya*), he writes them down separately, beginning with "Those gods... and ending with "...salutations again and again. Those who have taken refuge in the Blessed One, having resorted to him in whatever manner possible; therefore...

Thus, these virtuous ones are of good character and possess equal vision; their pure songs are celebrated by the gods, the Siddhas, and the illustrious Sanaka and others, and their pure stories are extolled. Therefore, do not attend upon them—do not even approach their vicinity—and abandon even those who live as their neighbors; this is the meaning. Why?

And [they are] protected on all sides by the mace Kaumodakī; the sense is that, having come into their presence, you shall slay them with that [mace]. Even if some sin were somehow committed against them, no one would be able to do anything [to you], because by the very fact of having taken refuge in the Blessed One, the destruction of all sins is accomplished.
He said: "Not for these. The plural number [in "we"] is used in reference to one's own servants and so forth. Even time, which is the age, has no power when it is subject to a controller. ||27||
The sequential composition: He instructs them by first restating their greatness—“those gods,” etc. “They do not approach”: the sense is that even if one should fall near them, it is still so. ||27||
Viśvanātha says: Therefore, whatever has been done up until this day has indeed been done;

she was protected by destiny alone. But henceforth, listen to what I instruct—thus he says, "ta" (those). "Gāthās" means stories; "samadṛśaḥ" refers to one's own and others' happiness, suffering, and so forth.
"Seeing you all protected by the mace, I believe that this single transgression of yours today has been forgiven by the messengers of Viṣṇu. However, if you go near the devotees again,
then you shall be ground to dust by the very mace of Hari held in their hands."

This is the state of affairs: you are indeed wretched; as for us—even Brahmā and the others together with me—we are but the time of our own youth, and even though we are the restrainer of Brahmā and the rest, [we are subject to it]. ||27||
Bring those who are turned away from the nectar of the lotus feet of Mukunda, which they have abandoned forever.
From this home, which is frequented by unattached paramahaṃsas who possess nothing, [I depart] toward that path of hell in which you have bound your thirst.
Śrīdhara: Who, then, should be brought for the purpose of punishment? To this he says with two verses, beginning with "tān" (them).

"Asataḥ" means the wicked. He specifies who they are: those who are averse to the nectar-like essence (*rasa*) in the form of the honey of Mukunda’s lotus feet. Of what nature is that [essence]? It is that which is constantly enjoyed by those possessing nothing (*niṣkiñcana*). Of them...

He states the proof: "The Eternal One [binds] those by whom thirst has been bound to the path of hell, to a home devoid of their own dharma" (Ha.bha.vi. 10.308). He describes those very same wicked, non-existent ones:
"From that essence which is the nectar in the form of the honey of Mukunda’s lotus feet, characterized by devotion..."

"Averse. To what state? "Constantly enjoyed" (juṣṭān), meaning served, by those who know the essence—those who understand the bliss of devotion or those who discern aesthetic flavor (rasa)—namely, by families of Paramahaṃsas; and for that very reason, by those who possess nothing, who are free from pride, or who are indifferent. Alternatively, the connection is: "constantly averse" (ajasraṃ vimukhān).
The meaning is: "those who do not turn their faces toward such a great flavor (mahārasa) even for a single moment.

He states the indicator of the wicked: "Bring here those who have bound their thirst to the path of hell, to a home devoid of one's own duty (svadharma), or to unrighteous enjoyments and the like, for the sake of punishment."
Thus, their finality has been stated. ||28||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: "In that case, what kind of people shall we approach? To this he says: "Those who are *asat*, i.e., wicked.
He states the characteristic of the wicked: [those who are deprived] of the nectar-essence of the lotus-feet of Mukunda.

"Those who are averse to the yoga of devotion (bhaktiyoga), which is the means for attaining that [state]"—the meaning is: those who do not practice such yoga of devotion. Now, one might object: "Since they are averse to it, surely that nectar-like essence (makarandarasah) should not be desired by them. Therefore, he qualifies the nectar-like essence as "by those who possess nothing" (niṣkiñcanaiḥ).

From that which is frequented and served by those solely devoted to bhakti and by the families of paramahaṃsas whose primary quality is devotion; therefore, from [that place], [he rescued] those who were bound by thirst for the home, which lies on the path to hell and leads to rebirth in the underworld.
The tongue does not utter the names and qualities of the Blessed One,
the mind does not remember His lotus feet,
and the head does not bow even once to Kṛṣṇa.
Bring them here—those who are non-existent and have failed to perform their duties toward Viṣṇu.

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the verse beginning with "jihvā" (the tongue), the grammatical construction is "yad yeṣāṃ jihvā" and so forth. By whom the "Viṣṇukṛtya"—the vow of the Blessed One—has not been performed. ||29||

*Sanātana* (Ha.bha.vi. 10.309): Furthermore, the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) begins with "those whose tongues... and so forth. Those by whom the *viṣṇukṛtya*—the service to Viṣṇu consisting of the Lord’s vows, such as the fast on Ekādaśī, the observances of Kārttika, and so on—has not been performed;
these are connected to the two preceding sentences by the word "even" (*api*). This is also the function of the particle *api*.
This applies everywhere. Therefore, the meaning is this: he does not even utter the name "Compassionate to the Wretched" (*dīnavatsala*) or any other name based on his qualities;
rather, he utters the name in whatever way possible, and that even for reasons such as fear or distress, but not preceded by a reflection on its meaning or with faith.

The meaning is that one properly utters the name of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Likewise, "even with the mind" and "even His lotus feet" means that somehow or other there is a touching of the limb by the mind alone, but not of the entire body; or else, it refers to the proper sounding [of praise] for the glorious lotus feet. Thus:

"Even the head for Kṛṣṇa" means that salutation consists merely in bowing with the heads, and that is directed toward Kṛṣṇa by observing anyone at all, rather than [saluting] the venerable form (śrīmūrti) and so forth directly with all one's limbs. Thus, even in some way, those who are devoid of a connection to devotion for Śrī Kṛṣṇa...

"Bring those very ones!"—it is for this reason that words such as "tongue" and so forth are employed; otherwise, since the functions of speaking and so on would belong to the tongue and other organs themselves, the further employment of those specific words would result in redundancy. This is the general direction of the argument. ||29||
The Sequence of Events: Let alone talk of those whose tongues do not speak;

for even one whose tongue does not, at any time during their entire life, ever speak of the qualities or the name of the Blessed Lord—how could such a person, lacking a tongue, ever [attain] His lotus feet with their mind?

One does not remember [the Lord], for when the mind is distracted, one does not bow the head toward the dark [Lord] while fixing the gaze upon the dark [object]. Even for one who performs a prostration to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow out of deceit, [the merit is lost].
The sin accumulated over a hundred lifetimes perishes at that very moment.

"Bring those who do not offer salutation to the greatness proclaimed in the Skanda Purāṇa. The reason for this is "the non-existent" (asataḥ). The reason for their non-existence is "those who have not performed the rites for Viṣṇu. And as it is stated in the Revākhaṇḍa of the Skanda Purāṇa, in the speech of Śrī Brahmā:
O Keśava, he who is devoted to you is the performer of all righteous deeds;
O Acyuta, he who is not devoted to you is the perpetrator of all sins.

O Hari, even a meritorious deed committed by those who are not devoted to you becomes sinful; O Hari, even one who has performed every possible dharma remains eternally in hell if he is devoid of devotion to you,
whereas even a slayer of a Brahmin is liberated if he is your devotee.
In the Śrī Padma Purāṇa:
"Even a sin committed for my sake results in well-being;
yet even dharma, if practiced while disregarding me, becomes sin through my power."
And that is appropriate, as shown by such passages as "Hearing and chanting about Him" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.11.10),

"From His mouth, arms, thighs, and feet" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.5.2), and "For all of them, worship of Me alone" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.18.43); thus, all injunctions and prohibitions would apply [as stated in the Padma Purāṇa].

And because [the text], beginning with "In the *Bṛhatsahasranāmastotra*," establishes such qualities as supreme eternity, it is stated in general that those who lack these three easily performed acts—recitation and so forth—will certainly lack all others; thus, they are devoid of the duties pertaining to Viṣṇu. [This applies to] the tongue and the other [senses].
Even though they function as instruments, they are designated as agents; thus, by the will of the Person, they somehow undertake activities such as chanting.

The specific designation of "the lotus-feet" (*caraṇāravinda*) serves only to manifest his auspiciousness and devotion, and does not restrict the recollection to those parts alone. In this regard, for those who are not devotees...
By means of bringing [the devotees], their non-bringing is indeed enjoined, because bringing is established as the general rule;
for the Śruti says, "The son of Vivasvat is the restrainer of creatures. ||29||

Viśvanātha: Furthermore, since even a single instance of chanting or remembering Mukunda becomes a means for attaining Him, those who possess such [devotion] are also designated by the word "good" (sat).
Therefore, should they not be brought here out of fear of that? To this he says: "The tongue," etc., and "In the absence of the tongue, the mind," and so forth.
Regarding the state of mental distraction, the phrase "to the dark ones" (*kṛṣṇāya*) and so forth is used. The term "even once" (*ekadāpi*) applies to every instance.

Those who have not performed any service to Viṣṇu—meaning they have failed to perform even the slightest act for Viṣṇu—are, for that very reason, "unreal" (*asataḥ*), that is, non-devotees of Viṣṇu (*avaiṣṇavān*). In this context, [it refers to] within a lifetime or within a year.
Or "during the day," as they explain according to their own respective views. ||29||
May that Blessed One, the ancient Puruṣa Nārāyaṇa, forgive whatever improper act has been committed by us through his own agents.
Oh, how great is the forbearance of my own people, who, though wise, have joined their palms in reverence; salutations to the Infinite Puruṣa!

Śrīdhara says: He asks the Blessed One for forgiveness with the words "tat" (that). The meaning is this: since that which was improper (*asad*) was done by our own men—that is, by those who stand as our own people (*svapuruṣaiḥ*), being our very own—therefore, let it be forgiven and endured by You Yourself. [This refers to] Your own, Your devotees.

"Of us"—that is, of us who are ignorant and lack knowledge. Oh! Toward that most venerable one, forbearance is indeed appropriate. In the reading *mahaḥ*, the meaning is: "May he grant forgiveness to us, who are unaware of our own greatness. (30)
The sequence of the composition: "Whatever has been done improperly by us through our own servants acting as intermediaries"—Viśvanātha [comments]:

reflecting upon his own guilt according to the maxim that "the master is punished for the offense of the servant," he bows down with humility: "Therefore, may He forgive us; [whatever was done] very well... by our own servants.

"By non-men" means by wicked men. "Something improper was done"—by what kind of people? By their own servants. "Alas! expresses astonishment. And yet, even that [was done] not by the wise; rather, it was done precisely because they were ignorant, even as they stood with palms joined in reverence.

Is it not the case that those who are truly unable to punish are the ones who practice forbearance? To this he replies: "Forbearance is more weighty"—even toward one who is most great, forbearance alone is appropriate. [This applies] to those who do not recognize the "glory" (mahaḥ)—that is, the majesty—of their own [servants], according to the reading "svānāṃ mahaḥ," which refers to the messengers of Viṣṇu. ||30||
Therefore, O Kauravya, know that the chanting of Viṣṇu’s names is an auspiciousness for the world and the certain atonement even for the great sins of men.
Śrīdhara: "Therefore," and so forth, is the speech of Śuka. Even for the world, [He] is of the nature of auspiciousness. ||31||

The sequence of the composition: "Therefore," and so forth, is the speech of Śrī Śuka. Therefore, the congregational chanting (saṃkīrtana) [is the destroyer] of all great sins of the worlds—whether committed by those with offenses or those without offenses—even including the most grievous transgressions. ||31||

Viśvanātha: If, by the authority of the words of Viṣṇu’s messengers and of Yama, even the mere mention of anything [His name] results in the destruction of all sins, then what need is there to speak of its proper chanting? Thus he says, "Therefore," which is the statement of Śrī Śuka. ||31||
For those who repeatedly hear and proclaim the exalted heroic deeds of Hari,
the self becomes purified through well-born devotion in a way that it cannot be by vows and other such practices.
Śrīdhara says: He states its exclusivity [by saying] "of those who hear. One would not be purified in that way by vows and the like;

however, by devotion in the form of love (*rati*) that has been well-born, the self—the mind—is purified up to the limit of liberation, so what need be said of mere sin? This occurs through the process of the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Regarding the sequence of the composition: [it is as follows].
The meaning is that one would not be purified by means of vows and the like in that same manner. ||32||
Viśvanātha: For devotees who practice hearing, chanting, and so forth, even if they have committed offenses, their devotion alone shall become complete. As it has been said:
"For those who have committed offenses against the Name, the names themselves remove the sin."
"Those very [practices], when applied without rest, are what bring about the goal.
In that regard, for the virtuous, it is the individual soul (*jīvātman*) itself that would be purified; how much more so, then, the mind? Thus he says: "for those who listen.
Here, "self" (*ātman*) refers to the living being (*jīva*). Just as it is purified from the impurity of ignorance, it is not so purified by means of vows and the like.

The meaning is that even when sins are diminished through expiatory rites performed for their sake, because the seed of sin is not destroyed, the mind becomes pure only to a slight degree and merely on the surface. Therefore, O King, as for what you have objected— that "I consider expiation to be useless, like the bathing of an elephant" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.1.10)— [that is not the case].

That is indeed the truth. By means of this narrative, the established doctrine has been demonstrated: that for devotees, the destruction of root sins occurs through devotion alone, resulting in their non-entrance into hell and their attainment of the Blessed One; whereas for those who perform ritual actions, there is the repeated coming and going between hell and heaven due to the power of their merit and demerit.
Thus it is illuminated. ||32||
The bee that has tasted the honey of Kṛṣṇa’s lotus feet no longer takes delight in the qualities of Māyā, which bring only suffering.
But another, struck by desire, would strive to wipe away the dust from himself, only for that very action to cause the dust to arise once again.

Śrīdhara explains this as follows: he is so called because he licks—that is, tastes—the honey from the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa. Having been cast away by the honey-licker due to their extreme insignificance, those objects of the world which are the qualities of *māyā* no longer delight him. But another, being devoid of that tasting of honey, for that very reason...

Being overcome by desire, one might even endeavor in ritual action as a form of expiation to wipe away the passion and evil within oneself; however, because such action lacks the power to purify the *sattva*, the passion and evil will surely recur through that very action, like the bathing of an elephant. (33)

The sequential composition [of the commentary] elucidates that very point: "Kṛṣṇāṅghri," etc. Viśvanātha, who is otherwise devoid of devotion alone, states: "Thus, whether they have committed an offense or are without offense, devotees should simply practice devotion and not perform expiation. However, those followers of the Smṛtis who lack faith in devotion..."

But those whose intellects are hardened by fallacious reasoning, such as mere exegesis (*arthavāda*), claim that there is only penance (*prāyaścitta*) and not the chanting of the Name; therefore, he says that the scriptures on penance are also meaningful:
"Just as a bee is a honey-gatherer at the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa..."

Just as one who is dying of hunger does not become attached to fodder, grass, and the like—the food of cattle, humans, and other beings—so too the devotee, even if previously addicted to undesirable sense objects, does not take delight in those qualities of *māyā* that have been cast off upon attaining the state of devotion (*bhaktatva*). This is because of the use of the verbal root *ram* (to delight). Even though he may be a *kaniṣṭha-bhakta* (the lowest grade of devotee), [he does not delight in them].

"He serves them, yet even while enjoying those desires, he should condemn them as resulting in suffering"—according to this stated principle, he does not take delight in them at all. Another, however, who follows the Smṛti, would indeed strive for action in order to wipe away the dust of sin from himself; he must certainly perform expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
The sense is that just as dust and sin might be purified again by chanting, they would indeed arise once more due to the presence of offenses against the Name. ||33||
Thus, having recollected the greatness of the Blessed One as spoken by their own master, those servants of Yama were struck with wonder in their minds.
O King, from that time forward, they have neither suspected anyone residing in the abode of the Immortal, nor do they fear to behold him.

Śrīdhara: Their minds were not at all astonished; rather, they simply believed that what had been said was the truth. From that time forward, suspecting that he might kill them, and harboring such fear, they were afraid even to look upon him. According to another reading, however, their minds became astonished. And they—
The meaning is that from that time forward, they were afraid. ||34||
Kramasaṃdarbha: This has not been explained.

Viśvanātha: The ellipsis is "they do not go at all toward those who take refuge in Acyuta. Therefore, according to the reading *acyuta*, they became bewildered in mind, and furthermore, they were afraid. ||34||
The Blessed One, born from a jar (Agastya), while seated on Mount Malaya and worshipping Hari, narrated this secret history.

Śrīdhara: Agastya, who was born from a water-jar, was seated on Mount Malaya; being undistracted, he was worshipping Hari again and again, meaning that he touched Hari’s feet for the sake of instilling confidence in Him. ||35||
The sequence of composition: the meaning is that Agastya, also known as Kumbhasambhava, heard it from Śrī Dvaipāyana during the study of the Saṃhitā. ||35||

Viśvanātha: Agastya, the pitcher-born, was seated on Mount Malaya, worshiping Hari again and again with an undistracted mind; the meaning is that he touched the feet of Hari for the sake of establishing trust—thus say the venerable teachers. 35.

Thus ends the third chapter of the sixth book in the *Harṣiṇī*, titled *Sārārthadarśinī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted to the Lord; it is well-received by the virtuous.
Thus ends the narrative of Ajāmila in the Sixth Canto of the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā, the Pāramahaṃsyasaṃhitā, which is a commentary on the Brahma-sūtras within the glorious Mahāpurāṇa Śrīmad Bhāgavatam.
The Third Chapter;
now the Fourth Chapter: The Hymn to the Secret of the Haṃsa.
The illustrious King said: You have described in brief the creation of the gods, asuras, and humans, as well as that of the nāgas, beasts, and birds, which occurred during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara.
Śrīdhara:
With the intention of describing the birth of Viśvarūpa from the three [sons] beginning with the fourth,
the lineage of that Akṣa among the Pracetasas is now expanded.
In the fourth [chapter], however, the propitiation of Hari by Dakṣa for the sake of the creation of progeny is described,
both through his ascetic penance and by means of the hymn known as the Haṃsaguhya.
Having heard the power of the names in the lineage of Svāyambhuva’s sons through this incidental digression, one now desires to know the detailed account of the dynasties.
By means of the two verses beginning with "devāsura," that which was stated in brief and in summary in the third book [is here explained]. ||1||
*Caitanyamata-mañjūṣā*: Only the thirty-first verse has been commented upon.
*Krama-sandarbha*: It is concise, because it does not provide a detailed account of the origins of the sixth and subsequent Manvantaras.
*Viśvanātha*.
Furthermore, the nourishment of Indra, who had slain his preceptor, must be told;
he [Indra] was Viśvarūpa, born from the daughter of Dakṣa.
Therefore, the birth of Dakṣa, which was mentioned briefly at the end of the fourth [chapter],
shall be recounted here in detail in three chapters within this book.
The king also, having heard those two accounts concerning the lineage of the sons of Svāyambhuva during the discourse on creation, questioned him about that matter once again.
In the fourth [chapter], it is described how Dakṣa, born from the Pracetasas, while creating progeny,
propitiated the Lord with the Haṃsaguhyastava.
By means of the two verses beginning with "devāsura," that which was stated in brief and in summary in the third book [is here explained]. ||1||
O Blessed One, I desire to know from you the detailed account of that very [creation],
and by what power the Supreme Lord brought forth the secondary creation.
Śrīdhara: "Vyāsam" means expansion. I desire to know that power by which, and in what manner, You created [the universe] from Yourself;
I wish to know that power and its mode. "Anusargam" means the creation that has continued in succession. ||2||

The sequential arrangement: [It consists of] Vyāsa and the subsequent branches and sub-branches born during his respective Manvantara; it is a "sub-creation" (anusarga) because the previous creation had almost perished due to some cause. ||2||

Viśvanātha: *Vyāsam* means expansion. *Te* means from you. *Anusargam* means a creation that follows [the previous one]. By which power (*śakti*) and in what manner he created, that power and that method—[he asked] the Supreme Brahmā. ||2||
Śrī Sūta said:
Having heard this inquiry of the royal sage, Bādarāyaṇi—
Having greeted them, the great yogi spoke, O best of sages.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
Śrī Śuka said:
When the ten sons of Prācīnabarhiṣ, the Pracetasas,
emerged from within the ocean, they beheld the earth covered with trees.

Śrīdhara: To state that [the Lord] created through the forms of Dakṣa and others, he describes the manner of Dakṣa’s birth with the words "When... When the sons of Prācīnabarhiṣ were emerged and emerged from the midst of the ocean, they saw the earth (gāṃ) covered with trees. This was by the instruction of Nārada to Prācīnabarhiṣ.
Because, in the absence of a king, agriculture and other such activities would cease to exist. ||4||
The sequential arrangement [of the narrative] begins with the lineage of Uttānapāda, because his was the final reign. ||4||

Viśvanātha: To explain how [the Lord] created through forms such as Dakṣa, he describes the manner of rebirth for Dakṣa, who had abandoned his body due to the pain of humiliation following Rudra’s offense—beginning with the words "When... They beheld the earth (gām) covered with trees, according to the instruction of Nārada.
When Prācīnabarhis had grown weary of worldly life and departed for the forest, [the people] lived solely under Satyarāja, because of the absence of agriculture and other such activities. ||4||
Enraged by the drums, their fury inflamed by ascetic power,
they emitted wind and fire from their mouths with the desire to consume them.
Śrīdhara: [The compound] *tapasā dīpito manyur yeṣām* means "those whose anger was inflamed by asceticism"; the sequence of words [in the commentary] is not explained [here].
Viśvanātha: [He says] *tapodīpiteti* because asceticism (*tapas*) is the substratum for anger (*kopa*). ||5||
O best of the Kurus, perceiving them being consumed by those two,
King Soma spoke, as if to pacify his great wrath.
Śrīdhara: To those trees being consumed by that wind and fire, Soma, the king of the forest-dwellers (vanaspati), spoke with nine verses beginning with "mā drumebhyaḥ. (6)

Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: Soma is the presiding deity of trees; he alone is the king of trees. The sense is that [the poet says] "as if pacifying" because the departure of anger cannot occur through the means of conciliation (*sāman*) at first. ||6||
"O highly fortunate ones, you ought not to harm those who are wretched, such as the trees;
for you are remembered as the lords of all creatures, intent on their prosperity."
Śrīdhara: O illustrious ones! [The term] *kramasaṃdarbha* means those who desire to increase it, specifically wishing to cause it to grow. Viśvanātha: This has not been explained.
Oh, the Lord Hari, the imperishable Master of Prajāpati,
the omnipresent one, created the trees and the herbs for the sake of strength and nourishment!

Śrīdhara: He says with three verses beginning with "Alas! that the burning of the food and edibles belonging to the Prajāpatis was improper. *Ūrja* refers to nourishing food; *iṣ* refers to grain. ||8||
The sequence of composition: *ūrja* refers to food that remains over from the meal. "Food" (*anna*) means he created food for those who are strong and for those who are weak. ||8||
Viśvanātha: *Ūrj* refers to food other than grain, such as fruits and edible items derived from trees; *iṣ* refers to grain, such as wheat and other crops derived from plants. ||8||
Food is the immobile among moving things, for it is footless among those that walk on feet;
it is handless among those endowed with hands, and four-footed among those that have two feet.
Śrīdhara: [This is] the *Kramasaṃdarbha*; it has not been commented upon.

Viśvanātha: For the moving beings (*carāṇām*)—those that move by means of two wings, such as bees and the like—the non-moving things (*acarāḥ*), namely the flowers, creepers, and so forth, are indeed their food. For those who move on feet (*padacāriṇām*)—those that move by means of feet, such as cows, buffaloes, and the like—the footless (*apadaḥ*)...
Grass and the like are indeed food. Among those very things, cows and other animals are the food for tigers and others who possess hands;
four-footed animals such as deer are the food for two-footed humans who move on their feet; and by the word "and," non-moving things such as grains and wheat are also included.
"— O sinless ones, you have been commanded by your father and by the God of gods;
how then can you be fit to burn up the trees for the sake of creating progeny?"
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
—o)0(o— Follow the path of the virtuous; restrain your blazing anger.
It has been enjoyed by your father, your grandfather, and even your great-grandfather.
Śrīdhara: Therefore, "he took his stand" (ātiṣṭhata) means he resorted to the path of the virtuous, which is tranquility, and which is cherished by his father and others. ||11||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Follow the path of the virtuous, which is cherished by fathers and others, and which leads to tranquility. ||11||
He is the father and kinsman of the people, the eyelashes of vision, and the husband of women;
he is the lord of subjects, the home of mendicants, and the wise friend of the ignorant.
Śrīdhara: Since the Lord of Creatures alone is the kinsman of his subjects, one must not destroy their means of livelihood;
thus he says, by way of five similes: "The parents are for children (tokānām), that is, for the young; the wise man alone is the friend who bestows knowledge upon the ignorant. (12)
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: For you, O trees and others, are the protectors of subjects (prajā), and the subjects are those who depend upon you for their livelihood;
therefore, protect them.

Since it is not observed that protectors possess the power to destroy, he provides five examples here: "The husband is the protector of children and women; the king is the protector of his subjects. (12)
"—O! Within the bodies of all beings dwells the Self, Hari, the Lord. Behold all this as His abode; for in this way He is truly gratified by you."
Śrīdhara: And because [the body] is presided over by the Lord, injury to living beings is not proper; thus he says: "Within bodies... [and so on]. "By you" (vaḥ) means by yourselves. ||13||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: And because [the Lord] is the presiding authority, injury to living beings is not appropriate; thus he says: "Within...
Why is it that by you alone has this Lord been thus propitiated through compassion for all beings?
The intended meaning is "remember. ||13||
He who, through the desire to know the Self, restrains the fierce anger that has arisen within his body like a cloud from the sky, transcends the qualities.
Śrīdhara: "Suddenly arisen" means that which has emerged in the body from space [without cause]. One should restrain this through inquiry into the Self. ||14||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Now, one might ask: why such deliberation at a time of anger? To this he replies with the words "He who... (*yaḥ*). The meaning is that it arose suddenly in the body, like [a sound] from space; [it arose] through inquiry (*vicāra*) out of a desire to know the Self (*ātman*).

"Yacchet" means he should restrain or pacify them. By saying "saguṇān" (those possessed of qualities), [the Lord] utters a conciliatory word (*sāman*) implying, "Otherwise, you will be swallowed up by those very qualities," and thereby suggests the strategy of dissension (*bheda*). ||14||
"—Enough with these wretched, scorched trees! May it be well with you who are barren.
For this excellent maiden, born of the forest, should be accepted as a wife."
Śrīdhara: May there be welfare for you all, including those who remain.
He gives his daughter for the purpose of protecting the trees; she is "vārkṣī," one nurtured by trees. ||15||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Observing that there is still no cessation of conflict even through division, he speaks of giving, saying "Enough" (*alam*).
"Of the *khilas*" means of the remnants; she is a "tree-maiden" (*vārkṣī*) because she is protected by trees. (15)
Having thus addressed the beautiful Apsaras maiden, O King,
King Soma departed; they then married her according to the law.

Śrīdhara: Having addressed and consoled her; "āpsarasīm" means the daughter of the Apsaras Pramlocā. The sequence of the composition has not been explained [here]. Viśvanātha: "Āpsarasīm" means the daughter of the Apsaras Pramlocā. ||16||
