From them, it is said, Dakṣa Prācetasa was born upon her;
by his emission of progeny, the three worlds were filled.
Śrīdhara: [This] has not been explained in the *Kramasaṃdarbha*.

Viśvanātha: "He was born" (*samabhavat*) refers to his birth during the *Svāyambhuva Manvantara*, because Dakṣa belongs to the lineage of Svāyambhuva. "By whose emission of progeny" (*yasya prajāvisargeṇa*): the emission of progeny is...
And his [creation] was indeed through the eyes:

"When the interval of the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara had arrived, at the time when the previous creation had been dissolved, he who, impelled by the gods, created the desired progeny— he was Dakṣa" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 4.30.49).
Because it is mentioned in the fourth [chapter].
Therefore, it is understood that his very asceticism (*tapas*), which extends through the five intermediate *manvantaras*, was for the purpose of attaining sovereignty as he did in former times. (17)
Listen attentively as I describe how Dakṣa, who was devoted to his daughters, created living beings through both seed and mind.
Śrīdhara: By the phrase "affectionate toward his daughter," it is stated that he has only a lineage of daughters; the sequence of my own commentary does not explain this.
Viśvanātha: By the phrase "affectionate toward his daughter," the absence of a lineage of sons is indicated. (18)
In the beginning, Prajāpati created these creatures by means of his mind alone:
the gods, asuras, humans, and others, including those dwelling in the sky, on land, and in the water.
Śrīdhara: Prajāpati is Dakṣa. ||19||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
Having observed that the creation of beings was not yet increased, the Lord of Beings...
Having approached the foothills of the Vindhya mountains, he performed difficult austerities.
Śrīdhara: "Abṛṃhitam" means not increased or not grown. Regarding "the feet of the Vindhya," that is, the nearby mountains, the sequential arrangement has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: Prajāpati Dakṣa [went] toward the feet of the Vindhya, that is, the peripheral mountains. (20)
There is a supreme holy ford named Aghamarṣaṇa that removes all sins;
having performed ritual ablutions there at each of the three daily sessions, he gratified Hari through his ascetic penance.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
Haṃsaguhya praised the Blessed One, Adhokṣaja.
I shall relate that to you, and how Hari was thereby satisfied.
Śrīdhara: [He was liberated] by means of the hymn known as the Haṃsaguhya. Whose? Dakṣa’s. ||22||

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: By means of the hymn "Haṃsaguhya," which was established in the past and is Vedic (*naigama*), but not one composed by Dakṣa; this is the meaning. Of which Dakṣa? ||22||
Śrī Prajāpati said: Salutations to the Supreme One, whose experience is unfailing.

I offer my salutations to the Self-existent One, for whom the bondage caused by the appearance of the three qualities has ceased through the realization of the true nature of those qualities, who is the unseen abode, and whose pride has been dispelled by the intellect that perceives the reality of the gunas.

Śrīdhara: I offer salutation—that is, I perform an act of bowing—to the Supreme One, the most excellent of all. The reason for his supremacy is that he possesses unfailing experience, which is the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*). Therefore, he is the binder and controller of both the individual soul (*jīva*), which is a reflection of the three *guṇas*, and *māyā*. Even so, there is the notion of reality regarding the *guṇas*.

[He is] that whose abode—His own essential nature—is unseen by those living beings. The reason for this is: from whom pride has ceased. In another reading, it means: from whom pride and limitation have ceased—that is, have been cast out.
If so, how is He established? To this he says: "To the Self-existent One" (svayambhuve), meaning to Him who is self-luminous. ||23||

The Structural Arrangement: Whether by one possessing desire for the higher and lower [realms] or by one free from desire, the Supreme Lord alone is to be worshipped and no other, because He possesses the power that subjugates both Māyā and the individual soul (jīva), whereas any other possesses a meager power dependent upon His Māyā. For that purpose, he approaches with a specific hymn of praise, beginning with "Namaḥ" (Salutation).

"Unfailing" (*avitatha*) indicates the power of non-deviating knowledge and will. "The three qualities" (*guṇatraya*) indicates the power of such action, because [the Lord] is the controller of the individual soul (*jīva*) and *māyā* through those powers;

furthermore, although those powers exist as His very nature by virtue of having transcended each respective quality, they nevertheless reside within the qualities themselves, such as *sattva* and the rest.

To Him whose abode (dhāma)—the manifestation of such power—is unseen by those possessing the intellect of reality (tattvabuddhi) and knowledge of causes, being impossible even to infer, let alone to experience; and to Him whose essential nature and His full powers [are likewise beyond them]. The reason for this in every case is: "to the self-luminous one" (svaprakāśāya).

That in which there is the appearance of the three qualities—an imposition through one's own ignorance—is the *jīva*. Although the *jīva* is of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), its inferiority is manifested by the mere appearance of being touched by ignorance, because it stands in the position of a ray [of that consciousness]. ||23||
Viśvanātha: [The phrase] "to the Supreme, to the individual souls, and to those who are illusory" means this. Why?

For the sake of unerring experience—that is, for the sake of true realization—the individual soul (*jīva*) is the appearance of the three qualities (*guṇatraya*); *māyā* is the cause; and [the phrase refers to those who are] bound by these two. Thus, even so, by those individual souls who possess the notion that the qualities are the ultimate reality...
To Him whose true nature is unseen; though distinct from those [qualities], He is perfectly understood as the Abode—it is said:

"to Him for whom the limit of measurement, the boundary of pride, has ceased. The sense is that no one is able to say, "He possesses only this much" in terms of qualities, forms, and sovereignty. As it was said by Brahmā:
"Who is capable of measuring even those qualities of You, whose nature is the *guṇas*, who have descended for the sake of the world's welfare? (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.14.7).
In the reading "I offer [this] to him whose pride has ceased," *māna* means knowledge; *dadhe* means "I perform. In that case, it is "salutation" (*namaḥ*).

This is the section on action (*karmapada*). Then, as to how its accomplishment occurs, he says: "To the Self-existent One (*svayambhuve*), who is self-luminous (*svaprakāśāya*)—[he] whose friendship a person does not perceive, even though [He] is a friend."
I bow to that Great Lord, who dwells as a friend with those dwelling together in this city, just as a quality resides within its possessor for one whose vision is clear.
Just as a quality [is subordinate] to that which possesses the quality, so too there may be someone standing before one who has become a subordinate to a king who is the primary figure,
thinking, "This person is my friend. Even though the king thinks about him, that person does not know it—
just as servants know their own status as being dear to the king.
"Likewise, salutations to You, whom the individual soul does not know as a friend"—thus it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa. 24.

Śrīdhara, demonstrating that [the Self] has an unseen abode, says: "No. Although the Person—the Friend, the individual soul (jīva)—dwells in this city, the body, he does not perceive, that is, does not know, the friendship of Him who dwells right here with him, consisting of such things as the impelling of the instruments [of action]. Why? Because his vision is directed toward the manifest (vyaktadṛṣṭeḥ).
[This refers to] the one who perceives the manifold world (*prapañca*). For the seer does not become the object seen. In the reading with the nominative case-ending, it means:

he for whom there is vision only of the manifested manifold; just as that quality—the state of being an illuminator—does not know its friendship, that is, its relationship as the subject (*viṣayin*), with the sense organs and so forth which are the objects (*viṣaya*). ||24||

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: He establishes the state of being the abode of the unseen (*adṛṣṭadhāmatva*) with the words "not" (*na*). Of that Supreme Self (*paramātman*), the person—the individual soul (*jīva*)—does not perceive (*avaiti*), that is, does not know, its friendship, such as its role as the activator of the instruments (*karaṇa*) and so forth; in this [Self]...
Even though the Friend dwells within this very city of the body, and even though He causes the enjoyments of the objects desired by Him to be experienced through His very friendship—

even though He Himself is the Friend and experiences that various friendship while dwelling right here in the body— He does not know [this], because His vision is directed outward; such is the reading with the genitive case ending (*vyaktadṛṣṭeḥ*).

Even for that Lord, the knowledge regarding whatever object is manifested precisely through the illumination of the sense organs; or, according to the reading with the nominative case, for that very reason,

the individual soul (*jīva*) is also one whose knowledge is manifested, just as sound, touch, and so forth [are manifested] by the sense of hearing and the rest, which are the possessors of qualities (*guṇin*).
Just as one does not know the friendship of a sense organ, which is characterized by its communication of its own sweetness and so forth, so it is here. ||24||
The body, the vital breaths, the senses, the mental faculties, and the elements— they know these as the Self, and that which is other than them as the Supreme.
A person knows everything, yet even one who knows that [everything] does not know the qualities [of the Supreme]; I praise the omniscient and infinite One.
Vaiśravaṇa is indeed the conceitedness regarding the body; the Maruts are those who take pride in the vital breaths;
Indra and the others are the presiding deities of the sense organs; and Rudra is the essence of the internal organ (antahkarana).

"Deluded, these do not know themselves, nor even the Supreme; but Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures, who identifies with the individual soul, knows everything. Even he does not know Hari perfectly, for even the omniscient one [does not know Him completely]. Thus it is said. (25)

Śrīdhara: [Objection: But surely, because it is insentient, the *guṇa* does not know; why then does the *jīva*, who is sentient, not know? To this he says: "The body... and so forth. The body (*deha*), the vital breaths (*asavaḥ*), the senses (*akṣāṇi*), the minds (*manavaḥ*), the elements (*bhūtāni*), and the subtle constituents (*mātrāḥ*) constitute the self (*ātmānam*), the essential nature (*svarūpam*), which is the object of perception (*dṛśyam*).

They do not know the other group of senses, nor that which is beyond those two—the group of deities. But the person, the individual soul (jīva), knows all these three, and he also knows the qualities (guṇas) that constitute their root.
Though he is a knower of that, he does not know Him who is omniscient; Him, the infinite, I praise and extol. ||25||
The sequential arrangement: "The body," etc.; [it refers to] another class of deities and the Supreme Person. ||25||
The *Bhagavatsandarbha* (17): The body (*deha*), the vital breaths (*asavaḥ*) or life-forces (*prāṇāḥ*), the senses (*akṣāṇi* or *indriyāṇi*),
the minds (*manavaḥ*) or internal organs, the elements (*bhūtāni*), and the subtle potentials (*mātrāḥ*) or *tanmātras*—

one does not [perceive] oneself as one's own true nature (*ātmanam svasvarūpam*), nor the "other" as the aggregate of one's respective objects, nor that which is beyond both as the host of deities (*devatāvargam*).

The wise know that the person, namely the individual soul (*jīva*), knows everything as itself— its own essential nature— as well as the other cognizer, their respective domains consisting of the collection of objects such as the body and so forth along with the group of presiding deities, and likewise the qualities (*guṇa*) such as *sattva* and the rest which are the root of the body and so forth.
Even though he is a knower of this and that, he does not know Him who is the All-Knowing One, the Knower of everything from the body down to the individual soul (jīva);
for He is infinite because of His infinite qualities, as it is said: "Him they call Ananta" [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.18.19]. For this very reason, the text begins with:
"For where there is duality, as it were, there one sees another... and so forth.

Having stated that the individual soul (jīva) is a seer of other things, the text— by means of the passage beginning with "where one's own self has become all, then by what and whom should one see?"— denies its status as a seer of the Supreme Self; however,
it affirms that the Supreme Self is indeed the seer of all those various things and is also the seer of itself.
He says this with the words, "It exists; by what, O Maitreyi, would one know the knower? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14).

The meaning is as follows: where there appears, as it were, duality within the expanse of *māyā*, that [duality], although non-different from that [Reality] because it is rooted therein, is nevertheless insentient, impure, and perishable due to its being caused by the inconceivable power called *māyā*.

Because it is perceived as distinct from that [Self], it repeatedly arises as if possessing independent existence; thus, in that state, one living being perceives another object, because of the mutual compatibility between his instruments of perception and the objects of sight—this is the intended meaning. However, in the splendor of his own true nature, for that living being...

The Supreme Self, who is like the sun and whose nature is like the solar orb, has become everything by virtue of His own essential power; He exists as having existed from time immemorial, and not by entering into that [universe].
Therefore, what other object could that other—the individual soul—perceive there, and by means of what other instrument?

The meaning is that no one perceives anything at all. The point is that rays of light do not, by their own power, illuminate the majesty contained within the solar orb, nor do flames burn the fire itself.
This being so, he whose infinite majesty of essential nature is indeed such as this—him...

By what other instrument could one know the Knower, the Omniscient Supreme Self? The meaning is: by none at all. Thus, when the power of knowledge has been established therein, the powers of action and will are also indicated. ||25||

Viśvanātha: Now, one might object: "Granted that the *guṇa* does not know because it is insentient (*jaḍatvāt*), but how is it that the *jīva*, being sentient (*cetanaḥ*), does not know? To this he says: although he is sentient everywhere, in relation to the Supreme Lord he is indeed insentient; for there, the body, the vital breaths (*asavaḥ*) residing therein, and the senses (*akṣāḥ*) [are all insentient].
The Manavas, the internal organs, the elements such as earth and the rest, and the sense-objects such as sound and the rest,

do not know the Self— their own true nature— nor that which is distinct from themselves among all selves, nor the Supreme who is beyond all selves, nor even the individual soul-nature (jīva-svarūpa). Yet the person, the individual soul (puṃs), [does know it] because of its consciousness.

One who knows that (taj-jña) is so called because, in the state of liberation while living (jīvanmukta), he knows everything—himself, the body and its adjuncts, the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest which are rooted therein, and that Supreme Self;
yet even he does not know the Omniscient Supreme Lord. [Objection: But you say he is "one who knows that"; [Response: Even that is not so.
From where does he know this? To that he says: "Infinite," because of the infinity of His non-material qualities; even that [knowledge] is indeed ignorance.
As it has been said: "Even the lords of heaven did not reach its end because of its infinity" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.87.41).
When there is the cessation of the mind through the forgetting of the perception and memory of name-and-form and form.
Salutation to that Swan, whose abode is purity, who moves by means of his own absolute state.

"Of the honey" (madhvaḥ): by its own exclusive state. Although the soul's lack of independence is observed due to the cessation of the mind during dreamless sleep and so forth, it is known from the observation of dreaming and waking that there exists another, the Lord, who is its controller. Its "exclusive" nature (kevalatvam) arises from the absence of the soul's own volition.
When there is the cessation of the mind during states such as dreaming and deep sleep,
then Keśava exists as the cause for the awakening from those states and so forth.

"Because the individual soul (jīva) lacks independence, there exists another who is its controller; from the conformity of the soul's activity [to His will], that omnipresent Lord is known. Thus it is said in the Harivaṃśa. (26)

Śrīdhara: Having stated that [the Self] is beyond the reach of the unseen, he speaks of its self-luminosity. When there is the cessation of the mind—that is, *samādhi*, and not dissolution as in deep sleep (*suṣupti*), nor distraction as in waking or dreaming—then he says: "That by which name and form are manifested is such"; this is the cause for that cessation.

Seeing is the perception [of objects], and memory is the non-forgetting or non-destruction of those two. At that time, salutation to that pure *haṃsa* (the Swan), whose abode—the mind—is pure and stainless, and who is perceived solely through the knowledge of its own nature. ||26||
The sequential arrangement [is established] by its own constitution, that is, by the power of its essential nature. ||26||

Viśvanātha: Now, regarding what was said—that even the knower of that does not know—it is because that very object of knowledge is of two kinds: easy to know and difficult to know. Among these, he states the easily known nature as being without distinctions, beginning with "When... (yadā).

Alternatively, *smaraṇa* (recollection) is the cessation of the mind, a state of supreme cessation; it is not a dissolution as in deep sleep (*suṣupti*), nor is it a distraction as in the waking and dreaming states. Of what kind [of mind]? It belongs to that by which name and form are manifested. The cause of this supreme cessation is the loss (*sampramoṣa*) of both perception (*darśana*)—that is, seeing—and memory (*smṛti*).

Because it is destroyed by that very same [state] when it is perfectly [realized], then "by its own state alone" (svasaṃsthayaiva) means by way of being the mere reality (vastumātratvena), which is accessible through non-distinctive knowledge; "is perceived" (īyate) means it is cognized. To that pure state, the "pure" (śuci) mind is the "abode" (sadma), meaning the locus of cognition.

To him who is such: the fact that this essential nature is easily understood has been stated by Brahmā, as follows: "Nevertheless, O Infinite One, Your majesty and qualities can be fully comprehended only by those whose inner selves are stainless" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.14.6). ||26||
The wise perceive Him seated within the heart by means of their own ninefold and threefold powers.
Just as they extract fire hidden within wood by means of their intellect through the fifteen-fold friction.
He indeed is the experience of the bliss of nirvāṇa through the negation of all specific māyās;
He possesses all names and He is the universal form.
May [He], whose self-power is inexpressible, be gracious.
Madhva: By means of the threefold [powers] consisting of will and the rest;
for the powers beginning with Vimalā are threefold by way of will and so forth.
From those [powers], which are the very nature of Viṣṇu, there arise others bearing their names.
"They are born by His grace, and one should worship them in the *pīṭha*;
they possess souls distinct from His, yet by His very grace they remain near Him. Thus it is stated in the *Tattvanirṇaya*.
Furthermore, there are the ten senses, along with mind, intellect, vital breath (*prāṇa*), and *pradhāna*.
"Of these, the fourteenth is supreme; Hari is remembered as the fifteenth.
And because of the differentiation of the intellect (buddhi) among them, the fifteenth is established. Thus it is said.
However, there may be a distinction in terms of "limitedness" (iyattā) regarding bliss and the rest, due to their abandonment of that [limitation].

"The immutable Hari is said to be devoid of all specific qualities; because his nature is non-material, he is also called formless. And: "Since his form is always similar to the forms of everything everywhere..."

"Since He possesses all forms, His primary meaning is 'Sound' (Śabda), and He is the name of all things. And: "Because He is beyond the world of ordinary experience, Viṣṇu has not been etymologically defined;
nevertheless, because He is described in the Vedas, He alone is said to possess form. Thus it is stated in the Vyomasaṃhitā.

Śrīdhara: In response to the expectation of who perceives one who has become such as this, he says with two verses, "the wise" (*manīṣiṇaḥ*). The syntactical connection of the two verses is: "May He, whom the discerning ones extract by discriminating and meditate upon, [and] who is the experience of the bliss of liberation, be gracious unto me. Thus, for those who extract [Him] in this manner...
The meaning is that it is "perceived. What [is perceived]? They extract it. Hidden by its own powers (*svaśakti*), not manifesting;
by how many? By nine; and furthermore, by the twenty-seven limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) which are tripled—that is, threefold—they extract the twenty-eighth, hidden [by them]. This is the sense.

Or rather, they extract [the Self] by means of the nine forms consisting of primordial nature (prakṛti), the person (puruṣa), the great principle (mahat), the ego (ahaṃkāra), and the five subtle elements (tanmātra);
by the threefold [principles] whose essence is the three guṇas; and, by the word "and" (ca), by the sixteen forms of transformation (vikāra).
In what manner do they extract it? By means of wisdom (manīṣā), having established it within the heart and rendered it motionless.

The meaning is that, like the transcendental fire manifested by the fifteen *sāmidhenī* mantras, they extract the Supreme Self—which is distinct from the self that is the locus of egoity—as characterized by the state of being the fifteenth (*pāñcadaśya*). ||27||

By the negation of that *māyā* which possesses all particularities without exception, there arises the experience of the bliss of liberation (*nirvāṇa-sukha*), since a negation is impossible unless there has been a prior engagement [with the object]. He states this engagement: "He alone is the name of all;
he alone is the form of the universe. Even though he possesses such forms, negation is possible because they lack reality; thus he says:
He is one whose power, called *māyā*, is unmanifest within his own self. ||28||

The sequence of composition: the pair beginning with "manīṣiṇaḥ. [Objection: Since you are *trivṛt* (threefold) and thus transcend the nine powers (*nava-śakti*), how can it be that you are by nature devoid of power (*niḥśaktika*)? [Response: No; he says, "aśeṣa... (without remainder). Experience (*anubhūti*) must necessarily be admitted, for without it, the status of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) cannot be established. And regarding that experience which is to be admitted—
The sense is that the power of essential nature (*svarūpa-śakti*), though indivisible from those [powers], is nonetheless established as distinct.

He says this very thing with the words "May she be gracious. Now, one might object: if she is extracted from them, how can she possess all names and forms consisting of those [powers]? To this he replies: "indefinable" (*anirukta*). This is because of her inconceivable power (*acintya-śaktitvāt*).
The meaning. ||27||

[Objection: "Surely that nature of mine which is called Brahman, whose sole form is the bliss of liberation, must indeed be experienced; thus let it consist of the threefold [powers] and the nine Śaktis. But as for that nature which is augmented by the forms of the qualities (guṇas), would that not be identical with that [Brahman], because of its similarity to the world? To this, he says: "Whatever... [yad yad...].

By the triad [of qualities], and augmented by attributes and forms—that essential nature which is peerless and most exceedingly vast—even that does not become an object within the range of speech and so forth. The reason for this is: "He indeed" (sa vā).
You, whose essential nature is augmented by attributes and forms, are perceived through the dissolution and creation of those attributes.
It is merely to be inferred, and not directly experienced;

or rather, it is perceived—that is, seen as the presiding controller—in that eternally established Vaikuṇṭha, from which there is the departure or removal of all qualities (guṇas), and thus which is free from the creation [of the material world]. ||28||

Viśvanātha says: He describes the nature of that which is difficult to comprehend, along with its specific attributes: "The wise, who are pure devotees, [perceive] that which is hidden and situated within the heart" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 2.8.5).
According to this statement, through the devotion of hearing (*śravaṇa-bhakti*), [the Lord is perceived] within the heart.
Having been introduced, they again extract it by means of the intellect known as loving devotion (*prema-bhakti*).
The meaning is that, having extracted it from within the heart, they savor its sweetness— such as beauty and so forth— by means of the senses, beginning with the eyes.
Of what nature is He? They draw Him forth by means of their own powers, namely the powers of consciousness (*cicchakti*).

By how many? By nine, beginning with Vimalā and the others; even there, by threefold [powers], that is, by the three functions of consciousness itself: *hlādinī*, *sandhinī*, and *saṃvit*. As it has been said:
In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"Bliss (hlādinī), existence (sandhinī), and consciousness (saṃvit)—these three exist as one in You who are the support of all;
yet in You, who are devoid of qualities, there is no mixture of bliss and pain. [ViP 1.12.68]

Just as they extract from a piece of wood the extraordinary fire—which is manifested by the fifteen *sāmidhenī* mantras, representing the state of being fifteen—they [should] be propitiated; this is the connection with what follows. For those devoid of devotion, this Being, whose specific nature possesses infinite qualities not under discussion, is difficult to know.
Because they cannot be fully experienced—even while being experienced by devotees—the sweetness and sovereignty [of the Lord] remain beyond full comprehension. As it was said by Brahmā himself:
"Even for you, whose nature consists of qualities, it is impossible to measure those qualities."
"For one who has descended for the welfare of others, who can master him?
By whom have the particles of dust of the earth, the mists in the sky, or the rays of the sun been measured by time, however well-crafted? (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.14.7). Thus ends [verse] 27.
He says that what I must worship is precisely that which is distinct from the qualified form of the existent which is illusory:

"May He be gracious to me. By the negation of that *māyā* which possesses all particularities (*viśeṣa*), there is the bliss of liberation (*nirvāṇasukha*); and there are no arrows at all—the arrows of internal and other sufferings that pierce the heart.

"In that very bliss, he who has experience—[that experience] which is mixed, causing both delight and distress—is found in You who are devoid of qualities," according to the statement of the Vaiṣṇavas.
Since a negation of what is not applicable is impossible, he states the applicability: "He alone possesses all names; He alone..."
The meaning of "Viśvarūpa" (the one whose form is the universe) is that all names and forms, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, belong to him alone.

Since Māyā is his power (*śakti*), the entire universe—which is nothing but Māyā—is likewise his form. However, the power that constitutes his very essence (*svarūpa*) is distinct from both the power of Māyā and the universe produced by Māyā.
He said: He is one whose inherent power (śakti) is unexpressed—that is, not made an object of expression by illusory speech and mind. ||28||
Whatever has been expressed by speech, defined by the intellect, or perceived by the senses or by the mind; of that [He is the source].
Let it not be that its own nature is the form of the qualities;
for that [nature] is characterized by the departure and manifestation of the qualities.

Śrīdhara: Now, one might object that if [the Self] is perceived solely through its own state, then its status as a "universal name" (*sarvanāmatva*) and its "universal form" (*viśvarūpatva*) would be untenable, because it is beyond the reach of speech and other senses; having raised this doubt, [the author states that] its true nature is, in fact, expressible by all names and visible through perception and the other means of knowledge.

Nevertheless, demonstrating through three verses that [the Lord] acts by means of *māyā*, he offers salutation with the words "yad yad": whatever is expressed by speech, uttered; whatever is determined by the intellect (*dhī*), resolved;
or whatever is perceived and grasped by the senses (*akṣa*)—or even whatever is determined by the mind (*manas*).
Let that which has self-luminosity as its conceptualized property not be its essential nature (*svarūpa*).

The reason for its not being the essential nature is that, for [that which is so conceived], it is indeed the form of the qualities (*guṇa*) alone; in another reading, "increased by the qualities. But he [the Self] is distinct from the qualities, because [he is the source] of the qualities.
It is so called because it is characterized by the emission and withdrawal, or the dissolution and creation [of the world];

for these two cannot occur without the superintendence of a conscious being. Alternatively, the connection with the third [verse] is as follows: "Salutations to Him whose own nature may not be, or does not exist. ||29||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Speech, intellect, and so forth are all merely *māyic*; therefore, even that which is described by them must be *māyic* as well. But that [the Self] does not state its own essential nature [through them]; thus he says, "whatever... (*yad yad*). Whatever... [it is].

Whatever is expressed by speech, formulated by the intellect, determined, or perceived by the senses—that is, apprehended by the sense organs—or even whatever is perceived and conceptualized by the mind:
may all that not be His true nature; it does not exist as such. To Him, [the third verse] concludes, "Salutation! This is the syntactical connection.

For that [Self] has the very nature of the qualities (guṇas) augmented by the qualities; if the reading is "hi tad," the meaning is that it is increased by the qualities, yet it is distinct from those qualities. For he is characterized by the departure and emission—that is, the dissolution and origination—of the qualities. He who...

"He is the Lord who effects creation and dissolution; therefore, His existence is established prior to creation and subsequent to dissolution. Regarding this, it is said: "But He is seen by means of the highest intellect" (KaṭhU 1.3.12), "He is to be perceived by the mind alone" (BṛU 4.4.19), "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death" (ŚvetU 3.8), and "The Self, indeed... (BṛU 2.4.5).

"...should be seen" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5), and so forth. Therefore, O King, because of the contradiction with thousands of scriptural and traditional statements such as "Hari is to be heard of and glorified everywhere and at all times by everyone" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 2.2.36), [this view] belongs only to those who have not been graced by the Lord.
This should be explained as being by means of *vacā* and other such herbs.

Therefore, the name of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and so forth cannot be grasped by the senses; for when the tongue and other faculties are intent upon service, that [Name] manifests of its own accord. (Bhaktirasāmṛtasindhu 1.2.234)
And there is the statement beginning with these words.

However, some say that it has not been fully defined because of the absence of a complete definition, since in the passage, "from which speech turns back, unable to reach it along with the mind" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4.1), there is an indication of an ablative case (apādāna).

The state of being inaccessible to speech and mind; [the phrase] "they turn back" refers to the cessation of internal greed, just as it was said regarding the state of being inaccessible to speech and mind. ||29||
In which, from which, by which, for whom, for what purpose, who, and in what manner one performs or causes to be performed an action;
That Brahman, which is prior to all things high and low, is the supreme, already established; it is the cause, non-dual, and one.

"Madhvaḥ: Brahman alone is the cause of the seven case-meanings, of time, and of the modes. Viṣṇu, the Supreme One, is indeed the sole cause of the case-meanings, of time, and of the various modes, because he bestows all existence. Thus it is stated in the Bhaviṣyat Parva.
"It is non-different because of the absence of anything similar to it; it is one because there is no distinction in its form and so forth. Thus [it is said]. ||30||

Śrīdhara: Thus, having accepted that in reality there is an absence of the nature of the qualities (guṇas), [the Lord] has indicated by the phrase "His own power is indefinable" (aniruktātmaśakti) that He possesses the form of the universe through Māyā as the denotation of all things. [He explains this] in relation to that which is the locus (adhikaraṇa), from which He is the source (apādāna), and by means of which He is the instrument (karaṇa).

That which is related [to it], that which is the recipient for whom [it is intended], that which is most desired, that which is the agent who acts independently, and that which is caused to act by another as the instigating agent— each of these is connected individually with the term "Brahman."

And here, by means of the seven words beginning with *yat*, the meanings of the seven case-terminations are shown. Furthermore, by the word *yathā*, the meanings of indeclinables (*avyaya*) expressing the manner of the relationship between action and its factors (*kriyākāraka-sambandha-prakāra*) are indicated. By the words "he performs" (*kurute*) and "is caused to be performed" (*kāryate*), the connection with action for one's own sake and for the sake of others (*svārtha-parārtha-kriyā-anvaya*) is shown for all [the cases]. And by the word *ca* (and),...
The meanings of the suffixes prescribed for the agent, the object, and so forth, have been subsumed [within Brahman].
Why is it that this is Brahman alone? To this he says: "That is their cause," meaning it is the cause of those [suffixal meanings]. Why is that? Because it is established prior to all [of them].

But surely Brahmā and others are heard of in scripture as its causes, and others are seen [to be so] in the world; how then is Brahman alone its cause? To this he says: "[Brahman is] the supreme cause of both higher and lower causes. But if it is the cause of everything, what indeed could serve as its auxiliary cause at that time?
"Because of the non-existence of anything else"? True; he says that this cause is indeed independent (*nirapekṣa*).

It is "non-other," meaning empty of dissimilar things (*vijātīya-śūnya*), and "one," meaning empty of similar things (*sajātīya-śūnya*). The connection with the following [verse] is: "homage to Him. ||30||
The sequence of composition: he demonstrates that very point with the words "In which... (verse 30).

Viśvanātha: Now, if that form consisting of the qualities (*guṇa*) is not His essential nature (*svarūpa*), then it would follow that He is incomplete; therefore, he says: in whatever locus, from whatever source, by whatever instrument, belonging to whom, for whatever recipient, whatever is desired, and whoever is the agent.

"He acts independently" or "he is made to act by another as an instigating agent"—each of these is connected with the word "Brahman. Here, by means of seven instances of the word *yat*, the meanings of the seven case-endings are demonstrated. This applies to the senses of the indeclinables *yathā* and so forth, as well as to the phrases "he acts" and "he is made to act."

The connection with the performance of one's own welfare and the welfare of others has been shown; by the word "and" (*ca*), the meanings of the suffixes prescribed for the sense of being (bhāva) and action (karman), etc., are also included. Why is it that [Brahman] is that very thing? To this he says: "Its cause" (*taddhetuḥ*), meaning the cause of those [things]. This refers to causality.
Why? Because it is established from the outset.

[Objection: But are not Brahmā and others heard in scripture to be its causes, and are they not seen as inferior beings? To this he replies: "Of the higher and the lower," meaning that because it is the cause even of those causes, it is the supreme.
The meaning is "the cause.

Now, if it is the cause of everything, what indeed could its state of being a cooperative cause (sahakāritva) be? To this he says: the meaning is that it is a single cause, independent of anything else.

Surely, for it is heard that the ninefold functions of consciousness—namely the powers of consciousness such as Vimalā and others; the threefold expansions of those [powers], such as Hlādinī and others; their manifestations, such as Vaikuṇṭha and its attendants; and [the vyuhas] such as Vāsudeva and Saṃkarṣaṇa—are all eternally established.

But since there are scriptural statements regarding Time, Māyā, the individual soul (jīva), and the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) as causes of the world, how can it be said that [the cause] is one? To this he says: "Non-different" (ananya), because nothing else exists apart from it; for the powers of consciousness (cicchakti) and their manifestations are of the very nature of that [Brahman], and Vāsudeva and the others are its parts.
The meaning is that although time, māyā, and so forth do not constitute its essential nature, they are non-different from it because they are its powers (śakti). ||30||
Those powers of speakers and disputants indeed become the ground for both conflict and agreement.
And they repeatedly cause self-delusion for them;
homage to that Infinite One of boundless qualities!

Śrīdhara: But if Brahman is thus the cause of the universe, then why do the Mīmāṃsakas dispute this point, asserting that the world was never otherwise than it is now? They agree with others who maintain the doctrine of inherent nature (svabhāvavāda), and why is it that both of them persist in their views even when instructed by those who know the truth?
Why do they become deluded again and again? To this he says: "Salutation to Him whose powers of *māyā* and *avidyā* are the grounds—the places where there occurs either dispute or agreement. (31)

*The Casket of the Doctrine of Consciousness*: "Whose powers," and so forth. Salutation to that Great Person (*mahāpuruṣa*), the Infinite (*bhūman*) who possesses infinite qualities; whose powers—such as *māyā*, *avidyā*, and the rest—become the source of both conflict and harmony in various instances.
However, these [powers] repeatedly cause self-delusion.
It is indeed appropriate that there be delusion in the case of a dispute; however, one should not ask how there can be delusion in the case of agreement.
The intended meaning is that in the case of agreement, [the opponent's argument] produces delusion by contradicting the established tenets of one's own devotion. ||31||

The sequential composition: regarding the word "yat" (that which). Where, among disputing and even reflective proponents, despite the existence of various [reasons], it is precisely such fallacious arguments (*dustarka*) and their underlying powers that present themselves as the cause;
thus he says, "whose powers. For this very reason, its nature consists of infinite qualities and abundance (*bhūmatva*); this is the meaning.

The Bhagavatsandarbha (9): Furthermore, those two—māyā-śakti and svarūpa-śakti—are mutually contradictory, and likewise their respective functions are numerous and mutually contradictory within their own respective groups; nevertheless, their single repository is that very same [Bhagavān].
He says: "Those which are the powers... (31).
Viśvanātha: Now, in this view, other monists (advaitavādins), who cannot tolerate internal, external, or other-external distinctions within their own category, dispute [with us];
and by them, others—the Naiyāyikas—are disputed as dualists (dvaitavādins) because they maintain the doctrine of sixteen categories.

They, in turn, agree with other Vaiśeṣikas; and all of them, along with others who claim that the world was once not as it is now, dispute with the Mīmāṃsakas. Why do they continue to be deluded even when instructed by those who know the truth? To this, he says: "The powers of whom [belong] to whom..."

The functions of the power of *māyā* serve as the causes for the arising of both dispute and, in some cases, agreement among disputing speakers who maintain their positions; they are the grounds for the occurrence of contention and, occasionally, consensus.
He states the purpose: "the delusion of the self" (*ātmamoha*). This means: even for those who desire to know the Self. The word "repeatedly" (*muhuḥ*)...

In this regard, non-interruption is indicated. By the phrase "to the one of infinite qualities" (*anantaguṇāya*), since the word *ananta* has multiple meanings and denotes "imperishable," it is stated that the qualities are both imperishable and limitless.
As it is said: "O Blessed One, those and other great qualities which are eternal reside in Him" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.16.31).

Thus it is stated regarding the Earth; and by the phrase "eternal" (nityāḥ), as well as by the words "of the one devoid of qualities" (aguṇasya) and "masters of yoga" (yogeśvarāḥ) in the statement of Sūta: "The masters of yoga, headed by Bhava and Padma, have not reached the end of the qualities of the one devoid of qualities" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.18.14).

Furthermore, in the statement of Parāśara: "Knowledge, power, strength, sovereignty, valor, and splendor— in their entirety, these are denoted by the word 'Bhagavat,' [along with] all qualities and so forth that are free from anything to be abandoned"— the inclusion of the phrase "free from anything to be abandoned" indicates that his qualities [are likewise free from such defects].
The sense is: how could those who, despite understanding His transcendence, still claim He is merely subordinate, not be deluded by ignorance? ||31||
Regarding the two [conceptions] based on real entities, which reside in one and the same thing and possess distinct and contradictory properties: 'it exists' and 'it does not exist'."
Whatever has been observed in Yoga and Sāṃkhya is indeed equal; for that which is supreme is vast and favorable.
"Know that the demonic view is: 'There is no one who intoxicates [us] more than Madhva; he alone is the Lord of All.
The divine view is: 'He exists. For in both cases, Hari alone is the one required."
"Keśava is the object and the bestower of the fruit of both prohibitions and injunctions;
he is also the cause of such a cognition regarding the high and low states. Thus [it is said]. (32)
Śrīdhara: Now, what is that Brahman whose powers become the ground for disputes and so forth?

To this he says: "It exists. Yoga refers to the scripture of meditation (*upāsanā-śāstra*); for in that [scripture], when meditation is performed upon the form of Virāṭ, it is enjoined as an object of worship that the netherworld constitutes his feet and so on. "It does not exist" refers to Sāṃkhya.

The Science of Knowledge (Jñānaśāstra). In that regard, [the text] negates the existence of feet and so forth by stating, "without hands or feet," "without eyes or ears. Whatever is common to both Yoga and Sāṃkhya, which persists, is observed, and is recognized—that is the Great Brahman; the meaning is that Brahman is the subject of dispute.
He clarifies the dispute: [it concerns] two distinct, contradictory properties (dharma) such as "existence" and "non-existence" belonging to two things.

Even if those two have different objects, there would be no contradiction; therefore, he says "residing in one. Why [must they reside in one]? Because they are grounded in a real entity (vastu), such as the affirmation and negation of a foot or other limb.
Because it is grounded in a single object. The reason for their equality is "the Supreme" (*param*).
For (*hi*) because [it is] beyond the scope of affirmation and negation, since those two have as their objects the feet and so forth.
If that is so, then what is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of that which is beyond such scope? To this he says: "conducive" (*anukūlam*).

The meaning is that [the Lord] is established as the basis for those two, because the conception of feet and so forth is impossible without a substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), and because their negation is impossible without a limit (*avadhi*). "Salutation to Him" is the syntactic connection (*anuṣaṅga*) with what precedes;
such is the arrangement of the sequence. In that context, at the occasion of the dispute, His essential nature is augmented by such qualities and forms.

He says "it exists" to show that it is indeed established. For at the time of the dispute among those who argue over the scriptural injunctions and prohibitions regarding the Lord's possession of name and form, he establishes that very point by saying "it exists. Yoga is the scripture concerning gross meditation; for therein, the Lord's possession of name and form is heard in the scriptures.

This is because of the parsimony of postulating that which is already seen [in scripture]. It is enjoined—that it does not exist—that it possesses all names such as "pot" and "cloth," and that it has the netherworld (pātāla) as its feet and so forth. For Sāṃkhya is a science of knowledge;
for in that system, whatever is denied by the prohibitive scriptures regarding its having name and form, that [is what is being negated here].
Since the state of being mundane name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is merely imagined, it is determined that it does not exist in any way whatsoever.
This was stated previously regarding both views in passages such as "He has all names and He is of universal form" (*sa sarvanāmā sa ca viśvarūpaḥ*),
and "Whatever is described by speech and defined by words" (*yad yan niruktaṃ vacasā nirūpitaṃ*) [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.4.28–29], and so forth.

He clarifies that very dispute concerning those for whom there is a finality regarding an entity as "it exists" and "it does not exist": [the dispute] belongs to those two who possess such contradictory properties as "it exists" and "it does not exist," which are distinct from one another.
Now, let it be granted that these two have different objects; he says "no," because they reside in one [subject] and share the same object.
Thus, when there is a dispute, whatever object is perceived as being consistent and is regarded as such, that becomes great and highly favorable for both. What is that consistency?
The meaning is that there is some reality which is distinct from name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and from its absolute non-existence, and which is characterized precisely by name-and-form.
This is what is being said: within a single reality, through both the affirmation and the negation of being name-and-form.

Otherwise, the scriptural texts would contradict one another in their meanings. However, in this case, since both [texts] are supreme, it is consistent with the previously stated reasoning that the purport of the injunctions and prohibitions establishes nothing other than the state of being endowed with non-material names and forms; thus, each respective view is merely a matter of dispute.
In this very way, Śrī Dhruva has stated here that there is no dispute [regarding this]:
"The distinction between the existent and the non-existent is recognized by animals, trees, birds, reptiles, gods, demons, mortals, and others."
"O Unborn One, Your form is the most substantial, beginning with the Great Principle (mahat) and consisting of many;

I know no higher reality than this, wherein there is no dispute. [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 4.9.13]. Here, because the word "form" (*rūpa*) alone serves as the substantive in both instances, it refers to both the "formed" (*rūpa*) and the "formless" (*arūpa*) supreme reality.

And furthermore, according to the Vaiṣṇava statement beginning with "cāparam eva ca" (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.7.47), the meaning of *vapuḥ* here is the form characterized by having four arms and so forth; this will be demonstrated further ahead. [Bhagavatsandarbha 38]

Viśvanātha: [Objection] But why are those who know the scriptures censured? If you say it is because the scriptures themselves lack unanimity and are mutually contradictory, we reply: do not speak thus; for he says, "There exists...
[referring to] Yoga and Sāṃkhya—Yoga being the scripture on the yoga of devotion (bhaktiyoga), and Sāṃkhya being the scripture on knowledge (jñāna). Of these two...

That well-known, supreme, most excellent, vast Brahman was observed as being equal and favorable; the meaning is that in observing those two scriptures, which are mutually contradictory, there is no discrepancy or opposition whatsoever.
Of what nature are these two? They possess distinct and contradictory attributes, such as "it exists" and "it does not exist.

For in the Yogaśāstra, [the Lord] is enjoined as an object of worship through the description: "He who is dark, clad in saffron-colored garments, lotus-eyed, four-armed, and bearing weapons such as the conch and mace," and so forth; thus, "He exists" is established.
For in the Sāṃkhya treatise, that which is nameless, formless, devoid of qualities, without hands or feet, without eyes or ears,
and though one and without a second, is denied even the existence of name, form, and so forth; thus, when two such properties—
which are distinct and mutually contradictory— belong to two things, there is no contradiction provided their spheres of application are different.
"May it be so"—this refers to two [cognitions] residing in one [object]. The meaning is that they both take as their object the single Brahman alone, abiding in that very Brahman.
[Objection: If that is so, then how can there be non-difference or non-contrariety? To this he says: "because they are grounded in the real entity (vastuniṣṭhayoḥ)."

Those two [scriptures] have as their defining characteristic the establishment of a final conclusion regarding the vastu—that is, the actual reality itself. Therefore, by means of the method of the Bhakti-śāstra, they teach only the actual reality and not that which is unreal.
Thus, through that Bhakti-śāstra, [they establish] the Supreme Lord’s forms such as Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and so forth.

Once the establishment of entities such as name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) has been accomplished, even the science of knowledge (*jñāna-śāstra*), precisely because it is grounded in reality (*vastu-niṣṭha*), does not negate that name-and-form for him; rather, it negates it only for his illusory form (*māyika-mūrti*), namely the Virāj. For this very reason, the science of devotion (*bhakti-śāstra*) likewise...
One does not adopt the Virāṭ form as an object of worship, for it is prohibited by the scriptures of knowledge (jñāna-śāstra). As it has been said:
"These two forms of the Blessed One have indeed been described to you by me; the wise do not accept either of these, as they are created by Māyā" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 2.10.35).

Thus, even the inclusion of the form of Virāj in meditative concentration (*dhāraṇā*) is intended solely for the purification of the mind during the initial stage for certain individuals, and not for the purpose of worship at all times; therefore,
in reality, there is no contradiction between the scriptures on devotion (*bhakti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*), and thus there is no conflict between the scriptures.
The sense is that it is precisely the philosophers (*dārśanika*), who dispute while being ignorant of the intended meaning of the scriptures, who are at variance with one another.
He who, for the sake of bestowing grace upon those who worship at the soles of his feet...
The Blessed One is nameless and formless, infinite;
yet he assumed names and forms through his births and deeds— may that Supreme One be gracious toward me.
Because his actions are invisible, he is nameless; and because he is unseen, he is formless. Yet, through an incarnation, he displays forms and actions.

"Though he is eternal in form and eternal in action, he is called 'formless and actionless' with reference to his unmanifest state, because he is devoid of form and action. Thus it is said in the *Prakāśasaṃhitā*.
"He is nameless because his significance is beyond [conventional] limits; he is formless because of his unmanifest nature."
And it is said: "The forms manifested through incarnations possess the same nature as Kaṃsāri and others. Furthermore:
"The primary names of Keśava have meanings that transcend worldly perception;
however, names such as Dāmodara and others are indeed identical with worldly perception."
"Ānanda, however, is the manifest form, while the primordial form (mūlarūpa) has been described [as the unmanifest].
That very same [primordial form], having attained manifestation, is declared to be the incarnation (prādurbhāva). Thus it is said. (33)
Śrīdhara: Now, one might ask what benefit there is in offering salutation to one who is indifferent and equanimous; to this he says: "He who...

Though devoid of material name and form, for the sake of bestowing grace upon those who worship at the soles of His feet, He assumed through His births and incarnations pure forms that have conquered the quality of *sattva*, as well as names corresponding to those deeds.
Why is that? The Blessed One possesses inconceivable sovereignty; may he be gracious toward me. (33)
The sequential composition clarifies that very point: He who, being indeed devoid of name and form, assumed names and forms—that is, he manifested them along with his births and deeds.
He states the fault of the contrary case: if that Infinite One were not possessed of name, form, and so forth, then...
Otherwise, it would follow that the possession of those powers must itself be finite. As it has been said by the Pracetasas:
"For there is no end to Your manifestations; therefore You are celebrated as Ananta (the Infinite)" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 4.30.31).
The cause for the manifestation of each respective [aspect] is the Blessed Lord, who possesses power whose essence is *bhaga*.

He negates the illusory nature (*māyātva*) of that power: the sense is that in Him, *mā*—namely Lakṣmī—is of the nature of the power called *parā*, for otherwise there would be a contradiction of His supreme transcendence (*paratva*).

Therefore, it is not the case that everything arises from illusion or that everything originates from divine sovereignty; for since the Lord is indeed devoid of illusion (*amāya*), they know Him to be supreme. Thus it has been said.
Now, one might object: even if He possesses the form of all names and is yet devoid of them, there certainly exist various practitioners of those respective [forms].
This is the authority. Anticipating the question "Who might these be? he says: "For the sake of bestowing grace upon those who resort to his feet.
The true reality of Yoga and Sāṅkhya does not shine forth clearly; rather, it is in devotion alone.
This is because of such scriptural statements as, "Devotion alone reveals him," and so forth. Therefore, regarding what was said concerning those two:

The sense is that it is merely a matter of dispute. For this very reason, it will be stated immediately thereafter—in passages such as Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.4.356: "O best of the Kurus, the Lord, who is affectionate toward His devotees, appeared...
having placed His foot upon the shoulder of Suparṇa," and so forth. By the phrase "to those who worship at the root of His feet," He refers to them.

It is indicated that form exists even prior to its manifestation by such scriptural passages as, "The foot is pure, revealed, and ancient. The use of the past tense in the word *bheje* (he worshipped) indicates beginninglessness (*anāditva*) for the sake of strengthening its authority. Furthermore, the term *ananta* (infinite) refers to His names and forms.
And the sense is that they are indeed infinite; and here the commentary states: "even though devoid of natural name and form. ||33||

[Bhagavatsandarbha 38] Viśvanātha: Then, manifesting the non-contradiction between the two classes of scriptures through the injunctions and prohibitions regarding names, forms, and so forth, he prays for the grace of the Lord, who is affectionate toward His devotees, upon himself: ya...

Thus [it is said]: "Though devoid of name and form"—meaning, although free from material name and form, he who, through his births or incarnations, assumed pure forms and names by means of his activities; thus says the venerable Svāmīcaraṇa. He "assumed" (bheje)—that is, he manifested them within the phenomenal world (prapañca). ||33||
He who, dwelling within the bodies of people, shines forth according to their inclinations through the paths of ordinary knowledge— (o)0(o)— .
Just as the wind takes up the quality inherent in the earth,
may that Lord fulfill my heart's desire.
Regarding the Madhvas: the lowest declare Hari to be merely the individual soul (jīva) residing within one's own body;
the middling ones, however, hold Janārdana to be distinct from the individual soul, though not yet definitively determined as such.

The supreme ones declare Hari to possess qualities such as fullness and bliss, and to be distinct from all individual souls; and among those [souls], they describe them according to their relative gradations.

"According to the purification of the intellect, people of middling capacity speak of that which resides in the body as mere breath, following their vital strength, yet they do not determine it definitively; whereas those who know the vital breath call the thread [of consciousness] the Lord of the God of Gods, which is bliss. Thus [it is said]. (34)

Śrīdhara: Now, one might object: "Those like you, who possess desires, pray to Gaṇeśa and others; why then do you, abandoning them, pray to the Blessed Lord alone? To this he replies: He [the Lord], who [is attained] through the worldly, modern paths of knowledge—that is, the paths of worship—according to one's disposition, in accordance with that particular latent impression (*vāsanā*).

The inner controller residing within the body shines forth in various ways through the forms of this or that deity. Just as the wind, by resorting to the specific qualities of the earth such as the diverse fragrances of the *campaka* and other flowers, appears to possess manifold scents;
or just as it is perceived to possess manifold colors by resorting to the quality of dust, such as its greyish hue—in the same way, it is with that very [inner controller].
The meaning is this: since He alone, in the form of various deities, bestows the fruits [of action], may that very Lord make my desire come true;
what is the use of other deities who are like internal tumors? As it is said in the Gītā:
"Whichever devotee desires to worship whichever form with faith..."
"Whatever firm faith a person has, that very faith I establish for them.
Endowed with that faith, they strive for the propitiation of that [deity], and from that they obtain their desires, which are indeed ordained by me alone. Thus [it is said].
"In whatever way they approach me, in that same way do I favor them"—thus it is said.

Regarding the sequence of the composition: [an objection is raised]—"But surely, for you who desire specific powers (*vibhūti*), worship of me is appropriate only by means of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as Gaṇapati and others, each conjoined with their respective powers."
How can you praise [the Lord] as being entirely without attributes? To this he replies: "He who, by means of the material elements...

The point is that since it is established that in each instance it is the Lord himself—and not the limiting adjunct—who acts like the wind to produce his own effects, what is the use of conceiving of him as having an adjunct? ||34||

Viśvanātha: Thus, by the verse "He with whom there is no friendship" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.4.24), and by the verse "Every man knows his own qualities, but he who knows Him does not know them; I praise the omniscient Infinite One" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.4.25), the real distinction between the individual soul and the Lord is established through their states of limited knowledge and omniscience respectively.

Thus, their distinctness has indeed been established. Consequently, by the statements "when there is the cessation of the mind" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.4.26) and "within the heart of the wise" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.4.27),
that very same single Lord is shown to be accessible through both extraordinary non-dual and dual knowledge.
The nature of the Lord as both without attributes (*nirviśeṣa*) and with attributes (*saviśeṣa*) has been manifested according to my understanding.

Furthermore, by the three verses beginning with "He indeed is all" (*sa vai samāśeṣa*, Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.4.28), it is stated that although phenomenal objects possess His nature, they do not constitute His essential nature. Again, [it is said]: "He exists," "He does not exist."
[Śrīmad Bhāgavatam 6.4.31] By means of this twofold [verse], the non-contradiction between the scripture of devotion (*bhakti-śāstra*) and the scripture of knowledge (*jñāna-śāstra*), though hidden,

has been made clear. Now, regarding those who consider themselves wise (*jñāni-mānin*) and assert that the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) is merely caused by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and not real— that is their adherence to an improper path.

Manifesting the fulfillment of his own heart's desire, he prays: He who, by means of ordinary and recent paths of knowledge, shines forth as the individual soul (*jīva*), pervaded by the very qualities of those people— whether seen or unseen— without transgressing their respective inner dispositions (*āśaya*, i.e., the internal organ) residing within their bodies.
Just as the wind, by resorting to a foul or refined odor belonging to the earth, comes to possess various odors, yet not in reality. ||33||
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus praised by him who was offering praise during that *aghamarṣaṇa* rite, he...
O best of the Kurus, the Blessed One, who is affectionate toward his devotees, appeared.
Śrīdhara: As Dakṣa was offering praise, that Blessed One became manifest before his eyes. ||35||
The sequential arrangement: thus, [the section] ending with "iti" consists of five and a half [verses]. ||35||
Viśvanātha: [This was spoken] to Dakṣa as he was offering praise. ||35||
With his feet placed upon the shoulders of Garuḍa, possessing eight great arms that hang down,
he holds the discus, conch, sword, shield, bow, noose, and mace.
Śrīdhara describes him with four and a half verses: he whose feet are placed upon the shoulders—that is, the back—of Suparṇa; he who possesses eight long and great arms;
and he who bears the eight weapons, beginning with the discus. ||36||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— He is clad in yellow garments, dark as a rain cloud, with a serene face and eyes.
His body was draped with a forest garland, and he shone with the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem.

Śrīdhara: He whose face and eyes are serene; whose limbs, from the neck down to the feet, are draped with a forest garland (vanamālā); and whose [chest] possesses the shining Śrīvatsa and Kaustubha. Viśvanātha: This has not been commented upon.
Wearing a great crown and bracelets, with shimmering crocodile-shaped earrings,
he was adorned with a girdle, rings, bangles, anklets, and armlets.
Śrīdhara: He whose crown and armlets are great; he whose crocodile-shaped earrings shimmer;
he who is adorned with a girdle and other ornaments. Here, the *valaya* should be understood as an ornament for the feet, since the *kaṭaka* has already been mentioned. ||38||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: A *kaṭaka* is an anklet; a *valaya* is one worn on the hand. ||38||
Bearing a form that deludes the three worlds, the Lord of the Three Worlds was surrounded by his attendants, Nārada, Nanda, and others, as well as by the leaders of the hosts of gods.

Śrīdhara: [It refers to] the Trailokyamohana, known as Śrī Puruṣottama, [worshipped] by the leaders of the hosts of gods and the world-protectors. Viśvanātha: [This] has not been explained in the Kramasandarbha.
Being praised by the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Cāraṇas who sang his praises,
he was struck with awe upon beholding that great and wondrous form.
"By whom was this not explained?
Prajāpati, his soul filled with joy, prostrated himself on the ground like a staff.
He was unable to utter anything because of his intense joy,
which filled the gates of his mind like torrents from a mountain spring filling a lake.

Śrīdhara: The doors of the mind, which are the senses, were filled by those [words]. Just as rivers are filled with torrents, so too, because he was enveloped by the fullness of great bliss (*mahānanda*), he was unable to say anything at all through speech or other means; this is the meaning. ||41||

The sequence of composition: By means of the doors of the mind—the cognitive senses—which are filled with intense and ultimate joy consisting of that very love abiding within one's own self, and which are thus filled with every part through their respective absorptions; by these [senses] which are like torrents or outpourings of water, being filled with every aspect of one's own self through those various states of immersion.
"Like lakes," so it is said. ||41||

Viśvanātha: Just as lakes are filled by torrents, so too were the gateways of the mind—the senses such as sight and the rest—filled with joy and bliss; for that reason, he was unable to utter anything, to speak, to see, or even to hear. ||41||
To Prajāpati, who was thus bowed down in devotion and desirous of offspring, Janārdana— who knows the hearts of all beings— spoke this.
Śrīdhara: Although he did not say this, nevertheless, knowing the [disciple's] mind, he spoke the following sequence; Viśvanātha: it has not been explained. )o(0o(0)
The Blessed Lord said:
O highly fortunate son of Pracetas, you have attained perfection through your austerity,
since by means of supreme faith directed toward Me, you have reached the highest state of being within Me.
Śrīdhara: *Bhāvam* means devotion (*bhakti*). *Gataḥ* means attained (*prāptaḥ*). ||43||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: "Supreme devotion toward me"—that is, the highest contemplation that "this very person is the Supreme Self."
I am pleased with you, O Lord of Creatures, because of this asceticism of yours which increases your strength; it is my desire that all beings may attain prosperity.

Śrīdhara: Since this austerity of yours causes the "udbṛhaṇa"—the increase—of this universe, therefore I am pleased with you. To the question, "What is the reason for my pleasure if my own austerity is for the sake of the world's prosperity? he says: "mameti" (mine). It is precisely this [desire] that [arises]: "May the prosperities—that is, the successes—of all beings flourish."
This is my desire; therefore, the meaning is that I am pleased solely because of the fulfillment of my wish. ||44||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: That asceticism of yours which was the cause of the expansion (*udbṛṃhaṇa*)—the growth—of this universe, is my very own desire; the meaning is that your asceticism was accomplished solely by my will. Now, [an objection]: "But..."
He states what the nature of his desire is there: "May the prosperities, that is, the abundant successes, of all beings be [mine]," as expressed in the words, "That this very one... (44).
Brahmā, Bhava, you Manus, and the lords of the gods—
these are indeed my manifestations, the causes of prosperity for all beings.

Regarding the term *madhvaḥ*: Śrīdhara states in the *Tantranirṇaya*, "The manifestations (*vibhūtayaḥ*) such as Brahmā and others are the vessels for the specific manifestation [of sweetness], while the incarnations (*vibhavāḥ*) such as the Fish and others are the inner controllers (*antaryāmiṇaḥ*) of that [sweetness]. He says "Brahmā" etc., meaning that the effort to expand the manifestations of beings is indeed appropriate for you.
O venerable ones, you are the Lords of Creatures, the causes of the emergence of all beings. ||45||
The sequential arrangement: [Objection] But how can there be a desire for manifestation in you, who are free from desire?
It is said in reply: it is solely through affection for the devotees, due to their connection with Him. Thus he says: "Brahmā... etc.
For Brahmā and the others, being My devotees, are indeed My manifestations (*vibhūtayaḥ*); and they, in turn, are the causes of prosperity for others. ||45||
Viśvanātha: But [the Lord] says that those like you are indeed base—"Brahma," etc. (verse 45).
"O Brahmin, my heart is asceticism, my body is knowledge, and my physical form is ritual action; the sacrifices have become my limbs, Dharma is my soul, and the gods are my vital breaths."
Madhu is Rudra, the presiding deity of austerity, who has taken refuge in the heart of Viṣṇu;
likewise, Umā, whose form is knowledge, has likewise taken refuge in the body of Viṣṇu.
"Indra, the subduer of Pāka, whose essence is action, assumes the forms of the erotic sentiment and the rest;
all sacrifices reside in his limbs, and the King of Dharma (Yama) resides in his torso.
Vāyu is his vital breath, Brahmā and the other deities reside in his mind, and each resides in their own respective [deities]. Thus it is said.
"That which exists depending upon something else is designated by that [latter's] name"—thus it is stated in the *Śabdanirṇaya*. (46)
Śrīdhara: It was stated that "I am pleased by your austerity for the sake of the world's prosperity.
Praising that very austerity, he incidentally praises other means such as knowledge (*vidyā*) which also bring about the world's prosperity.

Austerity (*tapas*) is meditation accompanied by restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*); it is my heart. Knowledge (*vidyā*) is the recitation of mantras along with their auxiliary branches (*sāṅga*).

She [is the sacrifice]. It is called *tanu* because it extends meditation (*dhyāna*); it is the body (*deha*). Action (*kriyā*) refers to the human activity directed toward meditation and so forth, which is denoted by the word *bhāvanā*, for by means of it meditation and the like are performed; thus it is the form (*ākṛti*). The sacrifices (*kratu*) that have been produced are the well-perfected limbs (*aṅga*). Indeed, the *pravargya* is the head, and the *upasads* are the neck.

This is based on the Vedic scripture stating, "The two eyes are the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāgau*)," and so forth. *Dharma* is the unseen potency (*apūrva*) of sacrifices and the like; *ātman* is the mind, because it has its locus in the heart. *Surā* refers to those who enjoy the sacrifice, who are indeed the vital breaths (*asavaḥ* = *prāṇāḥ*), because they are to be fully satisfied.
Regarding the sequence of the composition, he says "austerity" (*tapaḥ*), for devotion is indeed his internal power.

Viśvanātha says: "Listen to my form as it is appropriate for the yoga of action (karmayoga)"—thus he speaks. Austerity, consisting of restraints (yama), observances (niyama), and so forth, is my heart. Knowledge, consisting of the recitation of mantras along with their ancillaries (aṅga), is my body. Ritual acts, such as the obligatory (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites, are my appearance or form. Sacrifices are my limbs; indeed, this [body] is the head.

According to the Vedic revelation, "The Pravargya [ceremony] is the neck; the Upasad [offerings] are the eyes; the two Ājyabhāga [portions] are the eyes," and so forth, these have come into being. Dharma is my *apūrva* (unseen potential) arising from ritual acts; my mind is the *ātman*; my vital breaths are the gods.
For me, whose nature is Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*), austerity and the like are the manifestations of my heart and other limbs. (46)
—I was indeed alone in the beginning; there was nothing else, neither within nor without.
There was only the unmanifest state of consciousness, as if entirely asleep.
O Madhva, that form of mine which you have perceived through austerity was merely a manifestation; in the beginning, it was indeed that alone.
Yet Hari, though one, possesses various colors, many heads, and many arms by virtue of his form.
But that other [aspect] remained in a subtle form, devoid of splendor.

"Though not asleep, Hari appeared as if asleep with eyes closed; it is said that Śrī, out of disregard for Viṣṇu, seemed as if she had vanished elsewhere. Furthermore, because of its subtlety, other things are also considered to have dissolved from their place into Hari. Thus [it is stated] in the *Mātsya Purāṇa*. (47)

Śrīdhara: To demonstrate that austerity is the cause for the increase of progeny, he relates the history mentioned in the second and third [sections] in four verses. "I alone" excludes any other entity; "I was indeed" excludes any other action. "Internal" refers to the subject (*grāhaka*); "external" refers to the object (*grāhya*). It is merely consciousness (*sañjñāna-mātra*).
It is pure consciousness alone; it is unmanifest, not being made manifest by the functions of the senses; for this very reason, it is as if asleep everywhere, in all respects. ||47||

The sequential arrangement: In that regard, he says "I am" to show that the devotee alone is the cause for my connection with creation and so forth; it should be understood that this refers to this world as a lotus, and not to Vaikuṇṭha. ||47||

Viśvanātha says: "Listen to my true nature as it is appropriate for the yoga of devotion"—"I alone existed before creation, distinguished by this very form, clothing, ornaments, weapons, vehicle, and attendants; likewise, I shall exist in the future after the great dissolution."

The word *eva* [is used] because the word *agre* denotes both prior and subsequent time; however, the attainment of "I am indeed" (*asmy eva*) at the present moment is obtained by its own nature alone, thus demonstrating one's own existence throughout the three periods of time.
Furthermore, there is nothing else internal or external to me, because my essential nature is all-pervasive.
And its possession of inconceivable power has been demonstrated, as will be stated:
"That which is neither within nor without, neither before nor after;
that which is both before and after, without and within, and which is both the world and that which transcends the world."

"Thinking him to be his own son, though he was the unmanifest Adhokṣaja bearing a mortal form, the cowherd woman bound him with a rope to a mortar as if he were an ordinary being. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.9.13–14). Thus, he says "Listen to His true nature as it is appropriate for the yoga of knowledge": "He is mere consciousness, mere sentience."
The unmanifest is ungraspable by the functions of the senses everywhere and in all respects. ||47||

Within me, who am infinite and possessed of infinite qualities, there arose from my very qualities the one whose form is composed of qualities; from that alone was born the primordial, self-existent, and unborn one.
Regarding the sweetness [of Madhva]: "Infinite in terms of qualities.
It is proclaimed that the qualities are individually boundless;
that infinity is due to their qualities, for they are indeed infinite in number.
"Therefore, Viṣṇu possesses infinite qualities, and by virtue of those qualities, he is indeed infinite. Thus it is stated in the Tantrabhāgavata. ||48||
Śrīdhara: "From the qualities" means from Māyā. The cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) is composed of the qualities (guṇamaya). Therefore, at that very time, he was "unborn," meaning not born from a womb. ||48||
The sequential arrangement: he demonstrates devotion itself through the words "in me" (mayi) ||48||

Viśvanātha: Having taught the existence of his own essential nature, he tells a historical narrative (itihāsa) in order to impel [the world] toward creation, beginning with the words "In me" (*mayi*). "From the qualities" (*guṇataḥ*) means from Māyā. The "form of the qualities" (*guṇavigrahaḥ*) is the Great Universal Aggregate (*mahāsamaṣṭi*), the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*);
from that, right in its midst, is Svayambhū, the first of you all. (48)
When Mahādeva, empowered by my prowess, prepared himself for the task of conquering heaven, he indeed considered himself as if rendered useless.
Śrīdhara: It is like something fragmentary or incapable [of its purpose]. ||49||
The sequential composition is strengthened by potency; it is born from potency. ||49||
Viśvanātha: [He is] like something deficient or incapable. ||49||
Then, being thus addressed by me, the Lord performed severe penance,
by which the All-pervading One first created you nine creators of the universe.
Śrīdhara: Being addressed by me with the words "Tap, tap" (perform penance), [he performed] that penance by which... ||50||

The sequential arrangement: he demonstrates his devotion with the words "atha" (now). Therefore, even for you, the state of being the cause of the manifestation of prosperity arises precisely from being a devotee. ||50||
Viśvanātha: Being addressed by me with the words "Perform penance, perform penance," he [performed] that penance by which... ||50||
"O limb of Pañcajana, this daughter of Prajāpati,
named Asiknī, is offered to you; O Lord of Creatures, please accept her as your wife."
Śrīdhara: He states the means for the increase of progeny with the words "This [is]... O friend! O Dakṣa!
[This is] of the Prajāpati named Pañcajana. (51)
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* does not provide an explanation.
Viśvanātha says: "He says, 'Eṣā... (o)0(o), [meaning] "You too should strive in the paternal dharma which consists of all forms."
Possessing the nature of sexual union, you shall again bring forth this creation of beings in great numbers through sexual union with those who possess that same nature.
Śrīdhara: You are one for whom sexual union—that is, the pleasure of the couple—is itself the dharma; [I bow] to you who are thus disposed toward her. ||52||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha*: not commented upon.
Viśvanātha: —o)0(o)—
