Below you, all creatures shall come into being through my illusory power (māyā) by means of sexual union,
and they shall offer tribute to me.
Śrīdhara: By means of *māyā* acting as the instrumental cause, having united with women, they will come into being, arising in the form of sons and so forth. ||53||
Kramasaṃdarbha: "Having become united" means simply having become united.
Viśvanātha: "They shall come into being" means they will be born in the form of sons and so forth. ||53||
Śrī Śuka said:
Having spoken thus while he was looking on, the Blessed Lord, the creator of the universe, [disappeared].
Like an object perceived in a dream, Hari vanished right there.
It has not been explained by anyone at all. Thus [ends the section] in the *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose minds are devoted.
This fourth [chapter] of the sixth book has been completed, being well-composed for the virtuous.
Thus ends the Sixth Canto in the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā, the Pāramahaṃsyasaṃhitā, which is the Commentary on the Brahma-sūtras within the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, the Great Purāṇa.
The Fourth Chapter, titled "The Praise of Haṃsaguhya.
Now begins the Fifth Chapter.
Śrī Śuka said:
In that city of Pañcajanya, he was indeed augmented by the illusory power of Viṣṇu (Viṣṇumāyā).
The powerful lord begot ten thousand sons known as the Haryaśvas.
Śrīdhara:
It is described that in the fifth [chapter], having heard that his sons had been destroyed by Nārada through deceptive words, Dakṣa cursed him. 1.

The sequence of composition: "He spoke" (*uvāca*) and so forth constitutes a group of four. Where the five multiplied by five are of the nature of the supported (*āśrayin*), that house is of the nature of the support (*āśraya*) and is wonderful. (1)
Viśvanātha:
By means of a deceptive word, he indeed made the Haryaśvas and Nayas Vaiṣṇavas;
it is described that in the fifth [chapter], Nārada was cursed by Dakṣa. (1)
O King, all those Dākṣāyaṇas were of uniform character and conduct;
when commanded by their father regarding the creation of progeny, they departed toward the western quarter.
Śrīdhara: They are not distinct in their virtuous conduct; they are of one and the same character and behavior. ||2||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— Therein lies the holy site (tīrtha) of Nārāyaṇasaras at the confluence of the Sindhu and the ocean.
Where there is a very great confluence, frequented by sages and perfected beings.
Śrīdhara: The grammatical construction is as follows: they went to the holy place named Nārāyaṇasaras, situated where the river Sindhu and the ocean meet in that western direction;
it was *sumahat*, meaning exceedingly vast. ||3||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not commented upon.
Viśvanātha: In that direction lies the great Nārāyaṇasara Tīrtha, where there is the confluence of the river Sindhu and the ocean. ||3||
By the mere touch of that [water], their latent impurities were completely shaken off,
and their minds became fully awakened to the Dharma and the supreme state of the *paramahaṃsa*.
Śrīdhara: Those whose inner disposition (*āśaya*) is such that impurity, such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth, has been completely shaken off. ||4||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— Constrained by their father’s command, they performed fierce ascetic penance.
He beheld those celestial sages who were striving for the increase of progeny.

Śrīdhara: He saw that those beings, though composed of pure essence (*śuddhasattva*), were nevertheless striving with diligence for the increase of their progeny due to the dullness inherent in the command of their fathers. (5)
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: "Those who were thus prepared" (yattān udyatān). ||5||
And then Haryaśva said: "How indeed will you create progeny, O guardians, when you have not even seen the end of the earth? Alas, you are but fools!"

Śrīdhara: Alas, what a pity! These virtuous ones, who are qualified for the path to liberation, might be ruined by actions devoted to worldly engagement (*pravṛtti*). Out of compassion, [the Lord] instructed them with words of hidden meaning.
Thus he says in four verses beginning with "He said": "O you fools, though you are protectors, how [can you be so ignorant]?"
"Will you create progeny?"—the word "batā" expresses grief. In the reading "bālakāḥ," it serves as the reason for their childishness. ||6||
Kramasaṃdarbha: This has not been explained.
Viśvanātha:
These [beings], possessing pure internal organs, are qualified for the dharma of liberation (mokṣadharma).
Why do they immerse themselves here in this ritual act out of compliance with their father?
"Therefore, by teaching them the truth through cryptic speech, I shall liberate these beings"—
thus did the compassionate Nārada speak those deceptive words.

"O Haryaśvas! Having not seen the end of the earth, how will you create progeny? It is not explained here that they themselves will do it first after having explained [it]; therefore, you are merely childish fools, because you are children (*bālaka*). If the reading is *pālakāḥ*, then even though you are protectors of the subjects (*prajā*), you [are still fools]."
Only fools [think so]. "Batā" expresses astonishment. ||6||
Likewise, one should avoid a kingdom ruled by a single man, a cave from which there is no exit,
a woman of many forms, and a man who is the husband of an unchaste woman.

Śrīdhara: [The phrase] "that kingdom in which there was only one person" is to be supplied as the object of "not having seen. As for the words ending in the accusative case, such as "a hole" (*bila*) and so forth, their syntactical connection with the third verse—"how will you effect creation?"—is not explained in the *Kramasaṃdarbha*.

Viśvanātha: [The phrase] "that kingdom where there is but one person," and so forth—how will you create the world without understanding these words ending in the accusative case? Thus they are connected with the third [verse]. ||7||
A river flowing in both directions, a house with five times five wonders; in one place a swan of variegated speech, a barber’s shop, and wandering about oneself.

Śrīdhara: [It is] the wondrous abode of the twenty-five, consisting of five groups of five. "Made of *kṣaura-pavī*" means it is exceedingly sharp and firm, as if constructed from razors and *pavīs* (thunderbolts).
"Self-existent" (*svayam*) means independent. "Whirling" (*bhramim*) means having the nature of rotation. ||8||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.

*Viśvanātha*: Viṣṇu is the wonderful abode of the twenty-five principles—the five times five—flowing outward in both directions; he is so called because he bestows the supreme state of perfection (*sāṅguṇya*).
The sense is that those [weapons] ought to remain right there for the sake of the devotees; it is some kind of object made of razors, *pavi*-missiles, and *vajra*s, exceedingly sharp. ||8||
—o)0(o— How can you wise ones, not knowing the command of your own father, create a creation that is unsuitable and uncomprehending? Oh! How will you bring it forth?

Śrīdhara: Not knowing the command of their father, the omniscient Vipaścit, which was suitable for themselves, and not understanding what was previously stated—that the kingdom consists of a single person and so forth—the [demons] said, "Alas! How will you bring about creation? This is the syntactical connection. ||9||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: Of the wise one, the omniscient one. ||9||
Śrī Śuka said: Having heard that, the Haryaśvas, by means of their innate intelligence, [reflected].
They themselves reflected with their intellect upon the secret of the divine sage’s speech.
Śrīdhara: A "cryptic speech" (*vācaḥkūṭa*) is a statement that appears, through indirect expression, as if it were something else.
Those whose innate wisdom (*autpattikī saha-jā manīṣā*)—that is, their power of discernment—is such, reflected upon it themselves, having deliberated by means of that intellect. ||10||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: A "cryptic expression" (vācaḥkūṭa) is a statement that, by means of indirect speech (parokṣavāda), appears as if it were something other than its actual meaning. ||10||
The field known as the individual soul (*jīva*) is beginningless and its own bondage;
without perceiving its liberation (*nirvāṇa*), what would be the use of unwholesome actions?

Śrīdhara: With ten verses, he states the meanings determined by them after deliberating upon the ten statements spoken by Nārada. Regarding the phrase "not having seen the end of the earth" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.5.6), he explains the meaning of the word *bhū*:
"The earth (*bhū*) is the field (*kṣetra*); and here, that is the subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*) known as the individual soul (*jīva*). Which...
"One's own bondage" means the cause of one's own imprisonment. He states the meaning of the word "end": it is *nirvāṇa*, which is destruction.
What would come of actions that are non-existent and useless for liberation? Nothing at all. ||11||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.

*Viśvanātha*: He himself explains the ten statements spoken by Nārada in ten verses for the sake of easy understanding. Among them, regarding the verse beginning with "Without having seen the end of the earth" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 6.5.6):

He explains: "Bhūḥ" is the field (*kṣetra*). And here, that is the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) known as the individual soul (*jīva*). Since it is the beginningless—that is, devoid of a beginning—bondage of the innate individual self (*jīvātman*), its "extinction" (*nirvāṇa*) means its destruction through knowledge; that is the meaning. By means of those intermediate paths of action consisting of non-virtuous deeds (*asatkarma*), by that...
The intended meaning is: "On the contrary, you should strive precisely for the sake of nirvāṇa through karma. ||11||
There is but one Lord, the Fourth (turya), the Blessed One, the supreme who rests in Himself.
Without beholding Him, what can arise for a person through evil deeds?
Śrīdhara explains the meaning of the verse *ekapuruṣam* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.5.7) with the words "He alone," etc.

He is the Fourth (*turya*), the witness of all. "Self-supported" means having himself as his own substratum. "Unborn" means eternally liberated. "By unreal deeds" means by actions not offered to the Lord. ||12||

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: Likewise, he explains the passage from the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* (6.5.7), "The kingdom has but one person," with the word "one" (*eka*). The "Fourth" (*turya*) is distinct from the Viśva, Taijasa, and Prājña states; it is the fourth.

The kingdom is to be understood as the world. For devotees who strive, there is no longer existence—that is, the cycle of worldly birth (*saṃsāra*) does not exist. The sense is: "Without seeing [the Lord] through worship, He is not perceived; therefore, worship Him alone.
Since a man does not return once he has gone to that state, just as one who has entered the subterranean heaven [does not return],
what would be gained here by those who know the inner abode through unwholesome actions?

Śrīdhara explains the meaning of the verse, "And the cave whose exit is unseen" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.5.7): "The Person, having gone to—that is, reached—the cave-heaven, does not return at all, like one who has gone to Pātāla;
that is the inner abode, the Brahman in the form of light. For the ignorant person (*aviduḥ*), by means of the unreal..."
By means of ritual actions that are the instruments for attaining perishable results such as heaven. ||13||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha* explains the verse beginning with "a cave from which there is no exit" (*bilaṃ cādṛṣṭanirgamaṃ*, Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.5.7) as follows: "The person" (*pumān*).
Having gone to—that is, having reached—the abode of the inward-facing Lord (*pratyagdhāma*), namely Vaikuṇṭha... [he does not return].

"He returns no more; he does not turn back again. The meaning is that, like one who has gone to the subterranean heaven (pātāla-svarga), he remains fixed right there. The sense is: "Therefore, strive for the attainment of Vaikuṇṭha by those people who are ignorant (of this). ||13||
The intellect, which possesses various forms and is endowed with the qualities (guṇas), is like a wanton woman;
for one who has not attained steadfastness in that [intellect], what would be the use of evil deeds in this world?

Śrīdhara explains the meaning of the verse *bahurūpāṃ striyam* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.5.7) as follows: "Nānārūpā" means like a wanton woman (*puṃścalī*). She is accompanied by the delusive qualities of *rajas* and so forth.
"Tan-niṣṭhām" refers to her end, that is, discernment (*viveka*), which has not been reached—that is, not attained—by those who are wicked and unpeaceful.

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha* explains the verse beginning with "bahurūpāṃ striyam" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 6.5.7) as follows: "nānā... etc. Like a wanton woman, she is intent upon wicked objects; "guṇāḥ" refers to beauty, cleverness, and so forth.

And [the qualities] such as scholarship are endowed with those [faculties]. The meaning is: for one who has not reached its culmination—that is, for one who does not know and does not investigate the auspicious or inauspicious course of action. Therefore, the intention is: by means of discernment (*viveka*), turn the intellect toward Kṛṣṇa. ||14||
For one who, like a wretched wife, wanders through saṃsāra having lost his sovereignty due to attachment to that [world],
what could possibly come of evil deeds here for such an ignorant person?
Śrīdhara explains the meaning of the verse *pumāṃsaṃ puṃścalīpatim* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.5.7):
"One whose sovereignty and independence have been lost through association with her; one who possesses a contemptible wife, being like that;
wandering—that is, going—through her states characterized by pleasure and pain."
The living being of one who is ignorant and does not understand [the truth], by means of unrealities attained through the lack of discrimination of the intellect. ||15||

The sequence of the composition: "His sovereignty has been lost through association with that" (refers to the following). Thus, the soul's inherent capacity, consisting of its own knowledge and so forth, has been demonstrated. ||15||
Viśvanātha explains the phrase "the unchaste wife's husband" (*puṃścalīpatiṃ*) from Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.5.7 with the word *tat*:

"like a householder with a contemptible wife," he refers to the transmigrating individual soul (*jīva*). The absence of the genitive case (*abudhasya*) is an archaic Vedic usage (*ārṣa*); it means "of one who does not know"—that is, one who does not even know the destinies such as heaven and hell.
Therefore, the sense is: "Lift up yourselves by means of your own selves. ||15||
What can be gained by the improper actions of one who is intoxicated and ignorant of that Māyā, which brings about creation and dissolution and possesses the speed of the ocean's tide at its shore?

Śrīdhara explains the meaning of the verse *nadīm ubhayato vāhām* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.5.8): "It performs both creation and dissolution" (*sṛṣṭy-apyayau karoti*)—thus the flow from both sides is shown. *Velā* means the shore;
the exit point for those fallen into the current is the vicinity of that shore, which consists of austerity, knowledge, and so forth. *Vegitām* means "with great speed."

[He is] impeded from departing by anger, egoism, and so forth, which have generated momentum; thus, he is intoxicated and rendered helpless by that momentum. For this very reason, he is "unaware," meaning he does not reflect upon her being in such a state. [He is led] by the wicked, those who are deceptive. Alternatively, it means near the shore of the ocean, which is a place of worldly commerce.

Just as a river becomes turbulent on both its inner and outer sides due to the rising and falling of the ocean, so too does the Self—which is comparable to the ocean—become turbulent within the body at every stage of worldly activity (*vyavahārasthāna*) through birth, death, and so forth; this is the meaning. In the reading *veginīm*, it means "possessing velocity."
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha* explains [the verse] "flowing on both sides" (*nadīm ubhayato vāhām*, Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.5.8): she brings about creation and dissolution; thus, at the time of creation, the principles (*tattvas*) [arise] one after another from the preceding.

They emerge during the time of dissolution, each subsequent one entering the preceding one; thus, the flow is shown to proceed in both directions. "Velākula" means the vicinity of the shore, according to the lexicographical definition that *velā* refers to either the shore or the water.
For those fallen into the current of *saṃsāra*, the means of exit is austerity, knowledge, and so forth.

In that very state, [the mind] has been made impetuous by well-observed anger, egoism, and so forth—possessing asceticism, knowledge, and the like—for the sake of obstructing its departure; there is also a reading "vegītām" (impelled).
Thus, for one who is intoxicated and rendered helpless by those various impulses, and consequently ignorant and unreflective regarding it in such a state.
The sense is: therefore, having abandoned even worldly status and the like, go to the further shore. ||16||
The Puruṣa is the wondrous mirror of the twenty-five principles;
for the ignorant person here, what can come of unwholesome actions regarding the inner self?
Śrīdhara explains the meaning of the verse *pañcapañca* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.5.8):

"The Person is the inner controller (*antaryāmī*) of the twenty-five principles; He is the support, the wondrous form, the mirror of marvels; He is the presiding deity over the internal aggregate of causes and effects; [He is the refuge] for the ignorant."
By the wicked, who have fabricated false independence. ||17||

The structural arrangement: The Puruṣa is a marvelous mirror, consisting of the aggregate of the twenty-five principles like those of metals; he is the locus for the reflection of the Self, as a face is reflected in a mirror. [This is] the divine [nature], consisting of the Lord’s play (*līlā*), because it has been described as "wondrously variegated" (*citrakatha*). These are distinct words.
Because all objects [are derived] from that. ||17||

Viśvanātha explains the phrase "the house of five times five wonders" (*pañcapañcādbhutagṛham*) from Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.5.8, beginning with the word "five": "The Person, Viṣṇu, is the mirror of wonders. For devotees indeed offer their own thoughts and so forth—the twenty-five principles—to Viṣṇu alone, and these...

Having become stainless and non-material, they abandon their reflected state and come to possess the very nature of the mirror that is the form of Viṣṇu; such is the marvelousness of the mirror that is the form of Viṣṇu. However, a reflection such as a face in another ordinary mirror is merely the appearance of the object exactly as it exists.

The meaning is that he would not be one who grasps at the purity residing in a mirror. That person, Viṣṇu, exists within the self (*adhyātma*) as the Self itself; [the text speaks of] the ignorant one who does not know Him as the object of service.
Therefore, the intention is: "Surrender both the body and the self to Hari. ||17||
Having cast aside the scripture of the Lord which reveals bondage and liberation,
and failing to understand the state of solitude, what would one achieve through unwholesome deeds?

Śrīdhara: He states the meaning of the verse beginning with "kvacid dhaṃsam" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.5.8). "Aiśvaram" means that which establishes the Lord. The explanation of the word *haṃsa* is: that by which the distinct state (*viviktam padam*)—the reality consisting of both consciousness and the insentient—is [perceived]. It is so called because it demonstrates bondage and liberation. By this, [the verses are] diverse...

The phrase "of whom there is discourse" has been explained. Setting that aside, [it concerns] those who practice what is not [the truth], the ignorant, the undiscerning, and the wicked who are turned outward. ||18||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha* explains the verse "Sometimes he tells wonderful stories" (*bhā.pu.* 6.5.8): "Relating to the Lord" (*aiśvaram*) means that which establishes the Lord; [it concerns] bondage and liberation through various [means].

"He instructs by means of discourses" is explained as "wondrous discourse. "Like milk and water, he by whom the self and the reality of the self are distinguished" is explained as the "swan's footprint" (*haṃsapada*).
Since it is precisely there that words—namely, nominal and verbal endings—are distinguished and joined with investigation, it is appropriate that the finality resides right there.
Therefore, the intended meaning is: "One should worship Īśvara for the sake of liberation. ||18||
The sharp wheel of time revolves, drawing out the entire world;
for one who is independent in this world, what can be achieved by evil deeds?

Śrīdhara explains the meaning of the verse *kṣaurapavyam* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.5.8) with the words "the wheel of time" (*kālacakra*). He interprets the term *kṣaurapavya* by explaining that it is "rotating" (*bhrami*), meaning its nature is to revolve, and "sharp" (*tīkṣṇa*), meaning it "extracts" (*niṣkarṣayat*). Therefore, for one who is ignorant, because of the notion that the fruit is eternal, [it acts in this way].
Because of the great abundance of defects in the performance of rites for desired ends, [these are practiced] by the wicked. //19//
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* does not provide an explanation.

Viśvanātha explains the verse *kṣaurapavyaṃ svayaṃ bhrami* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.5.8) as follows: "The wheel of time (*kālacakra*); it has turned away as if by means of two razor-sharp arrows (*kṣura-pavibhyām*)."

Because it bestows fear, it is "Kṣaurapavya"; because its nature is wandering, it is "Bhrami"; because of its sharpness, it is "Tīkṣṇa"—it drags one away and destroys. The underlying meaning is: "By this [weapon], you will die tomorrow or the day after; why then do you not worship Hari? ||19||

How could one who does not know his father’s instruction from the scripture— which serves as the means of cessation— proceed toward that [instruction] by placing trust in the qualities of one who merely conforms to it?

Śrīdhara explains the meaning of the verse *svapitur ādeśam* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.5.9): "Of the scripture, which is the cause of his father's second birth; for one who conforms to that, i.e., for one who conforms to renunciation (*nivṛtti*). How can he who does not know the instruction that brings about cessation be one who places his trust in the *guṇas*?"
One who possesses confidence in the path of activity consisting of the *guṇas* should undertake it and proceed at the beginning of creation.

But for those whose intellects perceive liberation, the Lord, or Brahman [in the self], and for those who are the individual soul, *māyā*, or the inner self—what is the use of ritual acts when there is ignorance regarding the scriptures, the time, and the instructions? Thus it is said.
A verse summarizing the essence of speech. ||20||

The sequence of the composition: for knowledge corresponding to that, which is in accordance with cessation (*nivṛtti*). The implication is that if one does not know that, one would be bound right there. ||20||

Viśvanātha explains the phrase "not knowing the command of their own father" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.5.9) as follows: "Of the scripture" (śāstrasya). For the father is not merely the one who performs the *ādhāna* rite; rather, it is the scripture itself that constitutes the father's command, and that command serves only to restrain, not to incite. Therefore, regarding whose command...
If he does not know that which causes cessation, then how could he begin to act in accordance with that [cessation] or in accordance with the instruction?

For this person places his confidence solely in the path of activity regarding the qualities (guṇas), and thus believes, "This alone is the instruction. Therefore, there is the command of the scripture and of the father who follows the scripture regarding the dharma of cessation.
The explicit meaning (dhvani) is that service is real; one should protect that very service alone.

Therefore, the implicit meaning (anudhvani) is that since the teacher Dakṣa lacks true fatherhood—being contrary to the essential intent of the scriptures—there is no sin for you in failing to obey his command. Consequently, [you should receive] from me alone [the grace of] Viṣṇu...
"Having received the mantra, sit down in some secluded place and worship Viṣṇu alone"—this is the universal proclamation. (20)
"O King, having thus resolved with one mind, the Haryaśvas set out along that path from which there is no returning."
Śrīdhara: Thus they were resolved; having thus determined, being of one mind and possessed of unanimity, they circumambulated Nārada and departed upon the path from which there is no return. ||21||
Kramasandarbha: This has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: Those by whom [the matter] has been specifically concluded or ascertained—those who are of one mind, possessing a single consensus—having circumambulated...
Even acts such as honoring the guru, receiving the nectar of his feet, and prostrating like a staff are indicated—
in the resonance of Brahman, which shines forth as the lotus feet of Hṛṣīkeśa.
Having entered into an undivided state of mind, the sage wanders through the worlds.
Śrīdhara: "Nirbhāta" means manifested or directly perceived; [he] followed at the lotus-feet of that Hṛṣīkeśa—this is the meaning. ||22||

The sequence of the composition: This activity of Nārada is entirely due to his devotion to the Blessed Lord, which consists of the desire to direct [everyone’s] attention toward Him; thus he says, "In the Brahma-svara.
This is the inherent nature of the highest musical mode (*svara-jāti*). It is that which, in general, [directs one] toward the object of one's own longing.
The experience is that it specifically causes the devotees to remember the Blessed One. ||22||

Viśvanātha: "Alas, alas! So many living beings have been rescued from hell; I shall now offer glory to their Lord"—thus he describes Nārada’s immersion in an ocean of bliss. Regarding Hṛṣīkeśa, who is manifested there as the direct realization through the playful singing of the *brahman* which is the very notes, such as *ṣaḍja* and the rest:
At the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa, who attracts all the senses.
Having heard from Nārada of the destruction of his virtuous sons,
Kaḥ lamented, grieving that the possession of good offspring is but a locus for sorrows.

Śrīdhara: *Nāśam* means disappearance, invisibility, or the falling away from one's own duty (*svadharma*). They are so called because they shine or are resplendent by virtue of their character (*śīla*). Who is capable? [The answer is: "Possession of good offspring" means having virtuous sons.
It is the abode of sorrows—that is, of griefs. (23)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "Destruction" means, in the view of householders, the very loss of Vaiṣṇavism; that [loss] has occurred. Who was Dakṣa? He lamented: "Alas, alas! Such sons of mine have been led astray by Nārada."
He despaired. "Possession of good offspring" means having virtuous sons. "The abode of sorrows" means the place of griefs;
he lamented, thinking that it is only those who have witnessed the sorrow and suffering of the world who come to possess good offspring. (23)
Being further consoled by Aja, that Dakṣa begot upon Pāñcajanī thousands of sons known as the Valāśvas.
Śrīdhara: By Aja, that is, by Brahmā; "sahasraśaḥ" means by the thousands. ||24||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not commented upon. Viśvanātha: "Savalāśvān" means those named Savalāśva; "sahasriṇaḥ" means numbering one thousand.
Commanded by their father to create progeny, they, firm in their vows,
went to the Nārāyaṇa lake where their own ancestors had attained perfection.
Śrīdhara: "The supreme Brahman" refers either to the syllable *praṇava* or to the mantra that is about to be described. ||25||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
By the mere touch of that [water], those whose inner dispositions have had their impurities completely shaken off...
Chanting the supreme Brahman, they performed great asceticism there.
Śrīdhara: [This is] the *Kramasaṃdarbha*; it has not been commented upon.
Viśvanātha: "The supreme Brahman" refers to the mantra that is about to be described. (26)
For some months they subsisted on water, and for others on air;
practicing this mantra, they propitiated Iḍaspati.
Śrīdhara: They propitiated Viṣṇu, the Lord of Speech and the Lord of Mantras. ||27||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
Oṃ, salutations to Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person, the Great Soul.
We meditate upon the Great Swan, whose abode is the pure being.
Śrīdhara: We meditate upon the Supreme Swan, who has pure being as his support; salutations to him. ||28||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been explained. —
Thus, O King of kings, the sage [spoke] to those who were intent upon the creation of progeny.
Having approached, Nārada spoke deceptive words as before.

Śrīdhara: He spoke of those whose intellects are fixed upon re-creation, referring to the previously mentioned verses beginning with, "Without seeing the end of the earth, the peaks of speech... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.5.6). ||29||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
O descendants of Dakṣa, listen to my Vedic teaching as I speak it!
"O you who are affectionate toward your brothers, follow the path of your brothers as they search."
Śrīdhara says: "O daughters of Dakṣa, listen," and so forth; he speaks further as well. "Nigama" means instruction. "Anvicchata" means look for it. ||30||
Kramasaṃdarbha: not explained. Viśvanātha: "nigama" means instruction. ||30||
When brothers depart this life, that brother who, knowing the Dharma, follows after them,
becomes a man whose merit is shared with his kin and rejoices together with the Maruts.
Śrīdhara: *Prāyaṇam* means an excellent departure. He whose kinsmen are merit alone, and who is accompanied by the gods—the Maruts—who are affectionate toward their brothers. (31)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Departure (*prāyaṇam*) means renunciation (*pravrajyam*), by the gods who are brothers and thus affectionate toward their kin.
This very example has been stated: "But you [should depart] together with your elder brothers who are going to Vaikuṇṭha."
The meaning is: "you will rejoice. ||31||
Having said this much, Nārada, whose vision is never in vain, departed;
they too, O noble one, followed the path of their brothers.
Śrīdhara: He whose sight is never in vain. O Māriṣa, noble sir! ||32||
Kramasaṃdarbha: not explained.
Viśvanātha: "Māriṣa" means "O noble sir. ||32||
Having gone together toward the west along the path of the far horizon,
they have not yet returned, like the final watches of the night.

Śrīdhara: *Sadhrīcīnam* means favorable or appropriate. *Pratīcīnam* means obtainable through an inward-turned disposition. *Anupatham* means along a suitable path. They are like the final watches of the night that have passed. ||33||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: *Sadhrīcīna* means "concordant" or "proper. *Pratīcīna* refers to the path of devotion (*bhaktimārga*) which is favorable to the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) and is attainable through the inward-turning of consciousness (*pratyagvṛtti*); it is the "western," meaning the nights that have passed.
...as it were. ||33||
At that time, observing many portents, Prajāpati heard,
as before, of the destruction of his son brought about by Nārada.
He was not explained by anyone at all.
Fainted with grief for his son, he became enraged at Nārada.
Having encountered the divine sage, he spoke with his lower lip quivering in rage.

Śrīdhara: Having heard of his sons’ commitment to the state of the paramahaṃsas, Dakṣa too would likely become dispassionate; therefore, for the sake of bestowing grace upon him, the divine sage went to his side. Upon finding him there, Dakṣa spoke to him. (35)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Having approached the divine sage [Nārada], [it was said that] all the lineages of Svāyambhuva Manu—such as Priyavrata, Uttānapāda, Dhruva, and others—were indeed established by the Blessed One through me alone.

They were made his own; even the great Prācīnabarhis, though dulled by the weight of his karma, was uplifted. His ten sons, the Pracetasas, and his grandsons—the ten thousand Haryaśvas and the thousand Savalāśvas—were all delivered.
How so? For he alone, Dakṣa, remained in the midst of them, like one trapped in the blind well of a house.

Reflecting, "He plays about; I shall uplift him as well," and having now heard of his sons' attainment of the supreme state of *pāramahaṃsya*, Dakṣa himself grieves and dwells mostly in a state of world-weariness at home. Therefore, this is the auspicious time to bestow grace upon him. Even though—
Thinking, "Even now he does not seek me out; therefore, I myself shall go to his house," she spoke upon encountering Nārada as he arrived there. ||35||
—o)0(o— Śrī Dakṣa said:
"Alas! O wicked one, by you, who bear the outward mark of a virtuous man, the virtuous have been [betrayed] by us."
An improper course of action, unfit for children, has been shown as the path for a monk.

Śrīdhara: By you, who possess the outward appearance and dress of a virtuous man, an unrighteous act has been committed against our children. He explains that very point: "The path of a mendicant has been shown to the virtuous who are engaged in their own duty. (36)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "By you who possess the marks and dress of a saint (*sādhu*)," meaning by you, a great hypocrite. The plural number is used out of respect for "us," the saints. [The phrase] "of me, the saint, you... [is understood].

The sense is that even though you have not harbored enmity toward me even in a dream, by saying "you have done what is improper and inauspicious," a great offense has been committed by you in this time.
Now, one might ask: "What improper thing was done? To that he says: "Of the children"—that is, my boys.

Unable to endure the enjoyment of the pleasures of household life, you, out of envy, [spoke] to the mendicant, to the world of mendicants, and to children; because they were merely children, they were simple-minded and accepted the instruction of you, a hypocrite—this is the intended meaning. In this regard, [it is said]: "Since there is no one who is virtuous..."

He was such a person; by means of the marks of a saint—those who possess such marks or signs—he was shown to be one from whom no true saint exists, in such a manner that it might be so. Thus, the intended meaning of Sarasvatī should be understood. This applies likewise to the subsequent verses. Furthermore:
It has not been explained here for fear of prolixity. ||36||
For those who are not freed from the three debts and have not examined their actions,
an obstacle to the higher good is created, resulting in sin in both worlds.
Śrīdhara: [Objection: But surely the path of the renunciant is indeed excellent, because it is the cause of liberation. [Reply: True;

however, without the discharge of the three debts, there is only great misfortune. Thus he says: "By debts... According to the Vedic tradition: "A Brāhmaṇa, being born, is born indeed burdened with three debts—to the sages by means of celibate studentship, to the gods by means of sacrifice," and so forth.
According to the Vedic revelation: "He indeed is free from debt who has a son, who is a sacrificer, or who has lived as a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*).

For those who are not released from their debts—that is, those by whom the [three] debts have not been discharged through investigation and performance—there is no liberation from debt for the time being, because [liberation] occurs only after that period.

Due to the absence of both the procreation of sons and the performance of sacrifices, there is no liberation from the debts owed to the ancestors, the gods, and the sages. Therefore, O sinful one! by renouncing the enjoyment of sense objects, you have obstructed your welfare in this world;
and because you lack the qualification for liberation, you have also obstructed your welfare in the next world—this is the meaning.
And so Manu says:
"Having discharged the three debts, one should apply the mind to liberation;
but he who pursues liberation without having discharged them goes downwards" (Manu 6.35). ||37||

The *Kramasaṃdarbha* has not been explained. Viśvanātha says: Now, if it is argued that only the path of mendicancy is capable of delivering one from saṃsāra, and not the life of householders such as yourselves, he replies with the verse beginning "With debts" (*ṛṇaiḥ*). "A Brāhmaṇa, indeed, being born... [and so forth].

"One is born with three debts: to the sages through Vedic study (*brahmacarya*), to the gods through sacrifice (*yajña*), and to the ancestors through progeny (*prajā*). He alone is free from debt who has a son, who performs sacrifices, or who is a celibate student," according to such scriptural passages.
For those who are not released from these debts—those by whom their duties have not been scrutinized or investigated—for them, first of all...

There is no liberation from the debt to the sages (*ṛṣi-ṛṇa*). Furthermore, because they occur at a time subsequent to that [attainment], there is also no liberation from the debts to the ancestors and the gods due to the absence of procreating sons and performing sacrifices.
Therefore, O sinner! O betrayer of trust! by depriving me of the enjoyment of sense objects, you have deprived me of prosperity in this world.

"Obstruction": even though one lacks the qualification for liberation (*mokṣa*), because [the teacher] incites [him] toward dispassion (*vairāgya*), he has brought about an obstruction to the highest good (*śreyas*) even in the next world; this is the meaning. And so says Manu:
"Having discharged the three debts, one should direct the mind toward liberation."
"But one who pursues liberation without having discharged [his debts] goes downward. [Manu 6.35] ||37||
Thus, devoid of compassion, you wander shamelessly in the midst of Hara’s retinue, destroying the reputation of the simple-minded through your intellect.

Śrīdhara: He is so called because he shatters the minds of the ignorant regarding their attachments to sons and other worldly objects. Thus, being merciless and pitiless, how do you move among the attendants of Hari while acting as a destroyer of His fame? ||38||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: What can I say of you, a wicked man? You have brought even the Blessed One a bad reputation by acting as his servant; thus he says: "In this way," etc. "Niranukrośaḥ" means merciless or pitiless. [He says this regarding] the mind...

Because he destroys the intellect that is intent upon performing actions prescribed by the scriptures, you have become a destroyer of Hari’s glory; therefore, your offense extends even to Hari. By saying "in the midst of the assembly," it is implied that your offense has been committed against those like us—great souls who are Vaiṣṇavas—as well as against the Lord and His devotees.
It is indeed difficult to restrain him— the sense is that wicked deeds such as betraying the trusting are far from even being mentioned.
But surely the devotees of the Lord are always eager to bestow grace upon all beings?
Except for you, who destroy friendship and create enmity where none exists.

Śrīdhara: He expresses his very shamelessness with the words "nanu" (surely). The sense is: "Surely all the devotees of the Lord (*bhāgavatas*) are under the sway of a desire to favor all living beings; how is it that you do not feel shame while acting contrary to the welfare of living beings? ||39||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Furthermore, he says "nanu" (surely), meaning: "Since you have come before me, what kind of face will you show?
Therefore, shame on you, you shameless one! [The phrase] "except for you" (*ṛte tvām*) means "but you..."
The meaning is: "one who harms only living beings. The phrase "destroyer of friendship" implies: "even though he acts as a friend to us.
The phrase "causing enmity" implies: "having openly created enmity toward us, with what face do you appear before us again? Truly, you are shameless! How many more times shall I...?
The sense is: "I put you to shame. ||39||
"O Kevalin, it would be false for you to think that through this [teaching] men attain dispassion,
if you consider this [teaching] to be the severing of the bonds of affection."
Śrīdhara: Now, it is indeed through detachment that tranquility arises, and from tranquility comes the severing of the bonds of affection for living beings;
moreover, for one who is detached, the discharge of the three debts is not mandatory, as it is said:
"On the very day one becomes detached, on that very day one should renounce," or otherwise, "one may renounce even directly from the stage of studenthood."
Because of such scriptural passages as these, if you argue that by teaching detachment you have merely bestowed grace upon them, he replies:

"No. Even if you think thus, nevertheless, this detachment of men will not arise even when you, in the guise of an Avadhūta, attempt to unsettle their minds in this way through false knowledge, devoid of true realization.
It may be so. However, there can be no tranquility without dispassion, and without that, there can be no severing of the bonds of affection;
such is the meaning. ||40||
The sequence of events: This offense against Dakṣa by Śrī Nārada was due to the lingering evil impression from his ancient offense against Śiva. (40)

Viśvanātha: But surely their tranquility arises precisely from the dispassion instigated by me, and from that, the severing of the bonds of affection has already occurred. Furthermore, since it was inferred even today from the fact that they have not come to your father’s side, how can it be said that they lack the qualification for liberation? Nor is there a triple debt for one who is dispassionate.

Non-action alone is necessary, according to such scriptural injunctions as: "On the very day one becomes dispassionate, on that very day one should renounce," or "Or otherwise, one should renounce even from the stage of studenthood. If you argue that for this reason, I have already bestowed grace upon them by teaching them dispassion, we say: no. It is true that [grace was shown] through the compassion of Great Beings.

Dispassion (*virāga*) would indeed have occurred; however, although you—a false *kevalin*, devoid of knowledge, a mere ascetic, or one who considers himself a unique Vaiṣṇava—have thus caused such a disturbance of the intellect, even if dispassion were to arise for seven or eight days, from the standpoint of logic it would not be genuine dispassion. Even though you [possess] tranquility (*upaśama*),...
The meaning is that even what you imagine would not exist at all, because of your lack of being a Great Being (mahāpuruṣa). ||40||
A person does not know the sharpness of sense objects without experiencing them;
one becomes weary of them spontaneously, whereas one whose mind is divided by others does not do so in that way.

Śrīdhara: He states the reason why detachment would not arise in this way: "Without having experienced [them], one does not know the sharpness of sense objects—that is, their nature as causes of suffering. Therefore, [detachment arises] from the experience of sense objects and the resulting knowledge of their sharpness. ||41||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Therefore, he says "No," implying: "Since you are ignorant of this, hear from me the royal road.
One does not know the sharpness of sense objects—that is, their quality of producing suffering—without having experienced it; therefore, for that reason...
One might become weary of it by oneself simply through the knowledge of its extreme sharpness arising from the enjoyment of sense objects;
however, one whose mind is split—whose intellect is shattered—by others such as you does not do so. ||41||
Since you have committed an intolerable and disagreeable act against virtuous householders who are bound by their duties, it has been forgiven by me.

Śrīdhara: Therefore, you have indeed done us a displeasure; nevertheless, we do not act [upon it], as he says with the words "yat" (that which). Regarding "karmasandhānām," this means of those who maintain the boundaries of action (*karma-maryādā*). In the reading "kartum andhānām," the meaning is "those who do not know how to do what is disagreeable. That which you have done is difficult to endure.
"Marṣitam" means endured or tolerated. ||42||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: "In this way, just as you have harbored groundless enmity toward me, I too am certainly able to give back that very same retaliation, multiplied fourfold, of my own accord."
Nevertheless, he says "I do not give [it]," showing that even among us householders there is forbearance (*titikṣā*). He says "that which...

For those whose commitment (*sandhā*) or boundary (*maryādā*) lies solely within the path of action (*karmamārga*), or—in the reading *kartum andhānām*—for those who are blind to doing what is disagreeable to others; "unbearable" means difficult to endure.

The offense of you—an unrighteous man who has fallen from the bounds of knowledge, devotion, and decorum, yet possesses the eyes of a paramahaṃsa ascetic—to commit a supreme act of hostility against me, has been forgiven and endured. ||42||
"O weaver, because you have once again acted unkindly toward us,
therefore, O fool, there shall be no place for you to roam within the worlds."

Śrīdhara says: "Nevertheless, misfortune will surely befall you. O destroyer of the thread, O cutter of the lineage! Since you have brought about the misfortune of your sons—their displacement from their positions—therefore, there shall be no place or station for you as you wander through the worlds; this is stated under the guise of mildness.
The curse. ||43||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Nevertheless, he says that misfortune will surely befall you: "O weaver (tantukṛta), O destroyer of lineage (santānacchedaka), you have brought about (acaraḥ) misfortune (abhadram)—that is, you have caused the displacement from their positions of my sons."
*Pada* means a place. ||43||
Śrī Śuka said: Nārada, who is esteemed by the virtuous, accepted that proposal with the words, "So be it."
For such indeed is the praise of the virtuous: that the Lord himself endures it all.
Śrīdhara said: "Certainly, so be it," and thus he accepted. Although the Lord was capable of retaliating, he would simply endure it; that is all. 44.
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: "He accepted firmly" means he agreed, saying "So be it. "Approved by the virtuous" means that the virtuous indeed tolerate it in this very way. [This refers to] what is well-known.

He states that this same etymological explanation applies to the word *sādhuvāda* as well: "It is of such extent. Although the Lord was capable of responding, [Nārada] was indeed repeatedly insulted by Dakṣa even though he had come to bestow grace upon Dakṣa. In that regard:
Having heard those insults from Nārada, why did he not depart from his presence?

It is said: this was Nārada’s intention. "Let this man, being under the sway of anger, perform many insults and even cast a curse; for when [the time] comes, as it is said, 'this shall be the fruit arising from his anger.'"

When my anger shall be pacified, and when, seeing me enduring everything without offering even a word of contempt or the like in return, there arises in them a sense of remorse— just as it arose in Sanaka and the others who had returned from Vaikuṇṭha upon learning, "Alas, alas! This devotee of the Lord has been insulted and cursed"— then...

Thinking, "I shall depart after sowing the seed of pure devotion in this field which has become fit for the sowing of the seed of devotion," he remained there even for a moment. But Dakṣa, seeing that and remembering, "Alas!
How great is the intensity of the offense against the one who wears the crescent moon on his crest," withdrew from that place.

Thus ends the fifth chapter of the sixth [book] in the *Harṣiṇī*, titled *Sārārthadarśinī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted to the Lord; may it be well-received by the virtuous.
Thus ends the Sixth Canto in the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā, the Pāramahaṃsyam, within the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam*, the Great Purāṇa, which is a commentary on the *Brahma-sūtras*.
The fifth chapter, titled "The Curse of Nārada.
Now begins the sixth chapter.
Regarding the lineage of Dakṣa’s daughters,
the venerable Śuka said: Then the son of Pracetas, having been entreated by the Self-born (Brahmā), [beheld] Asiknī.
He begot sixty daughters who were devoted to their father.
Śrīdhara: In the sixth [chapter], the sixty daughters created by Dakṣa are proclaimed;
from them were born separate lineages, since Viśvarūpa was born from the son of Kīrti.
Fearing the destruction of his sons on account of Nārada, he begot daughters. ||1||
The sequential arrangement: It should be understood that these, beginning with Dharma, are also distinct from the aforementioned father-in-law and son-in-law. ||1||
Viśvanātha:
In the sixth [chapter], the lineages of Dakṣa’s daughters are described separately;
therein, from Tvaṣṭṛ, the son of Uditā, Viśvarūpa was born.

Thinking that Nārada, despondent due to grief for his son, would not abandon his enmity toward him even while resuming the life of a householder at the word of Brahmā, and fearing therefore the destruction of his own sons, he begot only daughters; thus he says, "Then," etc., [referring to] his wife Asiknī. ||1||
Ten [syllables] for Dharma, twelve from the body (Kāya), eighteen for Indu,
two each for Bhūta, Aṅgiras, and Kṛśāśva, and further, two for Tārkṣya.

Śrīdhara says: "To Kaśyapa" [is given]. "Dviṣaṭ-dviguṇāḥ" means those which are twelve (six doubled), that is to say, thirteen. "Indoḥ" means to Soma. "Triṇava" means twenty-seven. "Tārkṣyāya" refers to Kaśyapa himself who has obtained another name. The remaining four [verses] are the others. ||2||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: To Kāśyapa. "Twice six" means twelve, by which the lower number is excluded; thus, the meaning is thirteen. To Indra, that is, to Soma.

"Triṇava" means thrice nine, which is twenty-seven. "Dve dve" (two by two) refers to two for Bhūta and two for Aṅgiras. The remaining four are for Tārkṣya—namely, for Kaśyapa who bears the name Tārkṣya. ||2||
Listen to me as I recite the names of these women and their offspring,
by whose births and descendants the three worlds have been filled.
Śrīdhara: To those with offspring—that is, those accompanied by their children—listen to me. [This shall be told] through their progeny and descendants, such as sons, grandsons, and so forth. ||3||
*Viśvanātha*: The sequential arrangement has not been explained.
—o)0(o— Bhānu, Lambā, Kakud, Viśvā, Sādhyā, and Marutvatī.
The Vasus were his sons; listen now to [the account of] the Muhūrtas, the Saṃkalpas, and the wives of Dharma.
O bull among gods, O King, Indrasena was the son of Bhānu;
from Lambā came Vidyota, and from him were born the Stanayitnavas.
Śrīdhara: From that bull among gods. ||45||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon. —o)0(o— Since Kakuda was Saṃkaṭa, Kīkaṭa was his son.
From Yama came Bhuva, from whom Durga was born; from her came Svarga, and from him Nandi arose.
Śrīdhara: From Kīkaṭa were born the Durgas, the deities presiding over the fortresses of the earth; from Yāma was born Yāmya as his son, and from Svarga was born Nandi as his son. (6)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: From Kīkaṭa [come] the fortresses of the earth and the deities presiding over those fortresses; from Yāmi comes Svarga, the son of Yāmyā. (6)
The Viśvedevas were born of Viśvā, and they are said to be childless;
the host of Sādhyas was born of Sādhyā, and Arthasiddhi was their son.
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha; his son was the son of Sādhyā. ||7||
The sequence of composition has not been explained. —
Marutvān and Jayanta were born of Marutvatī.
Jayanta is a portion of Vāsudeva, whom they know as Upendra.
The hosts of deities known as Mauhūrtikas were born from Muhūrtā;
they indeed bestow upon living beings the fruits that arise according to their respective times.
Śrīdhara: Not commented upon.
Viśvanātha: Regarding the phrase "whom they know," the meaning is that Jayanta, like Upendra—the son of Aditi—is also designated by the name Upendra. ||8||
From Saṃkalpa, however, was born Saṃkalpa; Kāma is remembered as being born from Saṃkalpa.
The eight Vasus are the sons of Vasu; hear their names from me.
Śrīdhara: [The name] Vasu is mentioned at the end because his lineage is extensive. "Me" means from me. ||10||
The sequence of composition: because the lineage of Vasu is more extensive, it is mentioned at the end. From me [comes] Viśvanātha; this has not been explained.
Droṇa is Prāṇa, Dhruva, Arka, Agni, Doṣa, Vāstu, and Vibhāvasu;
from Droṇa’s beloved wife come joy, sorrow, fear, and the like.
Śrīdhara: His wife was named Abhimati, and their sons were Harṣa and the others. ||11||
The sequence of composition: his wife was named Abhimati; from her arose joy and the other [emotions]. ||11||
Viśvanātha: Not explained.
—o)0(o— Ūrjasvatī is the wife of Prāṇa; Saha, Āyus, and Purojava [are his sons].
Dharaṇī, the wife of Dhruva, gave birth to various cities.
Śrīdhara says: Saha, Āyu, and Purojava were his sons; *puraḥ* means cities. 12.
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
The wife of Arka is known as Vāsanā, and his sons are remembered as Tarṣa and the others.
The wife of Agni is Vasordhārā, and his sons are Draviṇaka and the others.
By whom was it not explained?
It was by Skanda, the son of Kṛttikā, and those such as Viśākhā and others thereafter.
The son of Śarvarī was Doṣa, who was a portion of Hari in the form of a porpoise.
Śrīdhara and Skanda, the son of the Kṛttikās and the son of Agni, are well known as Ṣāṇmātura and Agnibhū; [the lineage continues] from that Skanda. 14.
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Kṛttikā is the wife of Agni. ||14||
Vāstu, the son of Āṅgirasī, was Viśvakarman, the lord of forms;
from him came Manu Cākṣuṣa, and the Viśvedevas and Sādhyas were the sons of that Manu.
Śrīdhara: Ākṛtipati was the master craftsman (śilpācārya). From him, Viśvakarman, the Manu Cākṣuṣa, was born. ||15||

The sequence of composition: "Then Manu" constitutes half a verse. It is understood that although he was previously born in the lineage of Dhruva, he was born here again, just like Dakṣa, Vaśiṣṭha, and others. ||15||

Viśvanātha: [He was] the lord of Ākṛti. Therefore, although Manu Cākṣuṣa was born in the lineage of Dhruva, it is understood that he was also born here [in this lineage], just like Dakṣa, Vaśiṣṭha, and others. ||15||
The dawn, born of the sun, is the manifestation of light and heat;
it consists of five watches, by which living beings awaken to their duties.

Śrīdhara: The wife of Vibhāvasu is named Uṣas. Now, from the heat, the day has become five watches; for this very reason, the night consists of three watches (*triyāmā*). Since the periods of evening (*pradoṣa*) and dawn (*pratyūṣa*) are limbs of the day, their sequential arrangement has not been explained [separately].
Viśvanātha: Now, from sunrise, it is five watches; since dawn and twilight are parts of the day, the day consists of five watches. For this very reason, the night consists of three watches. ||16||
Sūta was the wife of Bhūta, and she gave birth to millions of Rudras:
Raivata, Aja, Bhava, Bhīma, Vāma, Ugra, and Vṛṣākapi.
Śrīdhara: Bhūta had two wives; he describes their lineage with the words beginning "Sarūpā" (verse 17).
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Bhūta had two wives; between them was Sarūpā. Raivata and the others are the eleven Rudras. ||17||
"Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Bahurūpa, and Mahān—
these and other fierce attendants of Rudra, such as the Pretas and Vināyakas."
Śrīdhara: Thus, the attendants (*pārṣada*) of Rudra, who possesses eleven forms such as Mahān, are the *preta*s and others;
others are born from different [sources]. ||18||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.
*Viśvanātha*: "Great" is the qualifying attribute; the other attendants (*pārṣada*) of Rudra were born of another wife. ||18||
Svadhā was the wife of Prajāpati Aṅgiras;
then that virtuous woman made the Atharvāṅgirasa Veda her son.

Śrīdhara: Aṅgiras had two wives, Svadhā and Satī; he describes their lineage with the words "of Prajāpati. His wife named Svadhā produced the Pitṛs as her sons, and Satī produced the Atharvāṅgirasa Veda. (19)
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Aṅgiras had two wives, Svadhā and Satī; between them, Svadhā—(o)0(o)—.
Kṛśāśva begot Dhūmaketu from his wife Arciṣmatī;
and from Dhiṣaṇā he begot Vedaśiras, Devala, Vayuna, and Manu.
Śrīdhara: Kṛśāśva had two wives, Arci and Dhiṣaṇā; he describes their lineage [beginning] with "Kṛśāśva" (verse 20).
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Kṛśāśva had two wives, Arcis and Dhiṣaṇā; between them, [the birth occurred] in Arcis.
Tārkṣya’s [wives] were Vinatā, Kadrū, Pataṅgī, and Yāminī;
Pataṅgī gave birth to birds, and Yāminī then gave birth to locusts.
Śrīdhara: [Not commented upon].
Viśvanātha: Of Tārkṣya, that is, of Kaśyapa named Tārkṣya. ||21||
Suparṇā gave birth to Garuḍa, the manifest vehicle of the Lord of Sacrifice;
Kadrū gave birth to Anūru, the son of the Sun, and to numerous Nāgas.
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha: Suparṇā is Vinatā; Anūru is Aruṇa. ||22||
The sequential arrangement has not been explained. —
O descendant of Bharata, the lunar mansions beginning with Kṛttikā are the wives of the Moon.
Due to the curse of Dakṣa, he was childless and afflicted by the seizure of consumption among them.

Śrīdhara: Due to his excessive love for Rohiṇī alone, he disregarded the other wives; consequently, being afflicted by the consumption-grasping (yakṣmagraha) and suffering from the disease of wasting (kṣaya), he became childless among them because of the curse of the enraged Dakṣa. ||23||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— Furthermore, having propitiated him once more, Soma obtained the digits that had been severed during his waning.
Listen to the names of the mothers of the worlds, which bring about well-being.
Śrīdhara: Having propitiated Dakṣa, she obtained only the digits (kalās), but not offspring.

Of what nature were they? They were those who had been "ditāḥ"—that is, shattered—in the *kṣaya*, meaning the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*). According to another reading, "when there was *kṣaya*," they were "edhitāḥ," meaning they were nourished and made to grow by him alone. ||24||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon. —o)0(o)— Now, that which was born from the wives of Kaśyapa is this world.
Aditi, Diti, Danu, Kāṣṭhā, Ariṣṭā, Surasā, and Ilā.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
The Sage, Krodhavaśā, Tāmrā, Surabhi, Saramā, and Timi.
The aquatic creatures were his attendants, and the beasts of prey were the offspring of Saramā.

Śrīdhara: Because they are few in number and easy to understand, he describes their lineages in their respective order, though not according to the sequence of the original list, beginning with the words "From Timer" (timer). ||26||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: She obtained only the *kalās* (digits), but not offspring—what kind of *kalās*? Those that were "split" (*ditāḥ*) or fragmented during the waning phase (*kṣaye*), i.e., the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*). According to the reading *kṣayaidhitāḥ*, it means those that were nourished again (*edhitāḥ*) once the waning had occurred.

Having increased them by that very same [process], he describes their lineages in the order of "the needle and the frying pan" (sūcīkaṭāhanyāya), beginning with the verse starting "of Timer" (timer). ||26||
—o)0(o— O King, from Surabhī came buffaloes, cows, and other animals with cloven hooves;
from Tāmrā came hawks, vultures, and the like; and from Muni came the hosts of Apsarases.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
O King, the serpents such as Dandaśūka and others are the offspring of Krodhavaśā.
All the trees of Ilā, as well as the Yātudhānas and the Saurasas.
Śrīdhara: The Saurasas are the sons of Surasā. ||28||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— As for the Gandharvas, they belong to Ariṣṭā; those with cloven hooves belong to Kāṣṭhā.
Danu had sixty-one sons; hear now of their principal ones.
Śrīdhara: Listen to the eighteen principal [categories] belonging to Pradhāna. ||29||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
Dvimūrdhan, Śambara, Ariṣṭa, Hayagrīva, and Vibhāvasu;
Ayomukha, Śaṅkuśiras, Svarbhānu, Kapila, and Aruṇa.
Pulomā, Vṛṣaparvan, Ekacakra, Anutāpana,
Dhūmrakeśa, Virūpākṣa, and the invincible Vipracitti.
Namuci, it is said, married Suprabhā, the daughter of Svarbhānu;
and the powerful Yayāti, son of Nahuṣa, married Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan.
It has not been explained by anyone whatsoever. And those four daughters of Vaiśvānara, who were beautiful to behold—
Upadānavī, Hayaśirā, Pulomā, and likewise Kālakā.
Śrīdhara, Viśvanātha, and Vaiśvānara were the sons of Danu; their sons were [the following]. ||33||
The sequence of composition has not been explained. —
O King, Hiraṇyākṣa was the Upādāna sacrifice, and Kratu was Hayaśiras.
Who indeed [married] Pulomā and Kālakā, the two daughters of Vaiśvānara?
Śrīdhara: The grammatical construction is: "Which Prajāpati, Kaśyapa, did she marry? ||34||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
Then the Blessed Kaśyapa, impelled by Brahmā, took a wife.
The Paulomas and Kālakeyas were Dānavas distinguished for their prowess in battle.
Śrīdhara: The reason for the marriage to Dānavī was that he had been urged by Brahmā. ||35||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: The cause for the marriage of Dānavī was urged by Brahmā. From those two, sixty thousand Nivātakavacas were born; and while you had gone to heaven, he [killed] them.
The grandfather Arjuna slew him. ||35||
O King, when his father had ascended to heaven, the grandfather of those two— who alone acted for the pleasure of Indra— slew sixty thousand sacrificial-slayers.
Śrīdhara: Sixty thousand sons, the Nivātakavacas, were born to them; and Arjuna, having gone to heaven, slew them along with their grandfather. 36.
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
Vipracitti begot one hundred and one sons upon Siṃhikā.
Those who have attained the state of a planet, including Rāhu as the eldest and a hundred Ketus.
Now, therefore, let the lineage of Aditi be heard in its proper sequence,
wherein the all-pervading Lord Nārāyaṇa descended by means of his own portion.
Vivasvān, Aryaman, Pūṣan, Tvaṣṭṛ, Savitṛ, Bhaga,
Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, Varuṇa, Mitra, Śatru, and Urukrama.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
From Vivasvat, Śrāddhadeva, Saṃjñā indeed gave birth to Manu.
And that illustrious lady gave birth to the twin pair, the god Yama and likewise Yamī;
then, having become a mare, she brought forth the two Nāsatyas upon the earth.
Śrīdhara: [He] generated those who were envious; [those] existing upon the earth. ||40||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Nāsatyau refers to the two Aśvinīkumāras. ||40||
Chāyā obtained Śanaiścara and then Sāvarṇi Manu;
she also obtained a daughter, Tapatī, who chose Saṃvaraṇa as her husband.
Śrīdhara: From him, Vivasvat [received it]. ||41||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— Aryaman’s wife was Mātṛkā; from those two were born the sons, the Carṣaṇis.
Wherein indeed the human race was fashioned by Brahmā.
Śrīdhara: *Carṣaṇayaḥ* refers to those possessing knowledge of what has been done and what remains to be done; it is listed as an object in the *Nighaṇṭu*.
"Wherein" (*yatra*) means in which [beings], for whom the human species is specially ordained through the particular contemplation of the Self.
And thus says the Śruti: "In the state of being a person (*puruṣatva*), the Self is more fully manifested. (42)

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: Of those two, Aryaman and Mātṛkā, the *carṣaṇayaḥ* (human beings) are those possessing knowledge of what has been done and what remains to be done. In whom—namely, in those distinguished by the contemplation of the Self—the human species is also manifested. And thus:
The Śruti says: "And in the state of being a person, the Self is more fully manifest. (42)
In ancient times, Pūṣan was childless, a consumer of flour, and his teeth were shattered;
he had laughed at Dakṣa while enraged, baring his teeth.
Śrīdhara: "Hara" is the understood object of the anger. "Vivṛtadvijaḥ" means having his teeth revealed.
"Kramasaṃdarbhaḥ" refers to [the sequence of events] in a former birth (purā). ||43||
Viśvanātha: [The phrase] "Rudra was enraged" is the ellipsis to be supplied. With his teeth bared, that is, with his fangs revealed—[he said:
"Tvaṣṭṛ’s daughter, a Daitya’s wife, a maiden named Racanā."
From those two, Sanniveśa and the powerful Viśvarūpa were born.
Śrīdhara: [This] has not been commented upon in the *Kramasaṃdarbha*.
Viśvanātha: The daughter of the Daitya was a girl named Racanā, the wife of Tvaṣṭṛ; by them—that is, by those two—(o)0(o)—.
The hosts of gods chose him as their kinsman on their mother’s side,
even though he had been abandoned by his preceptor Aṅgiras because of his lack of faith.

Śrīdhara: Whenever they were abandoned by Bṛhaspati, who was held in contempt and disregarded by them, they then chose Viśvarūpa—the nephew of their enemies and rivals—for the office of domestic priest. ||45||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
Thus ends the sixth chapter of the sixth book in the *Sārārthadarśinī*, the *Harṣiṇī*, which is perfectly suited for the hearts of devotees and is truly appropriate for the virtuous.
Thus ends the Sixth Canto in the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā, the Pāramahaṃsyam, within the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam*, the Great Purāṇa, which is a commentary on the *Brahma-sūtras*.
The sixth chapter, titled "The Lineage of Dakṣa’s Daughters.
Now begins the seventh chapter.
In the narrative of Viśvarūpa, the illustrious King said:
"For what reason did the preceptor abandon his own gods?"
O Blessed One, explain this to your disciples: the improper conduct toward a teacher.
Śrīdhara:
In the seventh [chapter], this Viśvarūpa was chosen for the office of domestic priest by the gods who had been abandoned by their preceptor; he then performed the duties of the priesthood.
For what reason, for what cause, have you abandoned your own disciples, the gods? This is an improper offense. ||1||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha:
In the seventh [chapter], by the gods who were defeated by the Daityas and abandoned by their preceptor...
Viśvarūpa was chosen as his preceptor for the instruction of the Veda.
The gods are his disciples. ||1||
Śrī Bādarāyaṇi said:
Indra, whose path of righteousness was transgressed by the intoxication of sovereignty over the three worlds, [acted].
O King, [he was honored] by the Maruts, Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, and Ṛbhus.

Śrīdhara: The construction of the eight verses is as follows: when that Indra did not welcome—that is, did not honor—the arrived Vācaspati, then that son of Aṅgiras departed from there and returned silently to his own home (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.7.9). He qualifies him [Indra] in order to show pride (*mada*), which was the cause of his disregard.
He by whom the path of the virtuous was transgressed through the intoxication of sovereignty over the three worlds. ||2||
The sequential arrangement: "Indra" consists of seven and a half [verses]. ||2||
Viśvanātha: When Indra did not welcome Vācaspati—that is, did not honor him—he returned to his own home; such is the connection of the eight verses [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.7.9]. ||2||
It was surrounded by the Viśvedevas, the Sādhyas, and the two Nāsatyas,
as well as by Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, and sages who discourse on Brahman.
Śrīdhara: "Pariśrita" means surrounded. ||3||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
[He was honored] by Vidyādharas, Apsarases, Kinnaras, birds, and serpents.
O Bhārata, while being served and praised, Maghavan [was pleased].
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
While being sung to in a charming manner, he sat gracefully upon his throne.
With a white parasol, as beautiful as the orb of the moon.
Śrīdhara: *Āsthānam* means an assembly hall; *adhyāsanam* in that [hall] refers to the lion-throne (*siṃhāsanam*), and he is seated upon it.
This sequence has not been explained [previously].
Viśvanātha: *Āsthānam* means an assembly hall; *adhyāsanam* in that [hall] refers to the lion-throne, and he has taken his seat there. ||5||
He was joined by other marks of supreme sovereignty, such as the yak-tail fans and so forth,
and he shone intensely together with Paulomī, who occupied half of his seat.
Śrīdhara: [He was] resplendent together with Paulomī, who stood upon half of his throne, adorned with the supreme insignia of a great king. ||6||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: [The phrase] "with the marks of a Great King belonging to the Supreme Lord" (*pārameṣṭhyair mahārājacihnaiḥ*). [The phrase] "by Paulomī, [that is] Śacī. [The compound] "she whose seat is half a seat" (*ardhāsanam evāsanam yasyās tayā*) is used here in the same manner as the expression "deer-eyed one" (*mṛgalocanā*), [referring to her] in the description of the one who offers the seat.
Inclusion. ||6||
When he did not welcome the arrival of the supreme teacher of the gods and of himself with rising from his seat, offering a seat, and other such honors;
Śrīdhara: He did not welcome him with rising from his seat and other such gestures; that is, he did not show him respect. ||7||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not commented upon.
Viśvanātha: [He approached] the teacher Bṛhaspati. ||7||
Indra did not rise from his seat even upon seeing Vācaspati, the best of sages, who is honored by gods and asuras, arrive at the assembly.
Śrīdhara says: "And he did not stir; even while remaining on his seat, he did not move in the slightest. ||8||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha* clarifies the very absence of rising to greet him: "Vācaspati. Although he had risen from his seat to another seat and was standing there, he did not move at all, nor did he stir. (8)
Then, having emerged suddenly, the lordly sage Aṅgiras,
the wise poet, returned silently to his own home, free from the agitation caused by pride.
Śrīdhara: Knowing—that is, being aware of—that transformation which arises from the intoxication of prosperity. ||9||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Then, from the assembly, the poet—knowing the future events as they will come to pass—[spoke].
The Lord is the ruler and the capable one; he [warned] the people because [the king's conduct] was a cause for disrespect toward his teacher. (9)
At that very moment, Indra, having awakened to his own offense against his teacher,
reproached himself by himself in the assembly.
Śrīdhara: Having awakened and recollected. ||10||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Having awakened from the sleep of the intoxication of Śrīmat; this is the meaning. ||10||
Alas! A truly evil deed has been committed by me, who am of feeble intellect, in that,
intoxicated by power, I treated my preceptor with contempt in the assembly."
Śrīdhara: Alas, the deed I have done is unwholesome! For by me, of dull intellect and small mind, he has been slighted and treated with contempt. (11)
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: "Kāt-kṛta" means disregarded or set aside. ||11||
What wise man would covet even the fortune of the Lord of the Three Worlds,
by which I, though once the sovereign of the gods, have today been reduced to the state of an asura?
Śrīdhara: I am also the Lord of the wise, the sattvic gods. 12.
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Having recognized that her own excellence is itself the cause for being treated with contempt, she censures it: "Who would covet [it]?"—that is, who would desire it? ||12||
Those who say that one who occupies the supreme position of Prajāpati should not rise to greet anyone do not know the highest Dharma.

Śrīdhara: Now, the elders say that a king seated upon his throne should not rise to greet [others]; to this he replies with two verses beginning with "He who... (verse 13). *Dhiṣaṇam* means a seat. (13)

The *Kramasaṃdarbha* has not been explained. Viśvanātha says: Now, those learned in the treatises on political ethics (*nītiśāstra*) say that a king seated upon his throne does not rise to greet anyone. True; however, they are indeed mistaken, as he says with the words "those who... [referring to] the state of being a supreme lord (*pārameṣṭhya*).
The seat of Parameṣṭhin is Dhiṣaṇā. ||13||
For those who follow the teachers of evil paths fall into the darkness below;
indeed, those who place their trust in their words sink like stone rafts.

Śrīdhara: Those who point out a wrong path are "those who teach a deviant path" (utpathadeṣṭāraḥ); their words are like a boat made of stone. Just as those with such a boat sink along with the sinking boat, so too is the arrangement of the sequence [of the commentary] not explained.

Viśvanātha: Just as those whose raft is made of stone sink along with the sinking raft, so it is here; thus, his anger toward his own courtiers, who were instructors in the principles of statecraft, was manifested. (14)
Then, free from guile, I shall propitiate that twice-born teacher of the immortals, whose intellect is unfathomable, by touching his feet with my head.
Śrīdhara: [He is] one whose intellect (dhiṣaṇā) is unfathomable and profound. Niśaṭha is one devoid of deceit (śāṭhya).
Kramasandarbha has not commented [on this].
Viśvanātha: Therefore, having reflected for a moment himself, [he considers] what indeed might be the remedy in this calamity.
Thus he said: "Then I... [referring to] Niśaṭha, being free from deceit (śāṭhya). ||15||
While Maghavan was reflecting thus, the Blessed One departed from his house;
Bṛhaspati, through the power of his inner self, went to an unseen state.
Śrīdhara: By means of His own supreme illusory power (māyā). ||16||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Disregarding Indra as he was thinking [of her], she [acted] with her own superior *māyā* toward him who was thinking [of her]. (16)
Not having received a name from his preceptor, the Blessed One, the self-ruling lord, examined it with his intellect; yet,
though joined by the gods as he meditated, he found no peace for himself.
Śrīdhara: Although he was examining the teacher’s name—that is, the means of knowledge—he did not find it; being unattained [to that goal], the sequence of the composition was not explained.
Viśvanātha: Although he was examining—that is, looking all around for—the name, which is the means of knowledge...
Not having attained, meaning not having reached [it]. ||17||
Having heard that, all the Asuras, relying upon the counsel of Uśanas,
being intoxicated with pride and acting as assassins, launched an attack against the gods.
Śrīdhara: "Assassins" refers to those with weapons raised. ||18||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha states: "It has not been explained."—
With their sharp arrows discharged, [the enemies] had their limbs, thighs, and arms pierced through.
With their necks bowed, they went together with Indra to Brahmā for refuge.
Śrīdhara: [This refers to] those whose limbs, heads, thighs, and arms have been pierced; this is the sequential arrangement [of the words]. Viśvanātha: [This has] not been explained.
Seeing them thus afflicted, the unborn Lord, the Self-born,
out of supreme compassion, spoke while consoling them.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
Śrī Brahmā said:
"Alas! O best of gods, you have indeed committed a great misdeed;
for you did not welcome the most excellent Brahmin, who was self-controlled and devoted to the Veda, because of your own power."
Śrīdhara: A great misfortune has been done to you, to you all.
He says this with the words "most devoted to Brahman" (brahmiṣṭham). They did not welcome it; they did not rejoice in it. ||21||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
This was the defeat of you [all] by others, resulting from his lack of policy.
O gods, that which belongs to those who have been enriched by their own vanquished enemies;
Śrīdhara: That which caused you to be defeated by enemies—that is, by your foes—was the fruit resulting from that misconduct, that injustice. And it has been said:
"A Brāhmaṇa endowed with noble lineage and devoted to the Great-souled Viṣṇu..."
"Seeing him approaching, one should not rise; he is overcome by sufferings.
[This refers to] those for whom their enemies are their own slayers. ||22||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: From others, from other [beings], from them. ||22||
"O Maghavan, behold those who were once your enemies, now utterly wasted by their transgression against their preceptor;
yet they are now being restored to prosperity once more by devotedly propitiating Kāvya."
May the deities of the Bhṛgu lineage take possession of my dwelling as well.

Śrīdhara: He states, by means of the example of the Asuras, that only the disrespect and honor shown to the guru are the causes of decline and prosperity—beginning with "O Maghavan. [They would seize] the enemies, the haters; those who had been made prosperous solely by serving the preceptor Kāvya Bhārgava. He explains this very state of being prosperous: "they would take" (ādadīran), meaning they would seize. ||23||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* has not been commented upon.

Viśvanātha says: "Only the disrespect and honor shown to the guru are the causes of misfortune and prosperity," and he expresses this by means of the example of the Asuras, beginning with the word "O Maghavan. Today their power is seen to be such that...
They might even take away my own abode, Satyaloka; the reason for this is that the Bhṛgu deities are devoted to their guru. ||23||
Why would those of the Bhrigus, who have mastered their purpose through indestructible mantras, take account of the triple heaven?
No misfortunes befall the Brahmins, Govinda, the cows, the lords of cattle, or the rulers of men.

Śrīdhara: For those whose mantra is indivisible, for those disciples who have been instructed in the meaning [of the truth], and for those Brahmins whose protectors are Govinda, the cows, and the Lord—only for them do misfortunes not occur; for others, however, they do occur. ||24||

The sequential composition [of the commentary] begins with the words "Tripiṣṭapa. Here, Viśvanātha introduces the example of Govinda. He states that here the means of conciliation, bribery, and force are not seen to be applicable;
even sowing dissension is impossible, as he says: "na bhedyo mantraḥ," meaning those whose counsel cannot be divided. This applies in all cases.

The reason is that they have indeed been instructed by the Bhṛgus, that is, by Śukrācārya.
