"Arthavantaḥ" means those for whom the goal (artha) is to be accepted as the supreme human purpose (puruṣārtha). [Objection: In that case, will we simply die? To this, he says reassuringly: "Not viprāḥ. "Viprāḥ" refers to those for whom Govinda, the cows, and the lords (īśvaras) are their protectors (anugrāhakas).
Of them. ||24||
Therefore, quickly take refuge in that ascetic son of Tvaṣṭṛ, the wise and self-controlled one who possesses universal form.
If you will forgive his deed, he, being honored, shall provide for your needs.
Śrīdhara: Therefore, for that reason; immediately thereafter, indeed, worship Him, whose activity is partiality toward the side of the demons. ||25||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Therefore, for that reason; he says that this alone is the present means: "Worship Viśvarūpa as your guru. For [he is] that Viśvarūpa whose action is partiality toward the side of the Asuras. (25)
Śrī Śuka said:
O King, having been thus addressed by Brahmā, they were freed from their distress.
Having approached the Ṛṣi Tvaṣṭra’s son and embraced him, they said this:
Śrīdhara: "Uditāḥ" means "spoken. ||26||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
The venerable goddesses said:
We have arrived at your hermitage as guests; may prosperity be yours!
O dear one, let the desire of our ancestors, appropriate for this occasion, be fulfilled.

For the supreme duty of sons toward their fathers is service, O Brahmin, according to the virtuous; this is true even for those who have sons themselves, let alone for those living as celibate students.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
—o)0(o— The teacher is the embodiment of Brahmā; the father is the embodiment of Prajāpati.
The brother of the Lord of Maruts is his very form; the mother is the manifest body of the Earth.

Śrīdhara: They speak thus for the sake of praising guests and ancestors—the *ācārya* is one who initiates [a pupil] and teaches him the Veda; he is the very embodiment (*mūrti*) of the Brahman, that is, the Veda.
{29} Kramasaṃdarbha: This has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: Ācārya means a teacher who instructs in the Vedas; of Brahmā, that is, of the Veda; [and] of Marutpati, that is, Indra. ||29||
She is the sister of compassion, the very embodiment of dharma, the guest of the self,
the personified arrival of fire, and all living beings of the soul.

Śrīdhara: [He is] the very self and embodied form of Dharma, the guest himself, manifest as the Self—that is, Śrī Viṣṇu—or else, the Self, that is, one's own self. The meaning is that one should cultivate the vision of the Self in all beings. ||30||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: The sense is: what need is there to say that a guest is the very embodiment of dharma? [He is] the Self (ātman) whom you behold. ||30||
Therefore, O dear one, you ought to fulfill their command by removing through ascetic power the suffering and the defeat of your distressed ancestors.
Śrīdhara: "From others" means defeat; that itself is "distress" (ārti). ||31||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Now, one might object: "Enough with these instructions on dharma and praises; state what you actually intend to say.
To this they reply: "Therefore... (verse 31).
We choose you as our preceptor, a Brahmin most devoted to the Veda and our guru,
so that by your splendor we may swiftly conquer our rivals."
Śrīdhara says: They speak the message—"We choose"—thus [ends verse 32].
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: We choose you as our teacher, [recognizing] you as a teacher. They state the purpose with the words "yathā" (as follows)—o)0(o—
For they do not censure the salutation of the feet of one younger in years regarding matters of substance;
O Brahmin, except in the case of Vedic meters, age is not the cause of seniority.

Śrīdhara: [Objection: "But you will perform salutation to me, who am the youngest, in my capacity as a teacher (upādhyāya), and that is censurable. To this they reply: "No. They do not censure the salutation of the youngest [brothers] when it is for the sake of specific purposes (*artheṣu*). Furthermore, [this applies] except in the case of the Vedas—that is, other than the mantras (*chandobhyaḥ*).
"Apart from age alone, there is no cause for seniority among those who possess the mantras;
therefore, by virtue of being the giver of the mantras to us, you alone shall be the eldest.
Or rather, apart from the Vedas—that is, excluding the *chandas*—age alone is the cause of seniority."
It is so; however, the Vedas alone are the primary cause. In the case of equality regarding those, age is the deciding factor.
And because you are the knower of the Vedas, you alone are the elder—this is the meaning. ||33||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Now, if you say, "Make me your guru," [the reply is: "Since I am your younger brother's son, how will you perform my salutation? To this they say: "No"—that is, except in the case of Vedic meters (*chandas*).
In other worldly affairs, they do not condemn saluting the feet of the youngest;
rather, they certainly do condemn it. For age alone is the cause of seniority and juniority:
one who is advanced in years is the elder (*jyeṣṭha*), and one who is younger in years is the junior (*kaniṣṭha*). This applies in the case of the Vedic meters (*chandas*), but not otherwise.
The meaning here is that knowledge of the *chandas* (Vedic meters) alone is the cause of seniority.
Therefore, because of your superior knowledge of the Vedas, you alone, by performing our priestly duties, shall be our guru who imparts the sacred mantras; such is the intention. ||33||
The venerable sage said:
Being requested by the hosts of gods to serve as their domestic priest, the one of great asceticism [consented].
Viśvarūpa, being pleased, spoke to them in a gentle voice.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
Śrī Viśvarūpa said:
"O Protectors, how could one such as I reject that which is requested by the Lords of the World— a thing censured by those of virtuous character and destructive of spiritual luster?
For it is said that for him alone who is his disciple, even that [rejection] would be called his own self-interest."
Śrīdhara says that, out of fear of disappointing your request, he will perform this task even though it is censured; he expresses this in two and a half verses.

Being a family priest (*paurohitya*) is condemned by those of virtuous character because it is a cause of unrighteousness (*adharma*). Furthermore, it causes the expenditure of *brahmavarcas*, meaning it depletes the spiritual luster already established previously.
And one such as I ought not to refuse; thus he says, "How indeed... He is worthy of being instructed by them.
For that very absence of refusal is said to be the disciple's own welfare. (35)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: The office of domestic priest has been condemned by sages of virtuous character;
for it involves the excessive expenditure of *brahmavarcasa*, that is, spiritual luster. Furthermore, that...
Thinking, "Even now, that must indeed be done by me," he asks: "How so? O Lords!
He is a disciple of you, the World-Protectors; he is a disciple of you all. Therefore, for a disciple, the very absence of refusal is his own self-interest. (35)
For those who possess nothing, the gleanings of grain are indeed their wealth;
by means of that, one performs the hospitable rites for the virtuous in this world.
O lords, how can I perform that which is censurable, by which the evil-minded one rejoices in his priestly office?

Śrīdhara: [Objection: Surely, through the office of a priest, the acquisition of wealth would result in the accomplishment of dharma; otherwise, how could there be dharma for one who is destitute? For this very reason, people rejoice in that [office]. To this, he replies: "For those who possess nothing, the gleaning of ears and stalks is indeed their wealth. Gleaning (*śila*) is the gathering of ears (*kaṇiśa*) that have been overlooked by the owner in the field.
*Uñchana* is the gathering of grains and the like fallen from marketplaces and such; by that alone, the religious duties of the virtuous are accomplished here in the householder stage of life. (36)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Now, one might object that through the office of a priest, wealth may be obtained and thus dharma accomplished; otherwise, how can there be dharma for one who is destitute? To this he replies: for those who possess nothing, the very act of gleaning ears of grain and picking up single grains is their wealth.

*Śila* is the gathering of ears of grain overlooked by the owner in a field; *uñchana* is the gathering of grains such as rice that have fallen on marketplaces and the like. A man of evil intellect alone rejoices in this practice associated with the sacrificial priest (*purohita*), but not one of good intellect.
Or rather, it is the corrupted intellect itself that rejoices because of its own conformity [to such conduct]. (36)
Nevertheless, how could I fail to respond to what my gurus have requested? Everything you ask for, I shall accomplish even at the cost of my life and my wealth.
Śrīdhara: "This which has been requested is but little; I shall do even more than that," he says with the words, "For you... (verse 37).
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: "I shall not refuse you, nor shall I reject your request; how small is this that you have asked for? It is indeed very little, and I shall do even more. Thus he says: "For you... (37).
Śrī Bādarāyaṇi said:
Having thus promised them, Viśvarūpa, the great ascetic, [acted accordingly].
Having been chosen, he performed the office of the domestic priest with supreme concentration.
Śrīdhara: By means of supreme meditative absorption and supreme exertion. ||38||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: By means of *samādhi*, that is, by one-pointedness of mind. ||38||
The Lord,
having snatched away the protected fortune of the enemies of the gods— even that which was secured by the science of Uśanas—
bestowed it upon Mahendra by means of the Vaiṣṇava science.
Śrīdhara: [He is protected] by the Vaiṣṇavī [mantra], which consists of the Śrī-Nārāyaṇa-kavaca. ||39||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
By her, the thousand-eyed Lord, though concealed, conquered the hosts of demons.
The noble-minded Viśvarūpa spoke to her concerning Mahendra.
Śrīdhara: "The hosts of Asuras" refers to the armies of the Daityas. ||40||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: That Vaiṣṇavī lore. ||40||
Thus ends the seventh chapter of the sixth [book] in the *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted, and which is perfectly suited to the virtuous.
Thus ends the sixth book in the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā, the Pāramahaṃsyasaṃhitā, which is a commentary on the Brahma-sūtras within the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, the Great Purāṇa.
The Seventh Chapter: The Narrative of Viśvarūpa.
Now begins the Eighth Chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Nārāyaṇa-Armour."
The King said:
"Protected by her, the thousand-eyed Indra,
as if in play, conquered the enemy forces along with their mounts and enjoyed the sovereignty of the three worlds."
O Blessed One, tell me that armor which is of the nature of Nārāyaṇa,
by which, being protected, one may conquer enemies who attack in battle.
Śrīdhara:
In the eighth [chapter], Viśvarūpa, however, spoke the armor consisting of Nārāyaṇa to Indra, by which Indra, being protected, then conquered the Daityas.
The glory belonging to the three worlds. ||1||
The sequential arrangement: "Yayā" constitutes a pair of verses. Tell me the manner in which he conquered by means of that Vidyā in the form of armor. ||1||
Viśvanātha:
Viśvarūpa taught Śakra the armor consisting of Nārāyaṇa, by means of which he conquered the Daityas; thus the eighth [chapter] is described. (1)
Śrī Bādarāyaṇi said:
The son of Tvaṣṭṛ was chosen as the family priest for Mahendra, who questioned him further.
Listen now with a one-pointed mind to this armor called Nārāyaṇa.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
Śrī Viśvarūpa said:
Having washed his hands and feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with the sacred grass (pavitra) in hand, facing north,
having performed the ritual assignment of mantras to his limbs and hands (aṅganyāsa and karanyāsa), remaining silent and pure, he [should proceed] with the two mantras.
Śrīdhara: He by whom the ritual placement (nyāsa) was performed upon his own limbs and hands with the two mantras consisting of eight and twelve syllables. ||4||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon. —o)0(o— When fear has arisen, one should don the supreme armor of Nārāyaṇa.
On the feet, the knees, the thighs, the abdomen, the heart, and then the chest.

Śrīdhara: One should arm oneself—that is, one should bind upon oneself—the armor consisting of Nārāyaṇa. In that regard, he describes the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the eight limbs, beginning with the feet, by means of the eight-syllable mantra, starting with the half-verse beginning "on the two feet" (5).
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Here, with the half-verse beginning "on the two feet," he describes the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the eight-syllable mantra upon the eight limbs starting from the feet. ||5||
One should place the syllables beginning with *oṃ* in sequence upon the face and the head;
one may use either "oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya" or its reverse.

Śrīdhara: One should perform the placement (nyāsa) by enclosing each individual syllable with the *praṇava* (*oṃ*), beginning with the syllable *oṃ*. Or, one may perform the placement in reverse order, from the head down to the feet.
The meaning is that one should perform either the placement of emanation (*utpattinyāsa*) or the placement of dissolution (*saṃhāranyāsa*). ||6||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: One should place each single syllable, beginning with the syllable *oṃ*, encapsulated by the *praṇava* (the *oṃkāra*). Or one may place them in reverse order, from the head down to the feet, or according to the sequence.
The meaning is that one should perform either the *sṛṣṭinyāsa* (creation-assignment) or the *saṃhāranyāsa* (dissolution-assignment) in reverse order. ||6||
Then one should perform the ritual placement (*karanyāsa*) using the twelve-syllable mantra,
beginning with the *praṇava* (OM) and ending with the letter *ya*, upon the joints of the fingers and the thumb.
Śrīdhara: The extraction of the twelve-syllable mantra begins with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ends with the letter *ya*.
One should place each syllable, encapsulated by the *praṇava*, upon the fingers starting from the thumb up to the right index finger.
The remaining four syllables should be placed on the first and last joints of the two thumbs. (7)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "Beginning with the *praṇava*" means that each individual syllable, enclosed by the *praṇava*, [is assigned] to the fingers starting from the right index finger up to the left index finger. The remainder...
One should place the four syllables on the first and last joints of the two thumbs. ||7||
One should assign the syllable *oṃ* to the heart, the letter *vi* to the head,
the letter *ṣa* between the eyebrows, and the letter *ṇa* to the crest-lock.

Śrīdhara: He states the placement of other mantras with the words "one should place. By separating the letters *ṣa* and *ka*, one should place the six syllables in the heart and the other [limbs]. (8)
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* has not been commented upon.
Viśvanātha says: He describes the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the heart and other limbs even by means of another mantra—“he should place,” etc. (8).
One should apply the syllable *ve* to the two eyes and the syllable *na* to all the joints;
designating the syllable *ma* as the weapon, the wise one becomes the embodiment of the mantra.
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha: having meditated upon the syllable *ma* as the weapon (*astra*). ||9||
The sequential arrangement has not been explained. One should direct that [mantra], ending with *phaṭ* and accompanied by the *visarga*, toward all directions.
Oṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu. Thus [it is said].
Śrīdhara: Therefore, one should employ that weapon-mantra of the letter *M*, namely "maḥ astrāya phaṭ," for the purpose of binding the directions. ||10||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: That weapon-mantra of the letter *ma*, namely "maḥ astrāya phaṭ," one should employ thus for the binding of all directions. ||10||
One should meditate upon the supreme Self as the object of meditation, endowed with the six powers;
one should then recite this mantra, which is the embodiment of knowledge, splendor, and austerity.

Śrīdhara: One should meditate upon the Self in the form of the Lord as the object of meditation. [One should meditate] upon Him who possesses knowledge, splendor, austerity, and form, and who is characterized by the six powers denoted by the word *bhaga*, such as sovereignty and the rest. This [meditation], which is about to be described, is known as the *Śrīmannārāyaṇakavaca*. (11)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.

*Viśvanātha*: One should meditate upon the Self in the form of the Lord as the object of meditation; this is the practice of *ahaṃgraha-upāsanā* (meditation through identification) performed with the desire for invincibility against others. [He is] that whose form consists of knowledge, splendor, and austerity.
This mantra known as the Nārāyaṇa-kavaca. ||11||
Oṃ! May Hari, whose lotus feet are placed upon the back of the king of birds, grant me complete protection.
Holding a shield, a sword, a mace, arrows, a bow, and a noose, he possesses eight arms endowed with eightfold qualities.
Śrīdhara: "Possessing eightfold qualities" means endowed with the eightfold sovereign powers, beginning with *aṇimā*. ||12||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* does not provide an explanation.

Viśvanātha [states]: Just as a river or a stream exists together with the ocean, so too, even though one has attained identity with the form of the object of meditation, one may remain distinct; thus, for the sake of praying for self-protection, one should recite the mantra.
He said: "Hari. He is endowed with the eightfold qualities, namely the eight sovereign powers beginning with *aṇiman*. ||12||
May my form as a fish protect me in the waters from the hosts of aquatic creatures and from the noose of Varuṇa.
May Māyāvaṭu-Vāmana protect me on dry land; may Trivikrama protect me in the sky.
Śrīdhara: The hosts of aquatic creatures themselves are the noose of Varuṇa; therefore [it is so called]. ||13||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.

*Viśvanātha*: He requests protection generally from all sides, and then states the protective mantras by means of the Lord in His specific forms as the presiding deities over particular places, beginning with "In the waters."
By three [verses]. The hosts of aquatic creatures themselves are the noose of Varuṇa; therefore [he recites these]. ||13||
May the Lord Nṛsiṃha, the slayer of the leader of the Asura hosts, protect us in difficult places such as forests and the front lines of battle.
As he let out a great, boisterous laugh, the quarters of the sky resounded and the fetuses fell from their wombs.
Śrīdhara: [The compound] refers to those difficult situations in which forests, the front of a battle, the commencement of combat, and so forth are the first [of the dangers]. (14)
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Ājimukha means the area at the front of the battle. ||14||
May that Boar, who upheld the earth with his tusk according to the ritual of sacrifice, protect you on your journey.
May Rāma, the elder brother of Bharata, who dwelt among mountain peaks during his exile together with Lakṣmaṇa, protect us.

Śrīdhara: May that famous Varāha protect me on the path—he who is so called because he is conceived and described through sacrifices performed in the form of his own limbs; he by whom the earth was raised up and rescued; [and] Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, among the mountain peaks, that is, the summits of the hills. ||15||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.

*Viśvanātha*: *Yajñakalpa* means whose very nature (*svarūpa*) is sacrifice; the suffix *-kalpa* is used here in its own sense (*svārthika*). Alternatively, he is so called because sacrifices (*yajñāḥ*) are capable (*kalpāḥ*, i.e., effective) through him. [This refers to] Rāma, the son of Jamadagni. ||15||
May Nārāyaṇa protect me from all fierce dharmas and from negligence; and may Nara protect me from laughter.
May Datta protect from non-yoga, and may Kapila, the Lord of Yoga and Master of Virtues, protect from the bondage of karma.
Śrīdhara: May Nara protect [us] from Ugradharma, characterized by malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) and the like, and from pride;
and may Datta, that is Dattātreya, protect [us] from non-yoga, which is the falling away from yoga. ||16||

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: With four [verses], he states the protective mantras against calamities arising from oneself or others: from *ugradharma*, such as malevolent magic (*abhicāra*); from laughter, that is, from pride; and from non-yoga, that is, from the loss of yoga. ||16||
May Sanatkumāra protect me; may Hayashirsha protect me from the offense against the gods on the path from Kamadeva.
May Hari in the form of the Tortoise, the best of divine sages, deliver me from this entire hell through the worship of the Supreme Person.
May Sanatkumāra protect Madhva from Kāmadeva. Hari, whose name is Sanatkumāra, entered another Sanatkumāra, the son of Brahmā, appearing in the form of celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
"May the Lord, the Sovereign of All, protect me equally from desire for what is fit and unfit.

Thus [it is said]. The best of divine sages [spoke this] because of the worship of another person, and because of the worship of another [deity] due to the perception that Viṣṇu is not their subordinate.
"May the divine seer Mahidāsa and the imperishable Viṣṇu protect me from those actions not offered to Him, as well as from the failure to remember Him. Thus [it is said]. (17)
Śrīdhara: [The fault] is that which occurs on the road—namely, proceeding without having offered salutation—which constitutes an offense against the gods;
it is not explained by Nārada as one of the thirty-two types of offenses arising from a breach in the worship of the Lord during the interval between the worship of the Puruṣa-sūkta.
Krama-sandarbha: It has not been explained [by Nārada].

Viśvanātha: From Kāmadeva—that is, from the impulse of passion. "On the path" refers to the offense of disregarding the gods, namely proceeding without having offered salutation. This means that from within the worship of the Supreme Person, there arises a flaw in the worship of the deity consisting of the thirty-two types of offenses. ||17||
May the blessed Dhanvantari protect us from unwholesome food,
and may the self-conquered Ṛṣabha protect us from the fear of dualities.
And Yajña descended from the world of Janaloka,
Bala from the Gaṇa, and the Lord of Serpents from Krodhavaśa.

Śrīdhara: May Yajña protect [us] from the world—that is, from public scandal—and may Balabhadra protect us from that destruction which has birth as its cause. In the reading "from Kṛtānta," may he protect us from Kṛtānta, that is, from Time (Kāla). [May he protect us] from the host of serpents belonging to the Krodhavaśa class. Ahīndra is Śeṣa. ||18||

The sequential arrangement [of the commentary] on the verse beginning with "yajñaś ca lokāt" shows that Baladeva possesses superior power, as he is distinct from Śeṣa and Kṛtānta (Yama). In the reading "janāntāt," the meaning remains the same: from the end, that is, the destruction, of people. ||18||

Viśvanātha: From the world—that is, from public scandal (*janāpavāda*). From "the end of people" (*janāntāt*): the end (*anta*) caused by people, namely harm; from that. There is also a reading *kṛtāntāt*. From the host of serpents due to the power of their wrath. The Lord of Serpents is Śeṣa. ||18||
The blessed Dvaipāyana became a Buddha due to a lack of awakening, while [others] became so due to the negligence of the hosts of heretics.
May Kalki, who has taken a great incarnation for the protection of Dharma, deliver us from the impurity of time that is the Kali age.

Śrīdhara: Kalki [is so called] because he arises from Kali, who has become the embodiment of impurity; he by whom a vast and great incarnation was assumed for the protection and preservation of Dharma. (19)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: From Kali, whose nature is the impurity of time. Of what kind is Kalki? "The protector of Dharma," and so forth.
May Keśava protect me with his mace in the morning; may Govinda, holding his flute, protect me during the forenoon; and may Nārāyaṇa, whose power is exalted, protect me at midday.
At midday, Viṣṇu holds the hand of the Lord of Enemies.

Śrīdhara: One should pray for protection during the six divisions of the day—known respectively as *prātaḥ* (morning) and so forth—and during the [six] divisions of the night known as *pradoṣa* (dusk) and so forth, using the three verses beginning with "māṃ keśava. This is to be done throughout the period from *āsaṅgava* up to *saṅgava*. ||20||
The *Caitanyamatamañjuṣā* states: "Govinda was present at dawn, holding his flute," and so forth.
The meaning is that it is understood that the two-armed Śrī Govinda, who is devoted to playing the flute and is higher than the highest, exists as an eternal form. This very [is the point].
The Great Vidyā of Nārāyaṇa-varma and Hayagrīva. ||20||

The sequential arrangement: "O Keśava, me" (one and a half verses). By this, the eternal manifestation of the Lords of Mathurā and Vṛndāvana is shown. Times such as morning and so forth are applied in this manner: first comes the forenoon (*prāhṇa*), then the morning (*prātaḥ*), and then the time of the sun's rising (*saṅgava*).

Its two parts are midday and the middle portion; the third part is the afternoon, which is further divided by the distinctions of the morning and evening twilights. At night, the first part is the onset of darkness (pradoṣa), the middle part is midnight (niśītha), and the half-night (ardharātra) is likewise situated therein.

Two *ghaṭikās* constitute the middle watch; the latter part of the night is the third division. The final two portions of that same period are designated as "dawn" (*pratyūṣa*) and "break of day" (*prabhāta*). Just as the twilights (*sandhyā*) are counted separately even though they are internal subdivisions of those periods, so it is in this sequential enumeration. However, in the case of sequential counting:

Since it would result in the transgression of the midday [period] and others, the forenoon (*prāhṇa*) is not counted as a distinct [period] in the Smṛti. For it is said: "The morning consists of three *muhūrtas*, and the *saṅgava* period is of the same duration."
Midday consists of three muhūrtas, and the afternoon is likewise; the evening consists of three muhūrtas and is censured for all ritual acts. Thus [it is said]. (20)

Viśvanātha: Regarding the specific times, the Blessed One speaks of protective mantras through three verses, assuming the form of their respective presiding deities. Keśava is the lord of Mathurā; [he is to be invoked] in the morning until the fifth *ghaṭikā* of the day. Govinda is the lord of Vṛndāvana; [he is to be invoked] until the time of *saṅgava*.

The forenoon (*prāhna*) extends from the sixth *ghaṭikā* until the tenth *ghaṭikā*, and from the eleventh *ghaṭikā* until the fifteenth *ghaṭikā*. Therein, from the sixteenth *ghaṭikā* until the twentieth *ghaṭikā* is midday (*madhyandina*), wherein [resides] the Lord of Enemies (*arīndra*), who holds a discus in his hand (*cakrahasta*).
May the god Madhu, whose bow is fierce, protect me in the afternoon; may Mādhava, who possesses three abodes, protect me in the evening.
May Hṛṣīkeśa protect me at the onset of night,
and may Padmanābha alone protect me at midnight.

May Śrīdhara, the abode of the three, the triad of forms beginning with Brahmā, the illustrious Mādhava—protect [us] at the time of dusk, deep night, the end of midnight, and at the hour of Niśītha; may Padmanābha alone protect [us]. 21.
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: The afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) begins from the twenty-first *ghaṭikā* and extends up to the twenty-fifth *ghaṭikā*;
therein, from the twenty-sixth *ghaṭikā* up to the thirtieth *ghaṭikā*...

In the evening, there [is this]: he whose abodes are the three—Being, Consciousness, and Bliss. Having described the protection of the day divided into six parts, he speaks of the protection of the night divided into five parts: *doṣe* means "in the evening," up until the fourth *ghaṭikā* of the night; there, the fifth *ghaṭikā*...

Starting from [the beginning] up until the fourteenth ghaṭikā, it is midnight because the latter half of the night constitutes midnight; therein, at the fifteenth and sixteenth ghaṭikās, it is the dead of night (niśītha). ||21||
The Lord whose abode is the Śrīvatsa is Īśa during the latter part of the night; at dawn, Janārdana is Īśa, bearing a sword.
May Dāmodara protect us at the junctions of the day, and may the Lord Viśveśvara, the embodiment of Time, protect us at dawn.

May the Lord Śrīvatsadhāmā protect [us] during the latter part of the night; may the Lord Śrījanārdana [protect us] at dawn; may Śrīdāmodara [protect us] at daybreak; and may Śrīviśveśvara [protect us] throughout the periods following the twilight prayers. (22)

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: He whose *śrīvatsa* mark is on his *dhāman*, that is, his body; *apararātra* is the time after midnight and before sunrise; *pratyūṣa* refers to the four *ghaṭikās* remaining at the end of the night; *anusandhyam* [means] at every junction of the day.
At the junctions of day and night. ||22||
The wheel, its rim blazing like the fire at the end of an eon, set in motion by the Blessed One, revolves on all sides.
Burn, burn quickly the enemy army, just as the wind-friend fire consumes dry grass!

Śrīdhara: That discus, whose rim is as fierce and sharp as the fire at the end of an eon, being employed by the Blessed One, "dandagdhi" the enemy host—that is, it burns them excessively. This is its very nature; the meaning is that nothing further need be prayed for from it. Or alternatively, "dandagdhīti" [is used].

The middle person [is addressed] with the word *loṇ*. Here, having stated the essential nature of the wheel as "you yourself are such a wheel" and having thus awakened [the deity], one prays: "Burn it exceedingly! *Kakṣa* means dry grass. ||23||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: He states the protective mantras with the divine weapons by means of four verses beginning with "the discus" (*cakra*).
[The discus] is that whose rim (*nemi*) is sharp (*tigma*) like the fire at the end of an eon (*yugāntānala*); O you who revolve all around!
O Discus, you who are by nature ever-rotating, being set in motion by the Blessed One, utterly consume the enemy host; burn them excessively, like dry grass in a forest thicket. ||23||
O you whose touch is like a falling thunderbolt and who emits sparks, crush him, crush him— you who are beloved by the Unconquered One!
Pulverize, pulverize the Kuṣmāṇḍas, Vaināyakas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, and Grahas; crush the enemies!

Śrīdhara: O Gada, you whose sparks have a touch like lightning—addressing you thus—you are the beloved of the Unconquered (Ajitā), while I am the servant of the Imperishable (Acyuta). Therefore, crush, crush the *kūṣmāṇḍas* and others; pulverize them! And pulverize the enemies as well!
Pulverize! The repetition [of the word] everywhere is for the sake of extreme speed. ||24||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Those whose touch is like lightning are the sparks (visphuliṅga) from which [they arise]. O Gada! Crush, crush them into powder, reduce them to dust! ||24||
You [ward off] the Yātudhānas, Pramathas, Pretas, Mātṛs,
Piśācas, and the terrible glares of the seizing spirits (vipragraha).
O Indra among heroes, filled with Krishna, let out a terrifying roar that puts the enemy to flight and makes their hearts tremble!
Śrīdhara: O Pāñcajanya, king of conchs! Drive away the Yātudhānas and the rest—the Brahmarākṣasas who seize Brāhmaṇas, and whatever others have terrible glances. (25)
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: O Darendra, O Pāñcajanya! ||25||
O Lord, being impelled by the Master, cut, cut asunder the enemy army with your excellent sword of sharp edge!
O you who possess the moon upon your banner, cover the eyes of our enemies with your shield; seize the sight of those whose vision is evil.
Śrīdhara: O you of sharp edge (tigmadhāra)! O best of swords (asivara), excellent blade!
Cut, cut my enemy's army! O you who possess a shield marked with a hundred moons (śatacandracarman), cover the eyes of the enemies, those possessed of sin (aghavat).
And take away the eyes of those with evil vision and fierce gazes.
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: O you of sharp edge! O best of swords! O most excellent of blades!
O you marked with a hundred moons! Seize and cover our eyes. (26)
that fear which we had from the planets, from comets, and from men; from reptiles, from fanged beasts, from spirits, and from calamities."
Śrīdhara: "From which" means from those [sources] from which fear arises; "from sins" (aṃhas) means from evil deeds. ||27||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
O Blessed One, all these [have arisen] from the proclamation of names and forms.
May those who oppose our welfare go to their destruction immediately.
Śrīdhara: "Obstacles to the highest good" (śreyaḥpratīpaka) means those which strike down what is desired. ||28||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Those who are hostile to or act against what is conducive to welfare (śreyas). ||28||
May the Lord Garuḍa— the master who consists of hymns, praises,
and meters— protect [us] from all misfortunes through his own names, as Viṣvaksena.

Śrīdhara: *Stotrastobha* refers to that which is praised (*stūyate*) by means of hymns (*stotra*), such as the *Bṛhat*, *Rathantara*, and other *Sāmans*. He is the embodiment of the *Chandas* (Vedic meters), being the personification of the Vedas, according to the Śruti: "You are Suparṇa, you are Garuḍa," and so forth. In the reading *aikapadya*, *stobhas* are the syllables that fill out the melody. In the reading *stotrastoma*, [it refers to the hymns and the chants].
A *stoma* is a collection of *ṛc*s that serves as the basis for a *sāman*. ||29||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Hymns (*stotra*) are the *Sāman* chants such as the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara*; that which is praised or extolled by these is the "Hymn-Praise" (*stotrastobha*). In the reading as a single compound (*aikapadya*), *stobhas* are the syllables that fill out the melody.
In the reading "stotra-stoma," *stoma* refers to a collection of *ṛc*-verses that serves as the basis for a *sāman*. ||29||
May the name, form, vehicle, and weapons of Hari, adorned by His attendants, protect us from all calamities, as well as our intellect, senses, mind, and vital breaths.
May the names, forms, vehicles, mounts, and weapons protect our intellect and other faculties; may those adorned by the attendants and the foremost of the attendants protect us. (30)
Kramasaṃdarbha: [This] has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: The attendants' ornaments are the chief among the attendants. ||30||
Just as the Blessed One alone truly knows both the existent and the non-existent,
by this truth may all our calamities come to destruction.

Regarding *madhvaḥ*: Just as the Blessed Lord alone, by virtue of being the regulator of both the existent and the non-existent, is described as having the nature of both the existent and the non-existent, so too:
"By this Truth, may the four-armed Lord Viṣṇu protect me. (31)
Śrīdhara: That which is both existent and non-existent, both manifest and unmanifest—all that is the world. ||31||
The arrangement of the sequence: "yathā" means in whatever manner or by which method. ||31||

Viśvanātha: That world, which consists of both the existent and the non-existent, is in reality the Blessed Lord alone, because it is the effect of His external power of *māyā*. "By this oath of truth"—if the Blessed Lord is indeed such as this, that He is Truth, then may our afflictions perish. If the Vedas are authoritative...
As in the case of "it" (itivat). ||31||
Just as one who possesses the experience of absolute unity, being himself free from conceptual construction,
assumes by his own *māyā* the powers known as ornaments, weapons, and emblems.
By that very measure of truth, may the omniscient Lord Hari,
who is omnipresent, protect us always and everywhere with all his essential forms.
Madhva: "The one supreme Viṣṇu alone is the unborn (aja) who dwells upon the banners as Bhūṣāha;
he himself abides there by bestowing his respective powers."
"By this truth, may Lord Hari, the sovereign of all, protect me. Thus [it is said]. ||32||

Śrīdhara: [It belongs] to those for whom there is meditation (*anudhyāna*) upon the experience of oneness (*aikātmya*); even though it is devoid of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which is [the notion of] difference (*bheda*). ||32||

The sequential composition: "Just as" (yathā) constitutes a couplet. Just as (*yathā*), in whatever manner (*yena prakāreṇa*), [the state] manifests for those who possess the experience of oneness (*aikātmya*) and are intent upon the vision of the absolute supreme nature (*kevalaparamasvarūpa*), being free from conceptual construction (*vikalparahita*) and shining forth as the supreme nature whose sole essence is the flavor of supreme bliss (*paramānandaikarasaparamasvarūpatayā*).

While His own [devotees] worship Him as their respective masters, by means of *māyā*—which here signifies grace—and by His own essential nature (*svarūpa*) which consists of manifold powers (*vicitra-śakti-maya*) acting as the cause, He assumes the powers known as the ornaments and so forth;
that is, He manifests them as His own manifestations consisting of power (*śakti-maya*). By that very [nature],...
By the authority of truth characterized by the experience of the wise— that is to say, if that [truth] were indeed true—
may He protect us with all those very forms characterized as ornaments and so forth, through the manifestation of His diverse forms.
For this very reason, in the *Viṣṇudharma*, within the hymn to the discus fashioned by Bali, following the verse beginning "Whose form is indefinable even for the highest yogins," it says:
"O Lord of the Earth, in the center of the hub of that revolving discus..."
"The Daitya beheld the entire triple world, beginning with Bhūr and Bhuvaḥ. Thus it is said.

In this very manner, in the ninth [chapter], this Discus was also praised by the illustrious Ambarīṣa: "The emblems, such as the banner in the form of Garuḍa and so forth... As for the fact that in some places it is heard as if it were something adventitious, that too—

This should be understood as being like the manifestation of the Blessed Lord (Śrī Bhagavat). Here, in the third [canto], the statement "the stainless jewel on His neck is the reality of the caitya" (Bhāgavatapurāṇa 3.28.28) also serves as supporting evidence.
Therefore, even in the twelfth [canto], the passage beginning with "The Unborn One bears the light of His own Self" (Bhāgavatapurāṇa 12.11.10) refers to the Virāṭ.

Although it has been shown for the purpose of meditation through the vision of non-difference by virtue of its being the "Gone-to" (the destination), it should also be contemplated, as far as possible, as the direct Śrī-vigraha (the divine form). For instance, in the *Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa*:
"The Self of this world is untainted, free from qualities, and stainless..."
"The Blessed Lord Hari bears the nature of the Kaustubha gem" (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.22.68).
Thus [ends the citation from] the *Bhagavatsandarbha* (48).
Viśvanātha: Oneness (*aikātmyam*) means having a single nature due to being composed of consciousness; it is the manifestation (*anubhāva*), that is, the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: may He—who is free from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) regarding those ornaments and powers; who is the consciousness-nature (*cidrūpatva*) of both Himself and them; and who, though devoid of difference from them, nevertheless bears those powers designated as "ornaments" and so forth—protect us by that very same true nature. In this context, the ornaments are...

He bears the Śaktis—the powers whose forms are the Kaustubha and other ornaments, the weapons such as the discus, the marks such as the four-armed form, and the names; he is joined with his own Māyā, that is, his inherent power (svarūpaśakti), which is eternal and called by the name Māyā. Therefore, Viṣṇu consists of Māyā.
"The wise declare [this]," according to the Śruti cited as authoritative in the Mādhva-bhāṣya.

Therefore, by that very truth—the means of valid cognition consisting of reality itself—the Lord bears ornaments, weapons, and so forth, as well as His four-armed form and other attributes, because they are composed of His own essential power (*svarūpa-śakti*). If it is true that He bears these as non-different from Himself, then...

If that were so, then Hari, being omnipresent in all places and times through the forms described in the mantras such as "may he ordain," should protect [us]. By the statement "the omniscient one," an oath is indicated, signifying: "The Blessed Lord alone knows the faith within our minds. (3233)
— in the intermediate directions, the cardinal directions, above, below, everywhere, within, and without, the Blessed One Nārasiṃha [is present].
Dispelling the fear of the world with his roar,
he has swallowed up all other splendors by means of his own brilliance.

Śrīdhara: Again, Śrī Nṛsiṃha himself is being entreated with the words "in the intermediate directions" (*vidikṣu*). The word "may he protect" (*pātu*) is to be supplied as a grammatical ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*). Alternatively, *Nārasiṃha* refers to Prahlāda. By his own roar—that is, by the thundering of the name of Śrī Nṛsiṃha—and by his own splendor—that is, by his own power—the [demons] were swallowed up.
He is the one by whom all the powers and splendors of the world-elephants, poisons, weapons, water, wind, fire, and so forth, have been [subdued]. ||34||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Thus, having completed the protection of himself through various forms, he again provides a single mantra for self-protection by means of a single, terrifying form of Nṛsiṃha that overcomes all adversaries.

He said: "In the intermediate directions" is to be connected with the word "protect. Alternatively, Nārasiṃha—the devotee of Narasiṃha, Prahlāda—by his own roar, that is, by the thundering of the name of Śrī Nṛsiṃha, and by his own splendor, [overcomes] the splendors and powers of all the elephants of the quarters, poisons, weapons, water, wind, fire, and so forth.
By which he [is characterized]. ||34||
"O Maghavan, this armor consisting of the essence of Nārāyaṇa has been declared;
clad in it, you shall swiftly conquer the leaders of the hosts of Asuras."
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha: "Daṃśita" means armored or clad in mail. ||35||
The sequential arrangement has not been explained. —
But whoever, while maintaining this, sees whatever with the eye;
Or if he should touch it with his foot, he is immediately liberated from that fear.
Śrīdhara: He too is liberated from anxiety and fear. ||36||
Kramasaṃdarbha: This has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: Even he is liberated from fear, how much more so one who wears this [amulet]! (36)
For one who maintains this knowledge, there shall be no fear from any quarter whatsoever—
not from kings, thieves, or demons, nor ever from diseases and the like.
Śrīdhara: But for him, indeed, no fear shall arise at all. ||37||
The sequence of the composition: Then, having raised the doubt as to why there is no fruit for one who possesses the vidyā, he says: "From some [cause]" (kutaścit). ||37||
Viśvanātha: This has not been explained.
—o)0(o— In ancient times, a certain twice-born man of the Kauśika lineage maintained this vidyā.
Through the practice of yogic concentration, he cast off his own body in the desert.
Śrīdhara: He explains this power of the vidyā through a historical narrative with three and a half verses beginning with "imām.
[The phrase] "in the desert, a waterless region" shows that this vidyā does not depend upon specific fields or sacred fords (tīrtha). ||38||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— Once, the Lord of the Gandharvas [arrived] above him by means of a celestial chariot (*vimāna*).
Surrounded by women, Citraratha went to where the abode of the twice-born was located.
Śrīdhara: Wherever the destruction—that is, the casting off of the body—of a twice-born man occurs, [it is] upon that [spot]. (39)
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: The destruction of the twice-born is the abandonment of the body. ||39||
At that very moment, he fell from the sky headlong along with his celestial chariot.
Having taken the bones at the word of the Vālakhilyas, he was filled with wonder.
Having cast [it] away and bathed in the eastward-flowing Sarasvatī, he returned to his own abode.

Śrīdhara: At that very moment, he fell from the sky. According to an alternative reading, it says "along with the women. Following the instruction of the Vālakhilyas, having cast away—that is, thrown down—his bones, he departed for his own abode, the world of the Gandharvas, filled with wonder. ||40||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: In the expression "prācīsarasvatyām," the absence of the masculine form [of the compound] is an archaic usage (ārṣa). The sense is that, otherwise, he would not have been able to depart for his own abode along with his celestial chariot (vimāna). ||40||
Śrī Śuka said:
Whoever should hear this at the proper time, or whoever should retain it with reverence, [attains the highest goal].
Living beings pay homage to him; he is liberated from all fear.
It has not been explained by anyone whatsoever.
Having mastered this lore from Viśvarūpa, Indra [became] the performer of a hundred sacrifices.
Having utterly defeated the asuras in battle, he enjoyed the sovereignty of the three worlds.
Śrīdhara: Having been attained, meaning having been reached. ||42||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been explained.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, which is perfectly consistent with the wise, in the *Sārārthadarśinī*, the *Harṣiṇī* commentary for those whose hearts are devoted.
Thus ends the tenth book in the *Śrīmad Bhāgavatam*, the Great Purāṇa, the commentary on the Brahma-sūtras, the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā concerning the state of the Supreme Swan (Paramahaṃsa).
The eighth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Nārāyaṇa Armor.
Now begins the ninth chapter.
Regarding the instruction of the Blessed One, Śrī Śuka said:
"O Bhārata, that Viśvarūpa had three heads."
We have heard that they were the drinkers of Soma, the drinkers of Surā, and the eaters of food.
Śrīdhara:
In the ninth [chapter], when Viśvarūpa had been killed by Śakra out of anger and Vṛtra had been produced by Tvaṣṭṛ, the gods, being terrified, offered praise to Hari.
That in which there is the drinking of soma—that is, the drinking of liquor—is "surāpītha. One who eats food is "annāda.
In this regard, the Vedic scripture beginning with "Viśvarūpa, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, was indeed the domestic priest of the gods" should be consulted. ||1||
The sequence of events: "He cut off his heads" refers to the loss of all power resulting from the transgression against Bṛhaspati and the offense committed against the host of gods. ||1||
Viśvanātha:
Śakra slew Viśvarūpa; Tvaṣṭṛ begot Vṛtra.
Praised by the gods, Hari spoke of the attainment of the thunderbolt as the ninth [chapter].

That in which there is the drinking—that is, the consumption—of Soma; [he is] an "eater of food" (annāda), one who eats food. In this regard, the Vedic scripture should be consulted: "Viśvarūpa, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, was indeed the domestic priest of the gods. ||1||
O King, he indeed visibly and loudly bestowed a portion upon the gods upon the sacrificial grass—
those very gods who were his ancestors— with great humility.

Śrīdhara says: He describes his partiality for the side of the asuras with two verses beginning with "sa vai. He openly and publicly proclaimed to the gods, with humility, the respective portions of the sacrificial oblation: "This for Indra, this for Agni," and so forth. The reason for this is that he whose ancestors were the gods [was thus inclined]. (2)
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* has not been commented upon.

Viśvanātha says: He [the Lord] expresses his partiality toward the side of the Asuras with two verses beginning with "sa vā" (He indeed...). Just as it is manifest (*pratyakṣam*), Hari humbly offered a portion to the gods, saying "This for Indra."
He gave it aloud, saying, "This for Agni. The reason for this is: "For whom the ancestors are gods. (2)
For he himself had secretly assigned a share to the Asuras;
yet, as the sacrificer, driven by the power of maternal affection, he offered that share to them.

Śrīdhara: He gave a secret, hidden portion to the Asuras. He explains that very point: while sacrificing to the gods, he brought a portion to the Asuras; by some means, he caused it to reach them, because he follows after the Asuras due to the power of maternal affection. (3)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "In secret" means having deceived the gaze of the gods, [he did so] two or three times; "lowly" is the sense. "He gave" means having given a portion, he "carried away" (avahat), that is, he caused it to reach [the destination] while remaining out of sight.
The reason for this is: "O Mother"—meaning she whose maternal grandfathers were the Asuras;
"terrified," meaning having perceived the manifestation of the Asura forces. ||3||
Seeing that offense against the gods and his deception regarding dharma, the Lord of the Gods was struck with fear and swiftly cut off his heads in rage.
It has not been explained by anyone at all. As for that *somapītha* [cup] of his, it became a *kapiñjala* bird.
The kalaviṅka bird is the drinker of wine; that which is the eater of food is the partridge (tittiri).
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha have not provided an explanation.
Kramasandarbha states: "Kapiñjala" refers to the *tittiri* (partridge). ||5||
Even though he was the Lord, he took upon himself the sin of killing a Brahmin with his joined palms;
at the end of a year, for the purification of all beings, he cast that evil away.
Hari divided [the earth] into four parts: land, water, trees, and women.

Śrīdhara: Although he was capable of warding her off, he nevertheless accepted her. Having remained in that state for a year, at the end of the year, fearing the reproaches of living beings and seeking purification in their midst to avoid public scandal, that Hari—Indra—[confessed] that sin to the Earth and the other deities.
The syntactical connection is: "having divided, he distributed. ||6||

The sequential arrangement is as follows: the half-verse beginning with "brahmahatyām" [is one unit]. Furthermore, although he is the Lord, he nevertheless accepted [the sin] directly with his joined palms (*añjali*), because even such a sin must be removed by such a means. However, the portion ending with "bhūtānāṃ viśuddhaye" remains in a subtle form.
The meaning is "indeed. The intention is that he will bring about even the slaying of Vṛtra. ||6||
Viśvanātha: "Alas! Alas! By suddenly killing him out of anger and fear, I have indeed committed a great sin intentionally; I am a most base person and know not into which hell I shall fall.
May I quickly obtain this fitting fruit!"—thus he was in a mass of remorse.
He says, "I have immersed myself," meaning "in Brahman. The sense is: "Kindle me with your own splendor.

Since [the Lord] is the sovereign manifestation of the Lord for the devoted one who is authorized (*adhikṛta*), how could such a person not feel remorse for his transgression? Thus, by means of this remorse, the force of his sins is exhausted.
Having remained in that very same state of reproach for a full year, at its conclusion,
he divided that sin into four parts for the purification of the elements— earth, water, fire, and air— which reside within his own body and had been rendered impure by the murder of a Brahmin.
Since it is impossible for space to be purified, the logical principle is that purification applies only to the four [other] elements, hence the term "fourfold.

Therefore, the sin residing in the internal organ remained indeed in a subtle form—that very seed which, through the slaying of Vṛtra, would again produce the murder of a Brahmin; such is the meaning. ||6||
The Earth indeed accepted the fourth part by means of the boon of filling the hollow;
thus the form of the Brahmin-slaughter appears upon the Earth as a barren wasteland.

Śrīdhara: "The fourth" means the fourth part. "By the filling of the pit" means by the act of filling the excavation; the meaning is that he accepted [the gift] under a formal agreement (*bhāṣābandha*), saying, "If the filling of the pit occurs spontaneously, then I shall accept it. "Īraṇa" means saline soil (*ūṣara*). Therefore...
In this way, study and other such activities are prohibited on saline soil. ||7||

Regarding the sequence of composition: although filling by means of digging and pouring could have occurred previously through rain or the falling of earth and so forth, it should nevertheless be understood that by this boon, the filling occurs through its own natural increase. ||7||

Viśvanātha: The fourth means the fourth part. By the "filling" (*pūra*) of the pit—that is, by that boon—meaning he accepted [the gift] under the verbal agreement: "If the filling of the pit occurs spontaneously, then I shall accept it. *Īraṇa* means saline soil (*ūṣara*). Therefore, on the saline soil...
Study and other such activities are prohibited. ||7||
The trees accepted the boon through the regrowth of their severed parts;
thus, the slaughter of a Brahmin appeared in the form of their resin.

Śrīdhara says: By means of the boon, "Let there be regrowth—re-sprouting—even when there has been cutting," it was seen that the Brahmahatyā exists in the form of resin; therefore, the resin is not to be eaten. (8)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: By means of a boon [granted by Śiva], let there be regrowth—that is, sprouting—upon being cut;
for this very reason, it is called *niryāsa*, and thus it is inedible. (8)
By means of the boon of eternal desire, women took upon themselves a fourth part of the sin;
that sin appears within them month after month in the form of the menses.

Śrīdhara: [He is endowed] with the boon of eternal fulfillment of desires, and with the boon of sexual enjoyment such that conception occurs without any injury to the embryo. Regarding the word "rajas" (menstrual flow): for this very reason, one should not engage in union or similar acts during the appearance of the menses.
This sequence of the composition has not been explained [here].

Viśvanātha: Constant desire, the absence of contentment even during extensive sexual enjoyment, and sexual intercourse that does not result in conception even for a pregnant woman—that alone is the "excellent" [state]; therefore, it is called *rajas*. For this very reason, a woman in her menses (*rajasvalā*) is unfit for social interaction. ||9||
By means of a boon consisting of an abundance of substance, the waters took up the fourth part as impurity;
that [impurity], seen in those [waters] as bubbles and foam, he (the Sun) carries away while casting it aside.
Śrīdhara: He states the fruit of that classification [of water] with the words "dravya... and so on. It removes—that is, it dispels—that sin.

Who is it that casts it away? The meaning is: one who casts it out from the water, such as bubbles and the like. Alternatively, "casting" (kṣipan) means that the water takes away—that is, it brings or seizes—the sin. And for this reason, water is not...

The meaning of the Vedic passage beginning with "paricakṣyā" has been stated. In an alternative reading, *harikilbiṣam* means the sin of Indra; [the phrase] "for Indra" means for the sake of slaying Indra, and "for the enemy" means for the sake of producing an enemy. ||10||

By the boon of the abundance of substance (*dravyabhūyovara*): it means that in whatever substance, such as milk and the like, water might be mixed, there should be its "abundance," meaning its predominance (*ādhikya*), by virtue of that boon; or else, it refers to the boon of its own abundance through the emergence of its own springs and so forth. Even with the reading *dravabhūya*, the meaning is exactly this. Or alternatively, *dravabhūyas*.
You possess innate fluidity by virtue of that boon; for it is stated in this Vedic revelation: "Of this [element], Viśvarūpa, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, is indeed [the lord]."

Regarding the sequence of composition: even in the alternative reading *dravyabhūyaḥ*, the word *dravya* denotes *drava* (fluidity) itself—either through the use of a primary derivative (*kṛt-prayoga*) in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*), or through a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) in its own sense. In the commentary, the term “mixed” (*miśrāḥ*) implies that prior to this point, they would not have been mixed at all. [The phrase] “the emergence of a waterfall” (*nirjharodgama*).

It is understood that prior to this, there was nothing such as the emergence of waterfalls and so forth. Regarding the reading "dravabhūyaḥ," Viśvanātha notes that it signifies natural fluidity (*sāṃsiddhika-dravatva*), which indicates that previously there was some solid substance; [the term] "bhūyaḥ" refers to the abundance of substances such as milk and the like through our contact.

Therefore, the very abundance [of water] is our boon. If the reading is *dravabhūyaḥ*, it means the state of being predominantly liquid (*dravabhūyastvam*), that is, natural fluidity (*sāṃsiddhikadravatvam*); by means of that, that impurity is seen in those waters through bubbles and froth.
For this very reason, he carries away the waters—taking them up—only by casting off and removing that [impurity] consisting of bubbles and so forth, but not [the water itself].

The meaning is that they are possessed of bubbles and so forth. And if someone were to fetch water that is indeed possessed of those [impurities], the sense is that he would be fetching nothing but sin. ||10||
His son having been slain, Tvaṣṭṛ then offered an oblation to Indra as his enemy, saying:
"O enemy of Indra, grow strong; do not delay; slay the one who hates you!"

Śrīdhara says: "Therefore he said, 'O enemy of Indra, may you prosper! Here, because the word *indraśatru* has the acute accent on its first syllable, the rule of the Smṛti stating that 'in a Bahuvrīhi compound, the first member retains its original form' applies; thus, by the definition of a Bahuvrīhi, Indra alone became his enemy. As it has been said:
According to Śruti, it says: "Because he said, 'O Indra's enemy, grow strong! therefore Indra became his enemy. And likewise, the Śikṣā states:
"A mantra deficient in accent or in phoneme..."
"Employed incorrectly, it does not convey that meaning;
that vajra of speech destroys the sacrificer, just as Indra’s enemy [did] due to an error in the accent. Thus it is said.
From the Anvāhāryapacana fire, which is the Dakṣiṇāgni.

The sequence of composition is as follows: "O enemy of Indra, may you prosper! Here, the word *śatru* means "slayer. In that case, if it were a *tatpuruṣa* compound, Vṛtra would be the slayer; however, since it is a *bahuvrīhi*, it results in Indra being the slayer.
And in that context, the status of the compound as a *tatpuruṣa* is established by the rule *samāsācca tadviṣayāt* (Pāṇini 5.4.68).

The fact that the compound-final vowel is oxytone is manifested by the rule prescribing the oxytone accent for the final member of a compound; however, its status as a *bahuvrīhi* is manifested by the rule "in a *bahuvrīhi*, the first member retains its original accent," which establishes the initial acute accent (*ādyudātta*) of the first member as its inherent property. For the word *indra* is indeed acutely accented on the first syllable.

Because the word *paramaiśvarya* is listed in the *udātta* class of gaṇas, its initial syllable is thus accented; consequently, by this reading of the initial *udātta*, a reversal occurred, and Indra alone became his enemy. ||11||

Viśvanātha: Regarding the previous statement, "At the end of the year, that sin [is removed]," as soon as the Moon was liberated from the murder of a Brahmin at the commencement of the month of Āśvina, Tvaṣṭṛ, having heard of the slaughter of his own son, returned from the penance grove and proceeded to protect his own month of Āśvina.
Out of anger and grief, he devised a means to slay Indra; thus it is said, "His son was slain. To Indra, his enemy—that is, to slay the enemy in the form of Indra—he uttered this mantra:
"O enemy of Indra, grow strong! This refers to the compound meaning: "being the enemy of Indra, grow strong."

Even though that was intended to be expressed, the meaning of a *bahuvrīhi*—namely, "one for whom Indra alone is the enemy"—has occurred by chance due to the violation of accentuation. For instance, because the root *idi*, meaning "supreme sovereignty," is listed in the group of [roots] with the acute (*udātta*) accent, the word *indra* is indeed *ādyudātta* (acute on the first syllable); and in that case, [the rule] *samāsasya*...

Because the rule *ceti* prescribes only the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) for a compound in general, the word *indraśatro* has its initial syllable accented acute by the rule *tatpuruṣe śeṣam anudāttam*. However, in the case of a *bahuvrīhi*,
the preceding rule *prakṛtyā pūrvapadam*— which supersedes the former— applies to the first member of the compound.

Because the rule for establishing the accent based on inherent derivation applies to the *bahuvrīhi* compound, the word *indraśatruḥ* has its initial syllable accented (*ādyudātta*). However, by fate, Tvaṣṭṛ recited it with that very same initial accentuation, and thus Indra alone became his enemy and slayer. This is stated in the Śruti: "That which he said..."
"O Śatru of Indra, prosper with Svāhā!"—therefore, Indra became his enemy. And likewise, the Śikṣā says:
"One who is deficient in mantra, whether in accent or in phoneme..."
When used incorrectly by one person toward another, it does not convey that intended meaning;
just as "Indraśatru" [meant to mean "one whose enemy is Indra"] [actually] destroyed the sacrificer because of a fault in the accent, for speech is indeed a thunderbolt. Thus [it is said]. (11)
Then, rising from the Anvāhāryapacana fire, he appeared terrible to behold,
like the God of Death at the end of an eon for all the worlds.

Śrīdhara: The connection with the fifth [verse] is as follows: "Seeing him, the people, terrified, fled in the ten directions. Of what nature was he? He was expanding daily by the distance of an arrow-shot (iṣuvikṣepa) on all sides, everywhere.
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Now, immediately thereafter, when a deviation from one's own recensional text is recognized, [the procedure begins] from the Anvāhāryapacana fire.

Because he was recited as a *bahuvrīhi* compound— characterized by the acute accent (*udātta*) on the first member obtained through its inherent nature— and subsequently recited as a *tatpuruṣa* compound— characterized by the grave accent (*anudātta*) on the first member obtained through external application— for that reason, he arose with a terrifying appearance; yet, due to his being recited according to his inherent nature, Indra shall be his slayer.

The sense is that later, by means of the *anvāhārya* [offering], even Indra will be slain by him, because he (Indra) along with his vehicle will be swallowed up by him. Since the word *anvāhārya* denotes the monthly *śrāddha* rite, no other interpretation is tenable. ||12||
Increasing on all sides by the measure of an arrow every single day,
resembling a scorched mountain and possessing the luster of a mass of twilight clouds;

Śrīdhara: [He is] black in color, resembling a burnt mountain; he whose radiance and luster are like a mass of twilight clouds; he whose crests and beard are like molten copper; and he whose eyes are fierce like the midday sun. (13)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: The connection with the fifth [verse] is as follows: "Seeing him, the terrified worlds fled in the ten directions. Of what kind [was he]? *Viṣvak*, meaning all around, in his own ten directions—above, below, and the eight cardinal points.
Increasing day by day by the distance of an arrow-shot. ||13||

Having impaled him upon a trident with three blazing points, which filled heaven and earth, he whose hair and beard were like glowing copper and whose fierce eyes were like the midday sun, [placed him there].
Śrīdhara: The meaning is "as if lifting up the two worlds (heaven and earth). ||14||

The sequential arrangement: therein, by means of the worlds of heaven and earth, one should indeed fix [the victim] upon the trident, because of the mental realization of the completion of its own threading onto that trident. ||14||
Viśvanātha: The meaning is "having repeatedly superimposed. ||14||
Dancing and roaring loudly, he shook the earth with his feet;
with a mouth as deep as a cave, he seemed to drink up the vault of heaven.
Śrīdhara: The grammatical construction is: "yawning again and again with a mouth as deep as a cave.
How so? With a mouth that was drinking the expanse of the sky, licking the stars with its tongue, and swallowing the three worlds. (15)
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: "By those who drink, as if by drinking [the nectar]. (15)
Beholding him repeatedly yawning with his great, fierce fangs, as he devoured the three worlds with his tongue while grasping the stars.
Terrified, all the worlds fled, looking toward the ten directions.
Śrīdhara: "By the great" means by the extensive. "In which there are fierce fangs" [is the meaning]. ||16||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha states: "It has not been explained.
—o)0(o)— By him, whose form was that of Tvaṣṭṛ’s son, these worlds were enveloped through his ascetic power (*tapas*).
He was indeed called Vṛtra, a wicked and most terrible being.

Śrīdhara explains the etymology of the name Vṛtra with the words "yenāvṛtā" (by whom [the worlds] were covered). He is the embodiment of that darkness; thus says the Śruti: "He covered these worlds, and that is the reason for Vṛtra's name, 'Vṛtra'. (17)

The sequential composition [is as follows]: "By which" refers to those [rays]. "By the form of Tvaṣṭṛ" (tvāṣṭramūrtinā) means that its very nature (mūrtiḥ = svarūpam) appears precisely through its connection with Tvaṣṭṛ; this is the meaning. ||17||
Viśvanātha: The meaning is that these worlds were covered by Vṛtra, who possessed a form belonging to Tvaṣṭṛ—that is, related to Tvaṣṭṛ. ||17||
The preeminent gods, accompanied by their hosts, rushed toward him and struck him down with floods of their own various divine missiles and weapons; yet he swallowed them all entirely.
Śrīdhara: "Agrasat" means he ate. ||18||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— Then they were all astonished, dejected, and their splendor eclipsed.
With concentrated minds, they approached the Primal Being who was facing toward them.

Śrīdhara: [He is] one whose splendor has been swallowed by them. [They praised] the Inner Controller (antaryāmin) who is within; for since the three worlds are pervaded by Him, it is impossible to go anywhere else. The meaning is that they remained right there and offered praise.
Thinking that there can be no protection from great fear other than him, the gods, afflicted by distress, take refuge in Hari alone. (19)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: "Pratyañcam" means that which is inward-turned, namely the inner controller (*antaryāmin*). ||19||
The illustrious gods said:
"The three worlds consist of air, ether, fire, water, and earth."
We, including Brahmā and the others,
who tremble with fear, offer tribute to him; he from whom even Death fears— that is our refuge.
Madhva says: Time, the Ender, Pradhāna, Death, and the Unmanifest—these are also spoken of by the names Śrī, Bhū, and Durgā, who is the subtle Prakṛti.
"She herself bestows fear upon Brahmā and the others, yet she remains under the control of Viṣṇu;
though she is fearless, it is proclaimed that she seems to fear because of being subject to his will. Thus [it is said] in the *Mātsya Purāṇa*. 20.

Śrīdhara: The five great elements, beginning with air, and the three worlds fashioned by them, as well as their presiding deities such as Brahmā and others, and even we ourselves who are posterior to them—all of us offer tribute to that Antaka, Kāla, before whom we tremble; yet even he is afraid of whom? Therefore—
May the Supreme Lord alone be our non-conflict, our refuge, and our protection. ||20||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Thinking that no one other than the Supreme Lord will be able to protect them from this fear born of Vṛtra, they take refuge in Him alone, saying "O Wind."

The twenty-three principles characterized by air and the rest, as well as the three worlds fashioned by those elements such as air, and likewise their presiding deities beginning with Brahmā, and we ourselves who are subsequent to them—
all these are terrified and afraid of death; for even this Antaka, Death himself, [is subject to it].
From whatever one fears, from that very Supreme Lord alone may there be for us *araṇam*—that is, refuge and protection. ||20||
To him, who was free from wonder, whose desires were fulfilled, and who was tranquil through his own attainment;
For the fool does not approach another [path] without [the right means];
he attempts to cross the ocean with the claw of a dog.

Śrīdhara: They state the reason for the restriction "from that very [source]" as follows: [He is] *avismitam*, meaning free from egoism or devoid of curiosity. Why? Because he is *praśāntam*, meaning free from passion and the like. And why is that?
Because his desires are fulfilled by his own attainment alone. And why is that? Because he is *samam* (equanimous).

It is empty of the delimitation of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). He who approaches anyone other than the Supreme Lord, who is of such a nature, for the sake of refuge, is a fool, an ignorant person; for he desires to cross the ocean by means of a dog’s tail—that is, its wagging tail. Just as by that [tail]...
The sense is that just as crossing the ocean does not occur [without a boat], so too crossing the ocean of calamity does not occur by relying on one who is not the Lord (nirīśvara). ||21||

The sequence of the composition: "Unsurprised" (*avismitam*) means free from astonishment because no other unprecedented object exists; therefore, he is one whose desires are fulfilled by the very attainment of his own self—which is both the object (*karmabhūta*) and the action (*kriyābhūta*)—and not by anything else. Consequently, he is equal toward all things. Therefore...

"Tranquil" means free from defects of the mind. Thus it has been said: "Those whose natures consist of *rajas* and *tamas*, being of similar character, indeed worship [them]" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.2.27), and so forth. Therefore, it was stated by the venerable Satyavrata:
"Not even a ten-thousandth part, nor even a fraction of that grace..."
Other gods, teachers, and people themselves, though united, are not able to do that for a man; I indeed take refuge in Him who is the Lord. [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 8.24.49]
And in the Śrī Mahābhārata: "But he who, out of delusion, abandons Viṣṇu and worships another, is like one who, casting aside a heap of gold, desires to grasp a heap of dust."
This has been explained in detail specifically in the Bhaktisandarbha. ||21||
Viśvanātha: Others, however, say that one should not resort to anything else with a discerning mind—hence the words "without wonder.

Apart from Him, only a fool—a great blockhead—and not a wise person, approaches another deity, or the yoga of action (*karmayoga*), the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*), or some other yoga for the sake of refuge; just as [one would approach] a dog.

He wishes to cross the ocean by means of his own tail; yet that dog is not even able to cross the ocean himself, much less one who seizes its tail! On the contrary, seeing one who grasps his own tail, that very dog first casts him into the middle of the sea and subsequently sinks down himself—this is the intended meaning.
They say that it is not at all surprising that one who takes refuge in the Blessed One crosses the ocean of saṃsāra;

thus they say, "without wonder" (*avismitam*). Wherein no wonder—that is, no marvel whatsoever—is found, even though crossing the ocean of saṃsāra is otherwise difficult to achieve, there is no cause for excessive astonishment elsewhere; in that regard, there is nothing [to be wondered at].
This is a state of wonder; the sense is that [the Lord] possesses the power to turn that very [ocean] into a mere cow's footprint at once.

"Together with the attainment of His own nature"—that is, together with the acquisition of the sevenfold sweetness consisting of beauty and so forth—"one whose desires are fully satisfied" refers to one for whom there are enjoyments granted by His own *hlādinī* potency.
To the one who is tranquil, compassionate, and forgiving even when an offense against his service occurs, because this is the characteristic mark of a distinguished devotee—
to him,
upon whose lofty horn he placed the earth like his own boat— o)o(o— him [I salute].
Just as Manu crossed the difficult passage after binding [the boat],
so surely you, though a dweller of the waters, will protect us who have sought refuge from the terrible fear of Tvaṣṭṛ’s son.
Śrīdhara says: "It is observed that He alone is the protector in great danger," and so they say with these two verses beginning with *yasya*.

Having tied the earth itself to His own boat upon His great horn, Manu Satyavrata crossed over that difficult crisis exactly as required; He, the one who moves in the waters, in the form of a fish, [protects] us.
He will surely protect and guard those who have taken refuge in him. ||22||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: But we, though extremely lowly and full of desire, even as we seek refuge in this one who is the source of great fear, must surely be protected by him, just as those of old were; thus they say with the two verses beginning with "yasya" (of whom). Of whom... [the rest of the verse follows].
The sense is: "Just as he crossed over the earth in the form of a fish, may we too cross over in that same manner.
Although he is a water-dweller moving within the water itself, by remaining right there, may he protect us who dwell on the earth, for he is the Lord. ||22||
In ancient times, even the Self-Existent One [Brahmā] was terrified in the waters of cosmic dissolution, which were formidable with the sounds of rising winds and waves.
One [lotus] fell from the lotus-pond; may He, by whom it crossed over that [fall] out of fear, be our protector.
Madhva: Wherein Prakṛti exists in the form of Vāyu, water, lotuses, and so forth, there Brahmā alone remained undivided; having reflected, he transcended fear.
"Haris entered within him and, being meditated upon, dispelled his fear. And:
"For the sake of establishing the natural state of people yet to be born, even a Brahmin who is full of qualities such as knowledge [attains] those [realms] in half a moment."
"Ignorance occurs four times, and fear twice;
even in this world, one can never become a Brāhmaṇa otherwise.
Even in that case, it would happen for him only through devotion to the Blessed One and through his own spiritual elevation. Thus, in the Brahmatarka.

Śrīdhara: In the waters of restraint—that is, in the waters of universal dissolution—within that which is terrifying and fearsome due to the roar of waves raised by surging winds, he alone, who was almost fallen from his lotus-navel and remained without a companion, crossed over that fear; he alone is our shore.
May he be our savior. ||23||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: In the waters of the dissolution (*saṃyama-ambhasi*), that is, in the waters of the cosmic destruction; "fallen from the lotus," meaning from the navel-lotus, or as if fallen—by which cause he [is so described]. (23)
That one Lord who, by his own *māyā*, created us, and through whom we create the universe;
We do not perceive the mark of even him who strives before us, for we consider ourselves to be lords.
We see only the indicative mark (liṅga) [of the soul] in Madhva.

However, at times, even for the gods, there may exist as it were a sense of ego (abhimāna); yet, generally speaking, throughout the various states of time, that too does not exist at all, according to the gradations [of their realization]. Thus it is said. (24)

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, they say with three verses beginning with "He who is one," "We were created and protected many times by the Blessed One alone; therefore, we go to Him alone for refuge. Being favored by Him, we create the universe.

"Are you yourselves not the creators? Is there no other benefactor for you, since none such is seen? To this they reply: "We do not perceive the mark or form of Him who was already exerting Himself as the Inner Controller even before us; the reason for this is that we are possessed of the conceit that each of us is a separate lord."
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: "May He—who indeed exists everywhere and even here, though invisible to us whose senses are turned outward, yet having become visible through His very grace—protect us," they say—*ya*.

Thus, with these three [verses]: "Even though He is manifesting His divine play (līlā) before us in forms such as Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, we do not perceive His true nature (liṅga); the reason for this is 'separateness' (pṛthak). (24)
He who is eternally present among gods, ṛṣis, animals, and humans, [protects] us who are being severely oppressed by our rivals.
Having made his descent through his own illusory power (māyā) by means of various bodies, he makes them his own and protects them age after age.
Let us all go for refuge to that very God, our own deity,
the supreme, the primary, the universal Puruṣa, the other,
who is worthy of refuge.
That great-souled one will bestow welfare upon us and our own people.
Śrīdhara: Having taken incarnations among the gods and others through forms such as Upendra, Paraśurāma, Matsya, and Rāma, he makes them his own and protects them. ||25||

The deity is one's own self. Why? Because the universe has the universe as its self. Nevertheless, they exclude any other modification. The reason for being the self of the universe is that it is the supreme cause. Now, if it is argued that both *pradhāna* (primordial matter) and *puruṣa* (the individual soul) are the causes of the universe, they reply: [it is] *pradhāna* and *puruṣa*; yet He is also of the nature of those two.
