The meaning is "he himself"; he alone will bestow welfare upon us. ||26||

*Caitanyamatamañjuṣā*: "He who [is not slain] by our enemies," and so forth. He is eternal indeed through his bodies; being eternal, he remains so. Now, is it not the case that the eternity of a body is untenable? No, he says: "by his own *māyā*, that is, by his inherent power (*svabhāva-śakti*). Here, the word *svamāyā* refers to inherent power, for power is...
Because it is inconceivable and beyond the reach of logic. ||25||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.

*Viśvanātha*: By means of his forms—such as Upendra, Paraśurāma, and others—he protects us by making us his own through his own *māyā*, grace, and conscious power (*cicchakti*), even while appearing as a child; for this very reason, at present...

The sense is that we do not shrink even from making a declaration for the sake of self-preservation. "That very one" refers to the universe, which is of universal form through the power of *māyā*, yet distinct from the universe through his own essential power (*svarūpa-śakti*). ||2526||
Śrī Śuka said:
O great king, as the gods were thus standing in attendance, [he spoke].
In the western direction, the bearer of the conch, discus, and mace appeared.
Śrīdhara first appeared in the western direction within the heart. ||27||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: In the western direction, on the shore of the western ocean, because that other excellent land was overrun by demons and it was impossible for the gods to remain there, [the Lord] sat down right there in a secluded spot.
Because it has been praised. ||27||
[He saw] the one with eyes like blossoming autumn lotuses, attended by sixteen beings equal to himself, excluding Śrīvatsa and Kaustubha.
Seeing him upon the earth, all [the people], overwhelmed by the joy of their eyes, fell prostrate like staffs; then, rising slowly, O King, they offered praise.
"Madhu’s [consort] Śrīvatsā is to be known as Prakṛti, and the Kaustubha gem named Brahmā is Puruṣa; He is also worshipped through sixteen forms that transcend those two. Thus it is said.
Excluding Śrīvatsā and Kaustubha, [the remaining forms] are equal to Himself because they transcend both Prakṛti and Puruṣa.
The meaning is that even the seventeen forms are equal. "Equal to his own self" means by those who are both identical to him and equal to him.
Because he is not dependent on the nature of a male, Hari [is the source] of Vāsudeva and the others.

"Keśava and the others are equal and are not different in any way," so it is said in the *Tantrasāra*. Furthermore, Janārdana eternally manifests his being through the Śrīvatsa and Kaustubha, which consist of the nature of Puruṣa and Prakṛti respectively.
"Because Hari has passed beyond these two, he is no longer under their control;
yet that very same state constitutes his separation from the Śrīvatsa and the Kaustubha. Thus it is said. (2829)

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, the grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: having seen him again before them, being overwhelmed by the joy of his sight, they fell prostrate on the ground like a staff;
then, rising slowly, they offered praise. Of what nature was he?
He was accompanied by sixteen attendants such as Sunanda, who were equal to himself, though without Śrīvatsa and Kaustubha.
He whose eyes are like fully blossomed autumn lotuses. ||29||

The sequential arrangement: the pair beginning with "the Self. [This is] due to the inherent nature of things and the certainty of attaining one's desired goal through the joy of contemplation. ||29||

Viśvanātha: [He is] endowed with the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem; though possessing four arms and other attributes, he is surrounded by his own attendants such as Sunanda and others who resemble himself, as if they were his own manifestations. ||2829||
—the illustrious gods said:
"Salutations to you, whose strength is sacrifice; salutations also to you, O Vayas."
Homage indeed to you, the eight-wheeled one; homage to you, the one well-invoked by many.
"Madhvaḥ" means "the life-force of all," because the Blessed Lord Puruṣottama is the one who causes all to grow; thus says the Śruti: "May He not cut the thread while weaving my intellect. (30)

Śrīdhara: Salutations to Him whose sacrifice is *vīrya*—the power to produce fruits such as heaven; and also to Him who is *vayas*, the very nature of time that delimits those fruits. To Him who, with such powers, cast His discus (*cakra*) at the Daityas who obstructed them, for the sake of the well-invoked [Indra].
To the one named Śobhanabahu. ||30||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Manifesting their mere conceit of being lords, [the verse states] that you alone are the cause of both the attainment of results and the obstruction thereof for worshippers such as ourselves through sacrifices.
They said: "Salutation!"—to Him from whom comes the *vīrya* (potency) of sacrifice, characterized by the power to produce fruits such as heaven;

the sense is: to Him who bestows the fruit. Furthermore, salutation to *vayasa*, that is, to Time, which destroys fruits such as heaven. Likewise, salutation to the Discus-weapon (*astracakra*), having cast the discus among the Asuras.

To him who has many names— such as "the subduer of those [demons]," "the protector of us," "the one who leads to heaven and so forth," "the destroyer of heaven and so forth," "the annihilator of the Asuras," and "the guardian of the gods"— to that Supuru-hūti (Indra). ||30||
O Creator, that supreme station of yours, the ruler of the three paths of destiny,
cannot be known by one who is recent to creation.

"Madhva said: That which is beyond the world of the gods, the world of the ancestors, and even hell—that supreme station, the Vaiṣṇava realm, is known as the goal of the wise. Thus it is stated in the *Māhātmya*. (31)

Śrīdhara: Now, why is it that, setting aside Your form which transcends the *guṇas*, You describe [Yourself] as possessing qualities such as being the "strength of sacrifice" (*yajñavīryatva*) and so forth, which are conditioned by the *guṇas*? To this they reply: That supreme state of Yours—which is the nature of the *niṣguṇa* (beyond the *guṇas*)—is the highest station of the three paths consisting of the three *guṇas*, belonging to You who are the Lord and Controller of those three *guṇas*.
O Creator, one who is posterior to the emission—that is, one like me at present—is not able to know You; therefore, let there be only salutation to You. ||31||

The Sequence of Composition (*kramasaṃdarbha*): Now, setting aside this form of mine which is directly perceived, why is it described as being characterized by qualities (*guṇa*) and adjuncts (*upādhi*), such as the potency for sacrifice and so forth? To that they say: "That which is yours," [says] Viśvanātha. Now, do you not praise [the Lord] merely for the sake of attaining the perishable and trivial state of heaven?
But what is the reason for seeking Vaikuṇṭha, which consists of imperishable, eternal bliss?

To this they reply: Your supreme abode, the realm of Vaikuṇṭha, belongs to You, the Lord and bestower of the three paths of gods, humans, and animals; it is not something that a person like us, who is within the sphere of worldly creation (visarga), can know.

It is not fit to be experienced [by them]. For the meaning is that a beast does not desire, nor obtain from anywhere else, anything such as milk and the like without fodder, chaff, and so forth. ||31||

—o)0(o— Oṃ! Salutations be unto you, O Blessed One! O Nārāyaṇa! O Vāsudeva! O Primordial Person! O Great Person! O Being of Great Majesty! O Supreme Auspiciousness! O Supreme Well-being! O Supreme Compassionate One!
O Kevala! O Support of the World! O Sole Lord of the Universe! O Lord of All! O Lord of Lakṣmī!

[By you] the door whose panels of darkness have been flung open by those wandering mendicants who are supreme *paramahaṃsas*, through the highest meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of self-yoga, and by whom the duty of the *paramahaṃsa* state has been made perfectly clear.
"In your mind, the light of the Self having been unveiled, you have yourself experienced the realization of your own innate bliss.

Śrīdhara [commented]: "The verses, though concise, do not measure the virtues of Hari. Thus, dissatisfied with the metrical compositions, they immediately praised him in prose, addressing him in many ways with an outpouring of devotion.

They elaborate upon its difficult-to-comprehend nature with the words beginning "O Blessed One" and so forth. That which contains the supreme auspiciousness— the pure Dharma— is that Pāramahaṃsya-dharma which has been thoroughly cultivated and well-practiced through the yoga of the Self, namely, the Samādhi which is one-pointedness of mind, and which is thus perfectly manifest.
Devotion to the Blessed One is that which has opened the door of the nature of darkness; when that door-like mind is thus uncovered and revealed, the world of the Self appears in its fresh form.
You are that very experience of one's own innate bliss which is spontaneously realized and manifested therein. ||33||

The sequential arrangement: *tamas* is *prakṛti* or ignorance. "In the world of the Self" means in the world that is one's own true nature; as stated in the scripture: "This is the world of the Self, this is the world of Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.32), and "For this Supreme Self is established in the divine city of Brahman" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.7), and so forth. That which is...
It should be known as subtle and supreme; they declare it to be the eternal state of all-pervading majesty. ||33||

[Bhagavatsandarbha 61] Viśvanātha: Since it was said, "to Puruhūta," they praise him by addressing him with many names, beginning with "Namaḥ. O Bhagavān! O you who are fully endowed with the sixfold opulences! They describe this very fullness thus—He...

O Nārāyaṇa! The meaning is that you alone, through the sequence of the increase of your own portions, exist as the one who reclines upon the ocean of milk, the womb of the waters, and the ocean of the causal waters, by virtue of being the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of both individual and collective primordial nature (*prakṛti*). Furthermore, because of your perfection even beyond that, O Vāsudeva, O primordial source of the emanations (*vyūha*)!
Furthermore, because of His perfection, O Primordial Person! O Lord of the Supreme Abode!
How indeed is this understood? To that they reply: He is one in whom there exist great majesties—that is, great powers corresponding [to the needs]—among the Great Persons who are His devotees.
Now, one might ask: what is the fate of my devotees, my abodes, and my forms during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*)?

To this they reply: "The auspicious things" refers to the natural (*prākṛta*) auspicious things, while "the supremely auspicious" refers to the non-natural (*aprākṛta*) auspicious entities, such as Your devotees, Your abodes, and so forth; [it is so called] because of their supreme well-being and welfare. Of these...
The sense is that [the Lord] is not subject to the constraints of time.
Furthermore, they say: "O You who are an ocean of boundless sovereignty and sweetness, we—who perceive only the external and are being devoured by time—take refuge in Your compassion alone.
But as for those who perceive the internal [reality], O Supreme Compassionate One!... [they perceive You differently].

You indeed become one who has directly experienced the realization of your own innate bliss. When? Through *samādhi*, which is one-pointedness of mind cultivated by means of *ātma-yoga*—namely, the restraints (*yama*), observances (*niyama*), and so forth. Why? Because the supreme duty of the *paramahaṃsa*, which is the yoga of devotion (*bhakti-yoga*), is perfectly manifest.

Thus, when the mind— which has its door of darkness flung open— is in such a state, you abide within that very palace of the mind, in the world of the Self, the abode of Vaikuṇṭha, being unveiled and free from all obscurations;
for when the mind is thus, you yourself exist right there in the midst of it as the world of Vaikuṇṭha.
It is called "bhāva" because it vibrates. ||33||
This mode of your sporting seems difficult to comprehend, in that you, being without shelter, without a body,
and regardless of our collective presence, being yourself unchanging, create and protect this world with its qualities while remaining yourself devoid of qualities.
Śrīdhara:
[Objection: But if You are of the nature of pure experience alone, how can You be the agent of creation and so forth?
To this they reply: This mode of Your play is difficult to comprehend, since You are without refuge and without support.
This is the universe. That sequence of events is one in which our collective association—our meeting and cooperation—is not considered.

Thus, while your sporting in Vaikuṇṭha is difficult to perceive, it is nonetheless established by logic because it is suited to you due to your transcendence of the *guṇas* and other such qualities. However, your sporting within the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) transcends logic.

They say that [the Lord] is difficult to comprehend because of the opposite nature [of His attributes], such as possessing qualities (*saguṇatva*). For a potter and the like possess qualities, rely upon a certain place and another kind of inherence (*samavāya*), and having set their own body in motion, they produce, protect, and remove objects such as pots—which themselves possess qualities—by means of other materials such as clay; but you...

The meaning is that [the Lord], though devoid of qualities (*aguṇa*) and indeed changeless (*avikriya*), manifests the world of plurality (*prapañca*) as possessing qualities by His own self through mere will, even without such supports as those [previously mentioned]. For the statement beginning with "without refuge" was spoken precisely with that intention. The word "as if" (*iva*) is used because of His inconceivable power; for even that [manifestation] is [due to His power].
The meaning is that it is not inaccessible even through excessive reasoning. ||33||

Viśvanātha: Furthermore, they say that although You sport eternally in Your own Vaikuṇṭha realm, being self-satisfied and transcending the material qualities (guṇātīta), You nevertheless sport in the world of manifestation through modes such as creation, which are difficult for those like us to comprehend;
thus, the "union of pastimes" (vihārayoga)—that is, the state of being engaged in play—is difficult to understand.
The meaning is that [this state] is easily understood by those wise in devotion to You, yet difficult for others to understand. Why?

Because one who has taken refuge in You is indeed without support (*nirāśraya*) and bodiless (*aśarīra*), being devoid of the activities of the embodied. For the Creator of the universe possesses form, according to such scriptural passages as "He of a thousand heads. This was not considered by us, Indra and the others.

He is one whose assistance consists in the conjunction of the presiding deities of the hands and other limbs. Even though the Self alone is the material cause (*upādāna*), it is not surprising that it remains unchanging, given the acceptance of the theory of illusory transformation (*vivartavāda*); indeed, it would be surprising only if such a theory were not accepted. For this very reason:
The Lord of Elephants will say:
"Obeisances, obeisances unto You, the cause of all, who are Yourself without cause, the wondrous cause" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 8.3.15).

Thus, the cause possesses a state of wonder: even while acting as the material cause (*upādāna*), it remains entirely free from modification. Being devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), you create the universe which possesses qualities (*saguṇa*). For a potter or the like, depending on some location, setting his own body in motion, and aided by external objects such as clay which undergo transformation, creates only that which possesses qualities.
"It is observed that [an agent] creates a pot possessing qualities"—this is one difficulty regarding creation. (33)
Now, in this matter, does your honor, like Devadatta, fall into the emission of qualities here and, through dependence on others,
experience the fruit of his own performed wholesome and unwholesome deeds; or rather, is he one who delights in the self and is characterized by tranquility?
"We do not know how the Seer of the Truth remained indifferent.
Madhva: Here, the objection is, "Is he like Devadatta?
The intended meaning is: "How could one who possesses inconceivable power and infinite qualities have dependence on others and so forth? ||34||

Śrīdhara says: They state another point that is difficult to understand: "Now, there... Just as Devadatta here, having constructed a house or the like, experiences therein the fruit of his own performed good and evil deeds, so too You, whose nature is Brahman, having fallen into the creation of the *guṇas* in the form of a *jīva*, experience [the fruits]. Or else:
He whose vision is correct and unerring is the power of consciousness; you, such as he, are indifferent (*udāsa*), meaning you remain as a witness in a state of detachment. ||34||

The sequence of the composition: "But we are unable to determine this," they say with sarcasm to address those whose minds are turned outward—beginning with "Now" (*atha*). In that regard, at the beginning of creation, during the process of action, like Devadatta or like a particular transmigrating soul (*saṃsārijīva*), having fallen into the emission of the qualities (*guṇa*) due to ignorance (*avidyā*).

He assumes forms such as those of gods or animals as the fruit of his own performed good and evil deeds; or rather, even while possessing the form of Devadatta, he remains one who delights in the Self through knowledge, and so forth—thus says Viśvanātha: for the protection of the virtuous cannot occur without the destruction of the wicked.
They state that even preservation, which includes destruction within it, is difficult to comprehend—beginning with the word "atha" (now).

Just as Devadatta, an ordinary living being, having constructed a house and the like, enters therein—the dense world of transmigration consisting of friends, enemies, neutrals, and so forth—and experiences pleasure and pain, the fruits of his own performed merit and demerit; [so too is the Lord's action].

Likewise, in that regard, you too— out of respect for the statement "so indeed is your lordship"— have fallen among those various emanations of the *guṇas* (the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*), namely the gods, asuras, rākṣasas,
and others who strike one another down, during your incarnations as Upendra, Kṛṣṇa, and Rāma.
Engaged in the protection of the virtuous and the restraint of the wicked, whatever enjoyment, sovereignty, and pleasure you obtain,

as well as the pain of fatigue from battle and the like— that is it; is that [result] due to dependence, being subject to karma, [namely] the wholesome or unwholesome pleasure and pain resulting from your own performed merits and demerits?

Does it appropriate and take possession [of them], or rather—what else?—does it remain indifferent as a witness, not taking possession of pleasure or pain because its power of consciousness is unimpaired and it possesses correct vision? We do not know; we do not know the truth of the matter. ||34||

Indeed, there is no contradiction regarding both [attributes] in the Blessed One, the Lord whose multitude of infinite qualities is unfathomable; for such contradictions are the province only of those debaters who rely on inner organs clouded by modern conceptualizations, conjectures, deliberations, fallacious means of knowledge, and the sophistry of false treatises.

There is no occasion for dispute in that which has ceased all that consists of *māyā*; for when the Lord alone has withdrawn His own *māyā*, what purpose could possibly be difficult to accomplish, given the absence of a second nature?
Madhva: [In the phrase] "in that which has ceased all that consists of *māyā," it means being devoid of a material nature; [it is] absolute.
"His own *māyā* is his innate power. This is the resolution [to the objection] beginning with "because of the absence of two natures," and so forth.
"Is he independent or dependent? Wise or ignorant? Suffering or happy?"—such doubts arise in which ignorant person?
Because Hari possesses infinite qualities and full power,
the wise know with certainty that His sovereignty and other attributes belong to Him alone;
for He is the accomplisher of the impossible and is entirely inscrutable.
They call this soul, which is ignorant of that power, "dependent";
thus, by means of this inscrutable power, the Supreme Lord remains unaware [of his own nature] to those who are ignorant.

Śrīdhara: Having thus stated that [the Lord] is difficult to know due to apparent contradiction, they describe the manner of knowing Him by means of its resolution, beginning with "For not... (*na hi*). "Contradiction" (*virodha*) means that which is contradicted. The meaning is that both [attributes] are not contradictory. For there is no doubt regarding You through any other example.

They say that [this] is appropriate because of His inconceivable sovereignty—referring to Him as "the Blessed One" (*bhagavat*). This means: in that independent Lord who possesses an immeasurable multitude of qualities; in Him whose majesty is unfathomable and beyond reasoning (*atarkya*);

where "doubt" (*vikalpa*) is the thought "it might be thus or otherwise," "speculation" (*vitarka*) is the inquiry "what is appropriate here?", and "deliberation" (*vicāra*) is the thought "it must be exactly like this."

In that regard, there are fallacious means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāsa*) and their supporting factors—namely, those modern sophistries (*kutarka*), conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), and so forth, which do not touch upon the true nature of things—in whatever treatises these exist; by them, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) becomes turbid and agitated. By such a [state], the basis of which is difficult to restrain, belongs to that disputant (*vādin*).

"Since this is not the occasion for dispute and is beyond the scope [of logic], is this not merely a matter of faith? Let a logical argument be stated. To this they reply: "He who has ceased from illusion—that cycle of existence (saṃsāra) within which [it exists]—even while remaining in that absolute state, having placed his own creative power (māyā) in the midst [of it], what indeed is the purpose?"

Agency and so forth are not possible. They say that if agency and so forth were to exist in reality, then there would be a contradiction; however, that is not the case, because of the absence of two distinct natures. ||35||
The Caitanyamata-mañjūṣā explains this very point at length: "Indeed, there is no contradiction in both [being present]," and so forth.

This is because two distinct natures do not exist; in reality, there is only one single nature. Alternatively, because there is an absence of duality within its own nature, its nature is indeed one alone, and that is precisely what is called Śrī Kṛṣṇa.

But anything else belongs to Him alone. Since You become whatever [is perceived], You are indeed the very form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa; thus, even in the act of bestowing grace, You remain as You are. You are eternal, and those [graces] are also eternal;
therefore, there is no contradiction in You, even though these two appear contradictory. The reasons for this are stated in the words beginning with "Bhagavatī" (the Blessed One).
These are the qualifiers; and the separate presentation of the reason is because of the absence of two distinct intrinsic natures. ||35||

The sequence of the argument: Since ignorance (*avidyā*) might be conceived wherever knowledge (*vidyā*) is conceived, they have said this for the purpose of mocking those who maintain that the Lord consists of the power of knowledge (*vidyā-śakti*) as a function of the power of illusion (*māyā-śakti*). Then, as if manifesting their own position with clarity, they say: "Certainly not," and so forth; [both].
Furthermore, this contradiction does not exist at all in the Blessed One; the reason for this is that he lacks two distinct natures.

This is because, unlike the transmigrating individual soul (*saṃsārijīva*), there is no distinction between the particular states of bondage and liberation. For if there were bondage, liberation would likewise be impossible; thus, even meanings characterized by various divine and super-divine incarnations (*avatāra*) and so forth would be difficult to establish.

It does not exist. The meaning is that she remains having concealed her own *māyā*—her power of will (*nijecchā-śakti*)—and having placed it within [herself], establishing it as an aid here and there. The reasons for this in both cases are "the Blessed One" and so forth. ||35||
Viśvanātha: Having stated the contradiction, they state its resolution from the perspective of the devotees—beginning with "na hi" (not indeed).

"Virodhaḥ" means that which is contradicted. The meaning is that both [qualities]—being one who delights in the Self (*ātmārāmatva*) and being subject to non-material pleasure and pain (*aprākṛta-sukha-duḥkhitva*)—are not contradictory in You. For there is no doubt regarding You by means of any other example.
"It is logical, because [the Lord's] sovereignty is beyond ratiocination"—thus they state the reason for the lack of contradiction, beginning with "the Blessed One" (*bhagavatī*).
First, they express the state of being happy and unhappy with the two words "the Blessed One" (*bhagavatī*);
for knowledge, power, strength, sovereignty, valor, and splendor in their entirety are denoted by the word *bhagavat*.

From the Vaiṣṇava statement, "without the qualities and so forth that are to be abandoned," it is understood that because you possess the sixfold sovereignty consisting of non-material knowledge and the rest, no material pleasure or pain whatsoever— which is rooted entirely in ignorance— exists in you.

[An objection: "In that case, from where do these other joys and sorrows in me arise? To this they reply: [They arise] from Him in whom there is a multitude of qualities such as being subject to love and affection for His devotees, which have not been fully cultivated by others; for it is by means of those qualities that Your devotees, such as Prahlāda and Vibhīṣaṇa, [are protected] from asuras, rākṣasas, and the like.

When suffering befell the Pāṇḍavas, the Yādavas, and others— your eternal attendants— as well as infinite practicing devotees, even those who were mere semblances of devotees, and deities such as ourselves,
your own sorrow was made known through the various efforts undertaken for the sake of destroying each respective evil-doer.
Likewise, for those very same people who have crossed over their respective calamities, whose crops were blazing with drought,
and who— like fields sprinkled by nectar rained down by a bank of clouds— have obtained the sight of you, when supreme bliss has arisen,
there is [the experience] of your wondrous happiness.
Because they are solely caused by the power of affectionate love for devotees, those pleasures and pains are indeed non-material (aprākṛta).
Furthermore, even those pleasures and pains are essentially of the nature of the bliss of consciousness due to that love.

Because their functioning consists of the essence of the power of consciousness (*cic-chakti*). Furthermore, as for the pleasure and pain produced by union and separation in the case of the women of Vraja and Vaidehī, since these consist of the highest pinnacle of love, they exist as nothing other than supreme bliss. And therefore—

It has been established that for you, whose nature is consciousness, and for pleasure and pain, whose natures are also consciousness, your state of being self-delighting (*ātmārāmatva*) while sporting with pleasure and pain is not at all contradictory due to their identity. [Objection: But in this way, am I not being described by none of the philosophers? To this they reply: "In You, the Lord..."

The sense is that it is indeed appropriate for those who are subject to His lordship to be unfit for such definition; for, according to Your own words, "I am to be grasped by exclusive devotion alone," their majesty— which is worthy of being fathomed— is unfathomable to those devoid of devotion.

Now, an objection may be raised: "Are not many logical inconsistencies pointed out by those [opponents] regarding the fact that the six sovereign powers (*ṣaḍaiśvaryāṇi*) and love (*preman*) are of the nature of consciousness (*cinmaya*), as established by you?
To this, they reply: "By those scriptures in which conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) and the like do not touch upon the true nature of empirical objects (*arvācīnavastusvarūpa*)."
The internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is thus agitated and confused, [oscillating] between "it is this way" and "it is that way. *Vitarka* is the thought, "What is appropriate here?";

*vicāra* is the thought, "It must be exactly thus. In that regard, fallacious means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāsa*) are those which support such [views]. Furthermore, there are those treatises in which [are found] fallacious reasonings (*kutarka*), modern [theories], and conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) and the like that do not touch upon the true nature of reality; by means of these [treatises]...

The *āśaya* (inner disposition) is the *kalila*, the agitated internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Those who always lie within it, remaining there forever, are the "difficult to restrain" (*duravagraha*), meaning those possessed of stubborn attachments (*durāgraha*). It is by these very [attachments] that the dispute of proponents—who harbor various dogmatic assertions—occurs, even when there is no occasion for it and it lies beyond its proper scope. In that regard, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is the mental form consisting of "thus" or "in this way."
Vitarka is uncertainty as to what is appropriate here; vicāra is certainty that it is exactly thus.
In this regard, fallacious means of knowledge (pramāṇābhāsa) are base forms of reasoning (tarka).
[Objection: But if there is a lack of logical consistency (anupapatti), how can there be an absence of dispute? To this they reply: all [disputes] have ceased.

The meaning is: "In that [reality] wherein all objects are composed of illusion (*māyā*) and are illusory (*māyika*), since disputes are the effects of the power of *māyā*, how could there even be the possibility of the occurrence of dispute for you, who are a reality distinct from both *māyā* and illusory objects?"
Is it not evident, moreover, that even He [the Lord] engaged in activities such as churning the ocean for the sake of assisting you,
acting as charioteer and messenger for the sake of assisting the Pāṇḍavas, protecting the Yādavas,
and fleeing from the fear arising from the oppression of Jarāsaṃdha and others?
Thinking, "How might my suffering, which is being witnessed by everyone, somehow take the form of happiness for me?

they say: "In You alone," and so forth. Only when You are devoid of the power of *māyā* (the creative energy of illusion), and having placed between [myself and You] that *ātma-māyā*—the inconceivable *yoga-māyā*—what indeed would be the purpose?
The meaning is that since your experience is filled with bliss, who would be able to enter what is difficult to accomplish?
Thus, perception and other means of valid cognition do not operate here; for there is the saying: "Those entities which are indeed inconceivable should not be subjected to logical reasoning."

Now, enough with the acceptance of an inconceivable power (*acintya-śakti*); let there be two distinct natures for me: one as the Lord (*bhagavat-svarūpa*), characterized by possessing happiness, sorrow, and so forth arising from affection for devotees; and the other as Brahman (*brahma-svarūpa*), characterized by self-repose due to remaining indifferent toward everything.
Thus, let these two natures possess their respective attributes in succession.

Regarding this, they say: "Because there is no duality of essential nature. For you, the one Lord alone, being accessible through non-distinctive knowledge is precisely Brahman-hood, while being accessible through extraordinary, distinctive knowledge is precisely Bhagavat-hood; thus it is perceived by those knowers situated at a distance.

The meaning is this: you alone are called "Bhagavān" by those devotees who dwell in the proximity of Brahman and are capable of perceiving extraordinary, transcendental qualities (*alaukika-viśeṣa*), whereas others are incapable of such perception.
It is precisely the atomicity (*paramāṇutva*) and the supreme magnitude (*paramamahattva*) of your grace that are the causes for [the experiences of] distance and proximity.
Regarding the object of knowledge. ||35||
—o)0(o— You follow the thought of those with both even and uneven minds, just as a segment of rope is perceived through the cognitions of a snake and so forth.
Madhva says: Just as a rope is perceived through the cognition of a snake and the cognition of a rope.
"Thus, Mahāviṣṇu is understood through both true cognition and false cognition by his own will alone, according to the fruit [of each individual's karma]. Thus says Śrīdhara in the *Tantrabhāgavata*:
"But [his] acts of grace, restraint, and so forth, occur through your Māyā, according to the differences in their respective understandings."
They say that [all things] manifest in You—the thought or intention of those whose minds perceive both the even and the uneven.
To those whose cognition has as its object a snake and so forth, a piece of rope appears exactly as it is [perceived].
Or rather, He demonstrates that very same non-contradictory Person through His supreme differentiation: "the even and the uneven" (verse 36).
The sequential composition [of the commentary]: "If that is so, then how is there a contrary perception for those whose minds are directed outward?

To this they reply: "In the same way" (*samam*). This means "for those of unascertained intellect. To establish that very point, they state the distinction from one who is liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*): "For he alone... (verse 36).

Viśvanātha: Furthermore, even for the sake of the ultimate liberation from saṃsāra, You do not destroy the views of those non-devotees; thus they say: "The minds of those who possess an equal [view] because it has Brahman as its object, and an unequal [view] because it possesses hostility toward Him. Or else, [it refers to their views] regarding the two [aspects] that constitute Your own nature.

Although You are identical and uniform in both Your states as Brahman and as Bhagavān, those whose minds are possessed of such inequality—thinking that while You are Brahman alone who transcends *māyā*, the state of being Bhagavān occurs only when there is an association with *māyā*—follow and reach Your very doctrine. They state that doctrine as follows: "In the case of the cognition of a rope as a snake and so forth..."

Just as in the case of Brahmā, the state of delighting in the Self alone is the truth; whereas qualities such as affection for devotees are merely manifestations of *māyā*, and thus the resulting pleasure, pain, and so forth are baseless and unreal. Therefore, there is no contradiction whatsoever. ||36||
For he alone is, moreover, the one whose nature is the reality of all things, the Lord of All,
who has become the cause of the causes of the entire world, because he is the inner self of everything.
Only that which is characterized by the manifestation of all qualities remains as one.

Śrīdhara says: Having thus resolved the contradiction, they state the determined ultimate truth: for that very reality, though perceived in manifold forms, is the nature of the thing itself, whose form is existence (*sadrūpa*). Of all qualities...
[The opponent asks: "Is it not the case that the individual soul (*jīva*) alone is characterized by the appearances—that is, the manifestations—of objects? [The author replies:

No, because [the Self] is the inner self (*pratyagātman*) of all and the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of all individual souls. Since the individual soul, through the superimposition of identity with the insentient, is itself almost as if insentient, there can be no manifestation without it; this is the intended meaning. Thus, [the Self] remains as the ultimate residue."
By such scriptural passages as “not this, not this” (neti neti) and so forth. ||37||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.
*Viśvanātha*: Since this is so, they say that we shall therefore abandon the doctrine of the Omniscient One (the Buddha) and follow instead the doctrine favored by his devotees—namely, he alone...
The true nature of reality is indeed distinguished by the aforementioned attributes such as being the Blessed Lord (*bhagavat*) and so forth.
Although this actual nature of reality is imperceptible— because it is the inner self (*pratyagātman*) of all and because it transcends the range of the senses—
it is nevertheless [perceived] through the manifestations and illuminations of all the qualities, such as the faculties of cognition and action.

"Characterized by preponderance" means known or inferred; as it is said: "You are inferred by the manifestations of Your qualities" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.2.35). You are "left as the remainder" by the negation of all things consisting of Māyā and its products through such scriptural texts as "not this, not this" (neti neti).

Having perceived the nectar of the Bhāgavata, following such verses as "Without bodily exertion, without doubt regarding the earth and so forth, and without assistants, that action of the immutable One is very difficult to attain," one should explain [the text] beginning with "difficult to understand. (37)
Now, indeed, by a single drop from the ocean of the nectar-essence of your greatness, once tasted,
there flows within one's own mind a continuous bliss.

O Slayer of Madhu, how indeed could these supreme devotees—who have forgotten even the slightest semblance of the pleasure found in objects seen or heard; who are single-mindedly devoted to the Blessed One, the beloved friend of all beings and the Self of all; and whose minds are utterly and incessantly absorbed in Him—ever again be intent on their own self-interest?
Virtuous people, who are dear to themselves and their friends, do not abandon service to Your lotus feet where this cycle of worldly existence does not recur.
Śrīdhara: Therefore, they say that devotion to You alone is the supreme human goal—now follows:

From the words "hetyādi" up to "paryāvarta": because you, O Supreme Lord, are of such a nature; "atha ha vāva" means for this very reason. O Madhumathana! the construction is: how could these supreme devotees ever repeatedly abandon the service of your lotus feet? For (hi) means because.

They are skilled and proficient in their own purpose, which is the goal of human life (puruṣārtha). For this very reason, those virtuous ones (sādhus), who are free from passion and other such afflictions, regard You alone as their beloved and their friend.
The reason for this is that Your majesty alone is an ocean of the nectar of immortality; by even a single drop (vipruṣ) of it—by a mere particle—[they are satisfied].

Those whose [minds] have been made to forget the mere semblances of fragments of pleasure found in objects seen or heard— objects that flow forth as an intense, continuous, and uninterrupted bliss once they have been tasted and experienced even a single time;
for this very reason, their minds are utterly and incessantly at peace in you, O Blessed One.
For those [beings], in whom that [state] exists, and in which [place], when such service is being performed. ||38||
The sequential composition: Having thus refuted those who are extroverted, they praise their devotees with the words "Now, indeed" (atha ha). ||38||

Viśvanātha: Having thus refuted those who look outward, [the authors] praise his devotees with the words "Now, therefore" (*atha ha*). Those who are *ekāntins*—because their minds are focused solely on his service—do not worship even the gods, sages, and others, having experienced the bliss of love (*premānanda*) produced by even a single taste or relish [of his grace]. Furthermore, as for those gods, sages, and others...

They say that people feel even greater devotion toward them, [thinking]: "He is the dear friend of all beings and the Self of all. The sense is that when one serves You, all of them have effectively been served. As for the phrase "those skilled in their own interest," it refers to those who would otherwise abandon service to You.
The meaning is that those such as the "bad yogis" are indeed destroyers of their own welfare. ||38||
O Soul of the three worlds, O Trivikrama, O Three-eyed One, O You whose majesty enchants the three realms:
even the sons of Diti and Danu are Your own manifestations; for this is the time for their subjugation.

O wielder of the rod of justice, just as you have inflicted punishment according to their offenses upon those with the forms of gods, men, beasts, and aquatic creatures through your own power of illusion, so too, O Blessed One, slay this son of Tvaṣṭṛ, if you so deem fit.

"Madhvaḥ": the three-eyed one in the form of Nṛsiṃha. For it is stated in the *Śabdanirṇaya*: "The names of Viṣṇu as Nṛsiṃha, however, begin with 'Trinetra' and 'Ugra'"; and also: "Because they are vessels for various states of being, all [deities] are manifestations (*vibhūti*) of Viṣṇu.
Śrīdhara explains the subject at hand from the verse beginning with *tribhuvana* until its conclusion:

"He whose self (*ātman*) and abode (*bhavana*) are the three worlds; or, he who is the self and the abode of the three worlds. He is one who possesses three strides (*vikrama*). He is so called because he leads the three worlds, or [because he is the leader] of the three worlds.

He whose majesty is captivating; thus it is explained in four ways—or alternatively, "the dwelling place of those [gods] at a time when they cannot be approached. He who possesses three strides; he who leads the three worlds;
likewise, he whose majesty is captivating to the three worlds. Thus it is explained in four ways.

They said to him for the sake of awakening: "Considering that this is not the time for their approach but rather the time for exertion, O wielder of the staff (*daṇḍadhara*), slay even this son of Tvaṣṭṛ just as you previously wielded and held the staff, if you deem it right to kill, if you so desire. (39)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Among those devoted to Him, indicating that they themselves are the most lowly due to possessing desires, they announce the subject at hand: "Those for whom the three worlds are their own abode..."

The sense is: "Having brought [him] from his presence, you shall give him to us. Regarding the word *triloka*: the sense is that even now, let the people dwelling in the three worlds behold your majesty; [therefore], destroy the Daitya.
Now, they say: "Surely you worship me with the aim of harming another"; to this they reply: "[He is] your own manifestation."
The sense is that, although even this [act] is not the time for their commencement, we shall inform them;
therefore, O wielder of the staff, you previously held the staff, and likewise now, at this very moment. ||39||
For us, your devotees, who are perpetually bowed down, O Hari, our hearts are bound by the fetters of meditation upon the pair of your lotus feet.

O Sinless One, you ought to pacify the inner torment of those who have been made your own through the disclosure of your true nature, by means of your compassionate gaze— clear, beautiful, and cool, colored with affection— and by the digit of the nectar of the sweet essence of your mouth.
Śrīdhara: First of all, you ought to pacify the inner torment of us who belong to you. Regarding the phrase "of those belonging to you," the reason is as follows: O Father, O Grandfather!
[we are those] whose hearts are bound by fetters—chains—consisting solely of meditation upon the pair of your lotus-like feet.

By whom? By means of a glance accompanied by a smile that was clear, beautiful, cool, and colored with affection—an affection kindled by compassion—and by which [glance] those who had been accepted through the disclosure of his own marks and the manifestation of his own form [were favored]. Likewise, by that very compassion, the sweet essence of his speech flowed forth.
Pleasant speech is that very digit of nectar (amṛtakalā), and by means of it... ||40||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.
*Viśvanātha*: Having thus offered praise, they pray for the nectar of the arrival of a comforting glance, sweet with compassion:
"O *asmākam* (of us)!"—O pervasive one, O Grandfather! Only the pair of your lotus-feet...

The meaning is: "We are unable to draw out the bee of our minds from Your lotus feet because our hearts are bound by shackles and chains consisting of meditation itself. [This occurs] through the manifestation of Your own form by the disclosure of Your true nature—that sweet [voice] which has emerged from the moon of Your face.
The essence of speech is pleasant discourse; that itself is a digit of nectar, and by means of it... ||40||
Now, O Blessed One, [we approach] you,
whose divine play of *māyā* serves as the cause for the origin, maintenance, and dissolution of the entire world.

He experiences, both within the hearts of all classes of living beings and externally as well, the nature of Brahman as the inner self (pratyagātman) and as the primary cause (pradhāna), according to the specific locations, times, bodies, and states, by virtue of being the material cause and the perceiver thereof.
Of the Supreme Self, the Supreme Brahman— who is the witness of all conditions, whose body is space—
how much of His specific nature can possibly be made known here, any more than sparks and such can represent the sacrificial fire?

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, your intention is already known to us; what is there for us to inform you of here? Thus they say: "Now, O Blessed One! How much of a specific matter could possibly need to be informed to you by us here? This is the grammatical construction (*anvaya*). Just as [it was told] to Hiraṇyaretas, Agni...

Just as illumination is not produced by sparks and the like, which are parts of that [fire], so too, the illumination of the purpose of the task is not to be performed by us for you; this is the meaning. Here, the qualifying attributes contain the reason: [by means of] divine *māyā*, which acts as the instrumental cause in the production and other processes of all worlds.

He whose delight is such; therefore, He is the inner controller (*antaryāmī*) and the inner self (*pratyagātman*) within the hearts of all classes of living beings as the nature of Brahman, and externally as well,
He experiences [all things] in that same form as the primary cause (*pradhāna*), without transgressing the specific distinctions of place, time, body, and state.
How? By being their material cause (*upādāna*) and by being the perceiver (*upalambhaka*), or rather, by being the perceiver of the material cause.

For this very reason, he is the witness (*sākṣin*) of all conditions (*pratyaya*), including bondage and so forth. The reason for his being the witness is that his essential nature (*svarūpa*) is a body (*śarīra*)—that is, his true form—which, like space (*ākāśa*), is untainted (*alipta*). There are two reasons for this untaintedness: first, because he is immediate (*sākṣāt*);...
Of the Supreme Brahman, the unconditioned Supreme Self, whose form is pure being (śuddhasattva). ||41||

The sequential arrangement: Now, having addressed him as "O Blessed One," [the author] intends that even though [Brahman] is of the nature of Brahman and the Supreme Self, the state of being the Blessed One (Bhagavān) alone is the most excellent;
therefore, it is said to be "in its primary form" and "in its most preeminent form," namely, by the name "Bhagavān."
The meaning is as follows: "Of him whose body is space" (ākāśa-śarīrasya) means that which shines and manifests itself everywhere—that is, the Supreme Brahman—is his very body. ||41||
Viśvanātha: The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "How much of a specific meaning (*arthaviśeṣa*) is to be communicated to you, in you?

[The meaning is: the inner self (*pratyagātman*) as the inner controller (*antaryāmī*); in that form, even externally toward objects, there is *māyā* as the primary cause, as well as the senses and so forth; and in that form, space (*deśa*), time (*kāla*), and the particular states of the body (*dehasyāvasthānaviśeṣāḥ*).

And childhood and the other stages do not transcend them; rather, they experience [them] as the material cause (*upādāna*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), the perceiver (*upalambhaka*), and the illuminator (*prakāśatva*) of those classes of living beings, such as the gods. The meaning is that he knows that which is to be made known within the heart. He whose body is, like space, unsullied by qualities (*guṇa*).
By us, who are like mere sparks and fragments of the fire whose essence is gold. ||41||

Therefore, you yourself must provide for us the shade of the hundred-petaled lotus-feet of our Blessed One, your supreme guru, which pacifies the exhaustion of this saṃsāra with its manifold afflictions.
Śrīdhara: Precisely because you are omniscient, we have been brought here by whatever desire [you had];
therefore, please yourself determine that task for which we were brought.

"Accomplish it. The very foot is a lotus with a hundred petals; its shade—which brings relief to the manifold exhaustion of saṃsāra caused by various afflictions—for those who have approached or reached it, is the sequence of the composition.
This has not been explained [previously].

Viśvanātha: Precisely because you are omniscient, we—who have been brought by you yourself to the shade of your lotus feet according to our desire—that is, by whatever longing we possessed—should have that task accomplished by you yourself. Of what kind of shade? That of those who have approached [you], namely the devotees.
It is that which brings rest to exhaustion. ||42||
Furthermore, O Lord, slay the son of Tvaṣṭṛ who is devouring the three worlds,
by whom our splendors, missiles, and weapons have been swallowed, O Kṛṣṇa.
Śrīdhara: Since the excellence of devotion was previously described, lest there be a suspicion that it is merely a desire, they state their own desire. "Atho" means immediately thereafter. ||43||

The sequence of composition: they express [this] quite clearly through longing. Viśvanātha says "atho" (then/therefore): because the excellence of pure devotion (*śuddhabhakti*) is described in all praises, the Lord sometimes grants devotion itself; such being the case, we are possessed of tears of love, trembling, and so forth.

"Out of a turning away from the pleasures of heaven, we shall wander upon earth alone, while our very enemies, dwelling in Amarāvatī, will shine resplendent"— with this apprehension and a lack of gravity, they clearly expressed their desire with the words "atho" (then). ||43||
to the swan, whose abode is the heart-lake, the observer,
to Kṛṣṇa of pure fame, who is beyond all effort; ||| o)0(o— ||| to Him.

Salutations to you, Hari, who provides for the gathering of the virtuous, who is reached at the end of the journey through existence as one arrives at his own hermitage, and who leads to the sought-after goal.
And it is said: "The enemy of the Madhvas makes no effort; indeed, he would always attack without exertion. (44)

Śrīdhara: They bow again quickly for the sake of his destruction: "Salutation to you, the pure Haṃsa, to Hari, the remover of distress. The reasons for his purity are as follows: to the one whose abode is the small space (the heart), whose dwelling is the ether of the heart; to the witness, the observer of the intellect and its functions; to Kṛṣṇa."
"To Him whose nature is eternal bliss.
According to the Nirukta: "The word *kṛṣi* denotes the earth (*bhū*), and the syllable *ṇa* denotes bliss (*nirvṛti*); the supreme Brahman, which is the unity of these two, is designated as *Kṛṣṇa*."

The reasons for his being the remover of suffering are as follows: he whose fame is pure and brings delight; who is free from the "uninitiated" (nirupakrama) and other such defects; who is thus embraced by the virtuous;
and who, like a traveler on the path of worldly existence, has reached his own hermitage upon that person.
To him for whom the fruit is the supreme state—sought after at the end of cyclic existence and honored in every respect—once he has attained his own refuge. ||44||
Kramasaṃdarbha: This has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: "We fall at your feet; kill [him] quickly!"—thus, out of agitation, they prostrate themselves, manifesting their entire desire directed toward him who possesses the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
To the swan who discerns the essential from the non-essential and grasps the essence; to the one whose abode is the deep pool, whose dwelling is the lake of our hearts;
to the one who observes even the desire manifested here within our hearts; and thus, to the one of pure fame, characterized by being the protector of us in great distress.
The intention is: "May the worlds sing Your glory.

To the one who is without beginning (*nirupakrama*), meaning capable of accomplishing our entrusted tasks even without any effort on our part; however, even with the exertion of the virtuous devotees, [Your] gathering [of them] does not [occur without Your grace].

And to Him who possesses nothing other than Himself, according to the scriptural statement: "Obeisance to Him whose wealth is His lack of possessions" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.8.32). Furthermore, for those travelers on the path of worldly existence—such as ourselves, who lead difficult lives and are devoid of pure devotion—to attain their own true abode, they must cross over ignorance.

The meaning is: "when there is the attainment of one's own bliss. It is for that [attainment], from which comes the desired or longed-for goal at the end of saṃsāra—that is, in every respect—whether it be union (*sāyujya*), residence in the same world (*sālokya*), servitude, or the love of a devotee. ||44||
Śrī Śuka said:
O King, having been thus respectfully praised by the gods, Hari—
Having heard his own reception, he spoke to them with joy.
Śrīdhara: "Abhinandita" means gratified or satisfied. ||45||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon. —o)0(o— The Blessed Lord said:
O best of gods, I am pleased with you because of this knowledge of my worship;
for by it, men attain the memory of their own sovereignty and devotion toward me.

Śrīdhara: By my *upasthāna*—that is, by the hymn (*stotra*) together with the knowledge (*vidyā*) consisting of the realization of the Self’s sovereignty and its state of being beyond transmigratory existence (*asaṃsāritva*), which is achieved through the remembrance (*smṛti*) of that [Self]. For there is no contradiction, since [the Bhāgavata Purāṇa], in passages such as 6.9.35, states that agency, enjoyership, and so forth are merely illusory (*māyika*). [This is] devotion (*bhakti*).
And by which it comes to be. ||46||
The sequential composition: "Self" (ātman) and "living being" (jīva), as well as "Lord" (īśvara), constitute "self-and-lord" (ātmeśvara).

The state of these two is "self-sovereignty" (ātmaiśvarya), with the lengthening of both word-components. The recollection of that is "discrimination" (viveka), which belongs to her. Now, regarding the passage beginning with "Is your honor like Devadatta? [46]

Viśvanātha: This hymn of praise is indeed my "vidyā" (knowledge). For those who praise me with this [hymn] by means of "ātmaiśvarya" (the sovereignty of the Self), there shall arise for them the remembrance of my sovereignty. This is because it is stated that my sovereignty is beyond logic: "By remaining unchanging within yourself, you create, destroy, and protect, adorned with qualities. (46)
What is difficult to obtain when I am pleased? Nevertheless, O bulls among the wise, one whose mind is single-pointedly fixed on me, knowing the truth, desires nothing other than me.

Śrīdhara: Now, with the words "O Blessed One" and so forth, he expresses his joy toward the devotee because devotion has been declared to be the most excellent of all things—asking, "What [is this]? (48).

* Caitanyamatamañjuṣā*: "What is difficult to attain? and so forth. The sense is: even if there were nothing difficult to attain when [He] is pleased, nevertheless, while you all possess desires, they do not wish for anything else but single-minded devotion toward me; even so, I am pleased. ||48||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: "Oh, what misfortune and folly is yours! Even after praising me with this knowledge, you do not pray for devotion," he says with the word *kim*. (47)
The miserable man who perceives only objects of sensory qualities does not know his own highest good;
if one should offer those very things to him while he desires them, even that [giver] would be of the same sort.

Śrīdhara: With the intention that it is improper for me, who am compassionate, to fulfill what was said by the gods—"prepare this for us ourselves," and so forth—he says in two verses beginning with "He does not know. One who perceives the truth regarding the *guṇas* (the objects of the senses) [does not desire them]; only one who is ignorant in that way [desires] those objects. 48.
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Although you are fools who desire sense-objects and do not know your own welfare or misfortune, nevertheless, how could I, being wise, give them to you? Indeed not.

He says that it is not as if a mother were to give poison to her sons with her own hand; rather, he who perceives only the objects of the senses—the *guṇas*—as the ultimate goal of human life does not know his own true welfare. Even if a wise man were to offer those very objects to such a person, that wise man would himself be as ignorant as the other. 48.
One who knows the supreme good himself does not speak of action to one who is ignorant;
for even the best of physicians does not prescribe unwholesome food to a patient, even if that patient desires it.

O Madhva: if he too were such [as you describe], yet not the most excellent, then your desire is indeed my own pleasure; otherwise, I would not give him away—this is the sense. For those who desire what is dear to Viṣṇu never give away anything that is not dear.
"Even if they desire what is unpleasant, he is indeed beneficial to men; for he is their lord. Thus it is said in the *Tantrabhāgavata*. (49)
Śrīdhara: He does not speak of action, nor does he speak of the path of worldly engagement; just as one who does not provide what is unwholesome, so is the best of physicians, the true healer. ||49||

The sequential arrangement: "by oneself," etc. Therefore, [the teaching] beginning with "one should not cause a division of mind" (Gītā 3.26) should be understood as referring to an instructor who is incapable [of guiding others]. ||49||

Viśvanātha: He does not speak of action; he does not teach the path of worldly engagement (*pravṛtti-mārga*). Just as he does not provide what is unwholesome, so too is he the best of physicians, the most excellent healer. ||49||
—o)0(o— O Maghavan, go! May prosperity be yours! Ask without delay for the body of Dadhyañc, the best of sages, whose essence consists of knowledge, vows, and austerity.

Śrīdhara: Having thus dispelled the impropriety by explaining the true state of affairs, he speaks in accordance with that intention, beginning with "O Maghavan": "With knowledge, vows, and austerity, [possessing] a firm and essential body."
Ask! Ask! ||50||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* has not been commented upon.

Viśvanātha says: "If you, because you delight in the body, pass away without [attaining] sense objects, then hear the means for that"—he says, "O Maghavan," [referring to] the essence [attained] through knowledge, pleasure, and austerity.
"Ask for a firm body; ask! (50)
Or rather, that Brahman without parts was attained by Dadhyañc for the Aśvins;
or else, it was that which they called Aśvaśiras, which bestowed immortality upon them.
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha: Regarding that, he describes his [Dakṣa’s] excellence in knowledge with two verses beginning with "sa vā.
For this is the well-known story told here: having heard from the Atharvans concerning Dakṣa’s expertise in the Pravargya ritual and the Brahma-vidyā...
Then the two Aśvins, having approached Dadhyañc, spoke to him.
Having heard, "O Blessed One, grant us the knowledge," he replied:
"I am occupied with ritual duties today; I shall speak later. Go now."
As soon as those two had departed, Śakra approached that sage and said:
"O Sage, do not teach the science of medicine to the Aśvins."
"If you speak while transgressing my word, I shall cut off your head instantly; of this there is no doubt. Having said this, Hari departed.
When Indra had departed, the two Nāsatyas approached and spoke to the twice-born man;
having heard what was spoken by Indra from his mouth, they both spoke again.
"O twice-born one, having first cut off your head and joined it to the head of the horse, we shall then speak; by that means, grant us the knowledge."
When his head has been severed by Indra, we shall join it back together again,
give you your own reward, and depart as we came.
Having heard this, Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa, being honored and free from suspicion, then spoke to the two of them concerning the Pravargya and the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*).
Thus, the meaning is this: Dadhyañc had attained—that is, he had realized—the partless, pure Brahman.

In another reading, however, the meaning is: "He attained—that is, he came to know—the Pravargya, by which wealth is thoroughly (niṣkṛtam) made; then he gave it to the Aśvins. The connection with the subsequent [verse] is that he "instructed" them—this is the sense. Of what nature was that Brahman? Since it was indeed proclaimed by Aśvaśiras...
The one named Aśvaśiras is well known. He bestowed immortality—that is, the state of being liberated while living—upon those two.
And so says the Śruti: "With the head of the horse, he spoke as he went forth. (RV 10.54.4) ||51||
The sequence of composition: the partless [reality] transcends Māyā.
—o)0(o— Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa gave to Tvaṣṭṛ an impenetrable armor consisting of my own self.
Since Tvaṣṭṛ gave [the sacrifice] to Viśvarūpa, and since you consumed it from that [act].

Śrīdhara: The phrase "I have obtained the armor consisting of my own self, the Śrī-Nārāyaṇa-kavaca," is to be connected with what precedes. The reason for this is that he gave it to Tvaṣṭṛ. What was it?
That which Tvaṣṭṛ gave to his son Viśvarūpa. Of what nature was it? That which you [obtained] from that Viśvarūpa.
"Then you have held [it] firm. The sequence of the composition means: "Ask for that very body which has knowledge as its essence"; this has not been explained [by others].
Viśvanātha: [He] gave the armor consisting of himself—the *Śrī-Nārāyaṇa-kavaca*—to Tvaṣṭṛ, which...
Tvaṣṭṛ gave the armor to his own son Viśvarūpa; since you have worn it from that Viśvarūpa, therefore, by means of this knowledge, ask for a body that is essential—this is the meaning. —o)0(o—
Requested by you, the Aśvins will give their limbs to him who knows the Dharma;
then, with those [limbs], he— strengthened by my own splendor— will take up that supreme weapon fashioned by Viśvakarman, by which he shall sever the head of Vṛtra.
"Even though they are capable, the gods, such as Indra and others, sometimes beg for honey;
it is solely by the command of Hari, and for the sake of His glory, and not otherwise. Thus it is said. (53)

Śrīdhara: [Objection: But how will he give his most beloved body? To this he says: being entreated for his limbs—that is, his bones—he will give them to you, because he knows what is right (*dharma*). Specifically, out of affection for his disciples, he will give them to the Aśvins. By saying "bones," the worthlessness of those parts is shown. With those bones...
The remainder [of the sentence] is: "The thunderbolt, the best of weapons, fashioned by Viśvakarman, shall come into being. (53)
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: [Objection: But in that case, who is the giver who would give even his own limb?
To this he says: "To you"—specifically, out of affection for his disciples, he will give it to the two Aśvins.
Or rather, [it was created] from the two Aśvins as its causes; the remainder is that it will come to be through those limbs and bones.
When he has been slain, you shall possess the excellence of splendor, missiles, and weapons.
You shall obtain prosperity once more, and they shall not harm those who are devoted to me.

Śrīdhara: "By means of which you shall take away Vṛtra's head, being strengthened by my splendor; and you shall obtain further splendor, missiles, weapons, and riches. That very one of massive body, who devours the three worlds, might otherwise destroy us."
To those whose minds were agitated by doubt, he said: "Since no one harms those who are devoted to me, it is indeed well for you. (54)
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not commented upon.

Viśvanātha: Now, [the demons might object]: "We are not able to fight with Vṛtra, who devours all; therefore, strive yourself to kill him. To this he says: "For they do not harm," [referring to] Vṛtra.

Because they have come under his control, the Asuras do not slay you, even though you are full of envy. Since Vṛtra was his supreme devotee and was willing to sacrifice even his own body for my sake, there is in reality no hatred toward you at all, just as there is none from you toward him—this is the intended meaning. ||54||
Thus ends the ninth chapter of the sixth [book] in the *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted, and which is well-suited for the virtuous.
Thus ends the sixth book in the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā, the Pāramahaṃsyasaṃhitā, which is the commentary on the Brahma-sūtras within the glorious Bhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa.
The Ninth Chapter, titled "The Instruction of the Blessed One.
Now begins the Tenth Chapter.
In the narrative of Viśvarūpa,
the venerable Bādarāyaṇi said: Having thus instructed Indra, the Blessed Lord, the creator of the universe, [departed].
Even as they gazed with unblinking eyes, Hari vanished right there.
Śrīdhara:
In the tenth [chapter], it was commanded by Keśava that Dadhyañc should provide the bone-born vajra; Indra, together with the gods and against the asuras, fought with Vṛtra. ||1||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*:
The construction of the thunderbolt was accomplished with the bones obtained from Dadhīca after he had been requested [to give them].
In the tenth [chapter], there was victory in battle for the gods over the asuras.
Thus requested by the gods, O Bhārata, that great seer of the Atharvans spoke these words with joy, as if smiling.
Śrīdhara: While feeling joyful, yet desiring to hear the dharma from his mouth, he spoke as if declining it with two verses beginning with "api."
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Even while rejoicing, as if laughing, he seems to treat them with contempt by rejecting their request. ||2||
"O you gods, do you not know that at the time of death, there is for embodied beings a cruel assault,
unbearable and robbing one of consciousness?"
Śrīdhara said: O gods! Do you not even know that suffering which is the malice [directed] toward one at the time of death? ||3||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon. *Viśvanātha*: [The word] *saṃsthā* means death. ||3||
To living beings who desire to live, the self is the dearest thing sought here in this world;
who would venture to give that away even to Viṣṇu when he comes as a beggar?

Śrīdhara: "The self" means the body. We certainly know this; however, if it is said that Śrī Viṣṇu is begging through our mouths, to that he says: "Who would venture to give even to Viṣṇu when he begs? (4)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "Self" means the body. We certainly know this; however, if it is argued that Śrī Viṣṇu is requesting through our mouths, to that he replies: "Who would venture to give even to Viṣṇu? (4)
The illustrious gods said: "O Brahmin, what indeed is that which is so difficult for men who are compassionate toward living beings to renounce?"
Of great beings such as you, whose deeds are worthy of praise by those of meritorious fame.
Śrīdhara: Those whose deeds are to be praised by those of meritorious fame. ||5||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— Surely, people intent on their own interests do not understand the distress of others.
If he knows, let him not beg; if the Lord says "no," let him not say "yes."
By the command of Mahāviṣṇu alone, and sometimes even for the sake of a task to be accomplished,
those who are superior in virtue beg even from the lowly on behalf of their master.
"They might even speak disparaging words to the gods;
by this much alone, their splendor would be diminished, just as a child [is diminished] by his father.
Thus it is stated in the *Tantramālā* by Śrīdhara: "If a beggar knows [the donor's worth], he should not beg; for if the Lord is capable of giving..."

If that were so, then he too would not say "no"; therefore, the sense is: "Just as you are in distress, we who are intent on our own interests do not know [of it]. By thus refusing, you do not understand our own distress. ||6||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: The Seer (*ṛṣi*) says—from "nūnam" up to "na yācata. The gods reply—the verse beginning with "nūnam" itself, excluding the four syllables "na yācata."

Therefore, the specific meaning of the *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general truth) here is as follows: The world of beggars is surely intent on its own self-interest—that is, intent on the enjoyment of sovereignty such as heaven and so forth—and does not perceive the distress, the pain of giving away even the bones of its own body, of another who is a donor. If it were a deity, it would perceive this because of its possession of discernment (*viveka*).

"In that case, you should not beg," they said. Hearing this statement by the sage—that because of your state of detachment you possess no divinity, but rather a status equal to beasts such as tigers—the gods replied: "Even the world of givers is surely intent on its own self-interest, for there is a sense of 'mine' regarding the body, senses, and so forth."

One who is intent on the happiness of long life for others does not perceive the distress of supplicants— the suffering caused by terrible enemies, calamities, and the like; even if, by virtue of being a seer (*ṛṣi*),
he perceives it due to his possession of discernment, wisdom, and compassion, he still says "no," meaning "I will not give."

One might say: since God is capable of granting that [knowledge], you too lack the status of a seer (*ṛṣi*) due to the absence of such knowledge and so forth; on the contrary, because of the presence of grief, delusion, and the like, your state is equivalent to that of cattle such as cows. This is the intended meaning. ||6||
The venerable sage said:
"Desiring to hear dharma from you, you have been addressed by me."
I now abandon this dear self of yours, who is about to depart.
Śrīdhara: "By me" means by myself; "counter-examples" means responses. "Abandoning me" means leaving behind the self, which is the body, as it departs. ||7||

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: "Desiring to hear from you the dharma"—that dharma has already been heard by means of your very reply; let it be so for now, [but] please make known your own intention.

He said: "This one. The meaning is: regarding this body which is casting off the self—that is, which will soon abandon it—I think, "I shall properly cast it off"; thus, as long as that body does not leave me, I myself shall abandon it and give it to you; may such good fortune as this be mine. ||7||
O Lord, that man who, with an impermanent self, does not strive for righteousness or fame out of compassion for living beings, is to be pitied even by the immobile things.
Śrīdhara: By means of the unstable self, which is the body; O Lords! ||8||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: O Lords! ||8||
This is the eternal dharma practiced by those of virtuous fame:
that the self grieves or rejoices through the grief and joy of living beings.
Śrīdhara: The meaning is that the nature of that very Self which grieves through the grief of beings and rejoices through their joy is itself imperishable; this alone is its extent. ||9||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: The self is the mind. ||9||

Alas, what wretchedness! Alas, what misery, that a mortal should not benefit others through quarrels with his own kinsmen— quarrels which belong to another, are momentary, and serve no purpose for oneself!

Śrīdhara: "By things belonging to others" means by those to be consumed by dogs, jackals, and the like; "not for one's own sake" means devoid of utility for oneself. "One's own wealth," "kinsmen" such as sons and so forth, and "the body"—that one should not benefit from these is what is meant. ||10||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: He censures the non-giver with the words "Alas!"—by means of others' food, such as that of jackals and the like;
by one's own wealth; by kinsmen, such as sons and so forth; and by physical bodies (*vigraha*). ||10||
Śrī Bādarāyaṇi said:
Having thus made this resolve, Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa [prepared] his body.
Completely surrendering himself to the Blessed One, the Brahmin abandoned [the world].

Śrīdhara: He by whom the resolve was made—that is, the determination was formed—abandoned his body while leading the self, the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), into union, making it one with [the Supreme]. 11.
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not commented upon. Viśvanātha: "The self" refers to the mind. ||11||
When his senses, mind, and intellect became the vision of reality and his bonds were destroyed,
he, established in supreme yoga, no longer perceived that his body had departed.
Śrīdhara: [He is so called] because by him the senses and so forth are restrained; thus he is one who perceives reality. He is one whose bonds have been destroyed. 12.
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: [He saw him] having attained yoga, that is, samādhi, yet fallen away from his own [state]. ||12||
Then Indra, uplifted by the powers of the sage and endowed with the splendor of the Blessed One, raised the thunderbolt fashioned by Viśvakarman.

Śrīdhara: The connection is with the following verse, "Then Indra shone. It was constructed from the bones, which were the *śaktis* (powers) of the sage. *Utsikta* means exalted or powerful. Alternatively, there is a reading: "by the bones of the sage" (*muner asthibhiḥ*). ||13||
Kramasaṃdarbha: This has not been explained. Viśvanātha: [The word] *sakthibhiḥ* means "with bones"; there is also a reading *śaktibhiḥ*. ||13||
Surrounded by all the hosts of gods, he shone atop the lordly elephant,
being praised by throngs of sages as if gladdening the three worlds.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
He rushed toward Vṛtra, the enemy, along with the leaders of the hosts of Asura armies.
O King, he was cast down by his power, like the enraged Rudra casting down Antaka.
Śrīdhara: "Paryastam" means surrounded by the leaders of the hosts of Asuras. ||15||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "Overturned" means surrounded; he says "like Antaka" (the Ender) with the intention that Rudra is indeed capable of destroying even Yama. Alternatively, this is like [the comparison] "a lion [attacking] a lion."
The example. ||15||
Then, at the beginning of the Tretā Yuga, in the first age, there occurred on the Narmadā a most terrible battle between the gods and the asuras.
Śrīdhara: *Raṇa* means battle. "At the beginning of the first Caturyuga," that is, at the commencement of the Tretāyuga. ||16||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: In the Tretā Yuga, at the beginning of the Tretā; in the first age, in the first of the four ages of the Vaivasvata Manvantara. (16)
— together with the Rudras, Vasus, Ādityas, the two Aśvins, the Pitṛs and Vahnis,
the Maruts, Ṛbhus, Sādhyas, and Viśvedevas, [he praised] the Lord of the Maruts.
O King, seeing Śakra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, shining with his own splendor,
the Asuras led by Vṛtra could not endure him in battle.
Śrīdhara: They did not tolerate it; they could not endure it. ||18||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
Namuci, Śambara, Anarvā, Dvimūrdhan, and the Asura Ṛṣabha.
Hayagrīva, Śaṅkuśiras, Vipracitti, and Ayomukha.
Pulomā, Vṛṣaparvan, Praheti, Heti, and Utkala;
and Daityas, Dānavas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas by the thousands.
Led by Sumāli and Māli, and clad in golden armor,
they repelled the vanguard of Indra’s army, which was difficult even for Death himself to approach.
Unperturbed and intoxicated with pride, they assailed [the enemy] with lion-roars,
using maces, iron clubs, arrows, spears, mallets, and lances.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
With spears, battle-axes, swords, *śataghnīs*, and *bhuśuṇḍis*...
They showered weapons and missiles from all sides upon the bulls among the gods.
Śrīdhara: The *śataghnī* has four hands and is bristling with iron spikes; the *bhuśuṇḍī* has iron spikes that rise in regular succession on all sides—such is the definition. ||23||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* has not been commented upon.
Viśvanātha states: "The *śataghnī* should be four cubits long and studded with iron spikes; the *bhūśuṇḍī* is defined as having iron spikes rising in succession on all sides. (24)
Covered on all sides by nets of arrows falling one shaft after another, they were no longer visible, like stars obscured by thick clouds in the sky.

Śrīdhara: *Puṅkha* refers to the base of a feathered arrow. It is so arranged that the base of one is joined to the base of another. By the phrase "like stars by clouds situated in the sky," it is indicated that they do not reach those [clouds]. ||24||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Those gods [were struck] by clouds situated in the sky, which had fallen following the feathered shafts—meaning, following the feathers of those arrows that had fallen one after another.
By the phrase "like the luminaries," their failure to reach that [state] is indicated. ||24||
Those floods of showers from weapons and missiles did not reach the celestial soldiers;
severed by the gods with their dexterous hands in mid-air, they were split into a thousand pieces.

Śrīdhara says: He explains that very point with the words "na te" (not them). The floods (*ogha*) of the showers (*varṣa*) of weapons (*śastra*) and missiles (*astra*) did not reach (*nāseduḥ*), meaning they did not attain him, in the path of the Siddhas, that is, in the sky (*ākāśe*). ||25||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
Now, their floods of missiles and weapons exhausted, [they fought] with mountain peaks, trees, and stones.
They rained down upon the host of the gods and cut them down as before.
Śrīdhara: [They were those] whose floods of missiles and weapons were exhausted by mountain peaks, trees, and rocks. (26)
