The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— Having observed them uninjured and safe...
Then, with multitudes of weapons and missiles, as well as trees, stones, and various mountain peaks,
the followers of Vṛtra wounded the soldiers of Indra and struck them with terror.

Śrīdhara: Having observed—that is, having seen—those soldiers of Indra to be unhurt (akṣatān), meaning free from wounds, well-being (svastimat), happy, and uninjured by trees and other obstacles due to the multitudes (pūgaiḥ) or collections of weapons and missiles; those for whom he was their protector (vṛtto nāthaḥ) became terrified (tatrasuḥ). ||27||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon. *Viśvanātha*: Having heard and seen [that], they were terrified (*tatrasuḥ*). ||27||
All the efforts made by the Daityas against the hosts of gods proved to be utterly fruitless, again and again.
Just as harsh and burning words uttered by the base against the great who are well-disposed toward Kṛṣṇa.

Śrīdhara: "Kṛtāḥ kṛtāḥ" means performed again and again. Among those hosts of gods for whom Kṛṣṇa is favorable, harsh, unpropitious, or rough words—whether literally "ruśatīḥ" (shining/bright) or "ruśatyaḥ" (ill-omened)—do not cause agitation, just as they do not when directed toward great beings.
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: "Repeatedly done, repeatedly done" means performed again and again, such as toward great Vaiṣṇavas;
"burning ones" (*ūṣatyaḥ*) refers to those who are inauspicious, saying, "May you die quickly! "Harsh" (*rūkṣāḥ*) means rough.
Such words as "O you lowest of men! and so forth [constitute verbal abuse]. ||28||
Having observed that their own efforts were in vain toward Hara, those who were devoid of devotion and whose pride in battle was shattered;
Having abandoned their lord at the front of the battle for the sake of flight, they set their minds on escape, having extracted all their strength.

Śrīdhara: Those whose pride was destroyed in battle; those whose strength—meaning their fortitude—was seized by their enemies. Although they were extremely famous, those Daityas, thus [described], did not suffer from tautology. At the front of the *āji* (battle), at the commencement of the fight, having abandoned their lord, they set their minds on flight.
Because they are not devotees of Hara. ||29||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
The wise Vṛtra [confronted] those Asuras who were his followers.
Seeing them fleeing and the army broken by intense fear,
the hero laughed and spoke this.

Śrīdhara: Having seen that army—the troops—already fleeing and broken by intense fear at the very outset, and observing them as they ran away in flight, he spoke these words which are about to be related. (30)
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon. —o)0(o— [This is] the beautiful [work], appropriate for the time, [intended] for the wise.
That hero among men spoke these words: "O Vipracitti, Namuci, Puloman,
Maya, Anarvāṇa, and Śambara, listen to me!"
Śrīdhara: He qualifies that very [speech]: "timely," meaning appropriate for the occasion; "pleasing to the wise. O Maya, O Anarvan, listen to my words. (31)
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— For one who is born, death is indeed certain in every respect.
If no remedy for this has been devised here,
and if there is neither worldly gain nor fame to be had from it, then who indeed would not choose this death as the proper course?
Śrīdhara: Therefore, if there were fame, worldly reputation, and heaven here from death, then indeed this death would be fit, proper, or appropriate. ||32||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Therefore, if there were fame and heaven here [in this world] as a result of death, then one should properly prepare for that death. ||32||
There are two deaths here that are difficult to attain, for one whose life-force has been conquered through the maintenance of Brahman.
Devoted to yoga, he should cast off his body, like a leader who, never turning back, lies upon the bed of heroes.
Śrīdhara: That one should cast off the body through the sustained concentration on Brahman (brahmasandhāraṇā)—that is one form of death.
That one should cast it off while lying as a hero on the battlefield, without retreating or turning back—this is the other.
These two are the deaths recognized here in this scripture. And so says the Smṛti:
"There are these two persons in the world who pierce the solar orb:
the wandering mendicant disciplined in yoga, and one who is slain facing the enemy in battle. (33)
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: One who has not retreated in a battle where heroes lie, remaining facing the enemy. ||33||

Thus ends the tenth chapter of the sixth [skandha] in the *Harṣiṇī*, titled *Sārārthadarśinī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted to the Lord; it is perfectly suited for the virtuous. *||*
Thus ends the sixth book in the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā, the Pāramahaṃsyam, which is a commentary on the Brahma-sūtras within the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa.
The Tenth Chapter: The Narrative of Viśvarūpa.
Now begins the Eleventh Chapter:
The Words of Vṛtra.
Śrī Śuka said:
O King, though their husband thus spoke words of righteousness, those senseless women, being utterly bewildered and intent on flight, did not heed his speech at all.
Śrīdhara:

In the eleventh [chapter], however, the various words of Vṛtra, uttered while fighting with the wielder of the thunderbolt and characterized by the excellence of devotion, knowledge, and strength, are described.
The words of her husband as he was praising and speaking. ||1||
The sequence of composition has not been explained.
Viśvanātha:
But in the eleventh [chapter], the deeds of Vṛtra in the midst of battle are described.
Some words consist of valor, and some consist of love. ||1||
The bull among the Asuras beheld the Asura host being shattered and driven away like one who is helpless by the gods, who were acting in accordance with Time.
Śrīdhara: By those who are favorable to time and who follow the course of time; "kālyamānām" means being driven away or dispersed. ||2||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not commented upon.
Viśvanātha: Like one without a protector, as if toward one who is without a protector. ||2||
Seeing this, O King, Indraśatru, filled with rage and unable to endure it, grew distressed;
restraining them by his power and rebuking them, he spoke these words.
Śrīdhara: Being indignant and unable to endure it, he restrained those gods, rebuked them, and spoke these words that are about to be related. ||3||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Those gods (tridaśān). ||3||
What is the use of words uttered by a mother, or of those who flee and are slain from behind?
For the slaughter of the terrified is neither praiseworthy nor leads to heaven for those who pride themselves on being heroes.
Śrīdhara says: He states that very point with the words "For not... (na hi). ||4||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: O gods, uttered by the Mother [Durgā] and equal to excrement—what fame or even what merit is gained by you from behind having slain the Daityas? In the reading where the instrumental case-ending occurs, it is an adjective qualifying the Daityas.
The killing of those who are terrified is not praiseworthy for either the agent or the victim, because it manifests a lack of fame and dharma; the meaning is that it is contemptible. ||4||
If you have faith in the primary goal or if there is even a slight essence in your hearts, O little ones,
stand before me for just a moment, provided you have no longing for vulgar pleasures."

Śrīdhara: In the great battle, if there is courage (sāra) in your hearts, then you petty, insignificant ones (kṣullaka), stand before me for just a moment (mātra), provided that you have no longing for the enjoyments of this world. ||5||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not commented upon.
Viśvanātha: O you petty, insignificant ones! In the great battle, the essence is fortitude. ||5||
Thus, enraged and terrifying his enemies with his physical form,
he of immense vital power let out a roar by which the worlds were deprived of their senses.
Śrīdhara: He whose vital breath and strength are the great hosts of gods; by whom they became senseless.
[Regarding] "the sequence of composition" (*kramasaṃdarbha*), Viśvanātha has not commented.
By that very shattering of Vṛtra, all the hosts of gods fell to the ground in a swoon, as if struck by a thunderbolt.
Śrīdhara: [It was] by the sound of the bursting of Vṛtra. ||7||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: And for the sake of the meaning "it increases," there is the slapping of the palms upon the broad shoulders, which is thus manifested. ||7||
Intoxicated by the pride of battle, he crushed with his feet the distressed army of the gods, whose eyes were closed in pain.
Shaking the earth with his might while raising his trident, he was like a rutting leader of an elephant herd shaking a forest.
Śrīdhara: [He is] one by whom the trident is raised. Just as a leader of a herd—an elephant whose pride has arisen from the forest of reeds (*nalavana*)—crushes it. ||8||
The sequential arrangement [of the commentary] has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: Because of his distress, his eyes were closed; a forest of *nalas* (reeds) is called a *nāla*;
a leader of a herd is an elephant (*hastin*). ||8||
Seeing him, the wielder of the thunderbolt, filled with extreme indignation, rushed at his enemy with a great mace.
He cast aside that most unbearable [missile] as it came flying toward him,
and caught it effortlessly with his left hand.
Śrīdhara: [Not commented upon].
Viśvanātha: *Abhidravate* means she comes forward toward him. ||9||
That Indra-foe, of great prowess, being greatly incensed by her, [struck] the mount of Mahendra with his mace.
Roaring in the fray, he struck Kumbha on the temple;
O King, everyone honored that deed.
By whom was it not explained?
Airāvata was struck by Vṛtra’s mace.
Reeling like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt,
Saptadhanu, along with Indra, fled with his mouth gaped open, vomiting blood and overcome with intense agony.
Śrīdhara: A space measuring seven dhanus. ||11||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: With split faces, meaning with mouths torn open; measuring seven bows or twenty-eight cubits. ||11||
To him who was not yet carrying away [the chariot] and whose mind was despondent,
that high-souled one did not hurl his mace again.
Indra stood firm, his horses unhurt and free from pain, as his hands touched the flowing stream of nectar.

Śrīdhara: He did not employ [the weapon] against him whose vehicle was either exhausted or fallen. Indra remained with his vehicle (elephant) wounded, yet freed from pain and suffering through the touch—the contact—of his own hand which flows with nectar (*amṛtasyandin*). ||12||

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: To him whose vehicle (or flow) is either present or absent; he whose own hand flows with nectar (*amṛta*)—by the touch (*abhimarśa*), that is, by the contact of that [hand], [he is] one whose pain has departed. ||12||
Having beheld that enemy, the wielder of the thunderbolt and slayer of his brother, with the desire for a duel against the lord of men, he [spoke].
Remembering that cruel and sinful deed, he spoke while laughing out of grief and delusion.
Śrīdhara: That Vṛtra—O King of men!—remembers the deed of that cruel and wicked one, the slayer of his brother Viśvarūpa, who stood there desiring battle with the intent for combat. 13.
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.
*Viśvanātha*: "Nṛśaṃsam" means cruel. ||13||
— o)0(o— Śrī Vṛtra said:
"By good fortune, you have appeared before me as my enemy."
O lowest of men, by good fortune I am today freed from my debt to the slayer of a Brahmin, the slayer of a guru, and the slayer of a brother,
for you have shortly pierced my heart with a stone by my trident.
Śrīdhara: You who have killed a Brahmin—specifically my own brother, a Guru—stand here before me. By good fortune, this auspicious event has occurred.
*Diṣṭyā* is an indeclinable used in the sense of joy. O most wicked one! You shall be pierced by my trident.
By you, whose heart is like a stone, acting as the instrumental cause, I shall very soon today become free from my debt to my brother; and this, by good fortune! (14)
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: By that [heart] of mine, pierced by my spear and appearing like a lotus, being thus disposed, I have today become free from debt. ||14||
He who [acted] toward our elder brother, a knower of the Self, a twice-born, a teacher, sinless, and initiated;
Trusting in his sword, he mercilessly severed their heads like those of sacrificial animals, desiring heaven.
Śrīdhara: You, who desire heaven, have cut [this]; or rather, it is like a sacrificer desiring heaven cutting [the victim] as if it were an animal. ||15||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: "One who desires heaven" refers to the sacrificer, and you are such a person. (15)
O you who are abandoned by the glory of your own heart and fame, and censured by man-eaters for your own deeds!
Vultures devour his body with difficulty, as it is pierced by my colic and has not even been touched by fire.
Śrīdhara: They devour you, who have not touched fire and whose body has not been burnt;
this is an expression in the present tense used for what is proximate to the present. ||16||
Kramasaṃdarbha: "They bite those who have not touched the fire"—this is a statement of impossibility made out of anger.

Viśvanātha: "They bite" (*samadanti*) is in the present tense (*laṭ*), according to the rule that the present tense is used for what is proximate to the present (*vartamānasāmīpye vartamānavat*). ||16||
And others here, those ignorant ones, who, with weapons raised, strike me in this cruel manner.
With their throats pierced by sharp tridents, I worship those lords of spirits together with their hosts.

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, if other ignorant ones here, following you, the cruel one, strike me while having raised their weapons, I shall sacrifice those lords of beings, Bhairava and the others, with them.
With what kind [of offerings]? With their throats pierced by my trident, which has been sharpened and made keen.
By those of whom [they are]. ||17||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: "I worship—meaning I shall sacrifice—with those others who have followed you, through the very gateway of the Asuras. And by that, I please the Asuras, the gods favored by the Asuras, and the lords of spirits."
The meaning. ||17||
Or else, O hero, may Hara here crush my head with his thunderbolt after having utterly overwhelmed me.
Having there discharged my debt by performing the offering to all beings, I shall take refuge at the feet of the wise.

Śrīdhara: Or rather, O Lord Indra! If you yourself shall take—that is, seize—my head, then, being thus freed from the bonds of karma, I shall offer my body as a tribute to all beings and attain the dust of the feet of the wise; that is, I shall reach the state of the steadfast.
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Or else (*atho*), having offered (*vidhāya*) a sacrificial oblation (*bali*) from his own body—which is exceedingly large—to the creatures (*bhūtebhyaḥ*) such as jackals and the like, being thus free from debt (*anṛṇaḥ*), having cleared his debt, [he becomes one] among the wise (*manasvinām*).
I shall obtain the dust from the feet of the devotees, such as the illustrious Nārada and others. ||18||
O Sureśa, why do you not hurl your infallible thunderbolt at me, your enemy, standing here before you?
Do not doubt this; let it not be as fruitless as a thunderbolt failing to strike, or like a supplication made for the sake of a miser.

Śrīdhara: With the intention that even death is preferable to life for me, he says "Sureśa" and so forth. "Na hinoṣi" means you do not cast [me] down. Do not entertain the doubt that [this weapon] will go back like a futile gadā (mace). It shall not be as fruitless as a supplication whose purpose is directed toward a wretched person.
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.
*Viśvanātha*: Just as you, having lived [this life], desire the enjoyment of heavenly objects, so too do I, having died, desire the direct service at the feet of the Lord in Vaikuṇṭha.

He says—"O Lord of the Gods"—asking, "May the desire of both you and me be fulfilled; why do you delay in slaying me? He further asks when he shall obtain such a target for the hurling of his thunderbolt.
The meaning is that [the enemy] stands right before him alone, not performing any counter-measure whatsoever.
"Indeed, O Great Being, I fear that the hurling of the thunderbolt might at some time be fruitless against you.

To this he replies: "It is *amogha*, meaning unfailing. "But surely, just as my own mace, once it has come into your hand, has become a direct cause of pain to me, if the thunderbolt were likewise to do so, then what [would happen to me]?"
Thinking "I shall do it," he says: "No. Just as a request made to a miser for some purpose or need is fruitless, so too the thunderbolt would not be fruitless [if this were done]. ||19||
"Is it not so, Śakra, that this thunderbolt of yours has been sharpened by the splendor of Hari and by the ascetic power of Dadhīci?"
Therefore, being directed by Viṣṇu, conquer the enemy; for where there is Hari, there is victory, prosperity, and all virtues.

Śrīdhara: Stating the reason for its infallibility, he encourages him with the words "nanu" (surely). *Tejas* means sharpened. "Slay me, your enemy. "Restrained" (*yantrita*) means impelled by Viṣṇu. ||20||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Stating the reason for its infallibility, he encourages [the listener] with the words "Now then" (*nanu*). By the splendor (*tejas*) of Hari, the Blessed One, and by the ascetic power (*tapas*) of Dadhīci, the weapon was sharpened (*tīkṣṇīkṛta*). By Viṣṇu...
Restrained means impelled; "yato" means from whichever side. ||20||
Having fixed my mind upon His lotus feet, just as Saṅkarṣaṇa has told us, I [meditate].
With the worldly fetters shaken off by the force of your vajra and having cast aside the world, I go to the state of a sage.
Śrīdhara: "Do not even doubt that I shall suffer from being killed," he says with the words "I am.
Just as my lord Saṅkarṣaṇa has spoken, so shall I fix my mind upon his lotus feet and attain the goal of the sage, the yogi. [Even though] shaken by the force of your thunderbolt...
He whose worldly fetter, characterized by the enjoyment of sense objects, has been severed; he who has cast off the world, having abandoned the body. ||21||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: Do not think that this very person, having enticed me, will again manifest his prowess and strike me down with the thunderbolt once more when I am rendered fruitless; for as to what I do— [the rest of the sentence follows].
"Listen with a one-pointed mind," he said—"I. Saṅkarṣaṇa is our Lord; as He has spoken, so shall I attain the goal of the sage, the yogi, having fixed my mind upon His lotus feet.
My body, which has the form of a worldly snare, has been shaken and shattered by the force of Your thunderbolt.
He, having cast off the world, had abandoned the sovereignty over the three realms. ||21||
Indeed, whatever riches belong to one's own people of single-minded devotion,
whether in heaven, on earth, or in the netherworld;
Neither does there exist hatred, agitation, mental anguish,
intoxication, strife, calamity, or excessive exertion.

Śrīdhara: "In that case, do not entertain the doubt that the Lord Saṅkarṣaṇa will grant the riches of heaven and so forth only to me, his own servant. To this he says: "Of men... He does not, indeed, certainly bestow—that is, give—the riches which exist in heaven, on earth, and in the netherworld (rasātala).
The reason for this is: that from which hatred and so forth arise. ||22||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Then do not say, "Sañkarṣaṇa, being pleased by your devotion, will grant you sovereignty over heaven and other realms"; listen, O Śakra! You [are merely] my master's...
"I am devoted, and he is also devoted; yet he grants enjoyment and sovereignty to you alone and not to me.
To this, he says—"Of men"—stating that the reason for this is the very nature of my Lord:
"Those prosperities which exist, He does not grant, nor does He give, to men whose intellect is single-mindedly fixed [on Him]. Why? Because..."
Since hatred and other such afflictions toward worldly attainments become distractions from the bliss of devotion, therefore [one should abandon them]. ||22||
"O Śakra, our Lord provides for man the destruction of the exhaustion caused by the pursuit of the three aims of life."
From that, the grace of the Blessed One is to be inferred—
that grace which is difficult for others to attain and which is the domain of those who possess nothing.
Śrīdhara: Then, what does He do for His own devotee? To this he says: He ordains the destruction of the exertion pertaining to the three aims—that is, the exertion concerning dharma, artha, and kāma.
Consequently, [the Lord] is to be inferred from the cessation of such exertion, and not by means of [His] sovereignty and other such attributes. Therefore...
The sense is that your prosperities will come about through the absence of the Blessed One’s perfect grace. ||23||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: [He said: "In order to lead me quickly to his own side, he has declared with the thunderbolt the means for my destruction;
that your lord grants you an abundance of enjoyments—by this very act, you [will attain] within yourself..."

One should consider that there is an absence of grace for him; thus he says: "The destruction of the exertion pertaining to the three aims—that is, the sphere of dharma, artha, and kāma—effects the destruction [of worldly attachment] for the person who is devoted from within.
From that very cessation of exertion, the grace of the Blessed One is to be inferred."
"But surely it does not appear thus in our experience. To this he says: "It is the domain of those who possess nothing;

it is difficult for others like you to attain, being indeed outside your range. Therefore, because there is no perfect grace of that [Lord] toward you, your riches will come to pass"—having become confident of this, quickly [take up] the thunderbolt.
The meaning is "let him cast down. ||23||
O Hari, I shall once again become the servant of servants at the sole root of your feet.
Let the mind remember the virtues of the Lord of Life;
let speech chant them; and let the body perform the appropriate action.

Śrīdhara: Having thus informed Indra of his intention, he prays to the Blessed One with the words "I am..."—I shall become, or may I become, once again the servant of those servants whose sole root and refuge is Your feet; [I shall sing] of Your qualities, O Lord of Life.

Let the mind remember; let speech also proclaim those very same things; let the body perform only your work. The *Caitanyamata-mañjūṣā* shows that the devotion to Hari established in his previous birth continues in exactly the same way even within this demonic body—beginning with "I am Hari," etc. O Hari! Your two feet...

I shall become a servant of servants to those Vaiṣṇavas for whom this alone is the sole root and means of livelihood; indeed, I was such before, and I am so now by virtue of being the servant of Śrī Nārada, and I shall become so again after this body has passed away—this is the intended meaning. [The verse continues: "O mind, remember the Lord of Lakṣmī... and so forth.
And so forth. The sense is that even by the mere contact of their limbs, such a state occurs. ||24||
The Sequence of Sentiments: And that pure affection is seen in the illustrious Vṛtra, as stated by him himself in the four verses beginning with "I am" [Prītisandarbha 72].
Viśvanātha: Seeing Indra not even casting down that thunderbolt, alas, alas!

Thinking, "Why do I speak of this wretched enemy who sees only the external? Why do I not inform the lotus feet of my own Lord? he beheld the Blessed One manifested through meditation and said: "I... [referring to] those servants whose sole root and refuge is Your very feet.
"I shall become, once again, no longer a servant. "How long will that delay be?
Please tell me; for I am worn out with longing"—this is the sense.
"Indeed, without any delay, I myself shall make you my own; choose the boons you desire."

She said: "May my mind remember you, the lord of my life and the lord of my breath; may my speech chant your virtues; and may my body perform service such as massaging your feet, fanning you, and offering betel."
This is my prayer with body, speech, and mind. ||24||
Neither the vault of heaven, nor the state of Brahmā, nor sovereignty over the whole earth, nor lordship over the netherworlds;
O Righteous One, I do not desire the perfections of yoga or even liberation from rebirth if I am separated from you.

Śrīdhara: Now, why should I give you great fruits as a servant? To this he says: O Samañjasa! O treasure-house of all auspiciousness! I do not desire the vault of heaven, the station of the pole-star, the world of Brahmā, and so forth, having separated from—or set aside—you.
I do not desire it. ||25||

From the *Caitanyamatamañjuṣā*: "Since heaven and other such realms exist, why do you not pray for the status of being a servant to the servants of His devotees? To this He says: "Not even the vault of heaven," and so forth. What of that? "I do not desire, nor do I long for, even liberation (*apavarga*). If so, what do You desire? He says: "Excepting You, [nothing else]."
The meaning is: "Having abandoned everything else, I desire nothing; I desire only you. ||25||

The sequential arrangement is as follows: the back of the celestial vault (nākapṛṣṭha) is the station of Dhruva; universal sovereignty (sārvabhauma) is like the great kingdom of Śrī Priyavrata and others; lordship over the realms of rasa (rasādhipatya) is mastery over Pātāla and the other regions;
and non-return (apunarbhava) is liberation (mokṣa). Herein lies the sequence of these four, beginning with the back of the celestial vault.

This is due to the intention to express a progressive diminution and a downward progression; consequently, there is also a "how much more" (*kaimutya*) argument for each subsequent stage. The preeminence of the *dhruva-pada* is due to its proximity to the station of Viṣṇu.
As for the pair beginning with the perfection of yoga (*yoga-siddhi*), however, because they are universal, they are placed at the end. Regarding the other two...
[The excellence of the subsequent:

25. Viśvanātha: Now, one might object: "I shall grant you all fruits, such as heaven and liberation; take them! To this, he replies with a shake of the head, saying "no, no. Not even the vault of heaven (*nākapṛṣṭha*). [Prītisandarbha 72]

The word "svargapada" (the state of heaven): The implied meaning (*dhvani*) is that by being separated from you—having abandoned you—my vital breaths are burning; what will heaven and the like provide me with happiness? If, through union with you, the three boons mentioned in the previous verse were to come to pass, then that alone would be for me heaven, liberation (*apavarga*), and so forth.
"What is the most excellent of all happiness? What is gained by grasping these?"—this is the underlying resonance. ||25||
Like birds with undeveloped wings toward their mother,
or like young calves afflicted by hunger toward her milk;
O lotus-eyed one, my dejected mind longs to see you, just as a beloved woman, sorrowful at the departure of her lover, longs for him.

Śrīdhara: What, then, do you desire? He says this: Just as birds whose wings have not yet grown are tormented by owls and the like, or as young calves bound by a rope [long for] their mother's milk, or as a beloved wife, distressed by longing, [yearns for] her dear husband who has stayed abroad in a distant land—so it is with me.
The meaning is that he desires to see you—who are afflicted by the three kinds of mental anguish, bound by karmas, and despondent due to desire and other passions. ||26||
The Caitanyamatamañjuṣā says: "What is your prayer to me? He replies with the verse beginning "Those whose wings have not yet grown," and so forth.
Just as [young birds], due to the inability to fly and the fear of owls and other predators, desire to see their mother, [so too do you].
If [you say] "therefore, let fear depart from you alone," then is your desire merely the absence of fear? No, it is not so; for one who desires...

I say "like a woman in love," but rather it was said "like a lover toward her beloved"; for between those two there is only pure love (prema), not carnal desire (kāma). Therefore, the meaning is: "May you likewise possess such love for [your husband]. ||26||

The sequential composition: Now he says, "unborn" (*ajāta*). Here, by the phrase "whose wings are not yet grown," his lack of dependence on others and his inability to follow after her are indicated. Likewise, by the phrase "to his mother" (*mātaram*) used in conjunction with that, his natural compassion toward no other and the intensity of her own compassion are suggested. By this—

And by this, an excess of affection toward their mother on their part is shown. Consequently, by analogy with that, a desire to see [the Lord]—caused by an even greater affection for the Blessed One—is manifested in themselves as well. Nevertheless, whatever other object is benefited by that [affection] alone is what they depend upon and what they relish.

And because there is an absence of exclusive devotion to that alone, he states another example out of dissatisfaction: "milk" (*stanya*). Here, although one could have simply continued with "the mother" (*mātaram*) for the purpose of connecting it to the desire to see (*didṛkṣā*), the use of the word "milk" is due to the mother’s intense cultivation of the notion that it is an abundance of those [elements] (the *rasas*); in reality, however, it is [the milk itself].
And because she is a portion of His body, there is an intention to express non-difference from Him.

Consequently, since "milk" implies the mother who consists of that portion in the form of milk, it is shown that such a mother alone is what they subsist upon and savor; thus, her preeminence over the former [the milk] is demonstrated.

Likewise, the young calves (*vatsatara*), being extremely young and bound to their owners, are incapable of following them; thus, even though they are common [to both], because much time has elapsed, they are afflicted by hunger—this distinguishes them from the previous case. Furthermore, this is due to the inherent nature of the bovine species to possess an excess of affection.
That should be reflected upon.

Now, even so, having considered the distinction between the mother cow and her calf in the subsequent example by way of their causal relationship, [the author]— in both examples— [qualifies them] with attributes such as "having wings not yet grown" for the sake of the future.

Observing the instability of such affection, he states another illustration: "the beloved" (*priyam*). Even though there are other expressive terms available, because both [the husband and wife] are designated by the word *priya* alone, they are understood here as possessing an innate and invariable affection. This applies to that state where, in old age...

Even in childhood, such things as dying together were witnessed; therefore, my mind also yearns intensely, like a certain beloved who, being dependent on no other, becomes despondent when her dear one has departed for a distant land and longs to see him in order to savor his presence through the eyes.

The meaning is "you. Here, even in the case of the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*), by not stating that the agency belongs to oneself but rather by highlighting the agency of the mind (*manas*), the fact that the activity occurs without prior deliberation is established; thus, the constancy of love due to its naturalness is made manifest. Likewise, [the phrase] "O lotus-eyed one" [refers to] the mind.

By indicating his similarity to a bee and by describing the supreme sweetness of the Blessed One, it is shown that He alone is the source of sustenance and the object of relish. [Prītisandarbha 72] Viśvanātha: Furthermore, even for one like me who is possessed of extreme longing, the attainment of You depends solely upon Your own will.
"And yet, I have no power whatsoever in that regard. To illustrate this, he gives three examples:

"When shall we reach our mother?"—thus thinking at every moment, young birds with undeveloped wings, terrified by owls and the like, and tormented by hunger, long to see her even when a single leaf moves; [they think], "She has come! to me.
Thinking "mother," they chirp softly and sweetly while extending their beaks.
Indeed, then, just as their mother comes and protects them from owls and other predators,
[the father] provides for them by means of small insects brought by those who are separate from him and killed within their beaks.

"Just as it pacifies hunger, so too shall I protect you from the threefold torments and from enemies such as Indra, and by bestowing upon you the enjoyments of heaven, the state of Brahmā, and other such rewards, I shall fulfill your desires.
To this [the soul replies], "In that regard, there is nothing at all desired by me other than your sweetness. Thus it is.

"There is no other triad of afflictions for me except for this bondage of the two bodies—the gross and the subtle—known as Vṛtra, which is adverse to attaining You. For this reason, he states another illustration:
"desiring milk," is the ellipsis; "calves" refers to very young calves in the house of a householder.

Bound by ropes and distressed by hunger, their minds solely intent on drinking their mother’s milk, even these young calves—though desiring their own happiness through that very milk—do not seek any service from their mother; dissatisfied with this as well, he states another illustration: "The dear... [etc.]

Just as a loving wife, despondent and shattered by separation, longs to see her joyful husband who has returned from dwelling in a very distant land, and seeks to delight him through the activities of all her senses while being captivated by his own beauty, sweetness of voice, and other qualities; so too [does the soul long for the Lord].

The sense is that she desires to delight all her own senses through [His] qualities, pastimes, cleverness, and so forth, and thinks, "In that very same way, may I also serve You. Therefore, she made three requests: "May my mind remember the qualities of the Lord of the Asuras, may my speech chant them, and may my body perform service"—this is the meaning. However, she...

While [others] might please their beloved with the amorous gestures of a maidservant or a female friend, I shall please you with nothing but the service of a maidservant; this is the only difference. ||26||
For me, who am wandering in the wheel of worldly existence by my own karmas, there is friendship with those people who are devoted to the One of Excellent Verses (Uttamaśloka).
O Lord, may there never be such a state for one whose mind is attached to self, children, wife, and home through your māyā.
Śrīdhara: May friendship with You, the One of Excellent Fame, exist only among Your devotees.
May there never again be attachment for one whose mind is attached to the body and so forth due to Your *māyā*.
[Krama-sandarbha: Now, considering that such good fortune of beholding Him was impossible for himself, he says this as well...

With tears, he said, "May it be mine," meaning, "May it be my supreme [possession]. Because this *Śrīmad-Vṛtravadha* consists entirely of the outpouring of pure love (*śuddhaprema*), it is counted as distinct from other Purāṇas due to its unique character; that work is endowed with the slaying of the demon Vṛtra.
"The Bhāgavata is desired" (Matsya Purāṇa 53.20). Thus ends [Prītisandarbha 72].
Viśvanātha says: Then, at that very moment, through the arising of a state of extreme wretchedness, he thought: "Alas, alas!
How could such good fortune be possible for one as lowly as I? Therefore, let this [Bhāgavata] be mine."
He prays: "May my friendship be with those of excellent renown, His devotees;

but may no one who is attached to the self, children, and so forth through His māyā have friendship with me—as there was friendship between the demons and me in this birth, and between me and Your devotees."
The sense is: "I experienced boundless suffering because there was no friendship. ||27||
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, perfectly composed for the virtuous, in the *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted.
Thus ends the Sixth Canto in the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā, the Pāramahaṃsyam, which is the commentary on the Brahma-sūtras within the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, the Great Purāṇa.
The eleventh chapter, titled "The Words of Vṛtra.
Now begins the twelfth chapter, titled "The Slaying of Vṛtra."
The venerable sage said:
Thus, O King, desiring to cast off his body in battle, he considered death to be better than victory.
Grasping his spear, he rushed at the Lord of the Gods, just as Kaiṭabha once assailed the Great Being within the waters.
Śrīdhara:
In the twelfth [chapter], the slaying of Vṛtra by Mahendra in a great battle is described— [an act] performed with extreme despondency [at first], but then emboldened by his own smile.
The Great Being, Śrī Viṣṇu; in the waters, that is, in the waters of dissolution. ||1||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*:
He by whose valor Śakra became dispirited, and by whom he was awakened.
Having praised him, he slew [the enemy] in a great battle; such is the story in the twelfth [chapter].

Thinking "he will kill me," this man, bewildered by his sense of duty, does not strike; therefore, I myself shall display my own beauty to both encourage him and provoke him, so that he might kill me quickly.

With this intention, he says [the verse beginning with] "The trident," and continues, "He has begun to fight again"—[referring to the words] "In the waters," meaning in the waters of universal dissolution (*pralaya*).
Then, brandishing his trident with force— its tongue as fierce as the fire at the end of an eon— the lord of the asuras [attacked].
Having hurled it at Mahendra and let out a roar, the hero said in rage, "O sinner, you are slain!"
Śrīdhara: That whose tongue and crest are as fierce as the fire at the end of an eon; having whirled it about, that is, having caused it to revolve. ||2||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: Having brandished and whirled the tongue and the crest [of fire]... ||2||
Seeing that [object] falling from the sky, as difficult to behold as a flickering meteor accompanied by planets, he remained free from any trepidation.
With his hundred-jointed thunderbolt, the wielder of the vajra severed both that arm and the coils of the king of serpents.

Śrīdhara: *tat* means that which was falling or coming from the sky; *vicalat* means wandering or revolving. *Graholka* refers to a meteor (a planet and a firebrand); it was as difficult to look upon as such. It had a hundred joints (*parvan*), and its shape was like the body (*bhoga*) of Vāsuki, the king of serpents. ||3||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not commented upon. Viśvanātha: Āpatat means coming. ||3||
With one arm severed by the mace, Vṛtra, enraged, approached him as he held the thunderbolt.
Hanu struck Indra and the celestial elephant,
and the thunderbolt fell from the hand of Maghavan.
Śrīdhara: [He struck] the jaw at the edge of the cheek; and [he struck] Airāvata, the elephant of the immortals. ||4||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: [The term] *hanu* refers to the region of the cheek. ||4||
That deed of Vṛtra was exceedingly wonderful; even the hosts of gods, asuras, cāraṇas, and siddhas [were amazed].
Beholding that peril involving Indra, they offered worship and cried out "Alas! Alas! most bitterly.
Śrīdhara: [This] has not been commented upon in the *Kramasaṃdarbha*.
Viśvanātha: Puruhūta is Indra. ||5||
Like Indra, ashamed in the presence of his enemies, he seized again the thunderbolt that had slipped from his own hand.
To him Vṛtra said: "O Hara, you who have taken up the thunderbolt, slay your own enemy; this is no time for despondency."
Śrīdhara: And Vṛtra spoke to him again: ||6||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— For those wishing to fight against aggressors anywhere...
Victory never belongs to those who are not the Supreme Self,
except for the one eternal, primordial Person, the omniscient Lord who is the master of creation, dissolution, and maintenance.

Śrīdhara: Victory is not always certain; rather, victory occurs in some cases and not in others. Or else, for those who desire to fight, victory is never always certain, but occurs only in some instances—meaning it happens only occasionally. "Those for whom the body is the supreme self" (paradehātmānaḥ), or alternatively, "those whose selves are dependent on another" (parādhīnātmanām). "The first" (ādyam) means that which is without beginning (anādim).
Eternal and constant. ||7||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: For those who possess weapons and are aggressors (*ātatāyin*), there is always victory over enemies in some cases, yet not victory over a single enemy in others;
just as you have constant victory over the Asuras, but no victory over me.

This is the meaning. Since the Supreme Lord is the "other" for those for whom He is not the self, not belonging to the self, and not under their own control, he says—"except for one"—to show that victory belongs eternally to the Supreme Lord alone. Therefore, unlike Arjuna and others who have brought the Supreme Lord under their own control, victory does not belong to you at all times.
The state of being. ||7||
He under whose control these worlds, along with their guardians,
pant helplessly like birds bound by a snare— he, Time, is the cause here.

Śrīdhara: He describes this very state of dependence with seven verses beginning with "The worlds. Remaining under whose control, they themselves being helpless, breathe and exert themselves. "Dvijāḥ" means birds. "Śicā" means with a net.
"Kālaḥ" refers to the Blessed One who measures time; he is the cause here for victory and other outcomes. (8)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Therefore, he says—"The worlds"—meaning that for you who are subject to karma, time alone, in accordance with auspicious and inauspicious unseen forces (*adṛṣṭa*), is the cause of victory and defeat, since [the worlds] remain under its control.
The birds, the twice-born ones, are gasping and struggling within the snare, the net. ||8||
Luster, endurance, strength, vital breath, immortality, and even death—
he who does not know him as the cause considers himself to be inert matter.
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha: Not knowing that Time, which consists of the odd and even [units], is the cause, one considers the dull body—the self—to be the cause. ||9||
The sequential arrangement [of the commentary] has not been explained. —
Just as a woman made of wood, just as a deer made of leaves;
Know, O Maghavan, that the elements are likewise dependent on the Lord.
Śrīdhara: Not commented upon.
Viśvanātha: Furthermore, even that person who is the subduer of anyone at all is himself under His control;
thus, [the Lord] says with an illustration that He Himself is the Bhagavān, the cause of all causes—"Just as... (yathā).
By two [reasons]: the tantras of Īśvara are dependent upon that Īśvara. ||10||
The Person (puruṣa), primordial nature (prakṛti), the manifest (vyakta), the self (ātman), the elements, the senses, and the latent dispositions—
none of these are capable of creation and so forth without his grace.
Those who consider the Lord—
who is the Supreme Self— to be a powerless soul in the form of an individual jīva;
having observed them, one should become partaker of hell due to such affection for them.
"Hiraṇyagarbha is said to be the Puruṣa, the Self, and Vāyu; likewise, Śeṣa is the Manifest (Vyakta), and Indra is declared to be the Āśaya. Thus [it is said]. ||11||
Śrīdhara: Now, it might be argued that it is logical for [the world] to have as its causes the Pradhāna, Puruṣa, and so forth, which originate from themselves;
to this he replies with the word "Puruṣa. The Manifested (vyakta) is the principle of Mahat; the Self (ātman) is the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra). ||11||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: The meaning is that the Person (*puruṣa*), the creator of the Great Principle (*mahat*), is even his own part, let alone [the parts] such as Primordial Matter (*prakṛti*) and the rest; the Manifest (*vyakta*) is the Great Principle, and the Self (*ātman*) is the Ego-principle (*ahaṅkāra*). These [exist] without his grace.
At the beginning of creation, they are not capable [of acting independently], nor is the *puruṣa* [capable]; for it must be stated how that very *puruṣa* is to be favored by Him.
Even the Supreme Brahman is to be favored by His lotus feet, as in: "And my own majesty is designated by the word 'Supreme Brahman'."
"You shall understand that which has been favored by me and revealed in my heart through these inquiries. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 8.24.38)—
Thus, the ignorant person considers himself to be the powerless Lord.
By means of the elements, it creates beings; by those same elements, it itself devours them.

Śrīdhara: Now, the Mīmāṃsakas maintain that the individual soul alone is the cause of creation and so forth by means of its own karma; to this he says: "Thus the ignorant person considers the self, which is actually powerless, to be the Lord and independent.
[Objection: But fathers and others are seen to be creators, while tigers and the like are seen to be killers?
To this he replies: "By the elements. He himself is the Lord. ||12||

Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: Now, the Mīmāṃsakas maintain that the individual soul (jīva) alone is the cause of creation and so forth by means of its own karma; to this he says: "Thus, the ignorant one regards the soul, which is itself powerless, as the Lord. Now, [an objection]:...
Are fathers and the like seen as creators, while tigers and the like are seen as destroyers? To this, he replies: "By beings" (bhūtaiḥ). ||12||
Longevity, prosperity, fame, sovereignty, and blessings— all these come to a person at that time, even if he does not desire them, just as their opposites do.

Śrīdhara: Now, one might object: "Since I have been defeated by you, I have no hope at all of victory; why then do you force me into battle? To this he replies with the verse beginning "āyuḥ" (life). At that time—that is, at the time of victory and so forth—the reversals are ill-repute and the like.

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: Now, one might object: "Since I have been defeated by you, I have no hope at all of victory; why then do you forcibly urge me toward battle? To this he replies with the verse beginning "āyuḥ" (life). At that time...
The meaning is: "Since this time is favorable for life and so forth, this is your time for victory; you shall be victorious.
The opposites are death, poverty, and the like. (13)
Therefore, one should remain equanimous toward ill repute and fame, as well as toward victory and defeat,
and likewise toward pleasure and pain, and even toward death and life.
Śrīdhara: Since everything is thus dependent upon the Lord, one should be equanimous; that is, one should be free from elation and despondency. 14.
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not commented upon.
Viśvanātha: "Equanimous" (samaḥ) means one who possesses a state of even-mindedness toward pleasure and pain. ||14||
Sattva, rajas, and tamas are the qualities of primordial nature (prakṛti), not of the Self (ātman).
He who knows the Self to be the witness therein is not bound.
Śrīdhara: He states the means for attaining equanimous vision: "sattvam" (the state of being). [The phrase] "is not bound by joy and so forth" is not explained in the *Kramasaṃdarbha*.
Viśvanātha: Victory, defeat, and the like are merely effects of the *guṇas*; the Self (*ātman*), however, is distinct from the *guṇas*.
Thus, by means of discernment, one should not experience joy or sorrow; this is what he says with the word "sattva. One is not bound—that is, one does not incur the bondage of saṃsāra. ||15||
"O enemy, behold me, vanquished in battle with my weapons and arms severed,
though I was striving to the best of my power with the desire to take away your life."
Śrīdhara says: "I myself am your teacher for the sake of removing both joy and sorrow"—thus he says, "Behold," referring to him whose weapon and arm have been severed. (16)
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: Regarding this matter, he says "Behold! [verse 16], meaning: "I myself am your guru."
"This battle, where life is seized, has arrows for its dice and mounts for its seats;
herein it is not known who will have victory and who will suffer defeat."
Śrīdhara: He concludes by means of the metaphor of gambling regarding its uncertainty. That in which life itself is the stake (*glaha*) or the wager (*paṇa*);
that in which arrows themselves are the dice (*akṣa*) or the gaming pieces (*pāśaka*); and that in which vehicles themselves are the moving seats or the gaming boards (*phalaka*). (17)
The sequence of composition: [It is that] in which the mounts—namely elephants and so forth—are the seats, being the wooden planks serving as the support for the warriors stationed there. ||25||

Viśvanātha: This battle is indeed nothing but a game of dice. He says that even those possessed by passion cannot abandon it because they perceive it as a fault: "Life itself is the stake (*glaha*) or wager therein; arrows themselves are the dice or pawns (*akṣa*);
and the mounts—elephants, horses, and so forth—are the gaming boards (*āsana*) or planks therein. (17)
Śrī Śuka said:
Having heard the words of Vṛtra, which were free from deceit, Indra honored them.
Having taken up the vajra, he spoke to him with a laugh, free from all astonishment.
Śrīdhara: "Free from falsehood" means being without guile. ||18||
The sequence of composition: one whose wonder has passed away, and one who has attained wonder. ||18||

Viśvanātha: "Gatavismayaḥ" (free from wonder) means that he was initially struck with amazement, thinking, "Alas, alas! How can even this demon possess such devotion, knowledge, and dispassion? Thus, he remained for a moment without a smile. Then, upon remembering Prahlāda, Bali, and others, [he realized] that his devotion is indeed millions of times greater than that of those like us.
The meaning is that, because the possibility [of his birth] even among the Asuras had arisen, his astonishment vanished, and he experienced laughter caused by great joy. ||18||
Indra said:
"O Dānava, you have attained perfection, since your intellect is such as this!"
A devotee, with his whole being, [should worship] the Lord of the Universe, who is the Self and the friend of all.
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha: You have served as a devotee. ||19||
The sequential arrangement [of the commentary] has not been explained. —
You have indeed crossed over the illusion of Viṣṇu that deludes all beings.
Having abandoned the demonic nature, he attained the state of a Great Being.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
Indeed, this is a great marvel, that you, whose nature is passion (rajas), [should speak thus].
A firm mind fixed upon the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, whose nature is pure being (sattva).
Śrīdhara: [The commentary on] *Kramasaṃdarbha* has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: "What a great wonder! Thus, once again, astonishment arises.
How can there be such firm devotion in you, whose nature is characterized by *rajas*, whereas in Prahlāda and others...

The sense is that, through the grace of great beings such as Nārada and others, one’s nature of passion (*rajas*) departs, and thus devotion arises there spontaneously; [this occurs] in Him whose self is *sattva*, the embodiment of pure *sattva*. ||21||
— for him who has devotion to the Blessed Lord Hari, the Sovereign of ultimate liberation,
what need is there for the meager water in ditches while he sports in the ocean of nectar?
Śrīdhara: What is the use of heavens and the like for you, which are comparable to the water in a ditch or a pit? [The sequence of the argument] has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: He says "yasya" (of whom) to show that your disregard for the enjoyments of heaven and so forth is indeed appropriate.

The sense is: what use have we for heavens and the like, which are like water in a pit or similar depressions—impure and turbid—since, due to the absence of devotion, our satisfaction comes from these very things? ||22||
Śrī Śuka said:
O King, while they were thus conversing with one another out of a desire to know the dharma, [the following occurred].
The two of great prowess, Indra and Vṛtra, the lords of battles, fought with each other.
Śrīdhara: The lords of battles, that is, the two foremost among warriors. ||23||
The sequence of composition by Viśvanātha has not been explained.
Vṛtra, the subduer of enemies, brandished his iron club.
O noble one, he hurled the terrible weapon at Indra with his left hand.
Śrīdhara: O noble one, O most excellent king! ||24||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Having whirled [it], O noble one (māriṣa), O venerable one (he mānya). ||24||
The god, with his hundred-jointed thunderbolt, simultaneously severed Vṛtra’s iron club and his hand that resembled an elephant’s trunk.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
With his two arms severed at the roots, the asura shone, dripping with blood.
Like a mountain with its wings severed, fallen from the sky and struck by the wielder of the thunderbolt.
Śrīdhara: [The two] by whom the root has been severed; "thus" means that blood flows from them. *Gotra* means a mountain. ||26||
Kramasaṃdarbha:
Viśvanātha; Gotra: Parvata. ||26||
Possessing great vital breath and great heroism, like a great serpent against an elephant,
the Daitya placed his lower jaw on the ground while keeping his upper jaw in the sky.
Śrīdhara: The connection of the verse beginning with "having made her lower lip... is with the third line, "he swallowed. ||27||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— [He is] one whose mouth is as deep as the sky, and whose tongue is flickering and formidable.
With fangs resembling the Ender of Time (Kāla), as if devouring the three worlds.
Śrīdhara: With a mouth as deep as the sky, and with a tongue as formidable as a licking serpent, he appears as if swallowing [the world] with fangs like unto Time (Kāla) itself. ||28||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: With a mouth as deep as the sky; like a serpent licking with a fierce tongue. ||28||
With his exceedingly massive body, he swiftly uprooted mountains,
crushing the earth with his feet like a walking king of mountains.
Śrīdhara: *Ākṣipan* means shaking; *nirjarayan* means pulverizing. ||29||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "He swallowed [it] swiftly, wearing it away—that is, making it decay. (29)
Having approached, he swallowed the wielder of the thunderbolt along with his mount.
Seeing him seized by Vṛtra, the gods, together with the Prajāpatis, [were struck with fear].
"Alas, what misery! cried the great sages in utter despondency.
Śrīdhara: He of great breath, of great strength, of great heroism, and of great power. ||30||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*, Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— Though swallowed by the lord of the Asuras, I did not enter his belly.
He was girt with the equipment of a Great Man and possessed the power of yogic illusion.
Śrīdhara: He was girded and armored by the Great Person, Śrī Nārāyaṇa, in the form of armor, through the power of yoga and the power of māyā. ||31||

The sequence of the composition: He states the reason for [the Lord] not having died in the phrase "sannaddho mahāpuruṣeṇa..."—[Arjuna] was equipped with the armor of Nārāyaṇa taught by Viśvarūpa. Now, one might object that it is contrary to the consensus of those learned in the scriptures that such knowledge should manifest even upon the killing of a guru; to this he replies with the word "yoga. It was obtained at that very moment.
The meaning is "by the power of the Lord's energy. By the use of the word "and" (ca), it is indicated that by that power, the emergence of the former energy also occurs. ||31||

Viśvanātha: Equipped and armored with the Great Person’s Śrī Nārāyaṇa-kavaca, he remained there through the power of yoga and the power of his own *māyā*. Yoga here consists of eight limbs; *māyā* is the state of remaining concealed by assuming forms such as that of the wind. (31)
Having pierced that belly with his thunderbolt and emerged from it, the powerful Lord, the destroyer of Bala,
severed the head of the enemy by his might, as if it were a mountain peak.
Śrīdhara: Balabhit is Indra; "uccakarta" means he cut off. ||32||
Kramasaṃdarbha: not commented upon.
Viśvanātha: He cut it off, he severed it. ||32||
But the vajra, moving with great speed and revolving on all sides, cut through his neck.
He struck down, in a single day's course,
those who had been felled over many days during the sun's solstice in the battle against Vṛtra.
Indra had made a pact with Vṛtra regarding the honey-wine;
then, having taken his hand in marriage, he wandered along the shore of the ocean and slew him with foam.
The Lord of the Gods, having engaged in a dispute over the touch of his foot, was provoked by jesting words and foam, and donned his armor for battle.

Having placed the thunderbolt within his foam and joined it with Viṣṇu, he hurled it; by meditating for a year, he [Indra] struck off the head of that [Vṛtra]. Thus it is said in the Āgneya Purāṇa. 33.

Śrīdhara: *tasya kandharam* means his neck. *Āśuvegaḥ* means possessing extreme speed. Regarding *jyotiṣām*, it refers to the sun and other luminaries. In the *ayana*, which consists of the southern and northern courses and constitutes a year, there is a group of days (*ahargaṇa*) consisting of three hundred and sixty; by such a group of days, [he is victorious] in the slaying of Vṛtra (*vārtrahatye*).

He struck [him] at a time suitable for the slaying of Vṛtra; or rather, the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is used in its own sense. The meaning is: "while engaged in the slaying of Vṛtra," that is, for the purpose of killing Vṛtra. ||33||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Although possessing great speed, it revolves all around, whirling in every direction from the cave rather than in a single direction; this is because the neck (*kandharā*) possesses great strength.

The state [of things]: having cut it with that many day-groups (*ahargaṇa*), he cast it upon the earth—meaning that the day-group should extend across both the southern and northern solstices (*ayana*) belonging to the luminaries, such as the sun and others. Of what kind are these solstices? They are *vātrahatye*, fit for the slaying of Vṛtra; [beginning with] the staff, etc.

When a suffix expressing the same meaning [as the base] is added to a word ending in a secondary suffix (*pratyaya*), the form *nānā* arises; in that case, it expresses the sense of "being" (*bhāva*). Alternatively, the form is *nānā*. (33)
And then, in the sky, kettledrums resounded, while the Gandharvas, Siddhas, and hosts of great Ṛṣis rejoiced.
Praising him with mantras containing the characteristic marks of the Vṛtra-slayer, they joyfully showered him with flowers.

Śrīdhara: Praising—that is, extolling—that Indra with mantras possessing the characteristics of the slayer of Vṛtra (*vārtraghnaliṅga*), which manifest the heroism of the destroyer of Vṛtra, such as "for the strength that slays Vṛtra and for victory over hostile armies," and so forth. ||34||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: [He praises] that Indra with mantras possessing the characteristics of "Vārtraghna" (slayers of Vṛtra), which manifest the heroism of the slayer of Vṛtra, such as "for the glory of the slaying of Vṛtra" and "for the conquest of armies," and so forth.
Praising [him]. ||34||
O subduer of enemies, the light of the Self that had emerged from Vṛtra’s body attained the realm beyond darkness while all the gods were looking on.
Śrīdhara: "Aloka" refers to the Blessed One who has transcended the world. ||35||
The sequential composition: "Of Vṛtra" refers to that which consists of the body of the attendants manifested from his own light;
"aloka" means the world of the Lord. ||35||

Viśvanātha: At that moment, as soon as Vṛtra had swallowed Indra along with his mount, [Vṛtra] resolved, "There is no other who can kill me," and having considered, "How is it that I do not quickly go to the side of the Blessed One by abandoning my body through the power of yoga?", he entered into meditative absorption (samādhi).

At that very moment, Indra, having burst open the belly of the insentient body of Vṛtra and emerged, proceeded to sever its head; this is to be understood from the illustration that he "cut it off like a mountain peak. The light consisting of the body of the attendant (pārṣada) of the self-luminous [Indra] became distinct from the body of Vṛtra. It is *aloka*, meaning beyond the world (*lokātīta*).
The Vaikuṇṭha of Śrī Saṅkarṣaṇa. ||35||
Thus ends the twelfth chapter of the *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted, appropriately concluded for the virtuous.
Thus ends the Sixth Canto in the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā, the Pāramahaṃsyam, within the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam*, the Great Purāṇa, which is a commentary on the *Brahma-sūtras*.
The twelfth chapter, titled "The Slaying of Vṛtra.
Now begins the thirteenth chapter.
Śrī Śuka said: O giver of many boons, when Vṛtra was slain, the three worlds were bereft of Indra.
Together with their herdsman, they immediately became free from fever, their senses at peace.
Śrīdhara:
In the thirteenth [chapter], it is described how Śakra, having been lost for a long time due to the great fear of the sin of killing a Brahmin (brahmahatyā), was protected by Viṣṇu. ||1||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha:
In the thirteenth [chapter], Indra dwelt for a long time out of fear of the murder of a Brahmin.
Therefore, from this horse sacrifice, there shall be protection for the stalk of his mind-lotus. ||1||
— the celestial sages, ancestors, spirits, Daityas, and the followers of the gods themselves.
Then Brahmā, Śiva, Indra, and the others returned to their own abodes;
however, Śrīdhara returned by himself, without even asking the unconsoling Śakra. ||2||
The sequence of composition: [the passage] beginning with "vṛtravikrama" is to be understood as occurring immediately after hearing Vṛtra’s speech. ||2||

Viśvanātha [comments]: "Brahmā, Śiva, Indra, and so forth. It is not logical that Indra went to his own celestial abode, because at the very moment of slaying Vṛtra, he was already afflicted by the calamity of Brahman-slaughter (brahmahatyā). Therefore, by the word "from there" (tataḥ), it means after the Horse Sacrifice (aśvamedha) had commenced following his arrival from Lake Mānasa.
This is to be explained. ||2||
Śrī Rājā said:
O sage, I wish to hear the cause of Indra’s lack of peace.
Since the gods were happy by means of this, how could there be any suffering for Hari?
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha [are the sons] of Hari (Indra). ||3||
The sequential arrangement has not been explained. —
o)0(o— Śrī Śuka said:
Agitated by Vṛtra’s prowess, all the gods together with the ṛṣis entreated Indra for his destruction; yet, being terrified of slaying one so great, he did not wish to do it.

Śrīdhara: To explain the cause of his sorrow, he relates an introductory narrative beginning with "Vṛtravikrama" and so forth. "Ārthayan" means they were entreating him. He was afraid of the "bṛhadvadha," that is, the killing of a Brāhmaṇa. ||4||
The sequential arrangement: [the passage] beginning with "vṛtravikrama" (the prowess of Vṛtra) is to be understood as occurring immediately after hearing the words of Vṛtra. ||4||

Viśvanātha: Seeking the slaughter of that Vṛtra, they entreated him; yet Indra did not wish to kill him, being afraid of the killing of a Brāhmaṇa—that is, the killing of one who was like a Brāhmaṇa. ||4||
Indra said:
"The sin arising from the slaughter of Viśvarūpa has been removed by women, trees, and water."
Where shall I wipe away my slaughter of Vṛtra, while you accept the portion allotted to you?
Śrīdhara: *Enaḥ* means sin. *Vibhaktam* means taken after having been divided. *Mārjmi* means I purify. The sequence of words has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: *Enaḥ* means sin. *Mārjmi* means I purify. ||5||
Śrī Śuka said:
Having heard that, the sages spoke thus to Mahendra:
"We shall cause you to sacrifice with the horse-sacrifice; may it be well with you, do not fear."
Śrīdhara: [Not commented upon].
Viśvanātha: "Do not fear; do not be afraid. (6)
By sacrificing with the Hayamedha rite to Nārāyaṇa, the divine Lord, the Supreme Self and Puruṣa, you shall be liberated even from the slaughter of the world.
It has not been explained by anyone at all:
"The killer of a Brahmin, the killer of a father, the killer of a cow, the killer of a mother, and the killer of a teacher are burdened with sin."
Even a dog-eater or a Pulkasa would be purified by the chanting of whose name.

Śrīdhara: Not explained. Sanātana (Ha.bha.vi. 11.338): "Aghavān" refers to another person who is engaged in sinful deeds; or one who is sinful by birth, such as a dog-eater (śvāda) or a Pukkaśa. ||8||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
[He worshipped] him with the great sacrifice of the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*).
Endowed with faith,
you shall not be tainted even by slaying all beings, both moving and unmoving, through what we have performed; how much less so by the suppression of the wicked?
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus urged by the Brahmins, Indra (Marutvān) slew his enemy;
when he was killed, the sin of Brahman-murder (brahmahatyā) overtook Vṛṣākapi.
Śrīdhara: Vṛṣākapi is Indra. ||10||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: When that Vṛtra had been slain, [he saw] Indra, the Vṛṣākapi. Here, by the power of expiation (*prāyaścitta*), even though he had previously committed sinful acts, this [suffering] was exceedingly intense due to the experience of misery.
Without mere expiation alone—
Indra endured that heat, yet tranquility did not enter him.
Even virtues do not bring happiness to one who possesses modesty when he has fallen into reproach.
"Madhva" indicates that their suffering is determined solely by previously commenced karma (*prārabdhakarman*);
it is not the cause for the arising of present karma, just as fire [is not the cause for the arising of fuel].
"Because gods and others possess the state of one whose wisdom is established, it cannot be otherwise;
however, even some *prārabdha* karma may, in certain cases, be neutralized. Thus [it is said]. (11)

Śrīdhara: By her, who was caused to be made by the gods and others; "sm" is used for emphasis. Indra alone endured the heat, and no one else. Nirvṛti (bliss) did not enter this Indra. To the question, "How could there be a lack of bliss for one endowed with virtues such as fortitude?", he says: "hrīmantaṃ," meaning possessed of shame.
*vācyatām* means "blameworthiness.
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: not explained.
Viśvanātha: *asahat* means "endured" (*asahata*). *Nirvṛtiḥ* means "bliss. *Amum* refers to Indra. Indeed (*nanu*).

How could there be lack of peace for one endowed with virtues such as fortitude? To this he says: [he avoids] a person possessed of modesty, [and thus avoids] the censure—the rumor that he is a slayer of a Brahmin. ||11||
He saw her running after him, like a Cāṇḍālī incarnate;
her limbs trembling with old age, seized by consumption, and smeared with blood.
Śrīdhara: "Seized by consumption" means afflicted by the disease of wasting (kṣaya). ||12||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— [She who] says, "Stay, stay!", having scattered her gray hairs.
Causing the pollution of the path with the foul odor of fish.
Śrīdhara: *Mīnagandhi* means that which has the smell of a fish; and that, being both *vasu* (wealth) and the wind of the breath, [is so called] by its scent. 13.
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— O Lord of the People, having gone to the sky, the thousand-eyed one [Indra] pervaded all directions.
O King, he quickly entered Lake Mānasa in the north-easterly direction.
Śrīdhara: Having gone quickly toward the north-easterly direction, he reached Lake Mānasa. ||14||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: First he went to the sky (*nabhas*), that is, to space;
seeing her pursuing him even there, he went to all the directions; seeing her likewise there as well, [he went] to the northeast (*aiśānī*).
Having gone there, he quickly entered Lake Mānasa. ||14||
He, Agnidūta, dwelt here upon the fibers of a lotus stalk, deprived of all enjoyment.
For a thousand years, he remained unobserved within,
contemplating how he might be liberated from the murder of a Brahmin.

Śrīdhara: That Indra dwelt for a thousand years upon the fibers of a lotus stalk. In what state was he? He was one by whom enjoyment had not been obtained. Why? Because, while dwelling here in the water, he himself became a messenger of Agni—the bearer of sacrificial portions who leads [the offerings] to Agni, his own messenger—within the water.
The meaning is that he has not obtained enjoyment because entry [into the sacrifice] is impossible; according to another reading, it means one by whom a share of the sacrifice has not been obtained.
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: The meaning is that [it was] "extremely imperceptible" among the fibers within the stalk of the lotus (*puṣkara*). It is "one whose enjoyment has not been obtained" because it is "concealed by fire" (*agnigūta*); [that is,] by fire, its own messenger.

The sense is that it is impossible for the bearer of the oblation to enter the water. Although water is not difficult for Agni to enter—since he carries the oblation even to Varuṇa who resides within it—nevertheless, that water is indeed difficult to enter because it is guarded by the attendants of Rudra. For this very reason...
It should be understood that even the sin of killing a Brahmin, which pursues one everywhere, was unable to reach him there;
for a thousand years, he remained unobserved and unseen by anyone. (15)
For so long did Nahuṣa rule over the triple heaven,
by virtue of the power and majesty of his knowledge, asceticism, and yoga.
His intellect blinded by the intoxication of prosperity and power,
he was led to the state of an animal by Indra’s wife.

Śrīdhara: *Triṇākam*: that which has no *aka* (suffering) is *nāka*, meaning the world of merit; the third *nāka* is heaven. [Objection: But how can a human have sovereignty over heaven? To this he says: he is one whose *anubhāva*—that is, his power—consists of knowledge and so forth, and who possesses the capacity for creation and protection. If so, then...

While he was thus [in power], how did Indra regain his sovereignty over heaven? To this he says: That Nahuṣa, whose intellect was blinded by the intoxication arising from prosperity and lordship, was brought—that is, led by a stratagem—to the state of a lower being, the womb of a serpent, by Śacī, the wife of Indra. For it is related as follows:
It is said that once Nahuṣa spoke to Indrāṇī, saying, "I am now Indra; therefore, attend upon me. When Bṛhaspati was informed of this situation by her, he said to her, "Tell him:
'I shall attend upon you when you have come riding in a palanquin carried by Brahmins. Then he [Nahuṣa]—

"He shall fall due to the curse of Brahmā. Having been told this by her, Nahuṣa made Agastya and others carry his palanquin. Then, quickly saying "Sarpa, Sarpa" (O serpent, O serpent), he touched Agastya with his foot.
Enraged by that, Agastya cursed him, saying, "Become a serpent," and he became a great serpent, an *ajagara*. ||16||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.

*Viśvanātha*: "Triṇākam" means the third heaven, i.e., *svarga*. Now, one might ask: how can a human being possess sovereignty over heaven? To this he replies: "By means of knowledge and so forth, his majesty consists in the power to withdraw all radiance."

He who [possessed that state]. While he was in power, how could Indra again attain heaven? To this he says: That Nahuṣa, whose intellect was blinded by the intoxication arising from prosperity and sovereign power, was brought to the state of a serpent—the destination of lower beings—and led there through a stratagem. For thus it is said:
It is told that once Nahuṣa said to Indrāṇī, "I am Indra; therefore, devote yourself to me. When she reported this occurrence to Bṛhaspati, he said to her, "Tell him:
'I shall devote myself to you when you have come riding in a palanquin carried by Brahmins.'"

"Therefore, he shall fall due to a Brahmin’s curse. Having been told this by her, Nahuṣa likewise made Agastya and others carry his palanquin. Then, quickly saying "Sarpa, sarpa" ("Go, snake! Go, snake!"), he touched Agastya with his foot.
Cursed by the enraged sage, he became a python. ||16||
Then, summoned by the voice of Brahmā, he departed,
his sins having been warded off by meditation that bears truth.
But Pāpa, his power destroyed by the deity of the quarter, could not overcome him who was protected by the consort of Viṣṇu.
Śrīdhara: Then Indra went to and reached heaven. In what state?

Having been summoned by the word of a Brahmin (brahmagirā). He was one by whom sin had been warded off through meditation on Hari, the upholder of truth (ṛtambhara) and protector of reality; yet he remained sinful even before, due to that [sin of] Brahman-slaughter.
He did not overcome Indra; he did not effect his defeat. Why? Because he was protected—guarded—by the deity of the direction situated in the north-eastern quarter, namely by Śrī Rudra. ||17||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Being summoned by the words, "We shall cause you to sacrifice with a horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) through the speech of Brahmā and the Brahmins," he departed from that Mānasa lake for heaven.

*Ṛtambharaḥ* means Viṣṇu, the protector of truth. *Agham* refers to the offense characterized by sinful conduct, which is neutralized by the power of expiation (*prāyaścitta*). *Pāpaḥ* refers to the sin characterized by the killing of a Brahmin; the masculine gender here is an archaic Vedic usage (*ārṣam*). [The text mentions] Śrī Rudra, the presiding deity of the northeast direction, and the Mānasa lake belonging to the consort of Viṣṇu.
By Lakṣmī, who dwells in the lotus forest. ||17||
And the Brahman-sages, O descendant of Bharata, having approached him, duly initiated him with the horse sacrifice through the propitiation of the Supreme Being.
Śrīdhara: By him [who performs] the worship of the Person, Hari, in which [work]. ||18||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— Now, while the Person, whose self consists of all the gods, is being worshipped...
When the horse sacrifice was being performed by Mahendra in the presence of those who discourse on Brahman.

Śrīdhara: Or there is a reading, "sarvavedamayātmani" (in the one whose self consists of all the Vedas). When the horse sacrifice had been spread out and performed by the exponents of the Veda, and while Mahendra was being worshipped as the Puruṣa [the Supreme Person]. ||19||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
O King, that accumulation of sin, even though great, consisting of the slaughter of Tvaṣṭṛ’s son, [was purified].
He was led by that very [path] to emptiness, like mist by the sun.
Śrīdhara: He was led to destruction by that very person; the meaning is that he was ruined. ||20||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon. —o)0(o— He [performed] the horse sacrifice (*vājimedha*) as previously described.
Having worshipped the Ancient Person, the Lord of Sacrifice, with rays of light being spread abroad,
Indra became great, his sins shaken off.
Śrīdhara: [He is] one by whom sacrifices have been undertaken. ||21||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— This Great Narrative [destroys] all sins.
The washing [of the world], the glorification of the feet of the Tīrtha,
the exaltation of devotion, the description of the devotees,
the liberation of Mahendra from Indra, and his victory.
Śrīdhara: He praises the narrative in order to prescribe its recitation and so forth, beginning with the words "This [is the story]...

"Prakṣālana" means that by which one is washed clean. It is that in which there is the proclamation of the "Tīrthapada" (the Lord whose feet are the holy ford). It is that in which there is the exaltation of devotion. It is that in which there is the description of the devotees. And it contains the liberation of Mahendra.
In which [battle] there was victory especially for Marutta. ||22||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: "Endowed with the height of devotion" means possessed of the excellence of devotion. "Wherein there is victory especially over Marutvat," that is, over Indra. (22)
Wise men should always recite this narrative, and likewise listen to it on every sacred festival day (parvan).
It is auspicious, conducive to fame, a liberator from all sins, bestowing long life, victorious over enemies, and a source of well-being.
Śrīdhara: [It is] an organ; that which makes it sharp. Or, it belongs to Indra (indrasambandhi). Āyuṣam means conducive to longevity (āyuṣyam). ||23||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: *Indriya* means that which produces clarity of the senses; *āyuṣa* means that which bestows long life. ||23||
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, perfectly composed for the virtuous, in the *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted.
Thus ends the Sixth Canto in the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā, the Pāramahaṃsyasaṃhitā, within the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam*, the Great Purāṇa, which is a commentary on the *Brahma-sūtras*.
The thirteenth chapter, named "Indra's Victory.
Now begins the fourteenth chapter.
In the narrative of Citraketu,
the illustrious Parīkṣit said:
"O Brahmin, regarding the sinful Vṛtra, whose nature was characterized by rajas and tamas..."
How did his mind become firmly fixed upon the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa?
Devotion to the feet of Mukunda generally does not arise even among the gods who are pure beings, nor among the sages whose souls are stainless.
Śrīdhara: Having heard [the topics] of knowledge, devotion, and so forth, and being questioned by Parīkṣit,
he stated the cause [of his realization] through four verses describing his conduct in a previous birth.
But when his fourteenth son, obtained with great difficulty, suddenly died,
an intense grief was manifested in Citraketu due to his excessive affection.
That whose intrinsic nature consists of both *rajas* and *tamas*.

"Sanātanaḥ" (Ha.bha.vi. 11.545): [This occurs] even among the gods who consist of pure *sattva*, and even among the sages whose souls are stainless and whose minds are immaculate. The word "generally" (*prāyeṇa*) means that it arises only occasionally for some particular individual. ||2||
