The Structural Arrangement (*kramasaṃdarbha*): Having stated the rarity of the knowledge of the Blessed Lord, he declares its accessibility through association with the virtuous, beginning with the words "Of the gods" (*devānām*). Although it has been said that "From *sattva* arises knowledge" (*Gītā* 14.17) and so forth, and that "Isolation is *sāttvika* knowledge" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 11.25.23), [the author proceeds as follows:]...

Although the fact that *sattva* is the cause of knowledge has been stated by such passages as "that which is the vision of Brahman is *sattva*" and so forth, nevertheless, regarding the knowledge of the Blessed One— even when *sattva* and the other qualities are present— as indicated by the expressions "of the gods who are pure *sattva*" and "even of the liberated perfected ones (*siddhas*)," [it is distinct].

Because even the knowledge of the Blessed One is absent; for, according to the statement beginning with "having the nature of *rajas* and *tamas*," since [the quality of *sattva*] exists even when those [other qualities] are absent, *sattva* is not their cause.
Rather, by describing his association with the venerable Nārada and others in a previous birth as being subsequent to them—it is not these...
In passages such as *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 7.5.32, and by the statement that those who possess nothing do not choose even the sprinkling of the dust from the feet of the Great Ones,

it is shown that the cause is indeed association with the illustrious and great, who serve as vessels for the fragrant nectar of the Lord's grace. And we would weigh even a fraction of such association against all else.
By stating this, because He is even superior to the state devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), He is indeed the Supreme One beyond qualities (*paramanirguṇa*).

Furthermore, in the first chapter of the seventh book [of the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa*], in passages such as "O Brahman, He is equal, dear, and a friend" (*Bhā.pu.* 7.1.1), His compassion toward those with qualities, such as the gods, is not real; rather, [it is merely apparent].

Since it is established that this applies specifically to illustrious beings such as Prahlāda and others, the fact that even association with them is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) is made evident by the manifestation of the qualitylessness of the great ones. ||12||
Viśvanātha:

In the fourteenth [chapter], regarding Citraketu, who was in a secluded place, there arose through the compassion of the virtuous both happiness and sorrow for his son, caused by the son's birth and death.

"Of those with pure beings" means those whose internal organs (antaḥkaraṇa) are pure. "Generally" implies that while knowledge arises spontaneously when the internal organ is pure, devotion does not; for devotion cannot occur without association with the virtuous (sādhu). ||12||
The living beings here on earth are equal in number to the particles of dust;
among them, only a few humans and others indeed strive for the highest good.
O best of the twice-born, among them, only a few are seekers of liberation;
indeed, among thousands of seekers of liberation, perhaps one may be liberated and attain success.
O great sage, even among millions of liberated and perfected beings, one who is solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa and whose self is perfectly tranquil is exceedingly rare.
"Of the Madhvas there are nine crores, and of the gods seven crores; all the sages and others who have Nārāyaṇa as their goal are devoted to Him. And:
"The gods, sages, and others who have Nārāyaṇa as their goal are devoted to Him."
"Only some, such as Brahmā and others, may be perfected ones who obtain the happiness of yoga," so it is said in the *Tantrabhāgavata*.
"In certain instances, there are words that are meaningless when applied to affliction, anger, passion, and the like," so it is said in the *Śabdanirṇaya*. (5)
Śrīdhara: He elaborates upon the rarity of devotion with these three verses beginning with "rajobhiḥ.
"Equal to earthly particles" means equal in number to the atoms (paramāṇus) of the earth; that is to say, they are infinite.
"Beings" refers to living creatures (jīvas). Among them, only a few, however many they may be, strive for the highest good, which is dharma.

They perform [these acts]. He is liberated; he is freed from attachment to home and the like. He succeeds; he knows the eternal reality (*sanātana-tattva*). "Equal to the earthly particles"—the meaning is that they are infinite in number, as numerous as atoms (*paramāṇu*). "Beings" refers to living creatures (*jīva*). Among them, whosoever...
A few strive for and practice the dharma that leads to the highest good. ||3||

He is liberated from attachments such as those to home and family; he is liberated. He succeeds; he knows reality (*tattva*). Or rather, "he may be liberated"—he becomes freed from *saṃsāra*; even in that case, only someone specific succeeds.
He attains the portion of bliss consisting in the experience of his own true nature (*svarūpa*). Thus, [the distinction] between liberation and spiritual perfection (*siddhi*)—

This is the distinction. Or rather, he would be liberated; that is, he would become one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). He succeeds; he merges into the Blessed One, the ocean of supreme bliss. Thus, in the state of being liberated while living, there is the experience of only a portion of the bliss consisting of the experience of one's own true nature (*svarūpa*); whereas in the state of perfection (*siddhatva*), [there is the full experience].

Furthermore, its superiority over the former [state] is already established by the experience of a particular kind of bliss (*ānanda-viśeṣa*). Even though there is absorption into the Lord (*bhagaval-layatva*), the plural form "of the perfected ones" (*siddhānām*) in the subsequent verse is used with the intention of indicating their separate existence. And this has indeed been thoroughly explained in the latter section of the *Śrībhāgavatāmṛta*.
"Even among millions of liberated ones and perfected beings, he is extremely rare and most difficult to attain.

Thus, by its extreme rarity, its status as the absolutely most excellent is stated. "One whose self is perfectly tranquil" (*praśāntātmā*) is a designation of his essential nature alone. His preeminence is due to the fact that his tranquility is complete.
"O Great Sage! You alone truly know this, and no one else; or rather, the sense is that you alone are such as this, and no other. (5)

The sequential arrangement: For this very reason, [the author] declares through three verses that those possessing pure affection alone possess supremacy in every respect—beginning with "by the dust-particles. *Śreyaḥ* refers to dharma and so forth, which are the means for attaining happiness in the next world. *Mucyeta* means one becomes liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). And as for such a person liberated while living, if by chance an offense against the Lord or others should occur...
He would not be established as such; rather, he attains the final liberation characterized by those various marks.

For, according to the method of explanation in passages such as *bhā.pu. 10.2.32*, "O lotus-eyed one, others merely imagine themselves liberated," we hear that even those who are liberated while living (jīvanmukta) may fall. Likewise...
In the *Vāsanā-bhāṣya*, a passage from the *Bhagavat-pariśiṣṭa* states:
"Those who are liberated while living fall back into the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of saṃsāra if they commit offenses against the Blessed One, whose power is inconceivable and great."

The meaning is that, based on the authorities shown in the *Bhaktisandarbha* and elsewhere, only a rare few attain freedom from obstacles even in that state. This is because, as stated in *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.9.21, "Even for those who are liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) or those who have attained perfection and liberation (*siddhamukta*),
this Lord is not easily attained," and so forth.

"Sometimes he grants liberation, but never the yoga of devotion" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 5.6.18). For this reason, one who is solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa is indeed very rare; for such a person alone is "one whose self is perfectly tranquil," meaning he is the most excellent among those established in the supreme reality of the Lord. Tranquility (*śama*) consists in being established in Me.

This is because it has been explained by the Blessed Lord himself in the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* (11.19.16): "Of the intellect... In that regard, even though the liberated ones possess material bodies, they are devoid of egoistic identification with them;
and among the millions of perfected beings (*siddhas*) who have attained states such as *sālokya* and the rest— [The original Sanskrit text continues: ...even in their midst.

One who desires only the service of Nārāyaṇa is very rare. Among those who are tranquil in soul, free from all afflictions, and devoted to the Lord of the Universe—whether they be humans, gods, gandharvas, or others—it is not every one of them who attains it; even among them, only some indeed [attain] the dharma of the highest good and so forth. [3] May such a person be liberated.
One becomes liberated while living. ||4||

Even among those who are liberated, only some achieve perfection (*siddhi*); this is what is meant by the statement that although many possess the means to liberation, they do not become liberated, but only some; and even among those who are liberated, not all are perfected, but only some.

"Even those liberated while living (jīvanmukta) undergo bondage again through their actions, if they have committed offenses against the Blessed One, who possesses inconceivable great power"—so it has been said.
Furthermore, those "perfected ones" (siddhas) are described as being in immediate proximity to union (sāyujya); among them, [is] the one solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa.

Thus, since a restrictive determination (*nirdhāraṇa*) is untenable, this genitive case has the sense of the ablative (*pañcamī*). Consequently, compared to those who are liberated and those who have attained perfection, one whose supreme goal is Nārāyaṇa is extremely difficult to find because of his preeminence. Alternatively, the distinction here is as follows: knowledge is indeed twofold—pure (*kevala*) and accompanied by devotion (*bhakti*). Among these, [the latter...]
Even those possessing mere knowledge do not attain liberation, just as those who merely husk grain are not freed from its coarse chaff.

Furthermore, knowledge accompanied by devotion is of two kinds: that which is accompanied by devotion even when there is disregard for the Lord's form due to perceiving it as an illusion (māyā), and that which is accompanied by devotion when there is regard for Him even without such [illusory] perception.

In that regard, those in the first category are certainly not liberated, but are merely conceited about being liberated. Having failed to properly dispel ignorance through such devotion and having failed to properly bring about the arising of true knowledge (*vidyā*), they vanish immediately;
and because they lack the knowledge of the reality of that state (*tatpadārtha*) without that [knowledge], they do not merge into Brahman.
In this regard, the authority is the statement: "O lotus-eyed one, those others who consider themselves liberated" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.2.32).
And the Bhagavad Gītā says:
"The deluded disregard me when I have assumed a human form."
Not knowing my higher nature as the Great Lord of all beings.
"Vain are their hopes, vain are their actions, vain is their knowledge, and deluded are their minds;
they have resorted to a delusive nature, both Rākṣasa and Āsura. (Gītā 9.11–12).
The meaning of these two verses is as follows: the deluded disregard me, who have assumed a human form, because of my omnipresence.
To perceive my human body as illusory is itself an insult to me, because of the fact that your own human body is seen to be illusory. What kind of human body do I have?
It is of the highest nature (*para-bhāva*), meaning the supreme, pure essence (*viśuddha-sattva*). Of what sort is it? It is the Great Lord of all beings (*bhūta-maheśvara*).

The Great Lord (Maheśvara) is the supreme cause of all beings, from Brahmā down to the smallest blade of grass; the meaning is that my human body alone has been assumed as the cause of all material things.
As for the phrase "vain hopes" (moghāśāḥ): if they were truly My devotees, then their hope for attaining Me would not be vain.

It would be futile. If they were performers of action (*karmiṇaḥ*), then their actions would be in vain and they would have no heaven; if they were possessors of knowledge (*jñāninaḥ*), then their knowledge would be in vain and they would have no liberation.
What, then, would happen to them? To this he says: "into a demonic [womb]" (*rākṣasīm*); that is, they would take birth in the wombs of demons and the like.

The meaning is as follows: in the second case, however, even when ignorance has ceased, those who have not [yet] ceased [from worldly activity] attain union with Brahman by knowing the referent of that word (*tatpadārtha*) through devotion that is free from the turbidity of [ordinary] knowledge. As it has been said:
Having become Brahman, serene in self, he neither grieves nor desires;
equal toward all beings, he attains supreme devotion unto Me.
"By devotion he comes to know Me in truth—both who I am and what I am;
then, having known Me in truth, he enters into Me immediately thereafter. (Gītā 18.55).
Furthermore, among those perfected ones, someone [attains this] through devotion.
If, at the time of beginning the experience of the meaning of that word (tatpadārtha), some pure devotee, by [the Lord's] grace,

attains complete and pure devotion, then— due to obtaining that sweetness— he will not desire *sāyujya* (union) but will become solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa; thus, the genitive case in the sense of "determination" (*nirdhāraṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*) is also to be explained.
In that regard, one who is devoted to the benefactor and is peaceful is called a "peaceful devotee" (*śāntabhakta*), such as a servant and so forth.
Because such a person is extremely rare and difficult to find, he did not employ the previously mentioned word "thousand," but rather said "even among millions" (*koṭiṣv api*). ||5||
"But how did that wicked Vṛtra, the tormentor of all the worlds,
come to possess such firm resolve in that fierce battle, O Kṛṣṇa? Thus he spoke.
Śrīdhara: [This section] *Kramasaṃdarbha* has not been commented upon.

Viśvanātha: Thus, he asks how this devotion—which is extremely difficult to attain and transcends the three *guṇas*—could have existed in Vṛtra, an asura blinded by the three *guṇas*, with the words "But Vṛtra... (6).
Herein we have a great doubt, O Lord, and a curiosity to hear it:
how he who satisfied the Thousand-Eyed One in battle through his manly prowess."

Śrīdhara: Nor did he seek refuge in Kṛṣṇa out of fear of Indra; thus he says, "He who [sought refuge] by means of manly effort," which is the sequence of the composition. Viśvanātha: This has not been explained. —o)0(o—
The venerable Sūta said:
Having heard the inquiry of the faithful Parīkṣit, the blessed son of Bādarāyaṇa greeted his words and spoke.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
Śrī Śuka said:
Listen attentively, O King,
to this ancient history just as it was heard from the mouth of Dvaipāyana, and also from Nārada and Devala.
Śrīdhara: Listen exactly as it is. ||9||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— There was once a sovereign king among the Śūrasenas, O monarch.
He was renowned as Citraketu, whose earth yielded all desires.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
He had ten thousand times a thousand wives.
And although he was a king of the Sāntānika lineage, he did not obtain offspring through them.

Śrīdhara: "Ten thousand thousands of wives" means ten million. Although he was himself worthy of progeny and capable of producing sons, he did not obtain offspring through them; the sense is that, by the turn of fate, all of them were indeed barren. ||11||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "Ten thousand times a thousand wives" means ten million (*koṭi*). He was one who sought progeny (*sāntānika*), meaning his purpose was for the sake of offspring; it was not merely for the sake of enjoying sense-objects that he had so many [wives].
The sense is "wife. ||11||
For him who was endowed with all virtues such as physical beauty, nobility, age, birth, learning, sovereignty, and fortune, the thought of the Lord of the Barren Woman became barren.
Śrīdhara says: He states that very point with the words "of the husband of a barren woman" (bandhyāpateḥ). ||12||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: The meaning of "the husband of barren women" is that all those [women] are indeed barren, yet by the turn of fate they have come together. ||12||
Neither all his riches nor his beautiful-eyed queens,
nor even this earth belonging to him as a sovereign ruler, became causes for his pleasure.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
Once, however, the venerable sage Aṅgiras came to his house.
Wandering through these worlds, he arrived there by chance.
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha have not commented [on this].
Kramasaṃdarbha: Furthermore, the cause for association with the virtuous is simply the independent movement of the virtuous themselves, and nothing else.
As it is said: "Once upon a time... [This occurs] by chance, that is, through their own free will, and not otherwise.

The meaning is "being impelled by another cause. According to Amara, *yadṛcchā* means independence or acting according to one's own will. Furthermore, even in the case of virtuous beings, the Supreme Lord’s role as the impeller occurs solely in accordance with their own desire. As it has been said: "I am dependent upon my devotees" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 9.4.63). In this case as well, at that very moment, his [Citraketu’s]...
It should be understood that the direct manifestation of the supreme reality (*paratattva*) has occurred, though it becomes fully evident at a later time.
For this very reason, it will be stated by the venerable Aṅgiras himself at the time of its playful manifestation: [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.15.19].
Having honored him according to the rules with rising to meet him, salutation, and other rites,
and having offered hospitality, he approached him as he sat comfortably, with a concentrated mind.
O great king, having honored him as he sat before him bowed low in humility upon the ground, the great seer addressed him and spoke these words.
Śrīdhara: He approached him; he sat down near him. Being composed and self-controlled, with his sequence of words well-arranged. Viśvanātha: This has not been explained.
Aṅgiras said: Is there well-being for you, and prosperity for your subjects as well as for yourself, just as a man or a king is protected by his seven constituent elements?

Śrīdhara: Is there also well-being? Health and freedom from illness? Prosperity and auspiciousness? For sovereignty is indeed dependent upon the constituent elements (*prakṛti*); thus he speaks with an illustration: just as the individual soul (*puruṣa-jīva*) is eternally protected by the seven principles beginning with the Great One (*mahat*), and does not remain even for a moment apart from them.
Likewise, the king also [is supported] by the seven constituent elements:
"The sovereign, the minister, the territory, the fortresses, the accumulation of wealth,
the army, and the ally— these are considered his seven constituent elements."
Thus, being constantly protected by those [qualities] whose characteristics have been described, the master, the teacher, or he himself [should act]. ||17||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Furthermore, is there health (*anāmaya*), well-being, prosperity, and auspiciousness for the ministers and other officials (*prakṛti*)? For the king’s happiness depends entirely upon the happiness of the ministers and others, and the happiness of the ministers and others likewise [depends on that of the king].

He provides a clear illustration that [the king's] happiness is dependent [on others]: just as the person— the individual soul— is eternally protected by the seven primordial principles beginning with Mahat, and does not remain even for a moment apart from them,
so too is the king [protected] by the seven.
The constituents of sovereignty are the ruler, the minister, the ally, the treasury, the territory, the fort, and the army; among these, the ruler is the most important. (17)
Having truly placed himself among his subjects, he shall attain prosperity;
likewise, the subjects, with their anxieties removed by the king, become like gods among men.

Śrīdhara: The meaning is that by placing himself directly and explicitly within the *prakṛtis* (constituents of sovereignty) and making himself conform to them, he would attain the highest good, which is the happiness of sovereignty. For the happiness of the *prakṛtis* is indeed dependent upon the king; thus it is said: "O god among men, in that way the *prakṛtis* also have their anxieties placed [upon you] by the king."

Those who have deposited their wealth become enriched with riches; according to an alternative reading, the meaning is that they become those whose mental afflictions are struck down on all sides, having cast away the sufferings of the mind. ||18||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "Having placed himself among his own subjects" means having cast the entire burden of his self upon them. *Śreyaḥ* refers to the happiness of sovereignty. It was entrusted specifically to the king, the lord of men (*naradeva*).

Those whose mental anguish—the root of which is craving for wealth, horses, elephants, and so forth—has been surrendered as a pledge; they, protected by the king, shall attain the highest good. (Alternatively, in the reading *āhatādhayaḥ*, those whose mental suffering has been destroyed by the god among men [the king] shall attain prosperity.)
Even his wives, children, ministers, servants, guilds, and counselors;
the citizens, the people of the provinces, other kings, and his own sons—all were subject to his will.

Śrīdhara: The subjects (*prajā*), the ministers (*amātya*), and the guilds (*śreṇi*)—referring to those such as merchants who exist in groups according to specific conventions; the citizens (*paura*), meaning those residing in the city; the country-folk (*jānapada*), meaning those holding authority over various regions; and the distinction between them is that a minister (*mantrin*) is an assistant in counsel (*mantra-sahāya*), whereas a minister (*amātya*) is an assistant in action (*karman-sahāya*). ||19||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Furthermore, he says "even" (*api*) to indicate that happiness occurs only when all people, even the king's subjects, are obedient to his commands; "guilds" (*śreṇyaḥ*) refers to oil-pressers, betel-sellers, and so forth. ||19||
If one’s own self were under one's control,
then all these worlds, together with their guardians, would bring offerings without weariness, remaining subject to that self.
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha: [The Lord] asks, by implication, whether your mind is under its own control—referring to the phrase "of whom" (yasya). *Anuvaśaḥ* means obedient or dependent. ||20||
The sequential arrangement has not been explained. —
The self does not find pleasure in the self through another, nor indeed by itself.
I perceive that you have not attained your desire, for your face is clouded by anxiety.
Śrīdhara: You are the Self. Why is it that you do not find pleasure or satisfaction in yourself? I perceive that you have not attained your desire, whether from another or from yourself. (21)

The sequence of composition: "Of the self," [Viśvanātha says], "because your face appears variegated with anxiety. Even though the king remained silent, he spoke to him again: "The self of your own body—whether by its own nature or due to some external cause—is not pleased; if you say, 'I am indeed happy,' it is not so."
He said: "Observe! ||21||
"O King, though he had been thus addressed by the wise sage,
he, bowing low with humility and desiring offspring, then spoke to the sage."
Śrīdhara: Even by one who is wise and omniscient. ||22||
The sequential arrangement: that which is conceptualized, having been made the object of various imaginings. ||22||

Viśvanātha: "Vikalpitaḥ" means made the object of various conceptual constructions. The sense is that even by a learned person, that is, by an omniscient one, that suffering must be heard from his very mouth alone. ||22||
Citraketu said:
"O Blessed One, what is not known by you through your asceticism, knowledge, and meditative concentration?"
For yogis whose sins have been destroyed, [it exists] externally and internally within embodied beings.
Śrīdhara: Speaking of the state of not having obtained one's desires, he addresses his son with four verses beginning with "O Blessed One. (23)
The *Kramasaṃdarbha*: not commented upon.
Viśvanātha: [He dwells] among embodied beings such as ourselves. ||23||
Nevertheless, O Brahmin, since you ask, I shall speak of what has been contemplated within myself;
for you are wise, and being urged by you, I shall do so with your permission.
Śrīdhara: Not explained. Kramasaṃdarbha: Since he has been urged and impelled, he should speak with his permission. ||24||
Viśvanātha: The meaning is that he is one who carries out the command of the Lord who asks. "Cintitam" refers to the thought conceived within the self, that is, the mind. ||24||
Even the riches of imperial sovereignty, sought after by the guardians of the world,
do not delight me, who am childless, just as other things fail to satisfy one afflicted by hunger, thirst, and desire.

Śrīdhara: "Childless" means having no son. Just as other things such as garlands and sandalwood do not provide pleasure to one who desires food and drink due to hunger and thirst, [so too do external objects fail to satisfy one who lacks a son]. ||25||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: For one who has a desire for food and water due to hunger and thirst, other things such as garlands, sandalwood paste, and so forth [are of no avail]. (25)
Therefore, O illustrious one, protect us from the darkness that has overtaken our ancestors;
ordain for us that by which we may cross over this difficult-to-traverse [darkness] with our progeny.
Śrīdhara: Act in such a way that we may cross over, together with our offspring, the darkness—the hell—that has been reached by us along with our ancestors, such as our fathers. 26.
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Act in such a way that we may cross over the darkness—that is, the hell—attained along with our ancestors, such as our fathers, by means of our offspring. 26.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus entreated, that compassionate Lord, the son of Brahmā, [replied].
Having cooked the *caru* offering for Tvaṣṭṛ, the powerful one worshipped Tvaṣṭṛ.

Śrīdhara: This has not been explained. Kramasandarbha: Because he desires to turn [the soul] toward the Lord by generating detachment under the pretext of giving away his son, he is compassionate; and so it will be stated by him himself:

"At that very moment, having come to your home, I grant you supreme knowledge; yet, knowing your deep attachment to another, I give you only a son"—thus says Viśvanātha. *Tvāṣṭram* means "having Tvaṣṭṛ as its presiding deity. [27]
O descendant of Bharata, the twice-born one gave the remains of the sacrifice to her who was the eldest, the most excellent, and the chief queen of the king, whose name was Kṛtadyuti.
Śrīdhara: "The remnant of the sacrifice" means the residue of the sacrifice. ||28||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Because she was the first to be arrayed, she is the eldest (*jyeṣṭhā*); and because of her excellence in auspiciousness, she is the most excellent (*śreṣṭhā*).
[He offered] the sacrificial remnant (*yajñocchiṣṭa*), the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) for the Lord of Sacrifice. 28.
"O King," he said to the monarch, "one son shall be born to you who will bring you both joy and sorrow. Having spoken thus, the son of Brahmā departed.
Śrīdhara: "It bestows joy through birth and sorrow through death"—having spoken thus, he departed. (29)

The composition of the sequence: Viśvanātha states that [the Lord] is said to be the bestower of joy and sorrow for the purpose of making one renounce one's own faults. In what manner is he the bestower of joy? In what manner is he the bestower of sorrow? Regarding this, what shall I now say concerning birth and death?

"The King alone will know in the future; moreover, even though these words are unpleasant, they must certainly be spoken now for the sake of providing a response to the reproach the King will later bestow.
Having reflected thus in his mind, he departed without stating the truth clearly, [saying only]: "My son is endowed with many virtues."

Thinking in his mind, "That which gives joy because it will come to pass, yet gives sorrow because of the excess of power it brings— let that sorrow be endured by me," the king should be known as being filled with bliss alone. ||29||
By consuming that very [substance], Queen Kṛtadyuti conceived a fetus from Citraketu, just as the goddess Kṛttikā conceived a son from the fire.
Śrīdhara: [Not commented upon].
Viśvanātha: The meaning is that from Agni, Kṛttikā [obtained her son], as if he were her own child. ||30||
O King, day by day her womb grew, like the moon in the bright fortnight,
slowly increasing through the splendor of the Lord of Śūrasena.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
Then, when the time had arrived, the prince was born.
Producing supreme joy for the Śūrasenas as they listened.
Śrīdhara: That embryo, which was the sequential composition [of the Vedas], grew through the splendor and heroism of the Lord of the Śūrasenas; Viśvanātha: this has not been explained.
The king, delighted, having bathed, purified himself, and adorned himself,
had the brahmins recite benedictions and performed the birth ceremony for the prince.
Śrīdhara: Jātaka is the birth-rite (jātakarman). ||33||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— To them [he gave] gold, silver, garments, and ornaments.
He gave away villages, horses, and elephants, as well as six hundred million cows.

Śrīdhara: An *arbuda* is ten *koṭis*. However, in the Veda, a *koṭi* itself is called an *arbuda*, because it is listed as such in the sequence following *niyuta* and *prayuta*: "a *niyuta*, a *prayuta*, and an *arbuda*. (34)
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
He showered the desires of other embodied beings like the rain-cloud.
The high-minded [king] performed that which was auspicious, conducive to fame, and conducive to long life for the prince.
Śrīdhara: "Dhanya" means wealth-bestowing; "āyuṣya" means life-prolonging. The phrase "mahāmanā atyudāraḥ kramasaṃdarbhaḥ" has not been commented upon.
Viśvanātha: He rained down the most excellent desire, which is "dhanya," and not that which is "adhanya" (unfortunate); he was "mahāmanāḥ" (high-minded).
Exceedingly noble. ||35||
Then, as the son of the royal sage was obtained with great difficulty, the father’s affection for him increased day by day,
just as the love of a poor man grows for wealth acquired with hardship.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
But a mother’s affection for her son is even greater, arising from delusion.
Among the co-wives of Kṛtadyuti, a fever of longing for offspring arose.
Śrīdhara: [The fever] in which delusion arises; the fever in the form of the desire for progeny is the heat.
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: not explained.
Viśvanātha: The fever in the form of the desire for progeny is the heat. ||37||
Citraketu’s excessive affection for his wife, who bore him children,
did not arise toward others in such a way, even as he daily indulged his young son.
They tormented themselves, reproaching themselves with indignation because of their childlessness, their own misery, and the king’s disregard for them.
Śrīdhara: The singular form "dāra" (wife) is an archaic usage (*ārṣa*). The sequence [of verses] is based on the cause of being childless, that is, the absence of sons.
Viśvanātha: This has not been explained.
Fie on that sinful woman who is childless and not esteemed as a housewife by her husband,
who is treated like a slave-girl by her co-wives who possess fine offspring!

Śrīdhara: [He does not take her] who is highly esteemed at home nor one who is highly esteemed abroad; or rather, the meaning is that she is esteemed as the very household itself, not merely as a wife. ||40||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: "A non-house" means a forest distinct from a house; "right there" means approved by her husband—that is, worthy of being granted residence in the forest. ||40||
What grief indeed can there be for female slaves who constantly receive honor through service to their master? Wretched as they are, they are like one slave serving another slave.
Śrīdhara: Just as a maidservant [is treated] by a slave, so are we unfortunate. ||41||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: "Like the servant of a servant"—the meaning is that we are as unfortunate as the servants of some unfortunate woman's servant. ||41||
As they were thus consumed by the excellence of their co-wife’s sons,
a powerful hatred arose in those whose conduct was displeasing to the king.
Śrīdhara: Those for whom a livelihood—that is, a means of subsistence—is not approved. ||42||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Those whose conduct or behavior is not approved by the king. ||42||
Their minds destroyed by hatred and their hearts cruel, the women,
unable to endure the king, administered poison to the prince.
Śrīdhara: Those whose minds were destroyed by hatred; *gara* means poison. *Durmarṣāḥ* means unable to endure [it]. ||43||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: "Durmarṣāḥ" means those who are unable to endure [it]. ||43||
Having performed her ablutions and being unaware of the great evil of her co-wives,
she wandered through the house, thinking to herself, "He is still asleep," as she looked about.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
Having observed the child lying there for a very long time, the wise woman [acted].
"Bring my son to me, O blessed lady," she thus urged the nurse.
Śrīdhara: [He saw] the nurse who was giving him milk. ||45||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha states: "It has not been explained.
—o)0(o— Having approached him as he lay down and seeing his eyes wide open...
Abandoned by her vital breaths, senses, and self, she fell to the ground crying, "I am slain!"
Śrīdhara: [He is] one whose eyes have pupils that have risen. 46.
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— Having heard her voice, which was then extremely distressed...
Even as she beat her breast loudly with both hands,
the queen entered in haste into the presence of her daughter and suddenly beheld her young son dead.
Śrīdhara: [This is] the *Kramasaṃdarbha*; it has not been commented upon.
Viśvanātha: The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "He saw that very son, though still a child, as dead. (47)
She fell to the ground and, with her hair and garments disheveled, fainted from the intensifying grief.
Śrīdhara: She whose hair and garment have fallen away. [This is] a sequential composition. Viśvanātha: Not explained.
Then the people residing in the king's inner apartments—
both men and women— hearing the wailing,
came forward, equally afflicted by the calamity and deeply distressed.
And they, having committed an offense, wept feignedly.
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha: And those [women] were even co-wives. ||49||
The sequential composition has not been explained. —
Having heard that his son had died, [his death] unnoticed by the Ender (Death),...
With his vision destroyed, stumbling and falling on the path,
he was utterly overwhelmed by grief intensified by the bonds of affection; losing his composure, he was surrounded by the twice-born.
He fell at the feet of the dead child, his hair and garments disheveled,
sighing deeply as he was choked by a torrent of tears.
With his throat constricted, he was unable to speak.

Śrīdhara: [He is] one for whom death is an unobserved ender—that is, whose cause of death is hidden. He is "anuprakṛti," meaning one whose ministers and other officials have followed him. He is one whose throat is "niruddha"—obstructed by being choked—due to the "bāṣpakalābhiḥ," that is, by drops of tears. 5051.
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: [He is] one whose end—death—is not perceived; *anu* refers to the ministers, friends, and so forth who follow his nature (*prakṛti*). "Surrounded by the twice-born, he fell"—this implies that the ministers and others [also fell].
And the meaning is that the Brahmins and others fell down. ||5051||
Then, beholding her husband overcome with grief for his wife and their only son, the infant, who was now dead, she was struck with sorrow.
The virtuous queen, causing heartache for the people and the subjects, lamented in many ways.
Śrīdhara: "Filled with great sorrow" means pervaded by much grief. "The single lineage" refers to the continuous succession; it has not been explained [further].
Viśvanātha: "That which is both single and a lineage"—meaning of the nature of a family line—bearing that heart-ache.
While she was flourishing, ||52||
Her two breasts, adorned with saffron paste, are drenched by drops of tears mixed with collyrium.
With her hair disheveled and her garlands falling away, she lamented for her son with a piteous cry, like a female osprey.
Śrīdhara: Those locks of hair from which garlands were falling. ||53||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— Oh, Creator, you are exceedingly childish!
But as for you, who strive for a self-creation that is inconsistent with reality:
while one [the Supreme] lives, there is the death of another;
and if you are the opposite, then you are certainly the Supreme.

Śrīdhara: You act in a manner inconsistent with and unbecoming of your own creation. He explains this very point: "Indeed, alas! That a child should die while the elder remains alive. For in that case, since the elder lacks the capacity for creation and the child has died, your creation would be lost; such is the meaning.

If it is argued, "But am I not now contrary to my own creation? he says in response: If you are contrary—that is, if you are the opposite—then you are a constant and eternal enemy to living beings because you cause them extreme suffering;
the meaning is that you are not compassionate. ||54||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: The Creator alone is the cause of such suffering for us; and his status as the cause is due solely to his own foolishness, [making it] "unlike" (*apratirūpam*) or "unsuitable" (*ananurūpam*) to his own creation.

You act [thus]. He says that very thing: "Indeed, alas! When another, the old man, is living, that which is the death of the other, the child"—for then, since the old man lacks the capacity for creation and the child has died, your creation would be lost; this is the meaning. [Objection: But now, am I not the opposite of my own creation? If you say this...

To this he says: If you are the opposite—that is, contrary [to what was said]—then you are a constant and eternal enemy to living beings because you cause them extreme suffering; the meaning is that you are not compassionate. ||54||
If there is no sequence here between death and birth for embodied beings, let it be so; let it be through their own actions.
This bond of affection which you yourself created for the sake of increasing your own progeny— that very bond you now sever.

Śrīdhara: [Objection: "But what fault is there in me, who undergo birth and so forth in accordance with the karma of the individual soul (jīva)? To this he replies: 'Not indeed... [The opponent argues: 'If it is argued that there is no fixed sequence—such as a father dying while the son is still alive, or a son being born while the father is still alive—because everything is dependent on karma, then [the Lord] must be subject to the very karma of those souls.'"
Let there be birth and so forth; what is to be done by you?
[Objection: But how could this be accomplished by inert karmas without me, the Lord? [Reply: Let it be so;
nevertheless, regarding that bond of affection which you formed for the sake of increasing your own creation—this very [bond]...

"You yourself are tearing [them] apart," "you are cutting them," and so forth—thus he cries out. The sense is that having seen such suffering, no one at all would ever feel affection for their sons and others. ||55||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Now, one might ask: "What is my fault when I undergo birth and so forth according to the karma of the individual soul (*jīva*)?
To this he says: "Not indeed... [For] while the son is still living, the father dies; while the father is already dead, the son...

If it is argued that there is no fixed order [in birth and death] because they are dependent upon karma, then let that birth and so forth arise from the very karmas of the self; what have you accomplished? [Objection:
But how could this be established by inert karmas alone without me, the Lord? [Reply: True.

Let that [suffering] be accomplished by you alone for the sake of increasing your own creation; yet you yourself cut asunder this very bond of affection which you yourself created. Seeing such suffering in affection, no one will ever form affection for sons and the like; for if one forms affection, how [can there be freedom from suffering] regarding sons and the rest?

The sense is that you are indeed a fool, since [if you think] "they will live," creation would be destroyed. Alternatively, the present tense (*laṭ*) is used in the sense of the imperative (*loṭ*); thus, the meaning is "cut it off. The point is that affection alone is the cause of pleasure and pain; in the absence of affection, whether a son is born or dies, neither pleasure nor pain would occur at all. ||55||
"O father, you ought not to abandon me, miserable and protectorless; look upon your father, who is consumed by grief."
May we easily cross over this darkness so difficult for living beings to traverse; do not go far away with your merciless Yama.
Śrīdhara: Difficult for those without offspring to cross; difficult for those without offspring to cross, along with one who is merciless. ||56||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: [Thinking] "Why do I converse with this foolish Creator? Why do I not instruct my own son in what is beneficial?"—having reflected thus, he says: "O Father! etc. O Father!
"By you, our son, may we cross over that darkness of hell which is difficult to traverse for those who are childless and without offspring.
Surely Yama is leading me to his own city; what shall I do? To this he replied: "Do not go with the pitiless one. (56)
"—O! Arise, dear child! These young companions are calling you to play, O delight of kings!"
For you have slept for a long time and are overcome by hunger;
eat, drink from my breast, and remove the grief of us, your own kin.
Śrīdhara: *Aśanayā* means by hunger (*kṣudhā*). ||57||
Kramasaṃdarbha: This has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: Thinking her son was asleep, she said, "Arise," [driven] by aśanayā, that is, hunger (kṣudh). ||57||
"— O son, I, whose auspiciousness has been destroyed, did not behold that lotus-face of yours with its charming smile and joyful gaze."
Or has he gone to another world, never to return, led away by that pitiless one? For I do not hear even a single word from you.
Śrīdhara: O son, my dear child, it was not when I first came to your side that I beheld your face with its charming smile; even now I do not hear your words.
Therefore, you have departed in such a way that there will be no further connection, meaning you will not return again.
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: O son! I have not seen your innocent smile upon your lotus-face; because you do not wake up, or rather, [have you gone] to another world?

Have you gone to the other world? What fault is there in your not returning again—that is, in your being devoid of a return—since you have been led away by the pitiless and merciless Yama? For this very reason, I do not hear your sweet and indistinct words.
Śrī Śuka said:
While she was lamenting thus with various expressions of grief for her deceased son, [the sage spoke].
Citraketu, deeply tormented, wept aloud with a full-throated cry.
Śrīdhara: [This is] the *Kramasaṃdarbha*; it has not been commented upon.
Viśvanātha: Together with her who is lamenting. ||59||
As that couple lamented, all the men and women who followed them wept; everything became devoid of consciousness.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
Thus, having fallen into such a state of dejection, he was lost to consciousness and without a leader.
Having learned this, the sage named Aṅgiras arrived together with Nārada.
Śrīdhara: Not explained. Kramasaṃdarbha: "A king without a leader," meaning one devoid of anyone to dispel his grief; this is the ellipsis. ||61||
Viśvanātha: Thus, perceiving that the entire city had lost its senses and that Citraketu was as good as dead, it was left without a leader. ||61||
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, perfectly suited for the virtuous, in the *Harṣiṇī* commentary known as *Sārārthadarśinī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted.
Thus, in the glorious *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam*, the great Purāṇa, in the commentary on the *Brahma-sūtras*, in the *Pāramahaṃsya-saṃhitā* composed by Vyāsa, in the sixth book,
in the narrative of Citraketu.
The Fourteenth Chapter.
Now begins the Fifteenth Chapter:
The Narrative of Citraketu.
Śrī Śuka said:
They both spoke to the king, who was lying near the corpse like one dead himself and overwhelmed by grief, awakening him with well-spoken words.
Śrīdhara:
Then, in the fifteenth [chapter], the removal of Citraketu’s grief was accomplished by Nārada, together with Aṅgiras, through the instruction of the ultimate reality (tattva).
Near the corpse, in the vicinity of the dead body. ||1||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha:
Now, in the fifteenth [chapter], the two sages rescued the king.
Out of grief, Nārada said nothing at all to instruct him in mantras.
"— O King of kings, who might this person be whom you mourn?
And who are you in relation to him in creation— before, now, or hereafter?"

Śrīdhara: And among his kinsmen, who are you? [The answer is: "In the creation of the form of progeny, this one is the son and I am his father. To that, they both replied: "Formerly... Those who were joined with him in a previous birth in the form of father and so forth, having been separated by death, [remain...]

The meaning is that in the present life, sons and so forth may belong to that very person or to another; in a future life, they may become his wife and so forth, or his enemies and friends, and thus there is no such fixed rule. ||2||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Who might this be of yours? If you say "a son," that may be true; but who are you to him? If you say "a father," then he says in response: "In the past, at the time of creation, or in a previous birth, or even now, who [are you]?"

Or, "beyond this" means in a future birth. Those who were joined with him in a previous birth as sons and so forth, being separated from him at death, may in the present birth become his own sons or those of another; likewise, in another birth, they may belong to him or to another.
The meaning is that they become wives and so forth, or enemies, friends, and so forth. ||2||
Just as grains of sand are carried away and come together by the force of a current,
so too do embodied beings, through the power of time, meet and part.

Śrīdhara elucidates that very intention with the words "just as": just as [bits of wood] in a stream go apart and come together by the force of the current, so too do embodied beings, the living souls, by the force of time. (3)
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* does not provide an explanation.

Viśvanātha elucidates that very meaning with the words "just as" (*yathā*): just as grains of sand are carried away and separated by the force of a stream's current, yet come together and join one another, so too [is it here].
By the force of time, even the living beings within bodies [perish]. ||3||
Just as grains within a heap of grain both exist and do not exist,
so too do beings within beings, impelled by the Māyā of the Lord.

Śrīdhara: "Even so, for all this time I had no son; that one born in my old age has died—this is my sorrow. To this, they both replied: "Just as within grains—that is, seeds—other grains exist, yet in some cases at certain times they do not exist, are not produced, and perish. But it is not..."

The restriction that "they must necessarily come into being" or "they must necessarily remain" does not apply here in the same way as it does to elements such as fathers and the like existing within elements such as sons and the like. Therefore, the sense is that although seeds possess the relationship of producer and produced, just as the status of father and son does not exist [inherently] there, so it is here as well; thus, one should not grieve.
For those impelled by the Māyā of the Lord, there is indeed becoming and non-becoming, but not in reality. //4//
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Now, enough of this inquiry as to whether "I am his father or his son in this birth or in another birth," or whether "I do not exist [there]," and so forth; rather—

If you ask, "By what offense do I experience the pain of separation from this one who is the object of my supreme love? Please tell me," they replied, "There is no offense here at all; rather, time alone is the cause.
They said: "Just so"—meaning that even though he was born when I was in old age, for all this time he was not my son.

If it is argued that there is great suffering because [someone] has died, they reply to that: within grains of barley, other grains (barley-seeds) sometimes come into being, and sometimes they do not, or they perish. Sons and others are of such a nature among beings such as fathers. Therefore, although there is the relationship of producer and produced among barley seeds, there is no such relationship of father and son.

The sense is that, likewise, one should not grieve in this case either. According to the lexicon which states that *dhānā* refers to parched barley or women, by means of a pun (*śleṣa*), the meaning is as follows: just as there are no *dhānās* (barley grains) in parched barley (*dhānāsu*), so too, among such beings as you—those who are devoid of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) required to produce offspring—the elements (*bhūtāni*) [do not persist].
"Offspring do not come into being; rather, O Lord, O King, they are impelled by *māyā*.
Thus, it is I, Aṅgiras, who have become your son through *māyā* for the sake of awakening you"—this is the intended meaning.
We, you, and all these beings, moving and stationary, who exist at the same time—
just as there was nothing before birth and death, so too, O friend, there is nothing now.

Śrīdhara: Since he is common to all, they say that the son alone is not to be grieved for—“And we,” etc. “Of equal time” means belonging to the present time. Just as [we] did not exist prior to birth and shall not exist after death, so too we do not exist now. O King! At the beginning and at the end...
The meaning is: "because of non-existence, like a dream. ||5||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.

*Viśvanātha*: [The commentators] say "We too" (*vayaṃ ca*) to show that it is not only the deceased son who is to be pitied, but rather that all others—the wife, ministers, kinsmen, and so forth—even while still living, are indeed objects of pity.

Just as things existing at the same time—abiding for a single moment—do not exist prior to birth or after death, so too they do not exist now; for here no entity existing across all three times is said to be real, nor is an unreal entity taken into account by the wise; therefore, even that [which appears to exist] is not ultimately true.
For one who is unreal, it is merely conceit. ||5||
The Lord of beings creates, sustains, and destroys beings by means of beings created by himself,
which are not independent; yet he remains indifferent, like a child.

Śrīdhara: [If the body] is non-existent, how can there be perception? Or how can there be such conceits as "I am the progenitor of this"? To this, they reply with the words "by the elements" (*bhūtaiḥ*). The sense is that because [the body] has been created by the Lord through *māyā*, this conceit belongs to the elements merely as the instruments of perception. But surely...

If there is something to be accomplished through the creation and so forth of the Lord, then He would be subject to incomplete desire; if there is nothing, from what cause would there be activity? To this, they reply: "Though independent, He acts out of sport (līlā), like a child. (6)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "And [he thinks], 'This son was not begotten by me; he has been destroyed by some unobserved, cruel person. Thus, the quality characterized by being the progenitor resides in himself, whereas the quality characterized by being the destroyer resides in the other."
They state that a fault must be raised [against this view]: [the Lord] creates by means of beings such as fathers and so forth; he protects by means of kings and so forth;

he destroys by means of serpents and so forth. The meaning is that these fathers and others are created by the Lord and are dependent upon the Lord because they are created by Him. Now, one might ask: what purpose does the Lord have, who possesses all desires fulfilled?
Regarding [the objection] concerning creation and so forth, he says: "Even though independent, He acts out of sport, like a child. (6)
O King, from the body of the embodied one, another body is born from that very body,
just as a seed arises from a seed; thus, O embodied one, the eternal purpose [of existence] is like this.
Śrīdhara: And they both state that this worldly activity of birth and so forth belongs only to bodies, not to the Self:
"The body of the embodied son is born from the body of the embodied father, which itself was born from the body of the embodied mother;
just as a seed is born only from a seed. But the embodied Self is indeed eternal. This is the meaning.
Just as with the earth and so forth, it is likewise [in this case]. //7//
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* has not been commented upon.
Viśvanātha says: "It is true that you have said, 'This son born of me by a father created by Īśvara has died;
therefore I grieve'? To that they reply: [this is grief] for the embodied son by means of the body of the father."

The body is born from the mother's body, just as a seed is born from a seed; therefore, since the body of the son produced by you exists right before your eyes, what is the reason for your grief now? This is the intended meaning.

"To this objection—that you grieve because the embodied soul, the *jīvātman*, is not present here now—they reply: The entity called the embodied soul or *jīva* is indeed eternal; it was not produced by you, and therefore you have no connection whatsoever with it. This is the sense. (7)
This distinction between the body and the embodied was formerly created by a lack of discernment,
just as this distinction between genus and individual is conceptually constructed with respect to a real entity.

Śrīdhara: But surely, because it stands in a relationship of mutual opposition with the perishable body, the embodied self (*dehin*) would also not be eternal? To this, they reply: This mutual distinction between the body and the embodied self is beginningless, produced by non-discrimination, and imagined through ignorance. "Jāti" is the universal (*sāmānya*), and "vyakti" is the particular (*viśeṣa*); [this verse refers to] the distinction between these two.

Just as [a distinction] is imagined with respect to a thing that is merely existent, because it cannot be defined due to its being established through mutual dependence, so it is in this case as well. //8//

The sequential composition: In reality, there is no state of being embodied for the pure Self; therefore, it has no body. In this regard, there is an illustration: just as there is no distinction between genus and individual in the Supreme Self, which is the cause of all things. (8)

Viśvanātha: [Objection: But surely, because it stands in a relationship of mutual opposition with the perishable body, the embodied self (*dehin*) must also be non-eternal? To this, the two [the authors] reply: This mutual distinction between the body and the embodied self is beginningless (*anādi*), produced by non-discrimination (*aviveka*), and imagined through ignorance (*ajñāna*). It is a distinction between the universal (*jāti-sāmānya*) and the particular individual (*vyakti-viśeṣa*).
Just as [the distinction] is imagined with respect to a thing that is merely existent, because it cannot be defined due to its establishment through mutual dependence— (o)0(o)—
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus consoled by the words of the twice-born, King Citraketu wiped his face,
which was withered by anxiety, with his hand and spoke.
Śrīdhara: A face withered by mental anguish. ||9||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
— o)0(o)— Śrī Rāja said:
Who are you two, endowed with wisdom and the greatest among the great,
who have come here in disguise, hidden by the appearance of ascetics?
Śrīdhara: Not explained.
Kramasaṃdarbha: "In the guise of an Avadhūta," because they assumed that form for the purpose of concealing their true identity.
Viśvanātha: "In the guise of an Avadhūta," because those two [the Lord and Lakṣmī] acted in that way for the sake of self-concealment.
Indeed, those Brahmins dear to the Blessed One wander at will upon the earth,
appearing like madmen for the sake of awakening those like me who possess vulgar intellects.
Śrīdhara: Those whose characteristics are like those of a madman. ||11||
The sequence of composition: [These] are dear to the Lord, who is especially affectionate toward his devotees and generally beloved by the gods who are devoted to Brahman. (11)
Viśvanātha: Not explained.
—o)0(o— Kumāra, Nārada, Ṛbhu, Aṅgiras, Devala, and Asita.
Apāntaratamas, Vyāsa, Mārkaṇḍeya, and then Gautama.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha, Rāma, Kapila, Bādarāyaṇi,
Durvāsas, Yājñavalkya, Jātūkarṇa, and likewise Āruṇi.
Romaśa, Cyavana, Datta, Āsuri, Patañjali, the sage Vedaśiras, Dhaumya, and likewise the muni Pañcaśikha.
Hiraṇyanābha of Kosala, Śrutadeva, and Ṛtadhvaja—
these and other lords of the perfected ones wander about for the sake of knowledge.
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha have not commented [on this].

Kramasandarbha: "Kumāra" constitutes a group of four. Even though Vyāsa, Bādarāyaṇa, and others were not yet manifest at that time, they are included by virtue of the perspective of the scripture alone. ||12||
Paramātma-sandarbha 69: In this regard, it should be understood from that very source that "Apāntaratamas" is a specific name for Śrī Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana himself in another birth.
Therefore, O lords of mine who am of deluded intellect,
let the lamp of knowledge be kindled for me, who am submerged in the blinding darkness of the domestic animal state.
Śrīdhara says: "Or rather, my two Lords are protectors capable of awakening me; therefore, let the lamp of knowledge be kindled by you both. (16)
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
Śrī Aṅgiras said:
"O King, I am Aṅgiras, the giver of sons to you who desire a son;
this is the venerable sage Nārada, the son of Brahmā himself."
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
Thus, you are submerged in the darkness of the grief for your son, a darkness difficult to cross.
Having recollected that which is not worthy of that [world], the domain of the Great Being.
O Lord, we two have come here for your favor;
you ought not to disregard us, who are devoted to Brahman and are devotees of the Blessed One.
Śrīdhara: You, who are devoted to Hari and whose sphere of concern is the Great Person (Mahāpuruṣa). ||18||

The sequence of composition: "Thus" refers to the pair of verses. [He is one] for whom the Great Person is the object—that is, within the range of his direct experience—because, as previously stated, the seed of devotion has arisen through the power of association with that devotee. (18)

Viśvanātha: [He is] one for whom great souls, supreme sages, and devotees of the Lord are the objects of his senses, such as the mind and the eyes; for this very reason, he is called "devoted to Brahman" (*brahmaṇya*) and a "devotee of the Lord" (*bhagavadbhakta*) because he is served by Brāhmaṇas and Vaiṣṇavas, but not because he was actually a devotee at that time—this is the meaning.
"— at that very moment, having come to your home, I bestow supreme knowledge upon you;
yet, perceiving your attachment to another, I give you only a son."
Śrīdhara: That very moment when I previously arrived. ||20||
The sequence of composition: "I give" means "I shall give"; and again, "I give" means "I gave.
Here, the present tense (*laṭ*) is used for the verbal suffixes according to the rule *tiṅāṃ tiṅo bhavanti*, which is an archaic Vedic usage. ||20||

Viśvanātha: "I give" means "I shall not give. And "I give again" has the sense of "I gave," according to the grammatical rule that verbal suffixes (tiṅ) may take the place of other verbal suffixes. ||20||
Now, the suffering of those who possess children is being experienced by you alone;
likewise [the suffering] regarding wives, homes, wealth, and various forms of sovereign prosperity.
Sensory objects such as sound and the rest are fickle, as are the splendors of sovereignty:
the earth, the kingdom, the army, the treasury, the servants, the ministers, and friends.
All these things of Śūrasena, which cause grief, delusion, fear, and suffering,
are like a city of Gandharvas, resembling dreams, illusions, and mental fantasies.
Śrīdhara: "Riches" means wealth; they are "fickle," meaning impermanent. (21) Furthermore, [he says] "the earth," etc. (22)

O Śūrasena, all these [objects of the senses] are indeed the causes of sorrow and the like; moreover, because they come and go, they are equal to a city of the Gandharvas. For it is well known that a city of the Gandharvas appears out of nowhere and then vanishes. Thus, their impermanence and their nature as causes of sorrow and so forth [are established].
And its nature of coming and going has been stated. He also speaks of its falsity: "Just as a dream, an illusion, and a mental wish, so it is. (23)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Thus, it has been stated that because wives and other such things are impermanent, they lack the nature of a real entity, they are causes of grief and the like, and they are subject to coming and going; yet those who [consider] others besides wives and so forth...

Objects that cause grief, delusion, fear, and suffering arise from a dream, yet they are indeed false; thus he says: "Like a gandharva-city, a dream, an illusion, a magician’s trick, and a mental wish"—these are the things arising from them. ||2123||
Mental phenomena, though appearing, are not seen apart from their objects;
through various actions, diverse karmas arose for the one who meditates upon the mind.
"From the mind arise hatred and attachment, from which merit and demerit are produced;
and from the merit and demerit of one's sons and others [merit and demerit arise]. Therefore, everything originates in the mind. Thus it is stated in the Nāradīya Purāṇa. (24)

Śrīdhara: Mental phenomena (*manobhava*) are manifested by the mind alone. The reason for this is that they are seen even without an object (*artha*) in its real nature (*tāttvika-svarūpa*). Why is that? Because they are not seen in the subsequent moment. For if they were real in nature, there would be no sublation (*bādha*) in the subsequent moment. Therefore—
The meaning is that they are false, like dreams and such, because they are merely the manifestations of the mind.
Now, the Mīmāṃsakas say that these [objects] are produced by merit and demerit; so how can they be said to arise from the mind?
To this he replies: for a person who meditates on objects through actions—that is, through the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of actions—it is from the mind alone [that they appear].

From the *nimitta* (the causal sign) the ritual acts (*karmāṇi*) came into being. According to an alternative reading (*pāṭhāntara*), the meaning is that the object most desired (*īpsitatama*) was meditated upon.
Since the ritual act also originates from the mind, the sense is that the objects to be accomplished by it likewise originate from the mind alone. ||24||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: [Objects] such as tigers, snakes, and so forth, which are seen even without an external object, are no longer seen when the dream state and the like cease; therefore, wives and other such things are unreal entities.

Dreams and the like are all unreal, being products of the mind. He explains their very nature as mental constructs: when a person meditates on objects through actions—that is, through the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of past actions—the mind itself becomes the cause, and thus actions come into being. In the reading *karmābhidhyāyataḥ*, [the meaning is] "meditating upon action."
The meaning is "not coveting that which is most desired. Since action also arises from the mind, the objects to be accomplished by it likewise arise from the mind; this is the intended sense. ||24||
for this body of the embodied one consists of substance, cognition, and activity;
it is declared to be the cause of various afflictions and torments for the embodied one.

"Madhu consists of the material substance, the gross body, the organs of action, and the organs of knowledge; the mind is declared to be of the nature of cognition. Thus it is stated in the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa.
"There would be the application of a single term to both cause and effect. Thus [it is stated] in the *Śabdanirṇaya*, verse 25.

Śrīdhara: Thus, it has been stated that sons and other objects of possessiveness are causes of suffering and so forth; in this regard, he says "for this... to show that the root cause is the connection with the body. The word "hi" (for) is used for emphasis. This very body—which consists of substance, knowledge, and action, and which takes the form of the objective, the divine, and the subjective—is indeed the [cause] of the embodied being.
It is so called because it produces various afflictions and torments for the embodied living being (jīva) who conceives the thought, "I am the body. ||25||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.
*Viśvanātha*: Thus, it has been stated that sons and other objects of attachment are causes of suffering and so forth;
therein, he says—"For this..."—that the root is the connection with the body. The word "hi" (for) is used for emphasis. This...

It is so called because it produces various afflictions and torments for the embodied soul— the individual living being who identifies with the body, thinking "I am the body"— which consists of substance, knowledge, and action, and which takes the form of the physical elements, the presiding deities, and the inner self. ||25||
Therefore, having reflected with a healthy mind upon your own destiny,
abandon the reliance on the permanence of dualistic objects and enter into tranquility.
And [as stated by] Madhva: "Hari alone is remembered as independent of anything else, while the other two are considered dependent.
Because of this dependence on another and because they are attained through him, duality is spoken of. (26)

Śrīdhara: With a mind that is healthy and undistracted, abandon this trust, confidence, or affection that [regards] the goal as certain—that it is "this" reality; instead, enter into and take refuge in austerity and tranquility. 26.
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: By one who is healthy and undistracted, the "course" is the reality (*tattva*). In this dualistic world—which abounds in the locus of "I-ness" (*ahaṃtā*) and "mine-ness" (*mamatā*), and which is the locus of "this-ness" (*idantā*)—it is constant...

Abandon the confidence, trust, or affection that this object is a real entity, for that thing is devoid of substantiality; rather, take refuge in tranquility (*upaśama*), which is eternal (*śāśvata*). As Amara states: "Eternal (*śāśvata*), firm (*dhruva*), constant (*nitya*), perpetual (*sadātana*), and primeval (*sanātana*).
Therefore, enter into and rely upon peace. 26.
Śrī Nārada said:
O you who are self-restrained, accept from me this secret Upaniṣad of mantras.
By retaining this for seven nights, one shall behold the all-pervading Lord Saṅkarṣaṇa.

"O Madhva, the Rudras and others, having realized Viṣṇu—known as Saṅkarṣaṇa—who resides within the body of Śeṣa and is the inner controller (antaryāmin) of Śeṣa, attained their own station effortlessly. Thus says Śrīdhara in the *Tantrabhāgavata*. Furthermore, the reality taught by Aṅgiras cannot be attained without the grace of the Supreme Lord.
To ensure that this is attained, Nārada instructs him in the mantra-vidyā: "This" (etām).
That which is seated near (upaniṣaṇṇam) the supreme good is an *upaniṣad*. This mantra itself is the *upaniṣad*; receive it, grasp it. You shall become its seer (*draṣṭā*). ||27||

The Sequence of Composition: Thus, being dissatisfied with that which was taught by Aṅgiras, Śrī Nārada said. Viśvanātha explains: "If that is so, then what indeed is the certain goal? [Please tell] that very thing to me out of compassion."
When it was expected that he would speak, Nārada, urged by Aṅgiras and being himself a great devotee of the Lord, said:
"This"—meaning, "Accept this," that is, take hold of this Upaniṣad in the form of a mantra. ||27||
O King, having approached the soles of whose feet in the past, Śiva and the other gods abandoned this twofold delusion.
They immediately attained his incomparable and unsurpassed majesty; you too shall attain it, though not so soon.

"Through duality, one abandons bondage; thus one becomes a renouncer of duality"—so it is said in the *Śabdanirṇaya*. The delusion consists in the conceit of "I" and "mine" regarding the body and so forth.
Indeed, the very words for those [entities] are the words for Viṣṇu.
Their greatness as well as that of Hari is subject to Him;
therefore, it is incomparable and even superior, leading each of them to liberation.
"Considering only his own former majesty, there is never any majesty of Hari that can be attained by another; for it is heard in the *Tantrabhāgavata*: 'O Viṣṇu, [this majesty] is not yours.'"

"That which cannot be attained even by the gods, such as Brahmā and Īśāna, is that very nature which is absolute liberation (*kaivalya*); you are that solitary Hari. Thus it is said in the *Skanda Purāṇa*.
Because [liberation] is obtainable through His grace, His own majesty is likewise incomparable and unsurpassed by any other.
Śrīdhara: They have attained, and shall attain, that supreme glory which is incomparable—meaning it is neither exceeded nor equaled—and is thus devoid of anything equal or superior. (28)
The sequential composition: Now he states the distinction regarding the instruction—beginning with "That which" (yad). ||28||
Viśvanātha: "He causes you to wander" means he makes you roam; "he approaches a second" means he will attain duality. ||28||
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, appropriately joined to the virtuous, in the *Harṣiṇī* commentary known as *Sārārthadarśinī*, for those whose hearts are devoted. *||*
Thus ends the Sixth Canto in the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā, the Pāramahaṃsya, within the Brahmasūtrabhāṣya of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa.
The fifteenth chapter in the narrative of Citraketu.
Now begins the sixteenth chapter.
In the narrative of Citraketu,
Śrī Bādarāyaṇi said:
"Then, O King, the celestial sage [Nārada] saw that the prince had passed away."
Having shown this, he spoke thus to his kinsmen who were grieving for him.
Śrīdhara:
In the sixteenth [chapter], having dispelled the king's grief by means of his son’s own words,
Nārada instructed him in the Mahāvidyā that propitiates Śeṣa.

First, in order to demonstrate through his son's very mouth that the relationship between father, son, and so forth is illusory, he showed him to his kinsmen by the power of yoga and spoke the words beginning with "O living soul. (1)
The sequential composition: having manifested by the power of yoga the deceased one who had attained the subtle body (*ativāhika-deha*), he showed him [to the others]. ||1||
Viśvanātha:
In the sixteenth chapter, having been awakened by the mention of his deceased son, the king received the mantra from Nārada;
after praising him, he acquired the remaining knowledge from his mouth.
The word "jñātīnām" (of kinsmen) is used in the sense of the accusative case. ||1||
Śrī Nārada said:
O Jīvātman, may you be blessed; behold your mother and your father.
Your friends and kinsmen are deeply tormented by the grief caused by you.
Śrīdhara: [This] has not been commented upon in the *Kramasaṃdarbha*.

Viśvanātha: Furthermore, observing that the remnants of grief and delusion were still difficult to overcome, he spoke through the mouth of his deceased son in order to awaken him, saying "O Jīva," etc., out of sorrow—that is, out of grief. (2)
Having entered your own body, surrounded by your friends,
enjoy the pleasures bestowed by your ancestors for the remainder of your life, and occupy the throne of kingship.
Śrīdhara: "The remainder" means that there is life yet remaining; the meaning is that [the person] has died by way of untimely death (*apamṛtyu*).

Regarding the sequence of the text: in the commentary, the phrase "by untimely death" refers to a specific sin appropriate as its cause, since it is precisely this that diminishes one's full lifespan. [He says: "having entered his own body."
Because of this contradiction, he states another alternative with the words "or else" (yad vā). ||3||

Viśvanātha: By pervading the remaining life—that is, the rest of his lifespan—the deathless one (amṛtyu) leads the king toward death. In reality, however, he has no life at all because it is illusory (*māyika*); [he eats] those given by the father, bestowed by the father. ||3||
The Jīva said:
In which birth did these become my fathers and mothers?
For one who is being whirled about by karmas among the wombs of gods, animals, and humans.
Śrīdhara: Having entered that very same body, the individual soul (jīva) arose and spoke; or rather, it should be understood that he did so after remaining in an intermediate preta-body. ||4||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: "The Jīva said"—the meaning is that the sage, having entered that very body, is called "Jīva" as if he were living. "To me" means to my [self]. ||4||
Relatives, kinsmen, enemies, neutrals, friends, indifferent parties, and adversaries—
all these indeed become one another's [relatives, etc. in turn for all people.

Śrīdhara: With the intention that, "If there is grief from the perspective of [them being] sons when I am dead, why is joy not felt from the perspective of [them being] enemies?", he states the non-fixity of these relationships: *bandhavaḥ* (kinsmen) are those related by marriage and so forth; *jñātayaḥ* (relatives) are those of the same *sapiṇḍa* lineage; *arayaḥ* (enemies) are slayers; and *mitrāṇi* (friends) are protectors.

The neutral are those distinct from both [the friend and the enemy] who are common to both; the hostile are those who harbor hatred due to wealth and other causes; and the indifferent are those distinct from these—such is the distinction. ||5||

The sequential arrangement: those situated in the middle meet within that [state], and those who are indifferent do not meet even with those two. In the commentary, regarding the phrase "or rather, the connection is thus," the words "of the two verses" are to be supplied as the ellipsis. ||5||

Viśvanātha: With the intention that "if grief is felt upon my death from the perspective of [me being] a son, why is joy not felt from the perspective of [me being] an enemy?", he states the non-fixity of relationships: *bandhavaḥ* (kinsmen) are those related by marriage and so forth; *jñātayaḥ* (relatives) are those of the same *sapiṇḍa* lineage; *arayaḥ* (enemies) are slayers; and *mitrāṇi* (friends).

The distinction is as follows: protectors (*rakṣaka*), neutrals (*madhyastha*) who are distinct from both [protectors and enemies], commoners (*sādhāraṇa*), enemies (*vidviṣ*) who are hostile due to wealth and other causes, and indifferent parties (*udāsīna*) who are distinct from those. ||5||
Just as commodities such as gold and other goods circulate among people here and there, so too does the soul pass through various wombs that act as its makers.

Śrīdhara: An illustration for being driven about by karmas is as follows: just as commodities fit for purchase, sale, and so forth circulate among merchants who engage in trade, so too does the individual soul (jīva) circulate among wombs, that is, among progenitors. 6.
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Now, if even an enemy were to become a son, how could there be affection for him by virtue of him being one's own? He resolves this with an illustration: "Just as... [regarding] commodities.

Gold and other such items, as well as gold rings and the like, are fit for buying and selling; yet that very same gold ring which, when situated in an enemy's house, serves as the cause of one's own death, becomes by chance the object of affection and the means of enjoyment once it has come into one's own house. It is exactly thus with respect to the wombs of living beings.
It enters into those who are the agents, the progenitors, the fathers, and the mothers among humans, cattle, donkeys, and so forth. ||6||
— for indeed, among men, the connection of an eternal object is seen to be impermanent;
for as long as one's connection with something lasts, so long does one's sense of "mine" persist.

Śrīdhara: With two verses, he explains, by means of an illustration, that even within a single lifetime, the relationship [to objects] is not fixed. Even for an object such as a domestic animal that is permanent—that is, still living—the relationship is impermanent and uncertain, because it ceases through sale or other means. (7)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: For this long time, my soul has been the son of Citraketu, and therefore he has indeed shown such affection. From now on, when I attain the status of being the son of another, will he show the same affection?

He states this by means of an *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by another matter): "Just as in the case of a single eternal object, such as a gold coin, even though it passes into the hands of another person on a single day through transactions like buying and selling, the connection—'this belongs to me, not to another'—is indeed impermanent; and in that regard, the phrase 'for as long as' is clear. (7)
Thus, the living being who has entered the womb is eternal and devoid of ego;
for as long as it is perceived in whatever place, so long does it possess ownership over that very thing.
