Śrīdhara: Thus, as long as one who has entered the womb remains connected [to the parents] and continues to exist under the influence of karma, so long does that ownership belong to the father and others; however, it does not persist even after the time of sale. Or rather, the connection is as follows: "having entered the body," as it was stated.

Regarding that, he states with an illustration that "my ownership over this body has now ceased": [it is like] gold and the like, which are eternal and persist through time; when it has entered the womb—that is, entered the body—in whichever body that may be, the ownership (*svatva*) of that living being (*jīva*) belongs to that body, but not [to anything else].
The meaning is "also after death"; the rest is the same. ||8||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: In reality, when a father or other [relative] is truly devoid of ego (*nirahaṅkṛta*), then [the consciousness] belongs to that father or other;
or rather, as long as the individual soul (*jīva*) is perceived in a particular body while being truly devoid of ego, for that long it belongs to that [body].

The sense of ownership belonging to the living soul (jīva) in that body does not exist at other times; therefore, since I currently lack ownership over this body, how can I exercise ego-identification (*ahaṅkāra*) toward it? Thus, the request "enter the corpse" is simply not tenable—this is the intended meaning. ||8||
He is eternal, immutable, and subtle; He is the refuge of all and the self-luminous witness.
By means of the qualities of His own *māyā*, the Lord creates the universe from Himself.

Madhva states: "This [Lord] is eternal and immutable; Hari is distinct from the impermanent ones such as the father and others who possess impermanent relations. And: "He creates Himself in the form of incarnations. (9)

Śrīdhara: [The Lord] establishes the eternity of the individual soul (jīva): "This one is eternal. The reason for this is that he is "indestructible" (avyaya), meaning devoid of decay. Why is that? Because he is "subtle" (sūkṣma), meaning devoid of birth and so forth. And why is that? Because he is the "substratum of all" (sarvāśraya); he is the substratum of the body and other things characterized by birth and so forth, but he is not of the nature of the body and such. For he is "self-luminous" (svadṛk).

It is self-luminous. It establishes its being the substratum of all: through the qualities of its own *māyā*, the Self creates the universe as itself, being the soul of the universe. This is because of the Vedic scripture stating, "He made Himself by Himself.
The meaning is that it is the substratum of all because it is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*). Since the individual soul (*jīva*) is in reality Brahman...

Since Brahman alone, as distinguished by its power of consciousness (cicchakti), is the Lord (Īśvara) and thus the creator, the expression "the individual soul (jīva) creates" is merely a figurative way of speaking. Alternatively, the soul is called a "creator" because it is the instrumental cause of creation through its own karma;
and since everything that is to be experienced rests upon the experiencer, it is said to be the substratum of all.
It should be observed. ||9||

The Structural Arrangement (*kramasaṃdarbha*): Having thus stated the dependence of the individual soul (*jīva*), he now demonstrates the Supreme [Lord] as well for the sake of establishing that [dependence], with three verses beginning with "This one" (*eṣa*).

This very Supreme Lord, established by both scripture and reasoning, is directly perceptible; the repetition [of the word "this"] is for the purpose of emphasis, and He is subtle and difficult to know. (9)

Viśvanātha: Thus, because the individual soul (*jīva*) is dependent and lacks sovereignty, it is understood that there exists another who is independent and the Lord (*īśvara*). In response to the inquiry as to what kind of being he is, [the author] says: "This one.
Because the soul is veiled by *māyā*, even though He is immediate, He appears as if remote.

The state of being denotable by that word has been stated. Because the Lord is not veiled by *māyā*, and because even the speaker Aṅgiras, being liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), is devoid of the veil of ignorance, he is said to be denotable by this word through immediate perception—as "this one" (*eṣa*). In that regard, there is eternality.
The three common attributes of the Lord— imperishability and subtlety— and the two uncommon attributes of the individual soul— dependence and lack of sovereignty— have already been indicated.
Now, this [text] is stated once again in order to describe all the uncommon attributes of the Lord, such as being the support of all.
"Having presented the word 'this' (eṣa)," [it refers to] the Self, because it consists of the power of the Self. 9.
for he has no one dear to him, nor anyone unpleasant, whether his own kin or a stranger;
he alone is the witness of all intellects and of the virtues and faults of their agents.

Śrīdhara: Regarding what was said—that he is "surrounded by friends" and that "his kinsmen are distressed"—to that also he says: "For not of him... The reason for this is that he is "alone," being free from association with friends and the like.
Why is that? Because of all the mental states (*dhiyaḥ*) belonging to friends and others who are the agents of benefit and harm, which are grave defects.
The cognitions are manifold; their witness is the observer. ||10||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: He states that for the individual soul (*jīva*), [distinctions such as] kinsmen, enemies, neutrals, and so forth, are based on ignorance, but not for the Lord (*īśvara*), with the words "For this [Lord],... As for the fact that a devotee is exceedingly dear and his own...
Regarding the notions that "one who hates devotees is unpleasant" or "another is a supreme enemy," it has been said:
"I am equal toward all beings; to Me there is none hateful and none dear.
But those who worship Me with devotion, they are in Me, and I too am in them" (Gītā 9.29).

"Those hateful and cruel ones, the lowest of men among transmigrating beings"—according to this statement from the *Gītā* (14.19), this is indeed an ornament, not a defect, for Him who is affectionate toward His devotees. Furthermore, while individual souls (*jīvas*) are many, the Lord (*īśvara*) is one alone; [He is distinct] from those who are the agents of virtues and faults, or of benefit and harm.
The witness is the observer of those various cognitions, which are the diverse mental states of friends and others. ||10||
The Lord,
who perceives both the higher and the lower, does not take on merit, nor defect, nor the fruit of action; for he remains like one indifferent.
"Madhva is the enjoyer because he enjoys the qualities of the Real; yet he is not an enjoyer [in the sense of being subject to them] because that [enjoyment] increases him.
And this is possible for the Supreme Lord due to His inconceivable power. Thus it is said. (11)
Śrīdhara: Regarding what was said, "Enjoy the objects of experience," and so forth, he says there too: "He does not take [them]," etc.

*Guṇa* means pleasure; *doṣa* means pain; and the fruit of action refers to sovereignty and the like. The reason for his indifference is that he is the witness of both the cause—the vision of the higher and lower—and the effect, but not their enjoyer. For he is the Lord.
He is devoid of dependence on the body and so forth. Therefore, since there is no relationship between me, who am such as this, and you, do not grieve; such is the meaning of the sentence. ||11||
The sequence of the composition: the Self is the Supreme Self. ||11||

Viśvanātha: Indeed, the individual soul (jīva) perceives the virtues and faults of both friends and enemies, because it experiences the fruits of its actions as pleasure and pain; the Lord (Īśvara), however, does not do so. Thus he says: "He does not take. For this very reason, seated as the inner controller (antaryāmin) of all like one who is indifferent, He remains as the witness over both the high and the low, the auspicious and the inauspicious.

"He sees"—that is, he perceives. "Like one who is indifferent" (udāsīna) means that he is not like an indifferent person who stands apart from such opposites as enemies and friends; this is the sense.

Therefore, for these individuals such as Citraketu and others, who are bound by the māyā of the Lord, this cycle of worldly existence consisting of grief, delusion, and so forth, cannot cease without their taking refuge in the Lord, which is rooted in the great grace of the Lord.
"It is indeed difficult to cross; what more need be said?"—this is the meaning of the section. ||11||
Śrī Bādarāyaṇi said:
Having spoken thus, Jīva departed; and then his kinsmen [did likewise].
Filled with wonder, they abandoned their grief, having severed the chains of self-attachment.
Having carried away the body of their kinsman and performed the appropriate rites,
the relatives abandoned that affection so difficult to relinquish, which brings the pain of grief, delusion, and fear.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
There, the destroyers of fools were ashamed, their splendor struck down by the slaughter of fools.
O great king, remembering the words spoken by the twice-born, they performed the vow of child-slaughter as prescribed by the brahmins on the banks of the Yamunā.

Śrīdhara: Remembering the words spoken by Aṅgiras—that sons and such are causes of suffering—the Brahmins were free from the desire for offspring and devoid of envy; this is the sense of the word "satya" (truthful). ||14||
The sequential arrangement: "The killers of children," etc., consisting of one and a half [verses]. ||14||

Viśvanātha: "The luster of child-murderers has been destroyed. When all [the women] realized the truth—that these very women were indeed child-murderers by the very definition of having their luster destroyed—then they were ashamed, saying, "Truly, we ourselves are fools who have killed a child."
Having become free from deceit, they performed the penance prescribed by the Brahmins, such as Aṅgiras and others. ||14||
Thus awakened to the Self by the words of the twice-born,
Citraketu emerged from the dark well of his home like an elephant from the mud of a lake.

Śrīdhara: Departure from a home that is like thick mud is appropriate only for one who is exceedingly steadfast, and not for anyone else; thus he says, with an illustration, "He, in this manner," etc., comparing him to an elephant (*dvipa*) emerging from the mud of a lake. (15)

The sequential arrangement: therein, he pays homage to him as the Blessed Lord (Bhagavat) with the words "of the Blessed Lord" (*bhagavataḥ*). As his manifestation (*vyūha*), he offers salutation to Vāsudeva; Saṅkarṣaṇa is mentioned at the end because [the worshipper] rests precisely there, having made him his own object of devotion.
Viśvanātha: Not explained.
—o)0(o— Having bathed in the Kālindī according to the prescribed rule and performed the meritorious water-rites, he...
With his vital breaths restrained through silence, he paid homage to the two sons of Brahmā.
Śrīdhara: He by whom the meritorious water-rites, such as the libations for the ancestors, have been performed; he whose vital breaths are restrained and whose senses are disciplined. ||16||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— Now, to that devotee who has sought refuge and whose self is disciplined...
The blessed Nārada, being pleased, indeed spoke this vidyā.
Śrīdhara: Not commented upon.
Viśvanātha: This [hymn], beginning with "Oṃ, salutations to you" and ending with "Salutations to you, O Supreme Preceptor," [is recited]. ||17||
—o)0(o— Oṃ! We meditate upon you, the Blessed One Vāsudeva;
salutations to Pradyumna, Aniruddha, and Saṅkarṣaṇa as well.
Śrīdhara: "We meditate" (*namo dhīmahi*) means we should contemplate; the sense is that we pay homage with the mind. ||18||

The sequence of composition: therein, he pays homage to Him as the Blessed Lord (Bhagavat) with the words "of the Blessed Lord. He offers salutation to Vāsudeva as His manifestation (vyūha), for Saṅkarṣaṇa is mentioned at the end [of the list], since [the author] finds his ultimate rest in that very [Vāsudeva] as his own object of worship. ||18||
Viśvanātha: Salutations to you; we meditate upon you—we contemplate you in order to propitiate you.

He describes the distinction of the Supreme Self from the individual soul (jīva) by means of nine attributes. To Him whose "measure" (*mātrā*)—that is, limitation—is consciousness (*vijñāna*), which is none other than the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*); whereas the individual soul has ignorance (*avidyā*) as its limitation.
The meaning is "retinue" (*paricchada*). According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *mātrā* refers to an ear-ornament, wealth, or measure; *paricchada* refers to a retinue.
Homage to the one who is consciousness-only, whose form is supreme bliss,
who delights in the self, who is peaceful, and for whom the perception of duality has ceased.
Śrīdhara: [He is so called] because from him the perception of duality has ceased. ||19||

The sequential composition: He pays homage by virtue of his being Brahman with the words "to Vijñānamātra" (Pure Consciousness). Here, "mūrtiḥ" means the essential nature; "nivṛttadvaitadṛṣṭayaḥ" means that when this is seen, no other vision occurs—this is the meaning. ||19||
Viśvanātha: He whose form consists of supreme bliss (*paramānandamayī*), whereas the individual soul (*jīva*) has a form composed of the five elements;

he who delights in the bliss of the Self (*ātmānanda*) alone, whereas the individual soul delights in the bliss of sense objects (*viṣayānanda*); he whose vision regarding the dualistic world of illusion (*māyikaprapañca*) is free from attachment, whereas the individual soul [is attached] to that world of illusion.
It adheres. ||19||
Salutations to Him whose surging waves of power are stilled by the very experience of the bliss of the Self;
salutations to the Great Hṛṣīkeśa, who possesses infinite forms.

Śrīdhara: By whom the waves of power (*śakti*) caused by *māyā*—namely attachment, aversion, and so forth—have been cast down and dispelled, such is the sequence of composition. He shows this specifically through the doctrine that does not admit the cessation of duality, beginning with the words "the bliss of the Self" (*ātmānanda*). Through the experience of the bliss of one's own nature (*svarūpa*), those other [states] are no longer perceived.
Since there is a succession of powers [within experience], even though experience is non-different from its own nature (*svarūpa*),

the power of the essential nature itself is established because of the addition of the meaning of the third case [instrumental]. He pays homage to Him as the Supreme Self with the words "to Hṛṣīkeśa," and as the cause of the universe with the word "the Great One."
"Having infinite forms by virtue of being the universe. ||20||

Viśvanātha: [He is] Viśvanātha, in whom the waves of power (śakti) caused by Māyā—namely attachment, aversion, and so forth—are utterly cast down and destroyed; whereas the individual soul (jīva) possesses the waves of attachment, aversion, and the like. [He is] Hṛṣīkeśa, the controller of all the senses, whereas the individual soul is controlled by the senses. [He is] Mahat, whereas the individual soul is minute.
He whose two forms are infinite and indestructible, whereas the individual soul possesses a destructible body. ||20||
When speech has ceased and that One who is reached by the mind alone—
devoid of name and form, pure consciousness, and beyond both being and non-being— may He protect us.
Madhva: When speech has ceased along with the external mind, Śrīdhara is to be attained by means of the mind consisting of pure consciousness (cinmātra).
Śrīdhara: When speech has ceased and is unattainable even by the mind, He alone shines forth.
The word "speech" (vacasi) is an elliptical expression for all the sense organs. May He, who transcends both the existent and the non-existent, protect us.
The cause of the effect and the cause [itself]. ||21||
The sequence of composition: Furthermore, he praises the Blessed One specifically as being of the nature of Brahman with two verses beginning with "In speech" (vaci). ||21||
Viśvanātha: He bows down to [the Lord] as the undifferentiated Brahman with the verse beginning "In speech... (21).

Salutation to You, that Brahman, in whom this world abides, from which it proceeds, into which it dissolves, and from which it is born, just as the nature of clay persists within all things made of clay.
"Like the class of clay in earthen vessels, the earth and mountains are likewise declared to be composed of clay;
within them, all classes of beings, beginning with the immobile, are born. Thus it is said. (22)

Śrīdhara says: He states that very point with the words "in which" (yasmin). To Him in whom this effect-and-cause resides and from whom it departs, and from whom it is born—to Him who is the all-pervasive thread, like the genus "clay" or mere clay in earthen jars and the like. ||22||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: He bows to [the Lord] as the cause of the universe: "In whom this world abides, from whom it is born, and into whom it also goes to dissolve; just as the genus 'clay' exists in clay-made objects such as jars."
The meaning is "the cause. ||22||
I bow down to that which neither the mind, the intellect, nor the vital currents of the senses touch, nor perceive;
which is spread within and without like space.

Śrīdhara: [Objection: If it were pervasive throughout everything, it would be perceived like the universal class-property "earth-ness" (mṛjjāti). How then is there no reach for the mind or speech there? To this he says: That Brahman, though extended like space, is not touched by the vital breaths (*asavaḥ*), which are the life-forces characterized by the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), nor is it known by the mind and so forth, which are characterized by the power of cognition (*jñānaśakti*). That...
I bow to Brahmā. ||23||
The sequential arrangement: he praises [the Lord] as the Supreme Self with two verses beginning with "That which... (yan na). ||23||

Viśvanātha: He prostrates [to Him] because He is inaccessible to the senses and so forth—with the words "That which... They do not touch it by means of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), nor do they know it by means of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*). If it is argued that this is because He remains at a great distance, he says in response: "Within the body and so forth, both internally and externally. (23)
These— the body, senses, vital breaths, mind, and intellect—
function in their respective activities only when pierced by a portion of Him.
At other times it does not do so at all, like unheated iron;
thus it receives the designation of "the seer" only in specific circumstances.

Śrīdhara states the reason for their ignorance of that [Self]: "These bodies, senses, and so forth, being pierced by its [the Self's] portion and entered by its portion of consciousness, function in their respective objects during the states of waking and dreaming; at other times, such as deep sleep or fainting, they do not function at all, just as..."

Unheated iron does not burn. Therefore, just as iron becomes a burner only through the power of fire and does not burn without fire, so too the body and other such things, though they proceed by means of the powers of knowledge and action residing in Brahman, do not touch it and do not know it— this is the sense.

"In that case, does the individual soul (jīva) know because it is a seer? No, he says: "In its various states, such as waking and so forth, it attains—that is, reaches—the designation of a seer, the appellation 'seer'; there is no other thing called the individual soul, for according to such scriptural passages as, 'There is no other seer than this' (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.23). Or alternatively:

The meaning is that the individual soul (*jīva*) reaches—that is, comes to know—that very thing which is designated as the "seer" and termed the "seer," but the soul does not know that [independently]. This has been stated in the *Haṃsaguhyastotra*: "The body, the vital breaths, the senses... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.4.25), and so forth.

The sequential arrangement: "Body and senses," etc. Here, even in the *Advaitaśārīraka*, Sāṅkhya is refuted as follows: "Now, if it were further imagined that the capacity to perceive in the *pradhāna* is caused by the Witness (the Self)—just as the capacity to burn in a mass of iron and the like is caused by fire—then [it would follow that...]"
"The state of being perceived as a sign belongs to the Pradhāna; that alone is the omniscient, primary cause of the world" (Śaṅkara-bhāṣya, 1.1.5).

And there is a scriptural passage on this point: "It is only by Him shining that everything else shines" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.2.15), and "Who indeed could breathe, who could live? (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7).

"By whom, indeed, could one breathe if this bliss were not present in this space? (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7), and "The eye of the eye, and the ear of the ear," (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.18), and so forth;
and in the scripture cited by the Commentary: "The individual soul (*jīva*) is not other than the Name; there is no self-established entity apart from it. However, [the soul is...]

The meaning is that He is indeed of that very nature. Thus, it should be explained as follows: "There is no other seer than Him" means that for the Seer of all, there is no other seer. ||24|| [Bhagavatsandarbha, Viśvanātha:
He states the reason for their ignorance of Him—beginning with "dehendriya"—by which they are pierced by His portions.]

And being permeated by the aspect of consciousness, they move within their respective objects during actions in the states of waking and dreaming; otherwise, in deep sleep, fainting, and so forth, they do not move at all. Or rather, unheated iron does not burn. Therefore, just as iron becomes a burner only through the power of fire, [so too do these elements function through the power of consciousness].

Just as fire does not burn itself, even so, the body and other factors, though operating within their respective domains by the very power of Brahman, do not touch Brahman, nor do they know it; this is the intended meaning. One might then ask: "In that case, let the individual soul (jīva) know [Brahman], since it possesses the quality of being a seer? To this, he says: regarding the designation of the soul as a "seer" in its various states, such as waking and the rest...

The meaning is that even the individual soul (*jīva*), which possesses the notion of being a seer and is the object of the action, becomes that very Brahman as the agent; for the sake of establishing the soul's status as a seer, Brahman itself attains it by bestowing upon it a certain measure of its own consciousness. Some also say that like me, the souls are likewise insentient.
Alternatively, the meaning is that Brahman itself attains—that is, knows—that [Self], but the individual soul (jīva) does not know Brahman.
As it is stated in the Haṃsaguhyastava: "The body, the vital breaths, the senses... [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.4.25], and so forth. ||24||
Oṃ, salutations to the Blessed One, the Great Being of great majesty, the Lord of great manifestations,
whose pair of lotus feet are cherished by the bud-like lotuses of the hands of the entire assembly of the leaders of the Sātvatas.
O Supreme Parameṣṭhin, obeisance to You!
Śrīdhara: He whose pair of lotus-feet is cherished by the buds—the closed calyxes—of the lotus-hands of the entire assembly, that is, the multitude of the foremost among the Sātvatas.
This is his address: O Supreme One, O Most Exalted One, O Sovereign Lord of All! ||25||

The sequential composition: He praises [the Lord] as being directly the Blessed One with the words "Oṃ namaḥ". Thus, even the worship of Saṅkarṣaṇa is merely a gateway, because he will be described as having the form of the Sātvata scripture; the intended supreme fruit, however, is Śrī Bhagavān himself. ||25||

Viśvanātha: Having stated that the Great Mantra (mahāmantra) reveals knowledge, he speaks of its being filled with the aesthetic flavor of devotion (bhaktirasa)—"Om. It is cherished by the cluster of lotus-like hands of the assembly of all the *sātvata* lords, those who are the most excellent among all devotees.
The desire is implied: "O You whose pair of lotus-feet has been gratified by the skill of light and gentle massaging, likewise place me also in the service of massaging Your feet."
Now, one might ask: "How can I employ you, who are so lowly, in that service which is so exalted?
To this he says: "O Supreme One, O Parameṣṭhin; O Supreme Lord, you are capable of acting otherwise or not acting at all. (25)
Śrī Śuka said:
Having instructed this knowledge to his devotee who had sought refuge in him, Nārada—
The Lord went together with Aṅgiras to his own primordial abode.

Śrīdhara: Previously, it was stated that Aṅgiras was the primary figure in the passage "Nārada and Aṅgiras came," because he was mentioned separately as the one who granted a son to Citraketu. Here, however, in the statement "Nārada went together with Aṅgiras," Nārada is designated as the primary figure; by his instruction, [the result accrued] to him.
Because of the arising of dispassion. O Lord, O Capable One! ||26||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "This" refers to this one great *vidyā* which contains many sentences. Here, Aṅgiras is primary because he granted [the boon] of a son to Citraketu, whereas [the other] is primary because he granted the mantra.

This is [the view] of Nārada. For this very reason, whereas it was previously stated that "Aṅgiras came together with Nārada," it is now said that "Nārada went with Aṅgiras. O Lord, you are supremely capable of knowing the underlying intention of this and other such matters. ||26||
Citraketu, however, subsisting on water alone and with a well-concentrated mind, retained that knowledge exactly as it had been spoken by Nārada for seven days.
Śrīdhara: He bore [it] exactly as it was. ||27||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— Then, at the end of seven nights, with the Vidyā being maintained [in his mind], he...
And he obtained unimpeded sovereignty over the Vidyādharas, O King.
Śrīdhara: He obtained the intermediate fruit of sovereignty over the Vidyādharas; it was unimpeded and unswerving. ||28||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: First, he states the intermediate fruit: "sovereignty over the Vidyādharas" (verse 28).
Then,
after a few days, his mental faculty, kindled by knowledge,
went into the presence of the feet of Śeṣa, the God of gods.

"By worshipping Viṣṇu, who is the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of others, a person, through that fitness, may either come into the presence of another or attain his station. Thus it is said in the *Nāradīya*.
In this manner, he went repeatedly into his presence.

"Let Citraketu worship Viṣṇu, the inner controller (antaryāmin) of Śeṣa; and having obtained boons from Hari who was possessed by Śeṣa, he attained the supreme goal. Thus it is said in the Tantramālā. (29)
Śrīdhara: [He departed] after a few days. [The phrase] "whose movement was characterized by a mind kindled and illuminated by knowledge" (vidyayeddhena dīptena manasā gatiḥ) has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: He states the primary fruit [of this practice] with the words "jagāma" (he went). ||29||
White as a lotus stalk, clad in dark blue garments, and adorned with a shimmering crown, armlets, waistband, and bracelets;
He beheld the Lord, whose face was serene and whose eyes were reddish-brown, surrounded by circles of Siddhas and Īśvaras.

Śrīdhara: [He is] fair-complexioned like a lotus stalk; clad in dark garments (śitivāsas), meaning wearing blue clothing; he upon whom the crown and other ornaments gleam; he who has a girdle (kaṭitra), meaning a waist-string; he whose faces are serene; and he whose eyes are reddish—[meditate on] him and him. (30)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon. *Viśvanātha*: "Clad in white" means wearing blue garments; *kaṭitra* is a waist-string. ||30||
With all his sins destroyed by the sight of him,
the sage, his inner self healthy and stainless, approached.
With eyes brimming with tears of affection and his hair standing on end from joy, he bowed down to the Primal Person.

Śrīdhara: And having seen that Primordial Person (Ādipuruṣa), he approached him and went for refuge. He bowed down; how so? One whose entire impurity was destroyed by the sight of Him, whose internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) was clear and stainless, and whose eyes were shedding tears of love.
He whose body hairs are thrilled is one with "thrilled body hairs. ||31||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Regarding the phrase "upon seeing that"—the term *kilbiṣa* should be understood as the mere suffering consisting of the impossibility of attaining the Blessed One. And having seen [him], he approached.
He approached him; having approached, he bowed down. ||31||
He repeatedly moistened the seat of the lotus feet of the Lord of Excellent Renown with drops of tears born of love.
With the flow of all his speech obstructed by love, he was simply unable to praise him for long.

Śrīdhara: He was not able—that is, he could not—for a long time to thoroughly praise or laud Him. The reason for this is that he was overwhelmed by love as he sprinkled—that is, he bathed—the seat, which is the lotus-feet of the One of Excellent Renown (Uttamaśloka), while his entire speech was obstructed from emerging or being uttered. ||32||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Having bowed, he says "He praised" (*sa...*) and so forth. [He praised him] who is the mind of Viṣṭaraśravas (Viṣṇu), while sprinkling [him], that is, performing an ablution. ||32||
Then, having composed his mind through his wisdom,
he regained his speech and spoke this.
Having restrained the outward movement of all his senses,
he [meditated upon] the Teacher of the World, who is the very embodiment of the Sātvata scripture.
Śrīdhara: Having composed his mind through the intellect—that is, by means of wisdom—he spoke this which is about to be told.
He is one by whom speech has been regained; he is that whose form is described in the Sātvata scriptures. (33)

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: The meaning is that he has regained his speech solely through her grace. By the phrase "one whose body (*vigraha*) is as described in the *Sātvata-śāstra*," [the author] refutes the notion—stated in the *Jñāna-śāstra*—that his body is composed of *māyā*.
Validity has been refuted. ||33||
Citraketu said:
"O Unconquered One, you have been conquered by those of equanimous mind."

By you, who are self-conquered, the virtuous have been conquered; and by those virtuous ones, who are free from desire, even You— who are most compassionate and the giver of the Self to those who worship You— have been conquered.
Śrīdhara:
Joyfully praising his master and servants, who were filled with the bliss born of mutual love,
he extols the Lord with fifteen verses.

O Ajita! Although you are unconquered by others, you have been conquered by virtuous devotees and brought under their control, because you are exceedingly compassionate. And they too, though free from desire, have been won over by you—you who, even to those whose minds are devoid of desire, give yourself alone. ||34||
The sequential arrangement: And in the *Haribhaktisudhodaya*, the speech from the mouth of the Blessed One (*Śrī-mukha*) addressed to Prahlāda is as follows:
"O child, abandon this fear and agitation caused by my own dignity."
He is not dear to me among my devotees; become one whose love is self-dependent.
Even though my desires are fulfilled, this is ever-new and dear to me:
that my devotee looks upon me and speaks to me with fearless intimacy.
Though eternally liberated, I am bound by the cords of affection for my devotees;
though unconquered, I am conquered by them; and though beyond subjugation, I have been brought under their control.
"He who, having abandoned affection for his kinsmen, finds delight in me—he alone am I to him, and he alone is mine; there is no other friend for the two of us.
Therefore, it has been rightly explained that the state consisting of the perception of the Blessed One is not composed of *māyā* and the like.

What then? It is that the Blessed Lord himself is dependent upon bliss, which is of the nature of the bliss of his own essential power (*svarūpa-śakti*). As it is said in the venerable *Gopālottara-tāpanī* Śruti: "A mass of consciousness, a mass of bliss, he abides in the yoga of devotion, which is of the single flavor of existence, consciousness, and bliss" (Goṭā.u. 2.79).
Thus [34].

[Prītisandarbha 66] Viśvanātha says: "May the two [of us] immerse ourselves in the ocean of the essence of bliss obtained through mutual subjugation, solely through devotion to the Lord. Thus he speaks while offering praise: "O Ajita! (the Unconquered One).

By the wise, the yogis, and other such virtuous devotees, You alone are conquered; that is, You are brought under their control by those of equanimous mind who, through self-mastery, have conquered the mind and—by virtue of having conquered the mind's attribute, desire—are free from longing, regarding their own pleasure and pain with equal indifference. Of them...

The implication is that freedom from desire alone is the cause for victory over You; even those saintly persons have been conquered by You, since You, who grant Your very self to those who worship You with a desireless mind—those who worship without selfish motives—bestow Yourself upon them. If you [the devotees] were to serve Me... what [could I give]?

"If you do not choose even liberation and the like from me, then serve me alone day and night as you desire and make yourselves my debtors"— thus, while giving himself to them, he forcibly [bestowed] his own beauty, sweetness of voice, fragrance, and other qualities.
The meaning is that he offers [the senses] for the sake of enjoyment by the lotus-like eyes, feet, and other organs.

Thus, the sense is that even Your own self-surrender (*ātmadātṛtva*) is the cause for victory over them. Here, "by the virtuous" (*sādhubhiḥ*) should not be explained as "even by the knowers" (*jñānibhiḥ*), because of the phrase "of those who worship with desireless minds" (*akāmātmanām*) in the second half-verse.

Because the two qualifiers serve to exclude others, the worship of the wise occurs only during the stage of practice for the sake of attaining liberation; however, here the present tense is used in the phrase "of those who worship. Furthermore, their state of desirelessness arises from the desire for the absolute cessation of suffering.
For them, it simply does not exist.
O Blessed One, the arising, subsistence, dissolution, and so forth of the world are indeed Your own power.
They are but minute portions of the portions of the Creator of the universe; yet there they vainly compete with separate notions of selfhood.

Śrīdhara: [Objection: But how can it be said that [the Lord] has been conquered by devotees alone? For victory is possible even over other lords who, though competing with Him, are the creators of the universe and so forth. To this, He says: "Thine" (tava). The arising and so forth of the world are Thy very *vibhava*—that is, manifestation, majesty, or sport (*līlā*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*),...
[They perform] entry, regulation, and so forth. However, Brahmā and the others who create the universe are not independent lords (īśvara);
rather, they are portions of that Person (puruṣa) who is a portion of You. Even though this is the case, they vainly compete with the conceit, "We are each separate lords. (35)
The sequence of composition: the creators of the universe, such as Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, and others, are "portions of portions," meaning they are extremely minute portions. ||35||

Viśvanātha: Having thus described the mutual subordination between the Lord and His devotee, He speaks of the Lord’s power with the three verses beginning with "tava" (of You). "Vibhavaḥ" means majesty. Now, one might object: Brahmā and others are seen to be the causes of the world's origin and so forth. To this He says: "viśva... (the universe...). Now, one might object...

Devotees of Brahmā, Rudra, and others, asserting that their respective objects of worship alone are the Lord of the Universe, compete with one another; therefore, he says: "In that regard, it is false.
This refers to those who possess the conceit of being distinct, such as the Hiraṇyagarbha-worshippers, the Śaivas, the Sauras, and so forth.
O You who exist within the beginning, the end, and the interval between the smallest atom and the greatest magnitude, You are free from the three [states of being].
Whatever is certain for sentient beings at the beginning and at the end is indeed the same in the interval as well.

Śrīdhara: He establishes that you alone are the agent of creation and so forth: the atom is the subtle root cause; the supremely great is the final effect. You alone exist between these two—the beginning and the end. That is, it is your nature to exist at the beginning, at the end, and in the middle (the interval).

He is, for that very reason, devoid of the three states, empty of beginning, end, and middle, and eternal. And these [states] are created by you, but they are not eternal. Why is this? To this he says: that which is eternal, unchanging, and present at the beginning, at the end, and also in the interval of beings—that is, of effects perceived as existing—is alone the eternal.
Like gold and so forth. ||36||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.
*Viśvanātha*: He establishes that you alone are the agent of creation and so forth, the nature of the ultimate reality—“The atom is the subtle primary cause; the supremely great is the final effect.”

You alone abide within the beginning and the end of those two; that is, you have the nature of abiding in the beginning, the end, and the middle (the interval). Therefore, you are eternally devoid of the three—that is, empty of beginning, end, and middle—because that which is constant as the cause at the beginning and the end of sentient beings and of all conditioned things [is you].

That very [Self] remains stable even in the intermediate state, like gold and other such substances. Therefore, you alone are the real cause and the only real entity; the meaning is that everything else, the entire collection of effects, is unreal. ||36||
This egg-shell, it is said, is enveloped by the seven elements beginning with earth, each ten times greater than the preceding.
Where even an atom-like portion falls, along with millions upon millions of cosmic eggs— that is Ananta.

Śrīdhara: Thus it has been stated that there is no limitation by time due to His immutability; now he states His lack of limitation by space as well—with the words "by earth and so forth. He is enveloped by each subsequent element ten times greater than the preceding one. Yet, even there, one who is like an atom—one equal to an atom—falls into You.
Because that [world] revolves, you are therefore infinite. ||37||
The composition of the sequence: the meaning is "by those [qualities] which increase tenfold in each successive stage. ||37||

Viśvanātha: Having thus stated the absence of limitation in terms of time, he now states the absence of limitation in terms of space: He is enveloped by earth and the rest—by earth, water, fire, ether, ego, the Great Principle (mahat), and primordial nature (prakṛti)—each ten times greater than the preceding one; yet in You, even that which is like an atom [finds room].
It falls and wanders about; therefore, you are infinite. ||37||
Those human-beasts, thirsting for sense-objects, worship your manifestations and not you, the Supreme.
O Lord, their blessings perish along with them, just like a royal household.

Śrīdhara: Since you are thus the Supreme Lord and other deities are merely your manifestations (*vibhūti*), those who worship others while abandoning you out of a desire for sense objects are extremely dull-witted; thus he says: "Those whose thirst is for sense objects are beasts in human form. Why? Because they [worship] the manifestations...

Indra and the others worship you, but they do not worship the Supreme You. What follows from that? To this he says: "Of them" (teṣām). "Thereafter" (tadanu) means after the destruction of the object of worship; just as after the destruction of a royal family, the blessings of its servants perish, so it is here. And this is the ultimate limit; even in the interim, [their blessings] perish.
Thus ||38||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Having thus described the pre-eminence of the Lord, he first states it by way of contrast through the censure of the non-devotee regarding the devotee as well—starting with the words "viṣaya... [The word] "vibhūtīḥ" refers to Indra and the other gods; [it does not mean] "not."
But you—after the destruction of those who worship you; just as, after the destruction of a royal court, the blessings of its servants perish. ||38||
Desires directed toward you do not take root at all, just as seeds of karambha do not grow.
From the multitude of qualities in this [world], which consists of the nature of knowledge and is devoid of qualities, arise the nets of dualities.

Śrīdhara: He says that even service performed by one desiring sense-objects has liberation as its fruit: "O Supreme One, if even the thoughts of desire—that is, desires for sense-objects—are directed toward You, they do not sprout;
they do not lead to the arising of another body. [They are like] *karambha* seeds, which are parched seeds."

For example: since the various pairs of opposites arise for this living being (*jīva*) solely from the collection of the *guṇas*, therefore, by worshipping You—who are devoid of *guṇas*—even through desire, one gradually attains freedom from the *guṇas* (*nirguṇya*); such is the meaning of the sequence of the composition, which has not been [further] explained.

Viśvanātha: He states the excellence of the devotee through the method of *kaimutika* (a fortiori) by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*): "If desires for kingship and the like, or the mental orientations directed toward those ends, have been fixed upon You, they do not sprout—that is, they do not lead to the arising of another body—just as parched barley seeds do not grow."

It is exactly so. Although it is observed elsewhere that desires which sprout do not become like parched seeds, nevertheless, they arise due to the excellence of their objects; thus he says: [desires arise] toward the Self of Knowledge, which consists of consciousness, is devoid of qualities (aguṇamaya), and is distinct from objects composed of the gunas. Therefore, just as an object fallen into a pit of liquid...

The meaning is this: since even thoughts of desire, having entered into you, would thus become composed of consciousness (cinmaya), how could they possibly be the cause of saṃsāra? For it is only from the multitude of the guṇas that the web of dualities—the causes of saṃsāra—arises. ||39||
Victory was achieved by you, O Unconquered One, when you proclaimed the faultless dharma of the Blessed One.
Those sages who possess nothing and delight in the Self worship Him for the sake of liberation.
Śrīdhara: When even the worship of You performed with a desire for results becomes a cause for liberation, then what need is there to speak of the greatness of the Lord’s dharma?
To express this, and because He is the founder of that tradition, he praises the Blessed One with the words "Victory! (Jitam). When...

You have spoken of the Bhāgavata dharma; therefore, O Blessed One, victory has been achieved by you, who abide in supreme excellence. The reason for this is: those sages such as Sanatkumāra and others, who possess nothing and yet serve you for the sake of liberation—it is by means of that [service] that you have conquered. Or, it may mean: "that dharma" which [they serve].

Regarding the sequence of composition: by the word "conquered" (jitam), his own excellence is revealed. The reading "Bhagavan" is favored by the Master (Svāmī), whereas "bhavata" is found almost everywhere. ||40||

Viśvanātha: If this is so—that devotion is preeminent even when it is performed with desire by virtue of its own greatness—then how much more so when it is free from desire? Furthermore, since the state of being free from desire in devotion was instigated by you, you are supremely compassionate even regarding that victory of yours previously established through disinterested devotion.

"Since you alone are the cause for bringing your own devotees under your control, in reality, victory belongs specifically to you alone"—thus he says, "Victory! O Unconquered One, as soon as you spoke of the faultless, desireless dharma of the Bhāgavatas, that very [dharma] was conquered by you alone; your devotees have been made your debtors.

Since You Yourself have declared that very yoga of desireless devotion by which You are won over by Your devotees, it possesses that quality; thus, while relishing a special grace that fulfills Your own longing for dependence upon Your devotees, Your devotees, on the contrary, remain as if they themselves have become indebted to You.

The term *bhāva* means "they become. Those who are from the very beginning destitute of possessions (*niṣkiñcana*) and pure, as well as certain sages (*munis*), ascetics (*tāpasa*), those who delight in the Self (*ātmārāma*), and those liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) who have abandoned their own fixed attachments through association with them—whatever dharma they worship; [that is what is meant].
Alternatively, these two are qualifiers of the very term "those who possess nothing" (*niṣkiñcana*). "Sages" (*munayaḥ*) means those whose nature is contemplation;

"delighting in the Self" (*ātmārāmāḥ*) means those who find delight in You alone. "For the sake of liberation" (*apavargāya*) means for that love from which even the fourfold group of goals is cast away; and there is also liberation [which results] from that, as in the passage beginning with "He who... and so forth.
Or, [the phrase] "to Bhaktiyoga," which possesses the characteristics described in the verse of the fifth chapter. ||40||
Where there is no uneven-mindedness among men regarding "I" and "you," nor "mine" and "yours," and where there is nothing else; ||| o)0(o— ||| [therein you abide].
That which is composed with a wicked mind is indeed impure, perishable, and full of unrighteousness.

Śrīdhara says: He states its very faultlessness: "Wherein," meaning in which Bhāgavata dharma, there is no "uneven-mindedness" (*viṣamamati*), as there is in other [kinds of] dharma, such as that which is performed for the sake of specific desires (*kāmya*). Now, one might object: "But even that [desire-based dharma] is indeed faultless because it was spoken by the Veda"; to this he replies: "Composed and enjoined by an uneven mind," meaning with the desire for the death of an enemy and so forth.
For that [Vedic dharma] is indeed impure because it possesses passion, hatred, and so forth; it is perishable because its fruit is transitory;
and it is full of unrighteousness because of the abundance of violence and similar acts. As it was stated by Śabarasvāmin:
"In this case, both the beneficial and the harmful are indicated by the Vedic injunction," and so on. (41)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: In this *Bhāgavata-dharma*, there is a "disparate mind" (*viṣama-mati*) regarding the locus of egoity (*ahaṃtā*) and the locus of possessiveness (*mamata*), expressed as "I" and "you," or "mine" and "yours"—this being seen in light of the meaning of the subsequent verse.

The meaning is that there is no thought characterized by the inequality rooted in hatred—such as "I am yours" or "you are my enemy"—which exists elsewhere in the context of desire-based dharma (*kāmyadharma*). He censures that very desire-based dharma: for that which is fashioned with a biased mind through the desire for the death of an enemy and so forth is indeed impure.

Because it consists of passion, hatred, and so forth; because it is perishable, as its fruit is transitory; and because it abounds in unrighteousness (*adharma*), due to the prevalence of violence and the like. As it was said by Śabarasvāmin: "In this [Vedic] injunction, two things are indicated here: the beneficial (*artha*) and the harmful (*anartha*)," and so on. (41)
What security is there for oneself and others, or what benefit is there for self and others through a dharma that harms them?
From treachery toward yourself comes your anger,
and likewise, from the oppression of others comes unrighteousness.
Śrīdhara elaborates on this: "What is security? What is well-being? Nothing at all.

By one who harms self and others (*svaparadhruk*)—that is, by one who injures both himself and others—because of that injury to oneself and because of extreme physical exhaustion, [there is no security] for you.
Anger and suffering arise. Thus it is said in the Gītā:
"Those mindless ones who emaciate the collection of elements within the body, and Me as well who dwell within the body—they know them to be of demonic resolve" (Gītā 17.5).

Likewise, there is unrighteousness (*adharma*) due to the oppression of others; and because of the word "and" (*ca*), there is also anger on your part. Therefore, although you are blinded by passion, you have somehow taught the dharma of desire (*kāmyadharma*) in order to lead people onto the path of the Vedas, and not from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvadṛṣṭi*). ||42||
The sequential composition [of the commentary] is as follows: because he is the cause of his own worldly existence, a person who harms himself cannot cross the ocean of transmigration;
this is because he is censured like a beast for harming himself, and likewise for harming others. "Kopa" refers to anger consisting of indifference. "Adharma" is impure dharma. ||42||
Viśvanātha: He clarifies the stated meaning: "What is security? What is well-being?

The meaning is that there is nothing for either oneself or another—for oneself (*nija*), the self who is the locus of the sense of "I," nor for another (*para*), such as a son or wife, who is the locus of the sense of "mine. [The one who acts thus] harms both himself and others.
By that [self-hatred], one harms both oneself and others;

for from self-betrayal comes unrighteousness (adharma), which is sin (pāpa), as well as your wrath, resulting from ascetic vows and the like that cause extreme affliction to one's own body for the sake of harming others. ||42||
Your vision does not deviate,
for by it the dharma of the Bhagavat has been proclaimed.
The noble ones, whose minds are not divided, worship you within the multitudes of both stationary and moving beings.
Śrīdhara: He says "no" to show that there is no hostility through the Bhāgavata-dharma. It does not deviate;

it does not abandon the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Your "īkṣā" is your vision. The reason for its non-deviation is "firm" (*sthira*). The Bhāgavatas possess an even-mindedness toward the multitude of beings, both stationary and moving, regarding that dharma which...
They serve. ||43||

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: Now, one might object: even though there is an abundance of defects such as perishability and so forth, people engage in the religion of desire (*kāmyadharma*) because its fruits are seen; yet, they do not engage in the religion of disinterested action (*niṣkāmadharma*), even though it is free from defects, because its fruits are not seen.

People have doubts regarding its operation; to that he says: "No. The reflection—that by your glance the individual soul (jīva) becomes one who has achieved his purpose—does not fail. While there may sometimes be a failure of the fruit even in the case of rites performed for specific desires (kāmyadharma), there is no such failure in your glance. For this very reason, those who are [devoted to you] are called "noble" (ārya), whereas others are "ignoble" (anārya).

The intended meaning is that they may indeed have doubts. "Those of non-dual intellect" refers to the Noble Ones (*āryas*), who are devoid of the notion of separateness regarding their own and others' happiness and suffering; thus it is shown that this is the meter known as *āryā*. ||43||
For indeed, O Blessed One, it is not impossible that through the sight of you, the destruction of all the evils of men occurs.
Indeed, by hearing it but once,
even a *pukkaśa* is liberated from cyclic existence.
Śrīdhara: It is not at all surprising that the destruction of all sins occurs simply from seeing you, who have become such a promoter of the Bhāgavata-dharma; thus he says: "Not indeed... (44).

*Sanātana* (Ha.bha.vi. 11.486): "He becomes liberated directly by himself"—thus is stated the fact that there is no other means. Alternatively, "directly" (*sākṣāt*) means in this very present body. And this has already been explained previously regarding the destruction of *prārabdha* karma. ||44||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: He says "not indeed" (*na hi*) to show that he himself has directly obtained the fruit of the dharma of desirelessness; "of men" (*nṛṇām*) implies "of me alone. What need is there to mention the destruction of sins? Even liberation [is attained].
He says: "It happens"—to one person alone, how much more so to many? At once, how much more so repeatedly?
Merely by hearing it, how much more so by chanting and other such acts? Even for a *pukkaśa* (outcaste), how much more so for others?
From mere worldly existence, how much more so from sin? Thus, even at the very commencement of the practice, the fruit is already seen.
Now, O Blessed One,
our mental impurities have been cleansed by your compassionate gaze.
How could that which was spoken by the celestial sage on your behalf be otherwise?
Śrīdhara: Therefore, he says "atha" (now), meaning "I have achieved my purpose.

For this reason, those whose impurities within their hearts (*āśaya*) have been wiped away—that is, dispelled—by the sight of you. And he states that his vision of you occurred through the instruction of the divine sage Nārada by saying "sura-ṛṣiṇā" (by the divine sage). ||45||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* has not been commented upon.
Viśvanātha says: "Therefore, I have achieved my purpose"—thus he says, "Now" (*atha*). ||45||
O Infinite One, you who are the self of the universe, all the conduct performed here by people is known to you.
What indeed could be reported to the Supreme Guru, like fireflies before the sun?
Śrīdhara says: "Just as I was previously extremely deluded, and just as I have been favored by Nārada—all this, O Inner Controller, what need is there for me to proclaim?
Thus he says: 'It is known' (viditam). That which is to be specifically made known—that is, proclaimed—is how much? Indeed, nothing at all."
The meaning is: just as there is nothing for the sun to illuminate by means of its own rays, so it is in that case. ||46||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* has not been explained.

Viśvanātha says: "Even though I am blinded by worldly objects (*viṣaya*), I have sent my devotee forth, lifted him from the well of *saṃsāra*, and brought him into the presence of my own feet"—to what more shall I report? He says: "It is known," regarding the Sun (*savituḥ*).
Like a boat on its own, what need is there for us, who are like fireflies, to illuminate you? 46.
Homage to you, the Blessed One, the Lord of the maintenance, dissolution, and arising of the entire world.
To the Supreme Swan (Paramahaṃsa), who is difficult for false yogins to comprehend due to their failure to realize the nature of the Self, [I offer salutations].

Śrīdhara: He pays homage to the Blessed One, whose characteristics have been described, with two verses beginning with "namaḥ. [He bows] to the Lord who is capable (īśāya) of the maintenance and other states of the entire world; to Him whose own course (ātmagatiḥ)—that is, His essential nature—is difficult to ascertain (duravasitā), being unknown; of whom? Of those of bad yoga (kuyoginām); by what means? By duality (bhidā).
By means of the vision of difference. ||47||

The structural arrangement [of the verse] begins with "namaḥ" (salutation). The term *bhidā* refers to that which is difficult for those of false yoga (*kuyogin*) to comprehend due to their perception of various distinctions among objects of worship. Alternatively, *bhidā* refers to devotion consisting of duality. This connects with the subsequent phrase "to the Supreme Swan" (*paramahaṃsāya*).
By means of that [devotion], he is one who sports within the heart-lotus in his pure form; such is the meaning. ||47||
Viśvanātha: The meaning is: "to the one who effects the liberation of those false yogins by means of *bhidā*—that is, through the perception of duality—from their state as *paramahaṃsas*. ||47||
Truly, after him as he breathes forth, all the world-creators breathe forth; after him as he perceives, their thoughts rise up.
Salutations be to that Blessed One of a thousand heads, upon whose crown the circle of the earth appears like a mustard seed.
Śrīdhara: They breathe and they exert themselves. Following after Cekitāna—the one who sees—the mental faculties, the organs of knowledge, look up and behold him as he is mounted [upon them]. ||48||
The sequential composition [of the verse] is as follows: they "behold" (uccakanti) its own nature;

the meaning is that by means of a mere portion of its power of knowledge (jñānaśakti), they obtain their respective cognitions. This is a form of the root *kan*, meaning "to shine," "to be beautiful," or "to move," in its yaṅluk (intensive without suffix) conjugation. ||48||

Viśvanātha: The organs of action of the Creator of the universe breathe and exert themselves while He breathes and exerts Himself; and the cognitive faculties (cittayaḥ), the organs of knowledge, look upon Him as the one who perceives and behold their respective objects. ||48||
Śrī Śuka said: Thus praised, the Blessed Lord Ananta spoke to him.
O best of the Kurus, being pleased, he [honored] Citraketu, the lord of the Vidyādharas.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
The Blessed One said:
O King, you have been perfected by that instruction which was imparted to Nārada and Aṅgiras by me, as well as by the sight of me.
Śrīdhara: My instruction is the teaching concerning my own domain; by that [instruction] and by that knowledge, you have attained perfection through this vision. ||50||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: By that [means], namely by my instruction—consisting of worship through hearing, chanting, and so forth—and by that *vidyā*, which is the great mantra taught by Nārada, as well as by the vision of me, which is accomplished thereby. ||50||
I am indeed all beings, the self of all beings, and the creator of all beings;
both the Brahman of sound and the Supreme Brahman are my two eternal bodies.

Madhva, however, [says]: "Hari, as the inner controller (antaryāmin) of all beings, should especially be understood through the primary function (mukhyā vṛtti) in all finite verbs (tiṅpada) as well as in all nominal stems (suppada). And so it is said. ||51||
Śrīdhara: To strengthen that realization, he himself teaches as follows, beginning with "I am...":
"I alone am all beings; I alone am the Self and the enjoyer of beings.
The meaning is that the entire universe, consisting of the enjoyer and the enjoyed, does not exist apart from Me. Since I am...
The creator of beings is the illuminator and the cause of all beings.
Now, one might ask: is not the Śabdabrahman the illuminator and the Supreme Brahman both the cause and the illuminator?
True; he says "the Śabdabrahman" to show that both of these are indeed my own forms. They are eternal, meaning they are two eternals.

The sequential composition is as follows: "I am. Here, by virtue of its association with the Śabdabrahman (the Brahman of Sound), the status of being a partial manifestation of the Parabrahman (the Supreme Brahman) also accrues to it. ||51||

Viśvanātha: Furthermore, you have already understood the essence of devotion (*bhakti-tattva*); in that regard, the hymn beginning with "O Unconquered One, You are conquered" (*ajita jitaḥ*, Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.16.35) is itself the authority. For the sake of showing that no further inquiry is required, He says "I indeed" (*ahaṃ vai*) to indicate that I myself shall teach the essence of knowledge (*jñāna-tattva*); listen! Herein is this...
This must be investigated. An entity (*vastu*) is first of all twofold: real (*vāstavam*) and unreal (*avāstavam*).
Only this triad—the Brahman, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), the Blessed Lord (*bhagavān*) together with His retinue—is the real entity;
this entire collection of the illusory phenomenal world (*māyika-prapañca*) is the unreal entity. And the unreal is also twofold: the effect (*kāryam*)...

And there is the non-actual (*akārya*). The actual consists of things found in dreams, magical illusions (*indrajāla*), and the like; the non-actual consists of things such as a sky-flower or a hare’s horn. Among these, because it was stated at the outset that "the object to be known is the real entity here" (*Bhāgavatapurāṇa* 1.1.2), in order to state that only the real entity is to be accepted, the non-real is first [discussed].

The text states: "I alone am all beings—the worlds consisting of both enjoyers and the enjoyed"—the sense being that this is because they are composed of my own power of the individual soul (*jīva-śakti*) and the power of *māyā*. Here, the unreal nature of individual souls is stated precisely because they are veiled by ignorance (*avidyā*).
He states the actual reality: "The second is the Self (ātman), the inner ruler (antaryāmī) of all beings, both in their collective and individual aspects;

and I am the third, the Puruṣa. Likewise, the first Puruṣa is 'I,' who brings those beings into being—that is, produces them. Likewise, [the fourth] is he who makes the beings possess states such as servitude and friendship."
I am the creator of beings; Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and I myself are now to be seen by you.

Furthermore, both that Śabdabrahman—the Veda which is the nature of my breath—and that Supreme Brahman which is realized by the wise as my own non-differentiated form, are both merely forms of my own body.

In order to dispel the suspicion that the Veda might be non-eternal because it consists of sound and is thus a quality of space, and likewise to dispel the suspicion that the Supreme Brahman might be a non-entity because it is indefinable, he says: "eternal" (śāśvatī), meaning they are both eternally real. ||51||
"I have spread myself throughout the world, and the world is woven within me;
both are pervaded by me, and both are established in me."
The world of honey [is] continuous within the self in the form of latent impressions (vāsanā). ||52||

Śrīdhara: Therefore, he says, "Behold that very [Self] in this way": behold the Self as spread out—that is, pervading—the world, which is the manifold of objects of enjoyment, by way of being its enjoyer; and behold the world as continuous—that is, permeated—within the Self by way of being its object of enjoyment.
Both of these are pervaded by Me, who am their causal Self; and both are made—that is, fashioned—within Me alone.
The word "smaret" (one should remember) connects with the third [verse], or the word "paśyet" (one should see) is to be supplied as an ellipsis. ||52||

The sequence of the composition is as follows: he causes [the disciple] to experience it in that very way—[as stated in the verse beginning with] "In the world" (*loke*). Behold the Self, which is the Supreme Brahman, existing as the pervasive substratum; behold that which is eternally supported within that Self by Me, who am the Blessed One in the form of the Supreme Brahman.

Because it is of the nature of the manifestation of that which is non-different from me; therefore, the meaning is that both [the offering and the acceptance] performed toward me are described as being caused solely by my knowledge. ||52||

Viśvanātha: Now, if you alone are everything, then are all beings themselves to be meditated upon as the object of worship by devotees, or rather [are they to be meditated upon] in the form of the Inner Controller (antaryāmin) and so forth? To this he says: [one should meditate upon] the Self—the individual soul (jīva)—which is spread out and pervading the world as the enjoyer within the world that is the object of enjoyment; and likewise, the world itself.

Both of these—which exist as a continuous and extensive state of being objects of enjoyment within the Self—are pervaded by Me, who am their causal Self. Furthermore, one should remember that both are produced as effects within Me, who am the underlying substratum-cause; this is the connection with the third [quarter of the verse]. Therefore, all beings are impermanent, being the products of My power.
The sense is that those things which do not constitute its true nature are not to be meditated upon as objects of worship. ||52||
Just as a person in deep sleep perceives the universe within himself,
yet upon waking from the dream, considers himself to be located in only one place.
Having thus understood that states of the self such as waking and so forth are merely products of Māyā, one should remember the Supreme, the witness of them.
The sweet [phenomena] are mere illusions, fashioned by primordial nature. ||54||

Śrīdhara: Now, one might object: "Since the universe, consisting of the enjoyer and the enjoyed, is clearly perceived through the distinctions of states such as waking and so forth, how can it be considered imagined? Anticipating this doubt, he says "Just as... in two verses, establishing the point by means of the example of the waking state and others occurring within a dream.

Just as one who is asleep in a dream perceives within himself alone the entire universe in the form of mountains, forests, and so forth, situated in another place— the meaning being that in the midst of a dream he perceives both deep sleep and the dream itself— so too,
having awakened within that very dream, he considers himself to be in one location while his body remains lying in the place of sleep.

One experiences the waking state. ||53|| Thus, having understood that even these well-known states of the living being (jīva)—waking and so forth—are actually states of the intellect (buddhi), which is the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the living being, and are therefore merely the illusory power (māyā) of the Self (ātman); one [should know] the Self as the witness of those states, and for that very reason, as the Supreme, devoid of those states.
One should remember. ||54||
The Structural Arrangement (*Kramasaṃdarbha*): Now, one might ask: "As long as one is not detached from the universe, how can that [detachment] occur?

Anticipating this doubt, he teaches the knowledge of that [reality] preceded by the knowledge of the true nature of the pure individual soul (*śuddhajīva*) through the following pair of verses beginning with "yathā" (just as). This is the meaning: just as one who is in deep sleep even in the midst of a dream...
Furthermore, a certain person, while dreaming, perceives the entire universe—including mountains, forests, and so forth—within himself due to a particular delusion;

he superimposes it upon his own self. Then, having awakened from that very dream as if having regained consciousness, he perceives himself as situated in one place, seeing a portion of the bed where he was lying.

One perceives that [world] of mountains, forests, and so forth as indeed distinct; having understood those states such as waking and the rest to be merely my *māyā*—for me, the Supreme Self—and having recognized them as the abodes of the individual soul (*jīva*), one should remember only me, the Supreme, as the witness even of the pure *jīva* who has attained realization. ||53||

Viśvanātha: On the contrary, having abandoned those unreal objects as if they were truly non-existent, one should worship my very form as the Inner Controller (antaryāmin) and so forth; thus he says with two verses beginning with "yathā. Just as a person who has fallen into deep sleep (suṣupta)—meaning one who is thoroughly asleep—while in the midst of a dream, sees that dream...
Due to a particular delusion, one perceives the entire universe— including mountains, forests, and so forth— within oneself, superimposing it upon one's own self.

Then, having awakened from that very dream and attained the state of waking, one considers oneself to be situated in a single location, namely, in that specific spot where one was lying down, as if in the waking state.
The meaning is that while experiencing it, one considers that mountain, forest, and so forth to be distinct [from oneself].

Thus, just as the waking state experienced in a dream is not a real entity, so too should the waking state known to be a real entity be understood as such, because it is perishable; this is what he says with the word "evam" (thus). [Now follow] the abodes of the individual soul (*jīva*).

Having understood that the states belong only to the intellect (*buddhi*), which is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the individual soul (*jīva*), and that these are mere illusion (*māyāmātra*) because they are the effects of the power of illusion (*māyā-śakti*) belonging to the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), one perceives their Witness— the Supreme, the Most Excellent, the Inner Controller— and thus the individual self (*jīvātman*) is excluded.

In this context, the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep within the dream-state are created by the individual soul (jīva) through ignorance (avidyā), and thus they are known to consist of ignorance alone and are indeed unreal. However, the well-known states of waking and so forth are created by the Lord through His power of illusion (māyā-śakti), and thus they consist of illusion alone and are likewise indeed unreal; nevertheless...

It must be discerned that the dream-objects—such as mountains, forests, snakes, tigers, elephants, horses, and so forth—are indeed non-existent, being created by the individual soul (jīva) through ignorance (avidyā). ||53||
Know Me to be that Self by which the sleeping person experiences sleep,
as well as the attributeless bliss of Brahman— that Self, know Me to be that.

Śrīdhara: Now, how can it be said that he is "the seer of those [states]," since during deep sleep there is an absence of objects to be seen and thus an absence of the state of being a seer? To this, he says: "by whom. By which form the sleeping person—the individual soul (jīva)—then, at the time of sleep, knows the sleep of the self, which is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) and a bliss beyond the senses; that Self...
Know me to be Brahman; for otherwise, since there would be no awareness of either the self or the pleasure during sleep, the recollection "I slept happily" would be impossible. ||55||

The sequential composition clarifies that very point with the words "by which": one knows sleep and the quality-less bliss therein by means of that specific principle (tattva-viśeṣa), which is a portion of the Great Consciousness-power residing in the individual soul (jīva) and so forth within the abode of the illusory ego (māyika-ahaṅkāra). Know that to be Brahman; know Me as the Self, the Supreme Self.
And understand the form of the Blessed One, based on such passages as: "Those who know reality say that [it is He]" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.2.11).
Viśvanātha says: "But how can I know that Seer, the Inner Controller?
To this he replies with the words "by whom": when the sleeping person—the individual soul (*jīva*)—is aware of sleep, that very state is deep sleep (*suṣupti*).

Know that very Self, the Inner Controller, by which cause one knows one's own bliss— which is devoid of qualities and free from distinctions— and by whom, out of compassion, the individual soul (*jīva*)— though its knowledge and bliss are obscured and firmly bound by the *guṇas*— has the *guṇas* eternally dissolved during deep sleep.

His quality-less bliss makes itself known to him; let it be clearly understood that He alone is the Inner Ruler (antaryāmī). For without Him, the dependent individual soul (jīva) could not, by its own power, release itself from its bondage and perceive its own bliss—this is the sense. [One should seek] that very Inner Ruler.

Know that Brahman is perceived as being without distinctions. Know me, the Blessed One, to be Brahman itself with distinctions. I alone—Brahman, the Supreme Self, and the Blessed One—exist in these three forms; yet there is no duality or triplicity in my essential nature. As it has been said:
By the gods—because of the absence of two distinct forms [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.9.36]. ||55||
That which persists for a person who remembers both [the states] of deep sleep and waking,
and from which [the former] is distinguished— that is knowledge; that is the supreme Brahman.
By means of the awakening from the honeyed [state], he himself, having awakened, would remain distinct while the two who were asleep were not awake. ||56||
Śrīdhara: [Objection: But how can one in the waking state remember what was seen by the witness of sleep?

For one person does not remember what was seen by another. To this he says: "Of both"—namely sleep (*prasvāpa*) and waking (*pratibodha*)—"he remembers," meaning he connects them; that which, by virtue of being the illuminator of those two, [sleep and waking]...

It follows through them and yet is distinct from them, because it does not perish even when either one of them perishes. The meaning is that this knowledge is the Supreme Brahman itself, and not something different from it. Therefore, the point is that just as there is memory of what was seen in childhood during youth, so too is the recollection of the bliss of deep sleep possible despite the difference in states.
Know that very Self, which is such as this, to be Brahman; this is the syntactical connection. ||56||

The sequential arrangement: For this very reason, he states that even the knowledge of the individual soul (jīva) has its ultimate purport (tātparya) in Brahman—namely, "both. That knowledge consists of the pure nature of the individual soul, and that [knowledge] is directed toward Brahman as its supreme goal. ||56||

Viśvanātha: [Objection: But how could one in the waking state remember what was seen by the witness of deep sleep, thinking, "I slept happily"? For one person does not remember what was seen by another.
To this, he says: [It belongs] to the person who remembers—that is, who synthesizes—both deep sleep and the subsequent awakening.

That which persists through both sleep and waking, being distinct from those two states because it does not perish even when either one of them ceases—that is knowledge; the meaning is that it is the *jīva*. Therefore, just as there is recollection in youth of what was seen in childhood, the recollection of the bliss of sleep is possible even though the states are different.
This is the state of being. That which is "beyond" (para) means the Supreme Brahman beyond that individual soul (jīva), and not that the soul itself is Brahman;
for although the soul possesses that form by virtue of being its external power (taṭastha-śakti), it lacks the status of being its essential power (svarūpa-śakti).
Therefore, the meaning is that Brahman is indeed distinct [from the soul]. ||56||
Because this nature of Mine, which is distinct from the self, has been forgotten by man,
there arises for him the cycle of existence: body after body, death after death.
"Madhva said: 'Forgetting the Supreme Self who is non-different from all, one wanders in this world;
remembering Him as non-different, one goes to the darkness—of this there is no doubt. (57)

Śrīdhara states the fault in the opposite case: if this Brahman, which is my own nature (madbhāva) and my true form (matsvarūpa), is forgotten, then it becomes separate from the self; consequently, saṃsāra occurs for this person. He describes the nature of saṃsāra: from body to body, following birth after birth.
Birth is followed immediately by death, and then there is death again. ||57||

The sequential arrangement: He states the fault in not knowing that [Brahman]: because Brahman has been forgotten, being obscured by beginningless ignorance; therefore, for this very reason, the transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) of this individual soul (*jīva*) arises.
And he shows that [Brahman], through a particular intention, as distinct from the individual soul and as distinct from himself—of the Self...

"Where there is difference, there my state of being—my existence—is," thus fear arises from attachment to a second [entity] (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.2.37). Therefore, it is entirely logical that saṃsāra exists in ignorance. ||57||

Viśvanātha: Therefore, he states that the very contemplation of the identity of nature between Brahman and the individual soul (*jīva*) is an offense and the cause of misfortune—with the words "That which this... Since [the Lord] is distinct from the self, that is, from the *jīva*, his own state (*madbhāva*), meaning his own essential nature (*svarūpa*), is indeed different; the neuter form [*madbhāvam*] is an archaic Vedic usage (*ārṣa*). If that [distinction] has been forgotten...
It would indeed be non-different; therefore, for this person who perceives it as non-different, there would be *saṃsāra*.

He explains *saṃsāra* itself by saying "from the body," and so forth. For this very reason, in such statements as "Thou art That" (*tattvam asi*), the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) with that [Brahman] occurs precisely through its being a power (*śakti*) residing within it, just as there is oneness between the sun and its rays.

The meaning is that it is "to be cultivated" (*bhāvanīya*). Thus, because the universe—which is not a real entity—is non-different from [the Self] by virtue of being the effect of its power, it possesses that same nature (*tādrūpya*). However, due to the absence of identity with that essential nature (*tātsvarūpya*), that which is different is indeed the cause of perishability; for the pure soul (*śuddhajīva*), however, is imperishable.

Even though they are included within the category of real entities (*vāstavavastu*), because their powers are extrinsic (*taṭastha-śakti*), they possess only that [extrinsic] nature and not that essential nature; however, Brahman, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), and the Lord (*bhagavat*) possess both the state of being real entities and oneness through the identity of their essential nature (*svarūpa-ekya*). This also applies to the eternal beloveds, the attendants (*pārṣada*), and the abodes of the Lord.

Because they are the playful manifestation (*vilāsa*) of the power of consciousness (*cic-chakti*), some possess the nature of a real entity (*vāstavavastutva*) and identity with that [consciousness] due to being eternally perfected (*nityasiddha*).
