As for other souls (*jīvas*) who possess latent impressions (*vāsanā*) such as servitude (*dāsya*)— whether they are perfected beings (*siddhas*) by virtue of being eternally liberated devotees (*nityamuktabhakta*) or by having attained the liberation of devotion (*bhaktikaivalya*)— [their status is likewise established].

Their identity with that [divine] nature arises precisely because they are not permeated by their own essential power (*svarūpa-śakti*), owing to the absence of inclusion within the group of servants (*dāsa*) and so forth; for those perfected living beings who have attained preeminence in devotion,
being devotees of the scripture, they lack inclusion within the group of servants and thus are not permeated by their own essential power.

Since "being of that nature" means being a real entity, non-duality is established as a result of the Blessed One possessing manifold powers; thus, by way of this incidental discussion, the Vaiṣṇava doctrine has been presented. ||57||
Having obtained here this human birth, which is the source of knowledge and discernment,
he who does not realize the Self shall never attain security.

Śrīdhara: Even though the attainment of enjoyments and so forth is possible in other wombs, one must strive for knowledge only here; thus he says, "Having obtained," etc. Knowledge is that which is declared in the scriptures, while realized knowledge (*vijñāna*) is direct perception; [he refers to] that [state] in which both of these are possible. 58.

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: He says "having obtained" (*labdhvā*) because one must certainly strive for the sake of knowing the characteristics already described—the occurrence (*sambhava*) of knowledge (*jñāna*) arising from the scriptures and realized knowledge (*vijñāna*), which is immediate perception.
In that [state], one perceives oneself—the individual soul—as well as the Supreme Lord. ||58||
Reflecting upon the suffering in this world, as well as the resulting reversal of fruits from desire,
and the fearlessness found in the absence of desire, the wise man should desist from all volitional intent.
Śrīdhara says: For the sake of detachment (*vairāgya*), he says: "In *īhā*, [that is] on the path of active engagement (*pravṛtti-mārga*); from that *īhā*.

But in *anīhā*, on the path of cessation (*nivṛtti-mārga*), fearlessness—that is, liberation (*mokṣa*)—occurs. Remembering this, one should desist from the mental resolve for results. According to another reading, "neither" refers to both suffering and the failure of the result.
And having thus recollected that "it does not exist," ||59||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* does not provide an explanation.

Viśvanātha says: "One who desires this knowledge—that is, one who has understood that the fruits of actions, whether seen or unseen, are [transient]—should abandon devotion to ritual action (*karmaniṣṭhā*). He states: "If there is desire in one's effort (*īhā*), then from that effort; if there is no desire..."

In the state of desirelessness, there is fearlessness, which is the total absence of fear from all sides. Regarding the reading "not both," it is traditionally held that neither afflictions nor misconceptions would exist. ||59||
Husband and wife perform their duties for the sake of pleasure and liberation from suffering;
yet from that, there follows neither the cessation of suffering nor the attainment of happiness.
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha explain this with the three verses beginning with "for happiness":
the non-cessation of suffering and the non-attainment of happiness. (60)
The sequential arrangement has not been explained. —
Having thus understood the inversion of those men who pride themselves on their discernment, [the wise should act accordingly].
And [he perceives] his own subtle state, which is distinct from the three abodes.
Śrīdhara: [This refers to] those who possess the conceit that "we are wise and proficient in exertion," having realized the fourth state (turīya), which is distinct from the three states. 61.

The sequential arrangement: he concludes in accordance with what preceded by means of the couplet beginning with "evam" (thus), citing such passages as "And the sages who delight in the Self" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.7.10). ||61||
Viśvanātha: [He perceives] the fourth state, which is distinct from the three states. ||61||
Freed from the impressions of what is seen and heard by his own splendor,
and fully satisfied with knowledge and realization, such a person shall become my devotee.
Śrīdhara: By means of the objects of the senses perceived and heard, both pertaining to this world and the next, and by his own splendor, which is the power of discernment. ||62||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: By means of the measures (mātrā), that is, the objects; by one's own splendor, that is, the power of one's own means. —o)0(o)—
To this extent alone should the true purpose of human beings—those whose intellects are skilled in yoga—be understood with their whole being: that it is the vision of the single Self within all.

Śrīdhara: He says "this much" (etāvān) because there is no higher human goal than this. It refers to those whose intellects possess proficiency in yoga—that which consists of the singular vision of the Supreme Self; this alone is the extent [of the goal]. (63)

The *Kramasaṃdarbha*: He praises that very thing with the words "this much" (*etāvān*). It is the singular, exclusive vision—that is, the direct experience—of the Supreme Self, the Blessed Lord Himself. [Prītisaṃdarbha, 2] Viśvanātha: The singular vision of the Supreme Self alone—the highest Self—and not [any other].
But [it is] of the object. ||63||
O King, you who are endowed with knowledge and realization, by holding fast to these words of mine with faith and vigilance, you will quickly attain perfection.
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha have not commented [on this].

The *Kramasaṃdarbha* states: "You are perfected" (*saṃsiddho 'si*). Both that which was said previously and what is now said, "you are being perfected" (*siddhyasi*), should be understood as referring to the immediate proximity of the present; in that regard also—
"Being heedful and retaining my words"— thus has the cause of future obstacles also been indicated.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having thus consoled Citraketu, the Blessed One, the Teacher of the World and Soul of the Universe, Hari,
vanished from his sight.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose minds are devoted.
The sixteenth chapter of the sixth [book] is concluded, which is well-connected with the virtuous.
Thus ends the Sixth Canto in the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā, the Pāramahaṃsya, within the *Brahmasūtrabhāṣya* of the glorious *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam*, the Great Purāṇa.
The sixteenth chapter in the narrative of Citraketu.
Now begins the seventeenth chapter.
In the narrative of Citraketu,
Śrī Śuka said: "Then Ananta, having vanished from that direction, offered his salutations to it."
The Vidyādhara Citraketu, who moves through the sky, traveled through the heavens.
Śrīdhara:
Then, in the seventeenth [chapter], having attained the great and unfailing prosperity and moving through the sky,
he laughed at Giriśa and, due to Umā’s curse, became Vṛtra.
Having paid homage—that is, having performed an act of bowing—to whichever direction it may be, [one should recite: "Salutation to that direction. ||1||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Citraketu, becoming the lord of the Vidyādharas in the seventeenth [chapter]...
Having laughed at Śaṅkara, he attained the state of Vṛtra due to the goddess's curse.
From whichever direction, in whichever quarter. ||1||
For a hundred thousand years, that great yogi, his faculties and strength unimpeded,
remained there while being praised by sages, siddhas, and cāraṇas.
Śrīdhara: The connection between the two verses is that Citraketu, causing Hari to be sung by the Vidyādhara women, took his delight;
he was one whose strength and sensory acuity were unimpeded. (2)
The composition of the sequence: that constitutes one hundred thousand [verses], thus a pair [of verses]. ||2||
Viśvanātha: Not explained.
—o)0(o— In the valleys of the great Kula mountains, where various intentions are fulfilled...
He sports with the women of the Vidyādharas, causing them to sing of Hari, the Lord.
Śrīdhara: [The phrase refers to] those [attainments] in which various kinds of supernatural powers (*siddhi*) are achieved through mere volition (*saṅkalpa*). ||3||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Even amidst the accomplishments of various mental resolves, he took delight only by making [others] sing of Hari, having abandoned all other resolves;
the meaning is that he remained solely devoted to the glorification of Hari’s qualities and the lotus of his feet.
Once, while traveling in a radiant celestial chariot given by Viṣṇu,
he beheld Giriśa surrounded by Siddhas and Cāraṇas.
Śrīdhara:
Due to pride in his wonderful sovereignty arising from past karma, you have unexpectedly entered an asuric womb; that indeed was because of the Lord’s decree.
Thus he says, beginning with "at one time," and so forth. ||4||
The sequence of composition: therein, he states that even in that case, another great offense against the ancients results in evil fruit—“once upon a time” (ekadā). ||4||
Viśvanātha:
Having granted devotion and prosperity, Hari, in order to experience his own separation,
brought him— who had been turned into Vṛtra by the Goddess’s curse— into his presence.
[She who was] not accepted [as his own], yet made half of his own body. ||4||
Having embraced the Goddess and taken her onto his lap with his arm in the assembly of sages,
he spoke while she listened, laughing loudly in her presence.
Śrīdhara, having accepted her by holding her close to his chest and embracing the goddess with his arm as he stood there, spoke and laughed while remaining near her. (5)
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
Citraketu said:
This teacher of the world, the direct speaker of Dharma for all embodied beings,
sits as the foremost member in the assembly, united with his wife.
Śrīdhara says: He speaks as one who proclaims the Dharma; and among embodied beings, he remains preeminent, having become a couple with his wife. (6)
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
Jaṭādhara, of intense austerity, was the presiding lord of the assembly of those who discourse on Brahman.
Embracing a woman, he remains there devoid of shame, like a common man.
Śrīdhara: [The commentary on] *Kramasaṃdarbha* has not been explained.

Viśvanātha: Regarding the phrase "just as a common person," the intention is that he should not be understood as an offender or a reviler of Śiva like Dakṣa, because he is not a common person in the sense of being an ordinary man, but rather because he is directly the Lord himself. ||7||
Generally, even commoners keep a woman in secret;
but this upholder of the great vow keeps a woman in public assembly.
Śrīdhara: [This is] the *Kramasaṃdarbha*; it has not been commented upon.

Viśvanātha: The meaning is that the Lord of Yogins, who maintains the great vow (*mahāvrata*)—that is, a lifelong celibate (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārī*)—bears what is dear; thus, his sovereignty is inconceivable. ||8||
Śrī Śuka said: O King, the Blessed One, whose intellect is unfathomable, having heard that, smiled and spoke.
He became silent in the assembly, and the members of the court likewise followed his lead.
Śrīdhara: He whose intellect (dhī) is unfathomable and profound. ||9||

The sequence of the composition: He whose intellect (*dhī*) is fixed upon the Blessed One, whose majesty is unfathomable and impossible to penetrate; therefore, because he did not direct his attention toward the body and so forth, he became silent. Regarding the phrase "those following him": the meaning is that, in accordance with his intention, they as well as his followers likewise became silent.
Viśvanātha says: "Laughing," etc.; the sense is that [the Lord] wishes to establish even me in right conduct.
He is one whose intellect is unfathomable and difficult for all to penetrate, because he immediately understood Citraketu's intention.
And this was Citraketu's intention: "This one is indeed the Lord himself; he is not [an ordinary being]."

Even if there is harm in [his] misconduct, there will be total destruction due to the fault of whoever, being ignorant, shall revile him—just as happened to Dakṣa. Therefore, if from this day forward I am able to establish him in right conduct, then it would be for the welfare of the worlds. And so it was.

"Viṣṇu is the Supreme Lord and truly auspicious because of his excellent conduct; Rudra, however, is inauspicious because of his wicked behavior"—lest such [a thought] arise in one who is not firmly established [in devotion], the Blessed Śambhu [declares]: "I do not become angry even with that well-wisher who speaks harshly to me, provided he is a devotee of Hari."

The members of the assembly, following his intention, remained silent and did not become angry; for it should be understood that had Śrī Śiva’s censure been intended by him, those members would have immediately covered their ears and departed from there. As it is said: "Having heard the censure of the Blessed One..."
"Or for another person devoted to that," and so forth. //9//
When he, ignorant of its true power, spoke such highly improper words,
the Goddess, filled with wrath, addressed the impudent one who was arrogant because he had conquered his own self.
Śrīdhara: "One who knows his [the opponent's] valor and power"—meaning one who knows that [the opponent] does not possess such valor—[speaks] toward him.

To one who has conquered the pride of the self (*nirjitātmābhimānin*), meaning one who possesses the conceit "I have conquered my senses," he speaks out of *ruṣ* (resentment), that is, out of anger. This is the sequence of the composition. But the Goddess was unable to endure this, and so she said: "one who does not know his [the opponent's] valor" (*atadvīrya*).

The meaning is that she was ignorant even of that state of being a great devotee (mahābhāgavata) which is initiated by such worldly conduct and consists merely of vigor. Thus it has been said: "of unfathomable intellect. (10)

Viśvanātha: "He does not know his [the Lord's] prowess or power"—the sense is that in Him, the independent Lord, there is nothing whatsoever to be done through the instruction of anyone. Regarding the phrase "speaking what is improper": since it is inappropriate to instruct the Lord of the Universe in ethics, the term refers to one who is audacious, meaning one who speaks without hesitation.

"To one who is excessively bold"—meaning to one who possesses the conceit that "I have completely conquered even my own self, the Supreme Self, Saṅkarṣaṇa, who is otherwise under the sway of love. As for the word "ruṣā" (with anger), it should not be explained as a conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) arising solely from ignorance of the intention of Mahādeva and the assembly; rather, it means "one who speaks much."

The reason for his anger should be understood as follows: although this [advice] is beneficial, he does not say it once or twice, nor even three or four times, but rather says it many times, which we do not wish to accept from him. ||10||
Śrī Pārvatī said:
Who is this lord who now, in this world, is the ruler and the wielder of the rod of punishment?
This is an offense committed against those like us—wicked, shameless, and ill-behaved.
Śrīdhara: One who acts in a contrary manner excessively is called *viprakṛt*. ||11||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: "One who brings about excellence (*prakarṣa*) in a special way (*viśeṣeṇa*)" is *viprakṛt*; the meaning is "one who acts for the benefit [of others] through the teaching. ||11||
Indeed, even the lotus-born Brahmā did not know Dharma, nor did the sons of Brahmā, such as Bhṛgu, Nārada, and others.
Truly, neither the youth Kapila nor Manu forbid us who transgress against Hara.
Śrīdhara: *Ativartinam* means one whose habit is to act by transgressing the scriptures. *Ye no niṣedhanti* means those who do not forbid or restrain [such a person]. ||12||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— Of these [authors], the pair of lotus-feet of the one to be meditated upon—
This arrogant man, a mere kṣatriya by birth, who treats with contempt the world-teacher himself— the very embodiment of auspiciousness— and who commands the learned scholars, must indeed be punished.
Śrīdhara: [He is] one whose pair of lotus feet are to be meditated upon by these [deities] beginning with Brahmā;

who is the most auspicious of the auspicious and the embodiment of the supreme Dharma; and who, having surpassed the learned and the ignorant alike, governs as the Teacher of the World—for that reason. (13)

Regarding the sequence of composition: in the commentary on the word "eṣām" (of these), if the reading is "avajñāṃ kṛtvā" (having treated with contempt), the word "teṣām" (of them) is to be supplied as the remainder. "Ajñān kṛtvā" means "regarding them as ignorant. ||13||

Viśvanātha: Having repeatedly insulted and disparaged the learned scholars with harsh words, and having recognized and disregarded even those present in this assembly as ignorant, he commands the Teacher of the World. ||13||
"O Vaikuṇṭha, this man, arrogant and with his mind inflated by false prestige, does not deserve to approach the soles of Your feet, which are worshipped by the virtuous."
Śrīdhara: If it is argued that this devotee of Hari deserves punishment, he replies to that: He does not deserve to approach the feet of Vaikuṇṭha, which are served by the virtuous;
for he is one by whom the notion has been formed that "I am superior," and for that very reason he is arrogant and unbending. (14)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: He whose mind possesses the conceit (*abhimāna*) that "I am a great devotee" who is highly esteemed—(o)0(o)—.
Therefore, O evil-minded one, go to the most wretched Asura womb,
so that hereafter you shall no longer commit an offense against the great ones, my son.
Śrīdhara: Having thus determined that he himself was deserving of punishment, he said to him: "Therefore," etc.
The meaning is: "O son, go in such a way that you will not commit, nor will you ever again commit, a great offense or transgression against the great. (15)
The sequence of the composition: Then, perceiving him to be afraid, he spoke with compassion—"Just as...
The meaning is that by means of this seed of an offense, another great offense like the former shall not be produced again. ||15||

Viśvanātha: This is indeed another curse. Then, filled with remorse, she says, "Alas! Why has this innocent devotee of Hari been cursed? addressing him as "O son. Just as a mother, though she strikes her own son with her own hand for his misconduct, naturally feels affection for him once again, so do I toward you.
The sense is that he is not to be punished. For this very reason, she speaks in a manner befitting a mother—beginning with "bhūyaḥ" (again).

Just as a mother, having struck a child who has caused offense in another's house through the restlessness of childhood play, says, "O untamed one! You shall not do this again," so too is her meaning here. Therefore...
That curse from Bhavānī did not affect Citraketu; on the contrary, his love for Vṛtra only increased.
This was because, when love is perfected, devotees do not perceive any distinction between having the body of a personal attendant (pārṣada) or the body of a demon. ||15||
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus cursed, Citraketu descended from his celestial chariot.
O descendant of Bharata, he propitiated Satī by bowing his head.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
Citraketu said:
O Mother, I accept your curse with my joined palms;
for that which has been spoken by the gods to a mortal was indeed preordained for him.
Śrīdhara: "Predestined" means precisely that which is obtained through past karma. ||17||
The sequence of the composition: "For it was previously indicated" (pūrvadiṣṭam) means that this understanding of mine arose precisely because of what was previously indicated.

Now, [an objection]: if [bondage, liberation, etc. were caused solely by qualities (guṇas), then for living beings there would be no bondage, liberation, and so forth, without a conscious agent? To this he says: "One" (ekaḥ). ||17||

Viśvanātha: [The meaning is: "I accept [this]; by this curse of mine, no harm whatsoever shall come to you, O Mahādeva, because you have committed no offense against me. He says—"by the gods"—to show that there is no fault in you either for having cursed me, who am innocent: "it was ordained by the gods from before."

The notion that it is "attained through past karma" is indeed appropriate for such a devotee due to his sense of wretchedness and his cultivation of that state toward himself; yet in reality, for one in whom love has arisen, there is not even a scent of karma,
for in the very stage of love, "his karmas are destroyed when I, the Soul of all, am seen."

Because of such statements as these, which declare the destruction of all karma; for the well-known fact that Hari is subject to his devotees would not be established if the devotees themselves were dependent on their karma, since one who is himself subject to karma could not bring under his control the Blessed One, who is independent of karma. And therefore, of him—
In order to proclaim his great power through his impartial vision regarding curses, favors, heaven, liberation, hell, and so forth;
in order to distance him from the unwholesome state of sovereignty over the Vidyādharas; and in order to increase the hunger of love through the heat of her own separation.

Furthermore, it is understood from the observation of the respective fruits that the curse was brought about by the Lord Śrī Saṅkarṣaṇa himself, out of affection like a father, through the goddess who was internally impelled by Him, for the purpose of bestowing upon him the experience of the great sweetness of direct service at His own feet once he had arrived in His own Vaikuṇṭha. This is the truth.
In this wheel of saṃsāra, a living being, deluded by ignorance,
wanders about and experiences both happiness and suffering everywhere and at all times.
Śrīdhara: And this is precisely the inherent nature of the wheel of saṃsāra; it is not surprising.
Thus he says: "The wheel of saṃsāra" (verse 18).
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* does not provide an explanation.
Viśvanātha says: "And this wheel of transmigratory existence is its very nature; it is not a wonder," thus he says: "Transmigratory... (verse 18).
Neither oneself nor another can be the agent of pleasure and pain;
the unwise person imagines both oneself and another to be the agent.
Whatever has been ordained by the Blessed One shall surely come to pass. ||19||

Śrīdhara: For this very reason, he says that there is no fault here for either me or you—"Not at all," etc.—the sequence of which has not been explained. Viśvanātha: "Aprājña" means one who lacks discernment. ||19||
In this continuous flow of qualities, what indeed is a curse and what is a favor?
What is heaven or hell, or what is pleasure or even pain?

Śrīdhara: Thus far, it has been stated while accepting [the existence of] pleasure, pain, and so forth. Now, he says that even those do not exist in reality: "In the flow of the qualities (guṇas), which consist of māyā, within saṃsāra. (20)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Thus far it has been stated by accepting pleasure, pain, and so forth; however, now, just as every drop of salt-water that falls into a salt-mine becomes salty, so too every single object within the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) [is of the same nature].

He says that in what is called "saṃsāra," the perception of distinctions such as pleasure and pain is not tenable, stating: "It is a flow of the guṇas. For one who has fallen into the midst of a current whose bottom cannot be touched, nothing at all is truly for the sake of pleasure until the banks are reached; therefore, everything—including curses, favors, and so forth—is suffering.
Such is the intended meaning. ||20||
The one Lord, partless and through his own creative power (māyā), creates all beings;
he alone ordains their bondage and liberation, as well as their happiness and suffering.

Śrīdhara: Now, if this is a continuous flow of the qualities of *māyā*, then because they are insentient (*jaḍa*), there would be no experience of bondage, liberation, and so forth; to this he replies: The one Supreme Lord, with *māyā* acting as the instrumental cause, creates living beings (*bhūta*)—that is, sentient creatures—and He also creates their bondage and the rest.
He is partless, himself devoid of bondage and the like. ||21||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Now, one might ask: "In this flow of the qualities (*guṇa-pravāha*), who is it that causes one to fall, and who is it that lifts one up from it? He says—"One alone"—that it is the Blessed Lord himself: by his own *māyā*, through *rajas*, he creates.
He protects through *sattva* and withdraws through *tamas*. Their bondage is by means of *avidyā*, and their liberation is by means of *sattva*;
pleasure is through *sattva* and pain through *tamas*. He is "without parts" (*niṣkala*), for *kalā* is *māyā*, and he is devoid of that. 21.
To him, no one was dear, nor anyone hostile; there was no kinsman or relative, no stranger, and no one his own.
For one who is equanimous everywhere and stainless, there is no attachment to pleasure; how much less, then, anger?

"He will not grant [boons] by His own name beyond what is worthy of service; nor is there anyone equal to Hari in [inflicting punishment] beyond the magnitude of the offense. Thus it is said in the *Māhātmya*. (22)
Śrīdhara: Now, one might ask what the cause is for such an unequal creation;

suspecting that this is because [the Lord] lacks partiality toward those who are dear and so forth, he says—in the two verses beginning with "na tasya"—that although there is no partiality toward the beloved and others, everything nevertheless occurs by the power of their respective karma.

"Pratīpa" means disagreeable; the sense is that he is neither a relative nor a kinsman. The reason for this is: "being equal toward all. Why is that? Because he is stainless and free from attachment. Therefore, there is no passion for the pleasure caused by him; how then could there be anger, which is bound up with passion? ||22||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Now, one might object that He must necessarily have some individual soul (*jīva*) who is dear to Him and some who is not dear, since He binds some, liberates some, and grants happiness to some; to this He says: "No."

There is no kinsman or relative; the reason for this is that [the Self] is equal toward all. The reason for this equality is that it is "stainless" (*nirañjana*); *añjana* (stain) is *māyā*, and it is devoid of that. Therefore, there is no passion or attachment to pleasure—that is, to sensory pleasure—and how could there be anger or hatred toward what is adverse to sensory pleasure?
Could it be so? This has been stated:
"Lust and hatred are established in the objects of each sense;
one should not come under their sway, for they are his adversaries" (Gītā 3.34).
The sense is that, for that very reason, he possesses neither affection nor aversion rooted in passion and hatred, nor does he have either a beloved or an adversary. ||22||
Nevertheless, the emission of their power leads to pleasure or pain, and to what is beneficial or harmful.
It serves for the bondage and liberation of embodied beings, and for the cycle of birth and death.

Śrīdhara: Even so, even there, that emission (*visarga*)—which, by his power (*śakti*) and through *māyā*, consists of action characterized by merit, demerit, and so forth—is capable of, that is, able to accomplish, the pleasure and other ends of these embodied beings. As it is said in the *Gītā*: "The emission is that which brings about the origin of the existence of beings."
Regarding the phrase "designated as action" (Gītā 8.3), the sequential arrangement has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: If his state is thus one of equanimity, then how does he bring joy to anyone?

"Does He cause suffering to anyone? To this he says: "Even so. Although He is equal toward all, nevertheless, by His power—that is, through *māyā*—there is an emission (*visarga*) which is the succession of karmas characterized by beginningless merit, demerit, and so forth; that very [succession] serves for the sake of pleasure and the like.

This is the meaning: although, because Māyā is His power, He Himself creates pleasure, pain, and so forth—which would indeed constitute partiality on His part—even so, since that [Māyā] lacks the status of being His essential nature (*svarūpa-śakti*), He does not create pleasure, pain, and so forth; thus, in reality, He remains impartial.
Thus, just as the illusory universe, although it is of the nature of the Lord,
is not identical with the essential nature of the Lord; and just as the heat associated with the sun causes suffering to owls and night-lotuses while causing pleasure to ruddy geese and day-lotuses.
The sense is: just as no one describes any inequality on the part of the sun toward those [planets] even when there is inequality [in their positions], so it is here.
—o)0(o— Now, O beautiful lady, I do not propitiate you for the sake of release from the curse.
Whatever you consider to have been poorly spoken by me, O virtuous lady, may that be forgiven.

Śrīdhara: Now, O beautiful woman, O angry one, I am merely propitiating you, but not for the sake of releasing you from the curse. To the question, "What then is the use of propitiation? he says: You consider my spoken word, though it was well-said, to be ill-spoken; therefore, let that be forgiven by you. (24)
The sequence of the composition: Even though you think, "I am favoring [you]," then let that which was poorly spoken by me be forgiven. ||24||
Viśvanātha: Therefore, for this very reason, I propitiate you alone, and not for the sake of release from the curse.
"O passionate one! O you who become angry without reflection! [The lover asks: "Well then, what is the use of propitiating?
To that he replies: "Whatever I have said, even if it was right, you consider wrong; let it indeed be wrong, for your sake."

"Forgive me. However, for me there would be an absence of both suffering and happiness whether in the curse or at its end; therefore, even though you are pleased, do not bring about the end of the curse"—this is the intended meaning. ||24||
Śrī Śuka said:
O subduer of enemies, having thus propitiated the two lords of the mountains, Citraketu—
He departed by means of his own celestial chariot while those two looked on with smiles.
Śrīdhara: Having propitiated Giriśa (the Lord of the Mountain) and Bhavānī-Śaṅkara (Pārvatī and Śiva), while they both remained smiling and filled with wonder. ||25||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon. *Viśvanātha*: While they were both feeling astonishment (*smayamānau* means "possessing wonder"). ||25||
Then the Blessed Lord Rudra spoke these words to Rudrāṇī,
while the celestial sages, Daityas, Siddhas, and his attendants were listening.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
Śrī Rudra said:
O lady of beautiful hips, you have witnessed the greatness of the servants of Hari, those great-souled ones who perform wondrous deeds and are free from desire.
Śrīdhara: This has not been explained. Kramasaṃdarbha: You have seen [the truth] even amidst the curse of Bhava; have you not considered it with freedom from fear? (27)

Viśvanātha: "O lady of beautiful hips!"—by this, a jest is implied: that you possess excellence and majesty solely through your qualities of beauty, and not through devotion, knowledge, detachment, or the like. Regarding the phrase "of the one of wondrous deeds," this is the wondrous deed of Hari which was seen by me: [that...]

By your granting of a curse, you have actually effected his own degradation; yet, because he did not suffer even the slightest deficiency in the abundance of love for his own devotee, and because you manifested the power of disregarding the curse of the Goddess, you have achieved nothing but his supreme exaltation.

It was done. Although she was filled with anger, the curse she uttered against him would have become effective even if she had been unable to inflict even the slightest suffering upon him; alas, alas, because this has proven utterly futile, [the power of curses] resides in great souls.
The instruction has been implied: "From this day forward, you must not behave in this manner toward those who are devoted with love.
All those who are intent upon Nārāyaṇa do not fear anything from any quarter.
They perceive the same essential purpose even in heaven, liberation, and hell.
Śrīdhara: Those whose nature it is to perceive that the purpose or motive is the same even in heaven and so forth are "tathā" (such). ||28||

*Sanātanaḥ* (from *Bhagavatsandarbha*, 10.190): They do not experience fear from anything whatsoever—be it from gods and the like, or from curses and the like—because they possess the disposition (*śīla*) to perceive that the same purpose or goal exists even in [the realms of] heaven and so forth; and likewise, there is nothing else.
Or rather, they even desire it; such is the meaning. ||28||

The sequential composition: those whose nature it is to see and experience the single goal— the goal of the person which is Nārāyaṇa— equally, whether in heaven or even in hell, as if in liberation, because they lack the perception of anything else as something to be rejected or acquired except for Śrī Nārāyaṇa.
The word *tulya* denotes singularity, just as in the rule *raṣābhyāṃ no ṇaḥ samānapade*. ||28||

Viśvanātha: Now, if such is the greatness [of the Lord], what is the cause for devotees [to attain it]? It is solely exclusive devotion to Nārāyaṇa and nothing else; thus he says: "Nārāyaṇa... Not only these, Citraketu and the others, but indeed all of them. The word "svarga" (heaven) applies to all three.
The meaning is that there is no distinction [between them] in terms of being unpalatable due to the absence of the bliss of devotion. ||28||
Due to the conjunction of bodies for embodied beings, pairs of opposites arise through the play of the Lord:
happiness and suffering, death and birth, as well as curse and grace.
Therefore, for others, the best [remedy] against the curse is the capacity to produce qualities and defects;
it is like the manifestation of distinctions inherent in those whose form consists of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

"The vision of that which exists within the mind again in dreams is due to being under the control of the Lord; therefore, that must certainly be known by all. Thus says Śrīdhara in the *Prakāśasaṃhitā*. Therein, he states the very reason for that in two verses: "The happiness of embodied beings..."

The pairs of opposites, such as suffering and so forth, arise for the non-Sovereign through his sport (līlā) and his illusory power (māyā); and within those, there is the conceptualization of qualities and defects—this is the logical connection. ||29||

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: He says "of embodied beings" (*dehinām*) to show that this would be so only in the absence of being established in Nārāyaṇa. "By the sport of the Lord" (*īśvaralīlayā*) means by Māyā, which has obtained its power through the sport of His glance. ||29||
For a person who lacks discrimination, there arises within the Self an apparent diversity of objects; likewise,
the conceptualization of qualities and defects is produced as if it were a real division, like that of a garland.

Śrīdhara: That differentiation of objects which manifests within the Self as if it were a distinction between the desired and the undesired—the differentiation of pleasure and so forth—is produced by non-discrimination for the person, just as in a dream. The meaning is that it is "produced" just as [the differentiation] is by means of a snake, a garland, and so forth, in the manner of a [real] garland (*srajivat*). Although one should have said *sragvat*, [he says *srajivat*].
The form "srajivat" is an archaic (ārṣa) usage; however, in the alternative reading, it is easily understood. ||30||

Regarding the sequence of the composition: in the commentary on the word *aviveka*, the words *te tu ca* have been supplied (*adhyāhṛta*), and [the phrase] *iṣṭāniṣṭa* [is understood]. Regarding the explanation of the distinction between qualities and defects, it should be understood that the word *bhidā* (distinction) also applies to the phrase *yathā*; this is because of the connection with the particle *ca*. Furthermore, there is an alternative reading: *tatkṛtaḥ*. ||30||

Viśvanātha: Therefore, one should understand that the illusory, unreal object—such as pleasure, pain, and so forth—is like a non-entity because of its instability; thus he says, "Through lack of discrimination... Just as in a dream there is a distinction of objects within the self, such as eating milk or the death of a son, even in the waking state there is the conceptualization of qualities and defects.

It should be understood as being created by the distinctions of pleasure, pain, and so forth. In this regard, there is an illustration: just as in a garland (*sraj*), there is indeed a distinction between "this is a rope" and "this is a snake"—the word *vat* meaning "just as";
for it is stated that *iva*, *vat*, or *vet* denote similarity. In the reading *sraji tat*, the meaning is "in the garland, because of its true nature."
*Bhidā* is like *bheda*. In the first reading, *bhit* ends in *kvip*; in the second, *bhidā* ends in *ṭāp*.
For those men who bear devotion toward the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva— (o)0(o)—
For knowledge, dispassion, and vigor have no dependence whatsoever.
Śrīdhara: Therefore, he states that it is indeed appropriate for the devotees of the Lord (bhāgavatas) to be free from desire—with the words "Vāsudeva" and so on.
For those whose strength (*vīrya*) consists of knowledge and dispassion (*jñāna-vairāgya*), there is no object to be sought as a refuge (*vyapāśraya*) through any special kind of intellect. 31.

Sanātana (Haribhaktisandarbha VI. 11.581): He confirms that very point through absolute independence by means of two verses beginning with "Vāsudeva. [The word *vīrya*] refers to the strength (*bala*) of knowledge and detachment;
or alternatively, it refers to those from whom even the strength of those two [knowledge and detachment] originates. [The term] *vyapāśraya* means taking refuge with a distinguished understanding.
There is no object to be resorted to. ||31||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Thus, for the wise (*jñānin*), even through the practice of knowledge, it is difficult to maintain the realization that dualities are not real entities. But for devotees (*bhakta*), since knowledge and dispassion are themselves forms of the power of devotion (*bhakti-anubhāva*), [this is possible] even without [them].
He says "Vāsudeva" to show that through the practice of knowledge, even the mental pursuit (*anusandhāna*) of those [objects] no longer occurs.
In this transmigratory world (*saṃsāra*), there is not even a single object that serves as the locus for distinction or attraction.
Only through the pursuit of devotion (*bhakti*) does the pursuit of the excellence or deficiency of illusory things cease to exist.
The sense is: "It is born"—understand that very thing for the sake of the devotees. ||31||
— I am neither Viriñca, nor Kumāra and Nārada, nor the sons of Brahmā, nor the sages, nor the lords of the gods.
We know his intended purpose, yet we— though we are but fragments of fragments— do not know his true nature, as we falsely imagine ourselves to be separate lords.
Śrīdhara: Since this [state] is his very nature by virtue of being a servant of Hari, it is not surprising;

to express this, he speaks of the majesty of Hari with the two verses beginning with "nāham. When we do not know His intention (*īhita*) or His pastimes (*līlā*), then, even though we are but parts of His parts, we do not know His true form (*svarūpa*).
Those who conceive of a separate Lord do not know at all. ||32||

The sequential composition: If they consider themselves separate lords, then even we—who are but parts of His parts—do not know His will or His true nature; however, if they are devotees, then everyone knows them.
This is the meaning. ||32||

Viśvanātha: He says, "Listen to the truth even for those such as us," beginning with "I am not [the Lord]. We do not know His intention (*īhita*) or His divine play (*līlā*), because we consider ourselves to be separate lords. ||32||
for he has no one dear to him, nor anyone unpleasant, whether his own kin or a stranger; because Hari is the self of all beings, he is beloved by all beings.
Śrīdhara: For this very reason, Hari too is dear to all beings. ||33||

The sequential composition: He clarifies the very greatness of devotion through the example of Citraketu with two verses beginning with "na hy asya. The meaning is that there is no distinction between the pleasant and the unpleasant, nor between self and others.
The reason for this is "because of being the Self" (ātmatvāt); the meaning is because of equality through the nature of the Self and because of the lack of need for anything else.

For the very reason that He is the Self, Viśvanātha is dear to all beings—that is, He is the object of unconditional love. Now hear the truth regarding Hari: "Not indeed," etc. That Hari, however, is indeed dear to all beings; yet, as for the fact that He is not dear to some and is even hated by others—
It does not exist; in that regard, illusion alone is the cause according to its varying degrees. Therefore, the reality of illusion has been made known. ||33||
And this illustrious Citraketu is his dear follower;
he is peaceful, impartial toward all, and indeed, like me, a beloved of Acyuta.
Therefore, one should not feel astonishment toward great-souled men who are devoted to the Great Being, who are peaceful, and who possess equal vision.
Śrīdhara: And I am indeed dear to Acyuta; therefore, the sense is that no resentment toward me arose in him. ||35||
The sequential arrangement [of the topics] is contradictory; for this very reason it will be stated later: "This meritorious history of the high-souled Citraketu" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.17.40). ||35||
Viśvanātha says: "However, listen to the truth regarding this Citraketu and myself"—even though he is equal toward all, [the Lord declares]:
"I am equal toward all beings; to Me there is none hateful and none dear."

"Those who worship me with devotion are in me, and I am also in them" (Gītā 9.29). According to this very statement, this follower Citraketu is dear to me because he is a devotee, and I too am dear to him; therefore, there is a mutual attraction between us two, both of whom are devotees of Saṅkarṣaṇa.
Because we possess mutual friendship and inner affection, even harsh words and the like serve only to nourish our happiness; yet you have become angry for no reason at all.
Furthermore, it is true that I am indeed such as you describe, but you consider yourself to be destitute of anything.

"You display yourself everywhere as one whose devotion is absolute; yet in secret you dally with a thousand Vidyādharīs. Therefore, you are a hypocrite, whereas I, showing myself to be full of passion for women, am truly free from deceit."

Moreover, you display devotion while concealing the enjoyment of sensual objects, whereas I behave in a manner quite the opposite; "let these courtiers themselves bear witness to the difference between us"— such a tasting of the flavor of playful banter would surely have occurred today as well.

"If you had not created obstacles here and there"—by this, the reproach is implied that he did not appear precisely because of the bitterness of your anger. Alas, alas! Even for you, the Lord who is an eternal great devotee, [this is the state of affairs] now that these base kṣatriyas have ascended the path of devotion.

Even toward such [beings], there is this much devotion; thus, to her who was filled with wonder, saying "Homage to you, therefore," he says "Therefore" (tasmāt) to show that this alone is indeed the true extent of devotion. ||3435||
Śrī Śuka said:
Having thus heard the speech of the Lord Śiva addressed to Umā, [the sages spoke].
O King, the queen became peaceful in mind and free from wonder.
Śrīdhara: [Not commented upon].
Viśvanātha: The meaning is that, thinking of his own former nature and feeling ashamed, he covered his face with the hem of his garment, being one whose mind was tranquil. ||36||
Thus, the devotee was most capable of replying to the goddess;
he accepted the curse with his head, for this much is the characteristic of the virtuous."
The gods alone are capable of that [power] over others; there is no doubt in this matter.
Even those who are powerless are clearly capable of cursing and so forth against those who possess power.
Nevertheless, those [rites] prescribed for those lacking power— such as curses and the like—
are indeed very slight and short-lived, and they do not produce their full effect.
There is no doubt that curses directed at superior beings are warded off by their power through great effort; rather, they result in the loss of knowledge and merit for those who utter them.
Without his grace,
Brahmā and Viṣṇu, though they possess wives, are entirely unable to destroy [their enemies] through boons, curses, and the like.
Therefore, all those performed by anyone else are certainly fruitless;
yet their curses are never found to be unreal anywhere.
"According to the sequence, [the boons] of Varuṇa, Viṣṇu, and Śrī, as well as those of Brahmā, shall be granted;
however, for the lowly, the boons of the superior [deities] become curses as previously stated.
These indeed grant the full fruit [of the request]; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. Thus it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa. (37)
Śrīdhara: Even though he is most capable and most powerful enough to bestow a curse... [37]
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Lest one should think that Citraketu, being a modern [figure], possesses little power, he says:
"Thus..."—even though he was *alam-tama*, meaning exceedingly capable, [he acted] for the sake of the Goddess. (37)
He was born from Tvaṣṭṛ’s southern fire, having taken recourse to a Dānava womb;
he became widely renowned as Vṛtra, endowed with both knowledge and realized wisdom.
Śrīdhara: [Not commented upon].
Viśvanātha: "Yonim" means birth. ||38||
All this that you asked me has been told to you:
the cause concerning Vṛtra, his birth as an Asura, and the opinion of the Blessed One."
Śrīdhara: Because he was born from the race of asuras with the nature of an asura, and because he held the view of the Blessed One. ||39||
The sequence of events: the cause of birth as an asura is a great offense; the cause of the Lord’s thought [to save one] is a great grace. (39)
Viśvanātha: Not explained.
—o)0(o— This meritorious history of the high-souled Citraketu.
Having heard the majesty of the devotees of Viṣṇu, one is liberated from bondage.
Whoever, having risen at dawn, recites this with faith while restraining their speech,
and remembers Hari while reflecting upon this history, attains the supreme goal.
Śrīdhara: This is this very thing. ||41||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Sārārthadarśinī*, known as the *Harṣiṇī*, for those whose hearts are devoted.
The seventeenth chapter of the sixth [book], which is well-connected with the virtuous, is concluded.
Thus ends the sixth book in the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā, the Pāramahaṃsyasaṃhitā, which is a commentary on the Brahma-sūtras within the glorious Mahāpurāṇa Śrīmad Bhāgavatam.
The seventeenth chapter in the narrative of Citraketu.
Now begins the eighteenth chapter.
Regarding the birth of the Maruts,
the venerable Śuka said:
Pṛśni, the wife of Savitṛ, [conceived] Sāvitrī, the Vyāhṛtis, and the Trayī.
The Agnihotra, the animal sacrifice, the Soma sacrifice, the Cāturmāsya, and the great sacrifices.
Śrīdhara: In connection with the lineage of Tvaṣṭṛ, the fourth of the Ādityas,
the slaying of Viśvarūpa and Vṛtra by Indra has been described.
In the eighteenth [chapter], through accounts of the lineage of the sons of Aditi beginning with Pañcajanya, the division of the Maruts from Śakra within the womb of Diti is described.
Having recounted the lineage of Tvaṣṭṛ in due order along with its collateral branches,
the lord of sages then described the lineages of the Ādityas and others.
In the account of the lineage of Dakṣa’s daughters, twelve sons of Aditi are mentioned:
Vivasvān, Aryaman, Pūṣan, Tvaṣṭṛ, Savitṛ, Bhaga,
Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, Varuṇa, Mitra, Śakra, and Urukrama.

Therein, having described the lineage of Tvaṣṭṛ starting from the sixth chapter through the narratives of Viśvarūpa, Vṛtra, and Citraketu, he now states the lineage of Savitṛ: "Pṛśni indeed... and so forth; in these passages beginning with "Sāvitrīm," the word "gave birth" (*prāsūta*) is to be supplied as a connective from the subsequent verse. *Paśum* refers to the animal sacrifice (*paśuyāga*). *Mahāmakhān* refers to the great sacrifices.
The five sacrifices. ||1||
The sequence of composition: "pṛśnis tu" and so forth is a triplet. ||1||
Viśvanātha:
In the eighteenth [chapter], Diti, whose son had been slain, undertook a vow;
from that womb, which was severed by her enemy, the host of Maruts was born.
Through the genealogical accounts of Tvaṣṭṛ, the son of Aditi and the fourth [in the line],
the events beginning with the slaying of Viśvarūpa have been introduced as a matter of context.
Having concluded this nectar-like narrative with the curse of Citraketu,
the lineage of the sons of Aditi, beginning with the fifth, is now described.
The animal sacrifice, the great sacrifices, and the five daily rites. ||1||
O dear one, Siddhi, the wife of Bhaga, gave birth to Mahiman, the all-pervading Lord,
as well as a daughter of excellent vows named Āśis.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
The elements are Kuhū, Sinīvālī, Rākā, and likewise Anumati.
One should perform the Darśa sacrifice in the evening and the Pūrṇamāsa sacrifice in the morning, in due order.
Śrīdhara: Kuhū, the wife of Dhātṛ, gave birth to a son in the evening; likewise, Sinīvālī [gave birth] to Darśa, and so on in succession. (3)
The *Kramasaṃdarbha*: not commented upon.
Viśvanātha: —o)0(o—
Immediately after the ritual act, he established the Purīṣya fires;
Varuṇa was the lord of the people, in whom Bhṛgu was born again.

Śrīdhara: Immediately thereafter, the Creator [performed] the five layers of the *purīṣya* fires within his wife during the ritual, according to the Vedic texts: "The *purīṣya* fires," and "These five fires are indeed the layers (*citayaḥ*). Formerly, Carṣaṇī was the wife of Varuṇa; into her, Bhṛgu—the son of Brahmā—was born again.
He was born. ||4||
Kramasandarbha: "agnīn" is the first half-verse.

Viśvanātha: The immediate creator [is the agent] in the ritual action; [he places] the fires known as *purīṣya* within the wife, for there is a Vedic scripture stating, "the five layers are the *purīṣya* fires. *Carṣaṇī*.
He was the wife of Varuṇa. Furthermore, although previously the son of Brahmā, he subsequently became the son of Varuṇa. ||4||
And the great yogi Vālmīki, it is said, arose from an anthill;
likewise Agastya and Vasiṣṭha were the two sages born from Mitra and Varuṇa.

Śrīdhara: Vālmīki was indeed the son of Varuṇa; these two were the exclusive sons of Varuṇa. Likewise, Utsarga and the others were also the exclusive sons of Mitra. He now mentions the two sons common to both of them: Agastya and Vasiṣṭha were the two sages born of Mitra and Varuṇa. (5)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Bhṛgu and Vālmīki were the unique sons of Varuṇa; likewise, Utsarga and others will be mentioned as the unique sons of Mitra. Of those two, Mitra and Varuṇa, there were two common [sons].
And he said to his two sons: "Agastya and Vasiṣṭha— these two sages were born from the seed of Mitra and Varuṇa,
which they quickly shed into a jar in the presence of Urvaśī."
Under the asterism Revatī, Mitra performed the ritual emission, which was unharmed and fruitful.

Śrīdhara: Because both of them poured their seed into the jar; for the Śruti says: "Born together at the sacrificial session, they poured their common seed into the jar with prostrations" (Ṛgveda 7.33.24).
*Drutam* means spilled. ||6||

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: Because of the words "since the semen," and so forth, according to the Vedic scripture: "They both poured the common semen into the jar" (*Ṛgveda* 7.33.24). "Druta" means spilled. ||6||
We have heard that Indra begot three sons upon Paulomī:
Jayanta, Ṛṣabha, and, O dear one, the third was the lord Mīḍhuṣa."
It has not been explained by anyone at all—
the [deeds] of the god Urukrama, who assumed the illusory form of a dwarf.
To Kīrti, his wife, Bṛhacchloka was born; he had sons such as Saubhaga and others.
Śrīdhara: [Not commented upon].

Viśvanātha: By means of *māyā*—either by his own essential power (*svarūpa-śakti*) or by that which possesses the form of Vāmana—he is joined with his own eternal power known as *māyā*. Therefore, the wise declare Viṣṇu to be composed of *māyā* (*māyāmaya*).
Thus, according to the scripture authenticated by the Madhva-bhāṣya. ||8||
We shall later describe the deeds, qualities, and prowess of that great-souled Kāśyapa, and how he indeed descended into Aditi.
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha [commented] later on the eighth book. ||9||
The sequence of composition has not been explained. —
Now, I shall proclaim to you the Daityas who are the descendants of Kaśyapa.
Wherein reside the illustrious Bhāgavata Prahlāda and Bali himself.
Śrīdhara: Regarding the word "atha" (now): having described the lineage of Kaśyapa’s sons, the twelve Ādityas, the meaning is that he now intends to speak of the sons of Diti. ||10||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Now, [the word] "atha" marks the commencement of another narrative; "dāyādān" means sons; "daiteyān" means those born of Diti.
There were two heirs alone, honored by the Daityas and Dānavas,
renowned as Hiraṇyakaśipu and Hiraṇyākṣa.
Śrīdhara: At first there were only two, namely Hiraṇyakaśipu and Hiraṇyākṣa; these two are celebrated in the Third Book. (11)
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been explained. —
The wife of Hiraṇyakaśipu was a Dānavī named Kayādhū.
She, the daughter of Jambha, gave birth to four sons.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
[He slew] Saṃhrāda, Anuhrāda, Hrāda, and Prahrāda as well.
His sister, named Siṃhikā, seized Rāhu from Vipracit.
Śrīdhara: Rāhu received his son from his master, the Dānava Vipracit. ||13||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Rāhu obtained—that is, received—as his son from Vipracit, the lord of the Dānavas.
Hari severed the head of Saṃhrāda with his discus while he was drinking the nectar; O Sūta, Kṛti, the wife of Saṃhrāda, then gave birth to Pañcajana.
Śrīdhara: From him, Saṃhrāda begot [a son]. ||14||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— Hrādasya’s wife, Dhamani, gave birth to Vātāpi and Ilvala.
Ilvala cooked Vātāpi for Agastya as a guest.
Śrīdhara: The grammatical connection is as follows: he who cooked Vātāpi in the form of a ram, [and] he whom he cooked—that Vātāpi—brought forth Ilvala. 15.
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: He who was Ilvala cooked Vātāpi in the form of a ram for Agastya; that is, he cooked Vātāpi, who had assumed the form of a ram, in order to feed Agastya. (15)
Anuhrāda’s sons by Sūryā were Bāṣkala and Mahiṣa;
Virocana was the son of Prāhrādi, and his son by Devī was Bali.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
From him, a hundred sons, with Bāṇa as the eldest, were born from Aśanā.
His glorious power shall be described later on.

Śrīdhara: Then, from the presence of Bali, there arose for him [Vāmana] a majestic power (*anubhāva*) worthy of excellent praise and meritorious fame. Alternatively, *anubhāva* means that which is experienced or praised by the virtuous;
the word "glory" (*yaśas*) is to be supplied as the object of "excellent praise" (*suślokya*). ||17||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: "The majesty (*anubhāva*) of that Bali"—this is an archaic usage (*ārṣa*), or it refers to his connection with external ritual action (*bāhyakarma*).
Bāṇa, having propitiated Giriśa, attained the status of a chief among his attendants;
indeed, even today the Blessed Lord remains by his side as the protector of the city.
Śrīdhara: His "chief status among the Gaṇas" means his preeminence. ||18||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— And the Maruts, the sons of Diti, are forty-nine in number.
They were all rendered childless and brought by Indra into a state of identity with his own self.
Śrīdhara: "Sātmatām" means having a common nature or identical form. ||19||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: The meaning is that they have been brought to the state of having the same nature (*sātmatām*), that is, to the state of being deities (*devatvam*).—o)0(o)—
The King said:
O Guru, how did they cast off their innate demonic nature and attain harmony with Indra? What was it that they did so well?
Śrīdhara: They have been brought to the state of divinity, which is natural to them. ||20||
The sequence of composition: *apohya* means having set aside or abandoned. ||20||
Viśvanātha: This has not been explained.
—o)0(o— O Brahmin, these sages indeed have faith along with me.
O Blessed One, you should explain that to us for the sake of full understanding.
Śrīdhara: This has not been explained.
Kramasaṃdarbha: Now, why do you wish to hear this external narrative?
To that he replies: "These [people] have faith," and by saying "together with me," he indicates his own subordinate role.
In the same way, while awakening [them], he likewise manifested [the teaching]. ||21||
Viśvanātha: "O sages, have faith"—in these words, he projects his own faith onto the sages in order to make them understand the secret meaning. (21)
Śrī Sūta said: Then that son of Badarāyaṇa [to] Viṣṇurāta...
Having heard those truthful words, brief yet full of meaning,
Satrāyaṇa, the all-seeing sage, honored him with a composed mind and spoke.

Śrīdhara: "Ādṛtam" means respectfully. "Alpam" means concise in syllables. "Arthavat" means endowed with great meaning. "Satrāyaṇa," O Śaunaka, refers to one for whom the sacrificial session (*satra*) is the refuge or support. ||22||

The sequence of composition: For this very reason, he praises [the work] with the words "that" (tat). It is "respected" (ādṛtam), meaning endowed with the reverence of the sages; it is "meaningful" (arthavat), and this can only come about through its connection to a specific form of worship of the Blessed Lord.
Thus, being joined with his own desired goal, [he speaks] with composure, preceded by the bliss of the Blessed Lord; therefore, that too [is established].

The intention is that [the author] will establish the connection with the Blessed One. Regarding the phrase "of manifold meaning" in the commentary, it means endowed with the success intended by the Seer (Vyāsa) and intended by Śrī Śuka. ||22||

Viśvanātha: "Arthavat" means possessing multiple meanings. Among these, one sought-after meaning is obtained from this narrative: namely, that even one who intends to harm others and performs devotion to the Lord out of tamas—even if his mind is impure—attains unwavering devotion that is free from tamas.

By attaining purity of mind, one obtains liberation from the cycle of existence as a secondary benefit, as well as the cessation of the desire to harm others; in this regard, Diti herself is the proof. Likewise, even those of discernment who possess crooked minds do not perceive within themselves those very faults that they observe in others.
Regarding this, the second [point] is that Diti alone is the authority because of the poet’s statement beginning with "worms and excrement.

The third is that Kaśyapa himself is the authority in the matter that even one of great wisdom can be deceived by the illusion of a woman. "A small amount" means concise; "with a composed mind" means with a complete and one-pointed mind.
Satrāyaṇa Śaunaka. ||22||
Śrī Śuka said:
Diti, whose sons had been slain by Viṣṇu acting as Indra’s ally, [was overcome with grief].
Burning with anger kindled by grief, she reflected:
Śrīdhara: [He was] with Śakra as his rear-guard ally, that is, as a helper from behind. ||23||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: By Śakra’s *pārṣṇigrāha*, meaning by one who acts as an ally from behind, that is, one who provides assistance from behind the scenes. ||23||
When indeed shall I lie down in peace, having slain that cruel slayer of his brother, that sinner who delights in sensual pleasures and possesses an unmelting heart?

Śrīdhara: Diti thought, "When shall I be happy after having killed Indra, the slayer of my brother? *Ulbaṇam* means cruel. *Aklinnahṛdayam* means hard-hearted; the sequence of these words has not been explained.

Viśvanātha: *Ulbaṇam* means cruel. "I sleep happily" (*sukhaṃ śaye*) means that I sleep with ease. [This refers to] he who was designated by the Lord as having the names "worm," "excrement," and "ashes."
One who harms living beings knows nothing of his own welfare for their sake, since hell awaits him.

Śrīdhara: Now, one might object: "A king certainly kills others for the sake of protecting his own body; what is surprising about that? To this, he says: "Kṛmi... etc. Even for one who is called a lord (*īśa*) or a master (*prabhu*), after the death of the bodies of former kings which remain for only two or three days, there are worms.
That which has been eaten by dogs and other such creatures is designated as "excrement," and that which is burnt is designated as "ashes.
For the sake of such a body, he who acts with hostility toward living beings—does he know his own true interest?
He knows it not at all. The reason for this is: because from hostility toward living beings, hell arises. ||25||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Even for a body that has been "struck by the Lord"—meaning even for a body designated as belonging to a king—after death, if it remains for two or three days, [the result is] worms; or if it is devoured by dogs and the like...

Regarding the term *viṣṭhā*, when [the body] has been burned by sons and others, it receives the designation *bhasma* (ashes). The use of the past tense (*bhūta*) is because this was observed to be the case for previous kings as well. One who does harm to the elements that constitute that body—does he know his own self-interest? Not at all; for it results in nothing but hell for himself.
Therefore, it suggests that Indra alone is devoid of discernment; yet she herself is likewise devoid of discernment, since,
desiring to slay Indra, she herself [seeks] one who harms living beings,

and though her own heart is not moist with compassion, she seeks one whose heart is not moist with compassion, and though she herself is ignorant of her own true interest, [she seeks] one who is likewise so.

It has thus been shown that even discernment, for those who lack discernment, only serves to further solidify their lack of discernment, because they consider Indra himself to be ignorant of his own true nature. ||25||
"For him who desires this with an uplifted mind,
may this [soma] surely become the drier of Indra's intoxication, by which my son shall indeed be born."

Śrīdhara: For what reason might my son become the witherer of that pride of Indra, whose mind was puffed up and unrestrained because he hoped for and considered this body and so forth to be permanent and eternal? ||26||
Kramasaṃdarbha: The meaning is that it is with the intention that whatever may belong to one who desires [the welfare of others] must indeed be the conduct dear to her husband.
Viśvanātha: By that very cause of his ill-conduct, his son became the drier-up of his pride.

"May it be mine"—this is the meaning of my prayer. For one who desires and considers this body and so forth to be permanent and eternal, whose mind is unrestrained—[of such a person] is this [state]. (26)
With this disposition, she repeatedly performed what was pleasing to her husband through service,
affection, humility, and self-restraint.
O King, through supreme devotion, charming and sweet speech,
and knowing his inner feelings, she captivated his mind with her smiling side-long glances.
Śrīdhara: With the thought that it was precisely the beloved conduct of her husband, she repeatedly performed what was pleasing to her husband. ||27||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: "When the husband is pleased, the desire of women is fulfilled; therefore, I shall satisfy my husband through service"—with this intention [she speaks]. (27)
Thus, even a wise man, rendered senseless by an attractive woman,
helplessly said, "Certainly. For this is no wonder in the case of a woman.
Śrīdhara: That he said, "Being helpless and dependent on women, I shall certainly fulfill your desire," is not surprising. ||29||
Kramasaṃdarbha: This has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: That he said, "Certainly, I shall fulfill your desire," is not surprising. (29)
In the beginning, Prajāpati, having observed that all beings were solitary,
fashioned a woman from half of his own body, by whom the minds of men were captivated.

Śrīdhara: He states the reason for this with the words "Having beheld" (vilokya). Having become solitary and detached, he created a woman solely for the sake of his own body, for the purpose of increasing creation through sexual union. ||30||

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: The mind has been captivated by things that have become solitary and detached; therefore, the meaning is that the flow of saṃsāra has remained uninterrupted. ||30||
"O dear one, having been thus served by the woman, the Blessed Kaśyapa smiled, and being exceedingly pleased, he spoke to Diti with words of welcome."
Śrīdhara: Thus, being served by his wife... ||31||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
Śrī Kaśyapa said:
"Choose a boon, O lady of beautiful thighs; I am pleased with you, O blameless one.
When a husband is well-pleased with his wife, what desire could possibly remain unfulfilled in this world?"
Śrīdhara: Here, by the word "and" (ca), it is meant both here and elsewhere. "Agama" means that which is unattainable. ||32||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: Āgama means that which is unattainable. ||32||
For the husband alone is remembered as the supreme deity for women;
Vāsudeva, the Lord of Śrī, is the mental deity of all beings.
That very same Blessed One is worshipped by men through the symbols of deities conceptualized as names and forms, and by women, assuming the form of a husband.

Śrīdhara: Now, it is well known that when the Supreme Lord is fully pleased, there is the attainment of all desires; regarding this, he says: "The Lord alone... Indeed, it is well known that Śrī Vāsudeva, residing in the mind, is the husband of Lakṣmī and the supreme deity. True; he himself, by virtue of his own authority, through various distinct forms...

He says that [the Lord] is worshipped by means of the verse beginning with "mānasa" (mental) and continuing for one and a half verses. He is characterized by the marks (*liṅga*) and forms (*mūrti*) of the deities.

He specifies those very things: "name" refers to Indra and so forth, and "form" refers to having a thunderbolt in hand and so forth; [he is worshipped] through various [conceptions] constructed from these two. 3334.
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Here, the "Lord" (*pati*) is indeed the individual soul (*jīva*). How could he be the supreme deity, the Lord (*īśvara*)? To this, he says: "Mānasaḥ"—Vāsudeva, who is the presiding deity (*adhiṣṭhātā*) of the mind (*manas*), that is, of consciousness (*citta*).

In this way, the Blessed One is worshipped by means of the signs and marks of the deities. By what kind [of signs]? Namely, by those variously imagined as having the form of Indra and others, such as [the mark] of holding a thunderbolt in the hand; [he is worshipped] by people belonging to the world of ritual action (*karmiloka*) through the distinction of names and forms, such as "Svāhā to Indra" and "Svāhā to Agni. Thus, the Blessed One is worshipped.
The meaning is that it is conquered by women in the form of a husband, just as [it is conquered] in that manner. ||3334||
Therefore, O slender-waisted one, women who are devoted to their husbands and desire their own welfare worship their husband as the Self and the Lord with undivided devotion.
"O blessed lady, since I have been honored by you with such a disposition and devotion,
I shall fulfill that desire of yours which is very difficult for unchaste women to obtain."
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
Diti said:
"O Brahmin, if you are a granter of boons to me, I choose a son who shall slay Indra—
one who is immortal, for I have lost my sons and by whom my two children were killed."
Śrīdhara: "Indra-haṇam" means the slayer of Indra; "amṛtyum" means devoid of death. By that Viṣṇu, acting as Indra's assistant, those two were slain. ||37||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "Indrahan" means the slayer of Indra (*indrasya hantāram*), because the root *han* has the sense of "going" [in this context]. Alternatively, it means one who follows Indra (*indrānugam*). "Amṛtyu" means incapable of being slain by anyone; alternatively, it means immortal due to his divine nature.
Because there is only one god, Māruta, [despite being composed of] forty-nine [components], the singular number is used. ||37||
Having heard those words, the brahmin became despondent and was deeply distressed:
"Alas! A very great unrighteousness has now come upon me."
Śrīdhara: Not commented upon.
Viśvanātha: "Dejected" means that the object desired by Diti would not be possible without the death of Indra; this is the sense. ||38||
Alas! Delighting in sense objects through the illusion consisting of women here on earth, my mind has been captivated; I am a wretch who will surely fall into hell.
It has not been explained by anyone. What transgression is there in a woman here who follows her own nature?
Fie on me, alas, for I am ignorant and have failed to conquer my senses regarding my own true interest!
Śrīdhara: What transgression or offense is there for a woman who follows her own nature? ||40||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Transgression is an offense. Cruelty is indeed the very nature of the female sex; [this refers to her] who conforms to, that is, follows, that [nature]. (40)
Their faces are a festival of autumn lotuses, and their speech is nectar to the ears;
yet their hearts are like the edge of a razor— who knows the conduct of women?
Śrīdhara: He describes the very nature [of the teaching] with two verses. In which [teaching] there is a festival, that is, a blossoming, like that of an autumn lotus;
in the ears—that is, the two auditory organs—there is nectar; and the mind is like the edge of a razor. (41)
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: He states the very nature [of the state]—“autumn,” etc. ||41||
Indeed, no one is truly dear to women who regard their own welfare as their primary aim;
for the sake of wealth, they will kill, or cause to be killed, even their husband, son, or brother.
Śrīdhara: [This refers to] those who, by their own nature, perceive themselves as most dear through the desire for their own welfare, as if they were their own selves. ||42||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: The meaning is that their effort (*ātma-yatna*) is directed solely by the desire for their own blessing (*āśis*), and not with regard to the happiness of their husbands and so forth. This is either a compound with elision (*aluk-samāsa*) or the word *āśis* ends in the feminine suffix *ṭāp*.
The word "I give" which was promised shall not be false;
and since even Indra does not deserve death, this [remedy] is appropriate in this case.

Śrīdhara: In this regard, the following is appropriate and fitting. The intention is this: I shall first instruct her in the Vaiṣṇava vow; by that alone, the anger of this woman of purified mind toward Indra will cease. Furthermore, her son shall become immortal. And as for the duration of the vow being long...
If some deficiency should somehow occur, even the slaying of Indra will not take place. ||43||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: In this regard, the following is appropriate and fitting. The intention is as follows: first, I shall instruct her in the Vaiṣṇava vow; when, through that very vow, her mind has become purified, then [her] anger toward Indra...
She will turn back. Consequently, because she does not desire the slaying of Indra, the Vaiṣṇava vow performed by her cannot yield an undesired fruit; thus, there will be no killing of Indra.
However, since the verb *han* (to kill) is used in both the request for the boon and the statement of its granting, and because of the nature of that verb—

Because it has the sense of "going," the son will be an immortal who follows Indra. Since the vow lasts for a long time, there will inevitably be some deficiency; through that very [deficiency], her mind will be pacified even though she is unaware of it. In reality, however, even if there is a deficiency in the Vaiṣṇava vow—
"Since the accomplishment of the fruit is inevitable, this exertion of hers will surely be fruitful"— having reflected thus, O descendant of Kuru, the Blessed Marīci [spoke].
He spoke somewhat angrily, censuring himself.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
Śrī Kaśyapa said:
"O blessed lady, if you maintain this vow for a full year without fail, a son shall be born to you who will be a slayer of Indras and a kinsman of the gods."
Śrīdhara: O blessed lady, if you maintain this correctly and exactly as it is, then you will become the slayer of Indra;
but if there is a deficiency, you will become a kinsman of the gods, because of the Vaiṣṇava nature of the vow.
This is because even if some deficiency should somehow occur, there is no total failure [of the vow]. (45)

The sequential arrangement [of the commentary] is as follows: "He is your son. If you maintain the vow, then he will be the slayer of Indra and likewise a kinsman to both the gods and the asuras. Otherwise, however, he will not be the slayer of Indra, and his kinship will belong to the gods alone; such is the meaning. ||45||

Viśvanātha: "Indrahā" means the slayer of Indra; "the kinsman of the non-gods, the asuras"—this is the meaning intended to inform Diti. "Indrahā" [also] means the follower of Indra; "the kinsman of the gods"—this is the meaning desired by himself. (45)
"—o)0(o— Diti said: 'O Brahman, I shall observe the vow; tell me what duties I must perform.'"
And those things which are forbidden here do not destroy one's vow.
Śrīdhara: [These are] necessary duties—those which do not obstruct one's vows, which are not mandatory, nor prohibited, but rather permitted. State all of those as well.
Viśvanātha: The sequence has not been explained.
Śrī Kaśyapa said:
One should not harm living beings, nor should one curse, nor should one speak untruth.
One should not cut one's nails or hair, nor should one touch anything inauspicious.

Śrīdhara: Regarding that, he states thirty-one prohibitions with five verses beginning with "One should not harm. One should not curse nor revile. One should not touch anything inauspicious, such as a skull or a bone. ||47||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: By the very first [injunction], "One should not kill," the apprehension of killing Indra was already prohibited.
One should not bathe in water, one should not become angry, nor should one converse with wicked people;
one should not wear unwashed clothes, nor ever wear a garland that has been worn by another.
Śrīdhara: One should not bathe by entering into water. One should not wear again a garland that was previously worn. 48.
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Having entered the water, one should not bathe; one should not wear unwashed clothing, nor put it on. One should not again wear a garland that was previously worn. ||48||
One should not eat the food of Caṇḍikā that has been left over, nor food containing meat brought by a low-born person;
one should not eat what has been seen by a woman in her courses, nor should one drink water from joined palms.

Śrīdhara states there are five prohibitions regarding eating, beginning with "not [the food of] the impure" (*nocchiṣṭam*). "The food of Caṇḍikā" refers to that which has been offered to Bhadrakālī, or that which is defiled by ants and the like. Regarding the phrase "one should not drink water with cupped hands," the sequence of the composition has not been explained.

Viśvanātha states five prohibitions regarding food: "Not [the food] left over," and so forth. *Caṇḍikānna* is food offered to Durgā. *Pipīlikāsṛṣṭa* means created by ants; for it is stated in the lexicon that *pipīlikā* is a synonym for *caṇḍikā*.
*Udakyā* refers to a woman in her menses. (49)

One should not go outside during the twilight hours while still having remnants of food on one’s person, without having touched water, with hair disheveled, without having performed worship, with speech unrestrained, or without being properly clothed.

Śrīdhara: He states seven prohibitions regarding going outside the house, beginning with "not [leaving] with remnants" (nocchiṣṭa). "Unhonored" means devoid of ornaments; "uncovered" means not clothed. ||50||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: He states seven prohibitions regarding going outside the house, beginning with "not [leaving] with leavings" (*nocchiṣṭā*). "Without having sipped water" (*apṛṣṭasalilā*) means one who has not performed the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*anācāntā*). "Unhonored" (*anarcitā*) means without ornaments. "Uncovered" (*asaṃvītā*) means with all limbs exposed.

One should not sleep with unwashed feet, nor while impure, nor with wet feet, nor with the head pointing north; nor should one lie on one's back, nor on one's face, nor with others, nor naked, nor during the two twilights.
Śrīdhara states eight prohibitions regarding sleeping: "Not with unwashed feet," etc., and "not facing west with the head toward the west. (51)

The sequential composition (*kramasaṃdarbha*): *aparākam* means that which reaches or touches the western direction (*aparām paścimāṃ diśam*) with its head; although it functions as an adverb (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), because the intended meaning lies precisely in its qualification of the subject, the sense is simply "having the head toward the west" (*paścimaśirā*). Alternatively, *aparācī* means "western. From that...

By the rule "after words denoting direction ending in the fifth case when a *lyap* suffix is elided," etc., the *astāti* suffix is applied in its own primary sense (*svārthe*).
