There is then elision of that [suffix] by the rule "elision of *añc*" (*añceḥ luk*), and subsequently, by the rule "elision of a secondary derivative" (*taddhitaluk*), there is elision of the feminine suffix. Thus, with the form *aparāg* established, starting from the west (*pratīcīm*) and reaching that [direction].
"Having made it one's own through the preliminary limbs"—the meaning is exactly as before. ||51||

Viśvanātha states eight prohibitions regarding sleeping: "Not with unwashed feet," etc. *Aprayatā* means impure (*apavitrā*). According to Amara, *pavitra*, *prayata*, and *pūta* are synonyms. "Not *aparāk*" means not with the head toward the west.
Wearing clean garments, always pure, and endowed with all auspicious things,
she should worship the cows, the Brahmins, Śrī, and Acyuta before her morning meal.
Śrīdhara explains the duties [to be performed] with two verses beginning with "dhautavāsā" (wearing washed garments). "Prātarāśāt" means from the first meal of the morning. ||52||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: He states what ought to be done—one should worship in the morning (*prātaḥ*), that is, before the morning meal (*prātarāśāt*). )0( )0( )0(
She should honor women who have heroic sons with garlands, perfumes, offerings, and ornaments;
and having honored her husband, she should attend upon him and meditate on him as being present within her womb.
Śrīdhara: [The term] *vīravatīḥ* refers to women whose husbands are living. *Ārcya* means having worshipped. *Koṣṭhagatam* means situated within the belly. ||53||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: "Possessing heroes" (*vīravatīḥ*) means those whose husbands are alive. "Contained within a chest" (*koṣṭhagataṃ*) means situated inside the womb.
If you shall observe this vow for a year, unswerving, which brings about the birth of a male child, then a son who will slay Śakra shall be born to you.
Śrīdhara: *Puṃsavana* is that which causes the birth of a son; *tubhyam* means "to you" (or "for you"). ||54||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Puṃsavana is that which effects the birth of a son. ||54||
"Very well," the high-minded Diti replied, O King, and having accepted this,
she conceived a fetus from Kaśyapa and observed a vow of chastity.
Not even by anyone has it been explained.
O giver of honor, Indra, having understood the intention of his maternal aunt— o)0(o — [he spoke].
The sage attended upon Diti while she was staying in the hermitage by performing service for her.
Śrīdhara: [This] has not been commented upon in the *Kramasaṃdarbha*.
Viśvanātha: [It refers to] Diti, his mother’s sister. ||56||
Day after day, at the appropriate times, he brought from the forest flowers, fruits, roots, sacrificial fuel, *kuśa* grass, leaves, sprouts, earth, and water.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
Thus, O King, for her who was established in her vow, Hari [removed] the breach of her vow.
Desiring to seize him, he moved about crookedly like a beast in the form of a beast.

Śrīdhara: Hari is Indra; "desiring to find a flaw" means wishing to obtain one. "Crooked" means deceitful, appearing in the guise of a virtuous man. Just as a hunter, a slayer of deer, assumes the appearance of a deer to deceive deer, so it is here. ||58||

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: Hari [Indra] desired to find a flaw in the vow; thus, even Indra’s lack of knowledge is established, because by the remembrance or chanting of Viṣṇu, even that which has a flaw [is purified].
It shall be without flaw. This vow of Viṣṇu remains truly flawless even if there is a flaw;

as it has been said: "By whose remembrance and by the utterance of whose name... (Skanda Purāṇa), and "A flaw in mantra or in ritual procedure... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 8.23.16), and so forth. Furthermore, even by Indra later on...

One who intends to experience the flawlessness of his vow will say: "The accomplishment of the worship of the Great Person is some incidental benefit" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.18.74). *Jihma* means crooked or deceitful.
Just as a hunter (*mṛgaha*), a deer-killer, assumes the form of a deer in order to deceive deer, so too does he assume the form of the people who serve him.
O Lord of the Earth, being intent upon that [task], he did not find any breach in his vow;
then Śakra fell into deep anxiety, thinking: "By what means might there be welfare for me here?"
Śrīdhara fell into reflection, thinking, "By what means might there be welfare for me? ||59||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— Once, at twilight, she was impure and emaciated by her vows.
Without touching water and without washing her feet, she fell asleep, deluded by fate.
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha: He is one who has neither touched water nor washed his feet. ||60||
The sequential composition has not been explained. —
Having obtained that opportunity, Śakra [struck] those whose minds were carried away by sleep.
The Lord of Yoga entered the womb of Diti by means of his yogic power.
Śrīdhara: She whose mind has been carried away by sleep. ||61||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.
*Viśvanātha*: By means of that *māyā* which serves as the means for attaining the perfection (*siddhi*) known as "entering another's body" (*parakāyapraveśa*).
With his thunderbolt, he cut the golden-hued embryo into seven pieces;
as each of the seven cried out, he cut them again, saying, "Do not weep!"
Śrīdhara: As if consoling them by saying, "Do not weep," he cut them again into seven pieces. ||62||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: As if consoling them by saying, "Do not weep," he cut them again into seven pieces.
Here, [it refers to] the soul (*jīva*) or the yogi who, in a very short time, consumes much merit and demerit.
Some maintain that, like a bodily manifestation (*kāyavyūha*), a single soul alone possesses the capacity to pervade forty-nine bodies.

Others hold that, from the perspective of what is yet to come, forty-nine souls who have entered a single body at the very outset attain individual bodies through a division made by Indra; [this occurs] within the portions created by Indra.
Likewise, there is the simultaneous entry of forty-eight other living beings at that very moment;

for instance, when certain creepers and shrubs are cut into pieces and planted in the ground, the separate entry of individual living beings is inferred from the emergence of growth from each distinct fragment. Thus it is said.
They said: ||62||
O King, as they were being torn apart, they all spoke with joined palms:
"O Indra, why do you wish to kill us? We are your brothers, the Maruts."
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha have not commented [on this].
Kramasaṃdarbha: "They said to him. Therefore, it is the superimposition of various bodies upon a single individual soul (*jīva*). Or rather, previously, there were many souls in one body.
It should be understood that for those who possess mental resolve, this occurs upon the attainment of the separation from the body. ||63||
"Do not fear me, O brothers," said Kauśika to his own attendants, the hosts of Maruts, who were devoted to him with undivided loyalty.
Śrīdhara: Kauśika is Indra. [He has] seven groups; for according to the Śruti, "The Maruts indeed consist of seven groups. ||64||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.
*Viśvanātha*: "To me" (*mahyam*) means to my [self]. *Kauśika* is Indra. "The seven hosts" (*gaṇān sapta*):
for according to the Vedic revelation (*śruti*), "The Maruts indeed consist of seven groups. (64)
By the compassion of Śrīnivāsa, the womb of Diti did not perish,
even though it was struck many times by the thunderbolt, just as you were by the weapon of Droṇa’s son.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
By beholding the Supreme Person even once, a person attains equality with Him.
For a year, slightly less than that, Hari was worshipped by Diti.
Together with Indra, those fifty gods became the Maruts;
having dispelled the defect of their mother, they were made drinkers of Soma by Hari.
Śrīdhara: This has not been explained. Kramasaṃdarbha: By Hari, meaning either by Indra or by Śrī Viṣṇu. ||67||
Viśvanātha: *Sātmatām* means having a nature identical to that of the *puruṣa*; *sajūḥ* means together with. ||67||
Having risen, Diti beheld the boys, radiant as fire;
together with Indra, the blameless goddess was filled with joy.
Then he said to Indra: "O dear one, desiring offspring who would bring fear even to the Ādityas, I have observed this most difficult vow."
"One son was intended, yet how did seven times seven come to be? If you know the truth, my son, tell it truly; do not speak falsely."
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
Indra said:
"Mother, having perceived your resolve, I have come into your presence; having gained this opportunity, my mind is set on wealth, not on righteousness."
Śrīdhara: When Diti had spoken thus without guile, Indra also spoke without guile: "O Mother!
[He is] one by whom an opportunity has been obtained; he whose intellect is fixed solely on wealth. (71)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: When Diti had spoken thus without guile, Indra also spoke without guile: "O Mother!
Having found an opening (*labdhāntaraḥ*), meaning having obtained a vulnerability. ||71||
"My embryo was cut into seven parts; there were seven little boys.
Each of them was also cut into seven pieces, yet they did not die."
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha have not commented [upon this].
Kramasaṃdarbha: "me" means by me. ||72||
Then, having witnessed that supreme marvel, I resolved:
"This is some incidental success resulting from the worship of the Great Being."
Śrīdhara: "Even supreme liberation" means even [the state of] liberation. ||73||
The sequential composition: "Then that" (tatas tad). "Determined" (vyavasitam) means deliberated. He says that very thing: "Mahā... [and so on].
Viśvanātha says: "Determined" (vyavasitam) means ascertained; he says that very thing in two and a half verses beginning with "Mahā...":
some perfection, even liberation, is a secondary consequence (ānuṣaṅgikī). ||73||
Those who, seeking the propitiation of the Blessed One, are free from desire for rewards—
even those who do not wish for anything else— are remembered as being skilled in their own true interest.
Śrīdhara: [This] has not been explained in the *Kramasaṃdarbha*.

Viśvanātha: "Even for supreme liberation, they are skilled in their own interest"—by this he means that those who desire liberation through worship are like those who seek a blade of grass in exchange for a present great treasure.
They are ignorant of their own self-interest; however, the meaning is that they too have indeed achieved their purpose due to the excellence of the object [of devotion].
As it has been said: "When requested by men, he truly grants what is desired. (74)
Having worshipped the God who bestows the inner self— the Lord of the Universe who is one's own Self—
who that wise man would choose the touch of worldly qualities, even if it were to lead to hell?

Śrīdhara: What wise person would choose contact with the qualities [of nature] and the enjoyment of sense objects, since such enjoyment of sense objects exists even in hell? [The *Kramasaṃdarbha*] does not provide an explanation.
Viśvanātha: The Lord intent on divine play; his own self, possessed of a beautiful form. ||75||
"O Great Queen, you ought to forgive this wickedness of mine, a fool; by good fortune, O Mother, the fetus has risen from death."
Śrīdhara: "O most great one" means the greatest; "having died, he has risen. (76)
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
— o)0(o)— Śrī Śuka said:
Permitted by her, who was pleased by his pure disposition, the lord Indra bowed to her and,
together with the Maruts, departed for the third heaven.
Thus I have related to you everything that you asked me:
the auspicious birth of the Maruts. What more shall I tell you?
It has not been explained by anyone at all. Thus ends [the section] in the *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted.
The eighteenth chapter of the sixth [book] is concluded, which is well-connected with the virtuous.
Thus ends the Sixth Canto in the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā, the Pāramahaṃsyasaṃhitā, which is the commentary on the Brahma-sūtras within the glorious Mahāpurāṇa Śrīmad Bhāgavatam.
The eighteenth chapter, titled "The Birth of the Maruts.
Now begins the nineteenth chapter.
Regarding the narration of the Puṃsavana vow,
Śrī Rājā said: "O Brahman, as for the Puṃsavana vow which has been described by you,"
I wish to know that by which Viṣṇu is propitiated.
Śrīdhara:
That very vow of Diti which was proclaimed by Kaśyapa in the nineteenth [chapter] has been explained here for the benefit of the world as a means of pleasing Hari.
The word "its" (tasya) refers to its mode; this is the ellipsis. ||1||
The sequential composition: "To you" (*te tubhyam*) means for your sake; the meaning is that there is no need for anything else. ||1||
Viśvanātha:
When questioned by the king once more in the nineteenth [chapter], the sage again declared that the propitiation of Viṣṇu is the vow for the destruction of mental cruelty.
The word "its" (tasya) implies "its manner" (prakāram) as the ellipsis. ||1||
Śrī Śuka said:
In the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, a woman, with the permission of her husband, [should perform the rite].
One should undertake this vow, which fulfills all desires, from the very beginning.
Having heard of the birth of the Maruts and having consulted with the Brahmins, she—
having bathed, her teeth white, wearing two white garments and adorned with ornaments—
should worship the Blessed One together with Śrī before her morning meal.

Śrīdhara: In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, during the bright fortnight, on the first day from the beginning [the first lunar day]—having addressed [her] and asked [for permission], she whose teeth are white—that is, one with clean teeth—being adorned, should perform the worship. ||3||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, that is, in the month of Mārgaśīra; from the beginning, on the first lunar day (pratipad). ||23||
Enough with you who are free from all expectations; O you whose desires are fulfilled, homage be to you! Homage to the Lord of great majesty, the source of all accomplishments!

Śrīdhara: First, he states the salutation mantras with three verses. "Everything is sufficient (*alam*) for you; there is no further task to be accomplished by others. Therefore, let there be salutation (*namaḥ*) to you alone. The reasons for this sufficiency are: "O you who are independent, O you whose desires are fulfilled (*pūrṇakāma*)."
To the Lord of great majesty, to the Lord of Lakṣmī; to Him in whom all supernatural powers, such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest, reside. ||4||
The sequence of the composition: *te* means "to you"; *alam* means "for your sake" or "there is no need for anything else"—this is the meaning. ||4||

Viśvanātha: Enough with excessive [praise]; let there simply be salutation unto You. He says that You are not like another deity who requires servants for the sake of accomplishing His own sovereignty—the meaning is "to the one who is independent," because of possessing innate, great sovereignty. Thus...

With what offering and the like can I please you, whose every desire is fulfilled? With what house, gardens, elephants, female slaves, dances, songs, or the sounds of drums and musical instruments can I honor you, the Lord of Great Sovereignty? Thus, for the sake of all accomplishments, to you who bestow the attainments of heaven, liberation, love, and the rest—
The underlying thought is: "How may I please [Him] through the collection of means such as the yoga of action, knowledge, and devotion? ||4||
O Lord, since you are endowed with compassion, prosperity, splendor, greatness, vigor,
and all excellent qualities, you are therefore the Blessed One, the Sovereign Master.
Śrīdhara: O Lord! Just as it truly is, you are endowed with compassion and other such qualities, as well as all other attributes such as the power of true resolve; therefore, for that reason. ||5||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.

*Viśvanātha*: He says that even all of that is possible through Your grace—"Just as You are favored by grace, so too by prosperity and the rest; therefore, O Lord, You alone are the Blessed One"—this is the syntactical connection (*anvaya*).
The meaning is this: being endowed with mercy and power, and even while requiring only a single *tulasī* leaf offered by a devotee, I become one who asks the devotee, "I am afflicted by hunger today;
give me something," thus remaining one whose desires are unfulfilled, [desiring] my own house, garden, and so forth.
Even though you are currently devoid of worldly power, you speak within your dreams, "Where shall I sport now that I am old?

and so forth; likewise, even though you are endowed with supernatural powers such as *aṇimā*, you are bound by the essence of the devotee's love and are unable to go anywhere—even with such prosperity, great fortune, power, and splendor.

By virtue of your independence from all, through your power, majesty, and glory, as well as your vital energy, strength, and all other attributes such as the truthfulness of your resolve, you exist everywhere in the universe characterized by self-sufficiency and the fulfillment of all desires; therefore, you alone are the Blessed One, you alone.
The sense is that the Lord is to be worshipped. ||5||
O Consort of Viṣṇu, O Great Illusion, O You who possess the marks of the Supreme Person!
Be pleased with me, O Fortunate One; O Mother of the World, salutations be unto you.
Śrīdhara: [This is] an address to her who possesses the characteristics of the Great Person, the Supreme Lord, such as independence and so forth. ||6||
The sequential composition: "O Consort of Viṣṇu," means O Mahāmāyā, whose nature is the power called Parā.
For this very reason, you possess the characteristics of the Great Puruṣa and have that [Puruṣa] as your sole essential form. ||6||

Viśvanātha: Having thus prostrated before the Lord, he says that one should likewise prostrate before Lakṣmī—beginning with the words "O Consort of Viṣṇu. O Mahāmāyā, since the word *māyā* denotes power (*śakti*), you are of the nature of the power known as Parā. For this very reason, you possess the characteristics of the Great Person, Viṣṇu.
[It is that] of which [the qualities] such as independence and so forth belong.
“Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, the Great Being, the one of great majesty, the Lord of great manifestations!”
"Along with great manifestations, I offer this oblation.
With this mantra, day after day, [one performs] for Viṣṇu the invocation, the offering of water for honor (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (upasparśana),
bathing, clothing, the sacred thread (upavīta), ornaments, perfumes, flowers, and incense.
One should present the offerings, such as lamps and other services, with a well-composed mind.
Śrīdhara states the mantra for worship: "Oṃ namaḥ" [etc. ||7||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: He states the mantra for worship: "Oṃ namaḥ" etc. ||7||
And one should offer twelve oblations of the remaining sacrificial butter (haviḥśeṣa) into the fire with the mantra:
*Oṃ namo bhagavate mahāpuruṣāya mahāvibhūtipataye svāhā*.
Śrīdhara: "Haviḥśeṣa" means the remainder of the sacrificial offering. He shows the mantra for the oblation: "Om"—this is the sequence of the text; it has not been explained [further].
Viśvanātha: "Haviḥśeṣa" means the remainder of the sacrificial offering. ||8||
One who desires all prosperity should always worship with devotion both Śrī and Viṣṇu, the givers of boons and the source of all blessings.
One should prostrate like a staff upon the ground with a mind bowed by devotion;
one should then recite the mantra ten times and thereafter utter the hymn of praise.
But you two are the all-pervading lords and the supreme cause of the universe;
for this subtle primordial nature (prakṛti) is the power of illusion (māyā-śakti), which is difficult to overcome.
Śrīdhara: "Prabhavau" means those by which [beings] arise pre-eminently (prakarṣeṇa bhavanti). ||911||

The sequential arrangement: "You two" refers to one and a half verses. He states the reason why those two, Parā and Parāparā, are also the cause of the universe: "For this... The intended meaning is that Prakṛti [acts] through the reflection of her own portion;
thus says Viśvanātha. It has not been explained [further].
You alone are her manifest sovereign, the Supreme Person;
you are the sacrifice, the object of worship, the ritual act, and you are the enjoyer of its fruit.
This goddess is the manifestation of the qualities, while you are the manifester and the enjoyer of the qualities;
for you are the Self who dwells within all bodies, whereas Śrī is the body, the senses, and the mental dispositions.
The Blessed One is name and form, while you are the cognition and the support.
Madhva [explains]: Viṣṇu is the inner controller (antaryāmī) of the sacrifice and so forth, while Ramā is [the recipient] through the act of worship and so forth;
therefore, they are denoted by those respective words, but not because they constitute the entire nature [of the sacrifice].
"Viṣṇu alone is the inner controller (antaryāmī) even of Śrī; of this there is no doubt.

There is no inner controller of Viṣṇu anywhere or from anyone whatsoever. Thus says Śrīdhara in the *Brahmatarka*. Sacrifice (*ijyā*) is the human activity that brings about a ritual, known as mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*); it is action (*kriyā*).

The worldly [convention] is the cognition that illuminates name and form; its support is their substratum, which is the sequential arrangement [of words]. "Of that" refers to this. In the *Sātvata-tantra*, it says: "Viṣṇu has three forms," and so forth.
He says the same thing in the passage beginning with "Thou," etc. (12–13).

Viśvanātha: *Ijyā* is the human activity that brings about a sacrifice, known as *bhāvanā*. *Kriyā* is worldly action. *Pratyaya* is that which manifests name and form. *Apāśraya* is their substratum.
Just as you two are the supreme lords who grant boons to the three worlds, so may my great blessings become true, O Lord of Excellent Renown.
Śrīdhara: [This is] the *Kramasaṃdarbha*; it has not been commented upon.
Viśvanātha: "The two Supreme Ones" means the two Supreme Lords. ||14||
Having thus praised Śrīnivāsa, the bestower of boons, together with Śrī,
one should remove that offering material, give water for sipping (ācamana), and perform worship.
Śrīdhara: [This is] the *Kramasaṃdarbha*; it has not been commented upon.
Viśvanātha: Having removed that—that is, having performed the removal of the *mālya* (garland)—[he says] "having removed" (niḥsārya). ||15||
Then, with a mind bowed by devotion, he should praise Him with a hymn;
having smelled the remnants of the sacrifice, he should worship Hari once again.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
And [he served] his husband with supreme devotion and the mind of a great being.
A husband who is naturally affectionate should personally provide those various things that are pleasing;
he should also perform all the duties for his wife, whether they be great or small.

Śrīdhara: With the mind of a great person (mahāpuruṣa), one should approach [the husband] with the thought that he is the Lord (īśvara) and worship him. Furthermore, the husband himself, being affectionate by nature, should support the wife's activities and be favorable toward her; this is the meaning. ||17||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— Even by one of the two, husband or wife, [the goal] is accomplished for both.
A husband, being composed, should perform this [rite] even when his wife is unworthy.
Śrīdhara: Since that which is performed by either one of a husband and wife belongs to both, the sequence of the ritual has not been explained [separately].
Viśvanātha: That which is performed by either one of a husband and wife belongs to both.
Bearing this vow of Viṣṇu, one should not fail it in any way;
[one should honor] Brahmins and women with heroic sons by means of garlands, perfumes, offerings, and ornaments.
Devotedly bowing day after day, she remained established in her religious observances.
Śrīdhara: One should not strike, nor should one cut. ||19||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "One should not strike" (*na vihanyāt*) means one should not cut off. The ablative case in *agrataḥ* is used with the elision of a suffix ending in *-lyap*; it means "having divided the front portion as is appropriate. ||19||
Having dismissed the deity to his own abode,
one should eat that which was offered before him for the sake of self-purification and the fulfillment of all desires.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
By this ritual of worship for twelve months or a year, [one attains the result].
Having performed this, the virtuous woman should then conclude on the final day of Kārttika.

Śrīdhara: If "twelve months" were stated, then if an intercalary month (*malamāsa*) should occur among them, the count would still be twelve, and thus one pure month would have to be excluded. If "year" (*hāyana*) were stated, the same contingency would apply to that intercalary month falling within it. To avoid both of these [consequences], [the term *abdapūrti* is used].
Both have been stated: he should perform the ritual service; he should fast. ||21||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: On the final day, which is the full moon (paurṇamāsī). ||21||
On the following day, having touched water and worshipped Kṛṣṇa as before,
one should offer oblations with milk-boiled rice mixed with clarified butter.
The husband [should offer] exactly twelve oblations according to the procedure for the *pākayajña*.

Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha: "When the next day has dawned" means when morning has arrived. "Cooked in water" means prepared by boiling. "According to the procedure for a *pākayajña*" means according to the procedure for the *sthālīpāka* offering of the *parvan* days. ||22||
The *kramasaṃdarbha* has not been explained. —
Having received the blessings uttered by the delighted twice-born, he took them upon his head.
Having bowed with devotion by touching his head to the ground, he should eat with their permission.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
Having placed the Master before him, he, restrained in speech, together with his kinsmen, [should proceed].
One should give the remainder of the sacrificial porridge to the wife for the sake of good offspring and great good fortune.
Śrīdhara: "Suprajāstva" means the state of having excellent sons. This is because, according to the sequence of the text, one must leave that remaining space in front;
for it is forbidden to eat in the space immediately preceding that [remaining portion]. (24)
Viśvanātha: The remainder [of the verse] concerns having good offspring (*suprajāstva*)—that which brings about good offspring and bestows great fortune.
Alternatively, it may be a separate sentence meaning, "From that, he shall have good offspring. (24)
Having performed this vow of the Lord according to the prescribed rule,
a man obtains his desired object in this world.
A woman, by resorting to this, may obtain good fortune, prosperity, offspring, a husband who lives long, fame, and a home.
Śrīdhara: [This is] the *Kramasaṃdarbha*; it has not been commented upon.
Viśvanātha: "Jīva" means he who lives (*jīvati*); he is both that and the Lord (*pati*), thus [the compound refers to] him. (25)
And a maiden shall find a husband endowed with all auspicious marks, while one who has no [living] son shall attain the state of one whose sins are destroyed.
One whose children have died becomes one with living sons; a woman who is a mistress of wealth becomes ill-favored, while one who is ill-favored becomes beautiful, possessing the highest form.
Śrīdhara: An "avīrā" is a widow. She who is very unfortunate, even though she possesses wealth, becomes fortunate [through this rite]. ||26||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not commented upon.
Viśvanātha: An "avīrā" is one who lacks a husband and sons; she whose children have died is a "jīvasutā," yet she does not become a "dhaneśvarī" (a mistress of wealth). ||26||
One who is deformed becomes beautiful; one who is diseased is freed from disease; and one whose body is impaired in its faculties becomes healthy.
Reciting this during rites for prosperity brings infinite satisfaction to the ancestors and the gods.
Śrīdhara: He who is afflicted with disease—that is, a sick person—is freed from that pain by means of a distinguished [healing] pain.

The ellipsis to be supplied is that he shall obtain a healthy body together with his senses. The meaning is that for one who exists while reciting this, there is infinite satisfaction for his ancestors and the deities. ||27||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: He who is afflicted by disease is liberated from that specific ailment; he shall obtain a healthy and capable body together with his senses. "In prosperity" (*abhyudaye*) refers to occasions such as the *ābhyudayika-śrāddha* (prosperity rites). 27.
At the conclusion of the fire offering, both the consumer of oblations (Agni) and the illustrious Lord Hari, being pleased, bestow all desired objects.
O King, you have related to me the great and meritorious birth of the Maruts, as well as the great vow of Diti.
Śrīdhara concludes with "O King. The great merit of his birth and his great vow have not been explained in the *Kramasaṃdarbha*.
Viśvanātha [concludes]: "The Fire-god and Śrī Hari are pleased. (28)

—o)0(o— Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, appropriately titled "The Essence of the Meaning," from the *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential truth for those whose hearts are devoted; it has been well-composed for the virtuous. *||*
Thus ends the sixth book in the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā, the Pāramahaṃsyasaṃhitā, which is a commentary on the Brahma-sūtras within the glorious Mahāpurāṇa Śrīmad Bhāgavatam.

The nineteenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Puṃsavana Vow," as analyzed by Cakravartipāda in his *Sārārthadarśinī* commentary on verse 1.2.21: [The text continues with the analysis of the verse.]
As it is said: "Compassion for the virtuous, service to the great, faith, taking refuge at the feet of the guru,
longing for devotional acts, devotion, and from that, the removal of what is harmful."
In the fourteenth [chapter], the meanings are: culmination, delight, non-attachment, passion, love, vision, and the experience of Hari’s sweetness.
This should be seen in that context.
Regarding the phrase "of him who was thus praising," there is an alternative reading, *bālakāḥ*, which was adopted by Viśvanātha.
"Veginīm" is an alternative reading favored by Viśvanātha.
The suffix "-kṛt" [is used here] (ga).
"Sakthibhiḥ" is the reading of Svāmī.
The following four verses are accepted in the Madhva tradition:

"Multiplicity, birth and destruction, decay and growth, the fruit of action, and the perception [of these] appear as attributes not belonging to the Seer, just as the transformations of the combustible object do not belong to fire. (1)
These [objects] appear to the self due to the conjunction with the body and through false grasping;
just as in a dream, so too one should not meditate on anything else, for all that is fear.

Just as the terrible cycle of worldly existence does not appear to one who is fast asleep because of the absence of the sense of "I," so it is for the liberated one who lives yet is free from the conceit of "I."
Therefore, abandon that which is other than this—the mere mind—along with the darkness of "I" and "mine";
fix the mind upon Vāsudeva, the Blessed One, the Self, the Lord. (4)
"There is no other seer but this" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.23);
the reading "sākṣāt" (directly) is found in the *Haribhaktivilāsa*.
This is according to the reading established in the *Haribhaktivilāsa*.
See Haribhaktivilāsa 11.376–377.
